name: MBA Year 1 — Core
tagline: Everything a top MBA teaches in the first year — accounting to strategy, explained from zero.

overview.about: The first year of every top MBA (HBS, Wharton, INSEAD, IIM-A, ISB) is a fixed core: how money is measured (accounting), how value is created (finance and economics), how customers are won (marketing), how work gets done (operations), how people are led (organisational behaviour) and how a company wins (strategy). This course follows that sequence. Each lesson has swipe cards, a quiz and deep notes with worked examples and Indian and global cases.

pattern.note: Financial and managerial accounting; business statistics and decision analytics
Corporate finance; managerial micro- and macroeconomics
Marketing management; operations and supply chain
Leadership, HR, competitive strategy, negotiation, communication, ethics and law

eligibility: Students preparing for CAT/GMAT who want a head start
Engineers and professionals moving into management
Founders who want the MBA toolkit without the fees

chapters.title: The accounting equation & double entry

cards.title: Accounting is a language
cards.body: Every business decision — hiring, borrowing, launching a product — eventually shows up as numbers. **Accounting** is the grammar that turns those events into three standard reports. Learn the grammar once and you can read any company in the world, from a kirana chain to Apple.

cards.title: The one equation
cards.body: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity.** Assets are what the business controls that will bring future benefit. Liabilities are what it owes outsiders. Equity is what is left for the owners. Every resource came from somewhere: either someone lent it or the owners put it in (or left profits inside).

cards.title: Double entry
cards.body: Because the equation must always balance, every transaction touches **at least two accounts**. Buy a machine for cash: one asset up, another asset down. Take a loan: cash up, liabilities up. This system was set down by **Luca Pacioli** in 1494 and it is still how every ledger works.

cards.title: Debits and credits
cards.body: A **debit** is simply the left side of an account, a **credit** the right. Memory aid **DEALER**: Dividends, Expenses and Assets rise with a debit; Liabilities, Equity and Revenue rise with a credit. Total debits always equal total credits — that is the built-in error check.

cards.title: Priya's café, step one
cards.body: Priya invests ₹10 lakh and borrows ₹5 lakh. Assets (cash) = ₹15 lakh; Liabilities = ₹5 lakh; Equity = ₹10 lakh. She buys a ₹6 lakh espresso machine for cash: cash falls to ₹9 lakh, equipment is ₹6 lakh. Total assets still ₹15 lakh. Nothing about her wealth changed — only its form.

cards.title: Profit lands in equity
cards.body: She sells coffee for ₹80,000 cash using beans that cost ₹30,000. Cash +₹80,000, inventory −₹30,000, so assets rise ₹50,000 — and **equity (retained earnings) rises ₹50,000**. Profit is not a separate box; it is the growth of the owners' claim.

cards.title: Interview habit
cards.body: When anyone describes a transaction, ask: **which two (or more) accounts move, and in which direction?** Consultants and bankers do this instinctively. If your mental equation does not balance, you have missed one side of the entry.

cards.q: A company buys inventory worth ₹2 lakh on credit. What happens?
cards.explain: Inventory (an asset) rises and accounts payable (a liability) rises by the same ₹2 lakh. Equity is untouched — no profit or loss yet.

cards.q: Under the DEALER rule, which account increases with a CREDIT?
cards.explain: Revenue increases equity, and equity-side accounts rise with credits. Cash, expenses and equipment rise with debits.

cards.q: Assets are ₹50 crore and liabilities ₹32 crore. What is equity?
cards.explain: Equity = Assets − Liabilities = 50 − 32 = ₹18 crore.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Imagine you own a cycle worth ₹20,000 that you bought with ₹15,000 of your savings and ₹5,000 borrowed from a friend. You have just discovered accounting. What you **have** (₹20,000 of cycle) equals what you **owe** (₹5,000 to your friend) plus what is truly **yours** (₹15,000).

Every company on earth — Reliance, Infosys, a Bengaluru startup — is the same picture at a larger scale. The **accounting equation**, **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**, is not a rule someone invented; it is a tautology. Every rupee of resources had to come from somewhere: either outsiders lent it (liabilities) or owners contributed it or chose to leave profits inside (equity).
Each side has precise meaning in accounting standards:
points: **Assets**: resources the business controls that are expected to produce future economic benefit — cash, receivables (money customers owe), inventory, machines, buildings, patents, brands bought in an acquisition.
**Liabilities**: present obligations to outsiders — supplier payables, bank loans, bonds, salaries owed, taxes owed, and **deferred revenue** (cash received for services not yet delivered).

**Equity**: the residual claim of owners = share capital put in + **retained earnings** (cumulative profits not paid out as dividends). In Indian statements you will see it as Equity Share Capital and Other Equity (reserves and surplus).

Revenue and expenses are temporary accounts that, at year-end, close into retained earnings. So the expanded equation is: Assets = Liabilities + Share capital + (Revenue − Expenses − Dividends) accumulated over time.

notes.p:
Because the equation must hold after every transaction, each event is recorded in at least two places — **double-entry bookkeeping**. The Venetian merchants used it; the Franciscan friar and mathematician **Luca Pacioli** codified it in his 1494 book *Summa de arithmetica*. Some historians argue it helped make large-scale commerce, and later capitalism, possible, because owners could finally trust the numbers of a business they did not personally watch.

**Debit** (Dr) means the left side of a ledger account and **credit** (Cr) the right side — nothing more mystical than that. The convention: assets, expenses and dividends increase on the debit side; liabilities, equity and revenue increase on the credit side (**DEALER**). Every journal entry has equal debits and credits, so a trial balance that does not tally tells you instantly that an error exists.

Example journal entry for a ₹5 lakh bank loan:
Dr Cash ₹5,00,000
  Cr Bank loan ₹5,00,000
Track the equation after each transaction (₹):
points: 1. Priya invests ₹10,00,000 → Cash 10,00,000 = Equity 10,00,000
3. Buys espresso machine ₹6,00,000 cash → Cash 9,00,000 + Equipment 6,00,000 = 15,00,000 (unchanged total)
4. Buys beans ₹1,00,000 on credit → Inventory +1,00,000, Payables +1,00,000. Assets 16,00,000 = Liabilities 6,00,000 + Equity 10,00,000
5. Sells coffee ₹80,000 cash; beans used cost ₹30,000 → Cash +80,000, Inventory −30,000; Equity +50,000 (profit). Assets 16,50,000 = 6,00,000 + 10,50,000

6. Pays rent ₹20,000 → Cash −20,000; Equity −20,000 (expense). Final: Cash 9,60,000 + Equipment 6,00,000 + Inventory 70,000 = **₹16,30,000**; Liabilities 6,00,000 + Equity 10,30,000 = **₹16,30,000** ✓

notes.p: Three lessons hide inside Priya's café. First, **buying an asset is not an expense** — the espresso machine changed the form of her wealth, not its size (it will become an expense slowly, through depreciation). Second, **borrowing is not income** — the loan raised cash but also raised an obligation. Third, **profit is simply an increase in equity** caused by operations. That is why investors obsess over retained earnings: it is the visible trail of value the business has created and kept.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how managers misuse it
notes.p: Beginners treat cash as profit — but Priya's cash fell from ₹15 lakh to ₹9.6 lakh while she was profitable. Managers sometimes 'improve' results by capitalising costs that should be expenses (recording routine repairs as assets), which inflates both assets and equity; WorldCom's fraud in the early 2000s was built largely on capitalising ordinary line costs. Another misuse: treating equity as cash the company 'has'. Equity is a claim, not a vault — a company can have large equity and an empty bank account.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Finance interviews open with 'Walk me through what happens when…' — the honest answer always starts with the two sides of the entry. GMAT/CAT data-interpretation sets assume you know that assets equal liabilities plus equity. In real jobs, product managers who understand double entry can talk to the CFO's team about why a big upfront customer payment is a liability (deferred revenue) rather than a win to celebrate this quarter.

points: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, always, after every transaction.
Every transaction affects at least two accounts (double entry, Pacioli 1494).
DEALER: Dividends, Expenses, Assets rise with debits; Liabilities, Equity, Revenue rise with credits.
Buying an asset changes the form of wealth, not its amount.
Loans raise cash and liabilities — they are not income.
Profit flows into equity via retained earnings.
Cash and profit are different things; track both.

chapters.title: The income statement: revenue, accruals, EBITDA to PAT

cards.title: The scorecard for a period
cards.body: The **income statement** (profit & loss account in India) answers one question: **did the business earn more than it consumed during this period?** It covers a span of time — a quarter or a year — unlike the balance sheet, which is a snapshot on one date.

cards.title: Accrual, not cash
cards.body: Revenue is recorded when it is **earned**, and expenses when they are **incurred** to earn it (the **matching principle**) — not when cash moves. A ₹12,000 annual app subscription paid in January is ₹1,000 of revenue each month; the unearned part sits on the balance sheet as **deferred revenue**.

cards.title: When is revenue 'earned'?
cards.body: Under **Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15** revenue follows five steps: identify the contract; identify the **performance obligations**; set the transaction price; allocate it across obligations; recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied. A phone sold with two years of service is two promises, recognised at different times.

cards.title: The waterfall
cards.body:
Revenue − COGS = **Gross profit**
− Operating expenses (SG&A, R&D) = **EBITDA**
− Depreciation & amortisation = **EBIT** (operating profit)
− Interest = **PBT**
− Tax = **PAT** (net profit). Each line strips out one more claim on the money.

cards.title: ₹1,000 crore company
cards.body: Revenue 1,000; COGS 600 → gross profit 400 (40%). Opex 200 → EBITDA 200 (20%). D&A 50 → EBIT 150. Interest 30 → PBT 120. Tax at 25% = 30 → **PAT 90**, a 9% net margin. Ninety paise of every ₹10 of sales reaches shareholders.

cards.title: Why EBITDA is popular — and dangerous
cards.body: EBITDA approximates operating cash before capex and financing, so it lets you compare firms with different debt and asset ages. But depreciation is real: machines wear out. Warren Buffett has long mocked EBITDA, asking in effect whether management thinks capital expenditure is paid for by the tooth fairy.

cards.title: Read margins, not just rupees
cards.body: Always convert lines into **% of revenue**. A rising gross margin suggests pricing power or cheaper inputs; a rising opex ratio suggests the company is buying growth. Comparing margins across years and rivals tells you more than any absolute number.

cards.q: A firm receives ₹24 lakh in April for a 12-month contract starting April. Revenue recognised by end of June (quarter 1)?
cards.explain: Accrual accounting: ₹2 lakh per month × 3 months = ₹6 lakh. The other ₹18 lakh remains deferred revenue (a liability).

cards.q: EBIT is ₹150 crore, interest ₹30 crore, tax rate 25%. PAT?
Which item sits BETWEEN EBITDA and EBIT?
cards.explain: EBIT = EBITDA − D&A. Interest is deducted after EBIT, tax after PBT.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
The **income statement** tells you whether a business created value over a period. Think of a month at a college canteen: money earned from selling samosas, minus flour, oil, gas, the cook's salary, the wear on the fryer, interest on the loan for the fryer, and tax. What is left belongs to the owner.

In India it is called the **Statement of Profit and Loss**; in the US, the income statement. Whatever the name, it measures **performance over time**, while the balance sheet measures **position at a point in time**.

notes.h: Accrual accounting and the matching principle
notes.p:
Cash accounting records money when it moves; **accrual accounting** records economic events when they happen. Listed companies must use accruals because cash timing can be wildly misleading. A builder who collects advances for flats not yet built would look hugely profitable on a cash basis; an exporter selling on 90-day credit would look loss-making.

Two rules drive accruals:
points: **Revenue recognition**: record revenue when the performance obligation is satisfied — goods delivered, service performed — under Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15 (ASC 606 in US GAAP), which share the same five-step model.

**Matching**: record expenses in the same period as the revenue they helped generate. Salespeople's commission on a sale is expensed with that sale; a machine's cost is spread over its useful life through **depreciation**.
Timing differences create balance sheet items: **receivables** (earned, not yet collected), **deferred revenue** (collected, not yet earned), **prepaid expenses** and **accrued expenses**.

notes.p: Each line removes one more group of claimants:
points: **Revenue (net sales)**: after discounts and returns; in India shown net of GST.
**COGS**: direct costs of what was sold — materials, factory labour, freight in. Revenue − COGS = **gross profit**, a test of the product's basic economics.
**Operating expenses**: selling, general & administrative (SG&A), marketing, R&D, head-office salaries.
**EBITDA**: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — a rough proxy for operating cash generation.
**D&A**: depreciation spreads tangible asset costs; amortisation spreads intangible ones (software, licences).
**EBIT**: operating profit, what the business earns for all capital providers.
**Interest** → **PBT** → **tax** → **PAT** (profit after tax), the owners' share. Divide by shares outstanding for **EPS**.

notes.p:
An illustrative consumer company (₹ crore):
Revenue 1,000
COGS (600) → Gross profit 400 — gross margin 40%
Operating expenses (200) → EBITDA 200 — margin 20%
Depreciation & amortisation (50) → EBIT 150 — margin 15%
Interest (30) → PBT 120
Tax @25% (30) → **PAT 90 — net margin 9%**
With 10 crore shares, **EPS = ₹9**.

Now a what-if. If the company raised prices 5% with no loss of volume, revenue becomes 1,050 and every extra rupee drops straight to PBT: PBT 170, tax 42.5, PAT 127.5 — a **42% jump in profit from a 5% price rise**. That is why pricing power is the most prized trait in business, and why Warren Buffett has said the single most important factor in evaluating a business is pricing power.

Analysts like EBITDA because it neutralises differences in capital structure (interest), tax regimes and depreciation policy, which makes cross-company comparison and **EV/EBITDA** valuation easy. Lenders use debt/EBITDA to size loans.

The abuse: companies with heavy capex (telecom, airlines, steel) present EBITDA as if it were cash, ignoring that towers, aircraft and blast furnaces must be replaced. Startups add further creative versions — 'adjusted EBITDA' that excludes stock compensation, marketing or even rent. **Charlie Munger** and Buffett have both been scathing about such metrics. The fix is simple: always look at EBITDA alongside capex and free cash flow.

Students confuse **revenue with cash**, and **profit with cash**. Others forget that one-off items (sale of a building, impairment, write-offs) distort a single year; look for 'exceptional items' and strip them out to judge underlying performance. Managers sometimes pull revenue forward — shipping extra stock to distributors at quarter-end (**channel stuffing**) — which flatters this quarter and hurts the next. Rising receivables faster than revenue is the classic red flag.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Expect questions like 'Revenue grew 20% but profit fell — give three reasons' (input cost inflation, discounting, higher depreciation from new capacity, higher interest). Case interviews constantly use **profit = revenue − cost** trees, which are simply the income statement in disguise. In jobs, every quarterly earnings call — from Infosys to Hindustan Unilever — is built around margin movement versus last year.

points: Income statement = performance over a period; balance sheet = position on a date.
Accruals: revenue when earned (Ind AS 115 five steps), expenses matched to revenue.
Revenue → Gross profit → EBITDA → EBIT → PBT → PAT.
Convert every line to % of revenue and compare over time and against peers.
Small price rises can multiply profit because they fall straight to the bottom line.
EBITDA ignores capex and working capital — pair it with free cash flow.
Watch receivables rising faster than sales and 'adjusted' metrics.

chapters.title: The balance sheet: assets, liabilities, equity, working capital

cards.title: A photograph, not a film
cards.body: The **balance sheet** shows what a company owns and owes **on one date**, usually 31 March for Indian firms. It is the accounting equation laid out in full: assets on one side, liabilities plus equity on the other, always equal.

cards.title: Current vs non-current
cards.body: **Current** items turn into cash or fall due within 12 months (cash, receivables, inventory; payables, short-term loans). **Non-current** items last longer (plant, land, brands, long-term debt). The split tells you whether a company can pay its near-term bills.

cards.title: Working capital
cards.body: **Net working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities.** Positive means near-term resources exceed near-term obligations. **Current ratio = CA ÷ CL.** Bankers usually like it comfortably above 1, but the right level depends on the industry.

cards.title: Illustrative balance sheet (₹ crore)
cards.body: Cash 50, receivables 120, inventory 150 → CA 320. Plant 500, intangibles 80 → total assets **900**. Payables 100, short-term debt 60, accruals 40 → CL 200. Long-term debt 250. Equity: share capital 100 + reserves 350 = 450. Total 200+250+450 = **900** ✓. Working capital 120; current ratio 1.6.

cards.title: Book value is not market value
cards.body: Assets are mostly recorded at **historical cost** less depreciation. A Mumbai office bought in 1990 sits at 1990 prices. Home-grown brands — think of Amul or Asian Paints — barely appear at all. That is why market value is often many times book value for great consumer firms.

cards.title: Negative working capital can be a superpower
cards.body: Some businesses collect from customers before paying suppliers — supermarkets selling for cash, food-delivery and e-commerce platforms, FMCG giants with strong dealer terms. Their suppliers effectively finance growth. Hindustan Unilever is often cited as an Indian example.

cards.title: Read it top-down
cards.body: Scan in this order: cash vs debt (survival), receivables and inventory vs sales (quality), equity trend (value creation), and any big goodwill (past acquisitions). Then ask what changed since last year and why.

cards.q: Current assets ₹480 crore, current liabilities ₹320 crore. Current ratio?
cards.explain: 480 ÷ 320 = 1.5. Net working capital = ₹160 crore.

cards.q: Which item is a LIABILITY?
cards.explain: Cash received for services not yet delivered is an obligation to deliver — a liability. The others are assets.

cards.q: Why is a famous brand's market value usually far above its book equity?
options: Internally built brands and growth prospects are mostly not recorded as assets
cards.explain: Historical-cost accounting omits internally generated intangibles and future growth; markets price them in.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
If the income statement is a film of the year, the **balance sheet** is a photograph taken at the closing bell. It lists everything the company controls (assets) and the claims on those assets — first the outsiders' (liabilities), then the owners' (equity). Because claims must equal what they claim, the two sides balance by definition.

Under Indian law (Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013), the format starts with **Equity and Liabilities** and then **Assets**, both split into non-current and current. US companies list assets first. The content is the same.
Know these line items cold:
points: **Cash and equivalents**: bank balances and very short-term deposits.
**Trade receivables (debtors)**: sales made on credit, not yet collected.
**Inventory**: raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods, valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (conservatism).
**Property, plant & equipment (PP&E)**: at cost less accumulated depreciation.
**Intangibles and goodwill**: purchased software, licences, and goodwill — the premium paid in an acquisition over the fair value of net assets.
**Trade payables (creditors)**, short-term borrowings, accrued expenses, deferred revenue, provisions.
**Long-term borrowings**: bank term loans, debentures, bonds; lease liabilities under Ind AS 116.
**Equity**: share capital (face value of shares issued) plus other equity — securities premium and retained earnings.

notes.p:
An illustrative mid-sized manufacturer, ₹ crore:

**Assets** — Cash 50; Receivables 120; Inventory 150 → **Current assets 320**. Net PP&E 500; Intangibles 80 → **Non-current 580**. **Total assets 900.**

**Liabilities and equity** — Payables 100; Short-term debt 60; Accrued expenses 40 → **Current liabilities 200**. Long-term debt 250. **Total liabilities 450.** Share capital 100; Reserves & surplus 350 → **Equity 450.** **Total 900** ✓.

What we learn: **net working capital = 320 − 200 = 120**; **current ratio 1.6**; **quick ratio** (excluding inventory) = (320 − 150) ÷ 200 = **0.85** — the firm leans on selling inventory to pay its bills. **Total debt = 60 + 250 = 310**, **net debt = 310 − 50 = 260**, **debt-to-equity = 310 ÷ 450 ≈ 0.69**. Moderate leverage, adequate liquidity. We will reuse this company in the ratio-analysis chapter.

notes.h: Working capital: the cash trapped in operations
notes.p:
Working capital is the money tied up in running the business day to day. If a company lets customers pay in 90 days but must pay suppliers in 30, it must fund 60 days of the cycle itself — and the faster it grows, the more cash it needs. Many profitable small Indian firms (MSMEs) fail for exactly this reason: large buyers pay late and the firm runs out of cash while showing profits.

The flip side is **negative working capital**. Retailers selling for cash, platforms that collect from customers before paying merchants, and strong consumer brands that collect from distributors quickly can grow while suppliers fund them. Amazon's early growth is a classic global case.

notes.h: What the balance sheet does not show
notes.p: Historical cost means the numbers are **reliable but often stale**. Land bought decades ago is shown at its old cost. **Internally generated intangibles** — brand, customer relationships, a culture of innovation, the Tata name — are not recorded at all, while the same brand would be recorded (as an intangible or goodwill) if someone bought it. This is why **price-to-book** ratios vary hugely: banks often trade near book value because their assets are mostly loans close to their recorded amounts, while asset-light consumer and technology firms trade at large multiples of book.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how managers misuse it
notes.p: Mistaking **reserves** for a pile of cash (reserves are part of equity; the cash may have been spent on factories long ago). Ignoring **off-balance-sheet** obligations — guarantees, contingent liabilities in the notes, or (before Ind AS 116) operating leases. Treating goodwill as a hard asset: when acquisitions disappoint, goodwill gets **impaired**, wiping out equity. Some managements 'window-dress' at year-end — collecting receivables aggressively or delaying payments just before 31 March to make liquidity look stronger, then reversing in April.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Credit analysts at banks like HDFC or SBI live on the balance sheet: can this borrower repay? Equity analysts track return on capital, which needs both statements. In case interviews, 'the client is profitable but short of cash' is a working-capital question. Exams test classification (is deferred revenue a liability? yes) and simple ratios.

points: Balance sheet = position on a date; assets = liabilities + equity.
Current = within 12 months; non-current = longer.
Net working capital = CA − CL; current ratio = CA ÷ CL; quick ratio excludes inventory.
Historical cost makes book values reliable but stale.
Home-grown brands are invisible; purchased ones appear as intangibles/goodwill.
Reserves are not cash.
Negative working capital lets suppliers fund growth; positive working capital consumes cash as you grow.

chapters.title: Cash flow statement & how the three statements link

cards.title: Profit is opinion, cash is fact
cards.body: Accrual profit depends on judgements — depreciation lives, revenue timing, provisions. Cash in the bank does not. The **cash flow statement** reconciles the two and shows exactly where cash came from and where it went during the period.

cards.title: Three buckets
cards.body: **Operating (CFO)**: cash from running the business. **Investing (CFI)**: buying or selling long-term assets and investments (capex, acquisitions). **Financing (CFF)**: dealings with capital providers — borrowing, repaying, issuing shares, dividends, buybacks. Their sum is the change in cash.

cards.title: Indirect method for CFO
cards.body: Start with **PAT**, add back non-cash expenses (**depreciation & amortisation**), then adjust for working capital: an **increase** in receivables or inventory **reduces** cash; an **increase** in payables **adds** cash. Most Indian and global companies present CFO this way.

cards.title: Free cash flow
cards.body: **FCF = CFO − Capex.** This is the cash the business throws off after maintaining and growing its asset base — what is genuinely available to repay debt, pay dividends or buy back shares. Valuation ultimately rests on FCF, not on reported profit.

cards.title: Depreciation +₹10, tax 25%
cards.body: Income statement: EBIT −10, tax −2.5, **PAT −7.5**. Cash flow: PAT −7.5, add back D&A +10 → **cash +2.5** (the tax saving). Balance sheet: PP&E −10, cash +2.5 → assets −7.5; retained earnings −7.5. **Balanced.** This is the most-asked finance interview question in the world.

cards.title: Sale on credit
cards.body: Sell goods for ₹100 on credit, cost ₹60, tax 25% paid in cash. Profit = 30. But CFO = 30 − 100 (receivables up) + 60 (inventory down) = **−10**. The firm is richer on paper and poorer in the bank — until the customer pays.

cards.title: Compare CFO with PAT
cards.body: Over several years, healthy firms convert most of their profit into operating cash. If PAT keeps rising while CFO stays flat or negative, ask hard questions — receivables may be ballooning or revenue may be aggressive.

cards.q: Inventory rose by ₹40 crore during the year. Effect on CFO (indirect method)?
cards.explain: Cash was used to build up inventory, so an increase in a current asset is subtracted from PAT in CFO.

cards.q: Which is a FINANCING cash flow?
cards.explain: Dividends are a payment to capital providers — financing. Machinery and subsidiaries are investing; customer receipts are operating.

cards.q: CFO ₹500 crore, capex ₹320 crore, dividends ₹100 crore. Free cash flow?
cards.explain: FCF = CFO − capex = 500 − 320 = ₹180 crore. Dividends are a use of FCF, not a deduction in computing it.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
A business can report a profit and still go bankrupt — because bills are paid in cash, not in profit. The **cash flow statement** exists to show the cash reality behind accrual accounting. It answers: how much cash did operations generate, how much was invested for the future, and how was any gap financed?

In India it is prepared under **Ind AS 7** (aligned with IAS 7). Lenders, analysts and short-sellers often read it first, because it is the hardest statement to dress up.

points: **Operating activities (CFO)**: receipts from customers, payments to suppliers and employees, taxes. Under the indirect method it starts from profit and adjusts for non-cash items and working-capital changes.

**Investing activities (CFI)**: capital expenditure on PP&E and intangibles, acquisitions, purchase and sale of investments. Usually negative for a growing company — that is fine if the investments earn good returns.

**Financing activities (CFF)**: proceeds from loans and share issues, repayments, dividends, buybacks, lease payments. Interest and dividend classification differs somewhat between standards and choices, so read the notes when comparing companies.
**Net change in cash** = CFO + CFI + CFF, which must equal closing cash − opening cash on the balance sheet.

notes.p: Think of the three statements as one machine:
points: **PAT** from the income statement is the first line of the cash flow statement and also flows into **retained earnings** on the balance sheet (less dividends).
**Depreciation** reduces PAT and PP&E, but is added back in CFO because no cash left.
**Changes in working-capital** balances on the balance sheet (receivables, inventory, payables) appear as adjustments in CFO.
**Capex** in CFI increases PP&E on the balance sheet.
**Borrowing, repayments and dividends** in CFF change debt and equity on the balance sheet.
The **ending cash** from the cash flow statement is the cash line on the balance sheet. If it does not tie, the model has an error.

notes.p:
Assume a 25% tax rate and that the extra depreciation is deductible.

**Income statement:** D&A +10 → EBIT −10 → PBT −10 → tax −2.5 → **PAT −7.5**.
**Cash flow statement:** PAT −7.5; add back D&A +10 → CFO **+2.5**. No change in CFI or CFF. Net cash **+2.5**.
**Balance sheet:** Assets — cash +2.5, PP&E −10 → total **−7.5**. Liabilities unchanged. Equity — retained earnings **−7.5**. Both sides fall by 7.5 ✓.

The insight: depreciation is non-cash, but because it is tax-deductible it **saves real cash** — the **depreciation tax shield** (D&A × tax rate).

notes.h: Worked example 2: one sale flows through everything
notes.p:
A company sells goods for ₹100 on 60-day credit. The goods cost ₹60 from inventory. Tax at 25% is paid in cash this period.

**Income statement:** Revenue 100 − COGS 60 = PBT 40; tax 10; **PAT 30**.
**Cash flow (indirect):** PAT 30; increase in receivables **−100**; decrease in inventory **+60** → **CFO −10** (exactly the tax paid).
**Balance sheet:** Cash −10, receivables +100, inventory −60 → assets **+30**; retained earnings **+30** ✓.

When the customer pays in 60 days: cash +100, receivables −100, CFO +100, no profit impact. Profit was recognised at the sale; cash arrived later. Grow this company fast on generous credit and it will run out of cash while posting record profits.

notes.h: Reading cash flows like an analyst
notes.p: Patterns matter more than single numbers. A mature, healthy business — think a large FMCG or IT services firm — shows **positive CFO, moderate negative CFI, negative CFF** (paying dividends and buybacks). A fast-growing startup shows negative CFO and CFI funded by large positive CFF (fundraising). A troubled firm may show **positive CFI** from selling assets to survive. Also compare **CFO to EBITDA** over several years: persistent gaps signal working-capital stress or aggressive revenue recognition. Several Indian corporate scandals were spotted early by analysts noting profits that never turned into cash, or large 'cash balances' that did not earn the interest they should have.

Treating dividends as operating outflows; forgetting that an **increase** in a current liability is a **source** of cash; double-counting depreciation; and treating 'cash profit' (PAT + D&A) as free cash — it ignores working capital and capex. Managers can flatter CFO by stretching supplier payments or using **supply-chain financing**, which quietly converts operating payables into something closer to debt.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: 'Walk me through what happens to the three statements when depreciation goes up by ₹10' is asked in almost every investment-banking and corporate-finance interview. Financial modelling tests require the statements to balance. In real jobs, CFOs manage to **cash**, not profit: monthly cash forecasts decide whether you can make payroll.

points: CFO + CFI + CFF = change in cash, which ties to the balance sheet.
Indirect CFO: PAT + D&A − increase in current assets + increase in current liabilities.
FCF = CFO − capex.
PAT links to retained earnings; capex to PP&E; borrowing to debt.
Depreciation saves cash through tax: shield = D&A × tax rate.
Fast growth on credit can be profitable and cash-negative at the same time.
Healthy firms convert most profit into operating cash over time.

chapters.title: Ratio analysis, DuPont ROE & accounting standards

cards.title: Ratios make firms comparable
cards.body: ₹90 crore of profit means nothing alone. Ratios divide one number by another so you can compare a firm with its past and with rivals of any size. Four families: **profitability, liquidity, leverage, efficiency**.

cards.title: DuPont identity
cards.body:
**ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier**
= (PAT/Sales) × (Sales/Assets) × (Assets/Equity). Developed at DuPont in the early twentieth century, it tells you **why** ROE is high: pricing, efficiency, or borrowed money.

cards.title: DuPont, worked
cards.body: Sales 1,000, PAT 90, assets 900, equity 450 (₹ crore). Margin 9% × turnover 1.11 × multiplier 2.0 = **ROE 20%**. Check: 90 ÷ 450 = 20% ✓. Two firms can both earn 20% — one through margins, the other through leverage. Only the second gets riskier when rates rise.

cards.title: Liquidity and leverage
cards.body: **Current ratio** = CA/CL. **Quick ratio** = (CA − inventory)/CL. **Debt/Equity** = total debt/equity. **Interest coverage** = EBIT/interest — how many times operating profit covers interest. Below about 1.5–2x, lenders get nervous.

cards.title: Efficiency in days
cards.body: **Inventory days** = Inventory/COGS × 365. **Receivable days** = Receivables/Sales × 365. **Payable days** = Payables/COGS × 365. **Cash conversion cycle** = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.

cards.title: Two roads to the same ROE
cards.body: A supermarket like DMart earns thin margins but turns assets over fast. A luxury brand earns fat margins with slow turnover. A bank earns a thin return on assets but uses high leverage. DuPont shows each model clearly — and warns when ROE is propped up by debt.

cards.title: Ind AS, IFRS and GAAP
cards.body: India's **Ind AS** are converged with **IFRS** and were phased in from 2016–17 for large companies. The US uses **US GAAP**: more rule-based, allows **LIFO** inventory (IFRS forbids it), and does not allow upward revaluation of PP&E. Always check the standard before comparing ratios across countries.

cards.q: Net margin 5%, asset turnover 2.0, equity multiplier 3.0. ROE?
EBIT ₹150 crore, interest ₹30 crore. Interest coverage?
cards.explain: Coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = 150 ÷ 30 = 5x.

cards.q: Which inventory method is allowed under US GAAP but NOT under IFRS / Ind AS?
cards.explain: IFRS (and so Ind AS) prohibits LIFO; US GAAP permits it.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Financial statements are long; ratios compress them into a handful of vital signs, like a doctor's pulse, blood pressure and temperature. A single ratio means little. The power comes from **comparison** — against the company's own history, its competitors and its industry — and from asking **why** a ratio moved.

points: **Profitability**: gross, EBITDA, EBIT and net margins; **ROA** = PAT/Total assets; **ROE** = PAT/Equity; **ROCE** = EBIT/(Equity + Debt) — the favourite of Indian analysts because it is independent of financing.
**Liquidity**: current ratio, quick ratio, cash ratio — can the firm pay bills over the next year?
**Leverage (solvency)**: debt/equity, net debt/EBITDA, interest coverage — can it survive a bad year?
**Efficiency (activity)**: asset turnover, inventory days, receivable days, payable days, cash conversion cycle — how hard do the assets work?
**Valuation** (covered later): P/E, EV/EBITDA, price/book — what is the market paying for all this?

notes.p:
The **DuPont identity**, popularised by the chemical company DuPont's finance team (credited to F. Donaldson Brown in the 1910s), breaks ROE into three drivers:

**ROE = (PAT/Sales) × (Sales/Assets) × (Assets/Equity)**

The sales and asset terms cancel, so the identity always holds. Each term maps to a strategy: **margin** reflects pricing power and cost control; **turnover** reflects operational efficiency; the **equity multiplier** reflects financial leverage. A five-step version further splits margin into tax burden (PAT/PBT), interest burden (PBT/EBIT) and operating margin (EBIT/Sales).

Why it matters: ROE built on margins and turnover is durable; ROE built on leverage evaporates — or turns negative — in a downturn or when interest rates rise.

Use the illustrative company from earlier chapters (₹ crore): Sales 1,000; COGS 600; EBIT 150; interest 30; PAT 90; cash 50; receivables 120; inventory 150; current assets 320; total assets 900; payables 100; current liabilities 200; total debt 310; equity 450.
points: Debt/equity = 310/450 = **0.69**; interest coverage = 150/30 = **5x**.
Cash conversion cycle ≈ 91 + 44 − 61 = **74 days** — each rupee is tied up for about two and a half months.
Diagnosis: healthy ROE driven by decent margins with moderate leverage; the weak spot is inventory. Cutting inventory to 60 days would release roughly 150 − (600 × 60/365) ≈ ₹51 crore of cash.

notes.h: Industry context: same ROE, different businesses
notes.p: A value retailer such as DMart (Avenue Supermarts) is known for thin margins but very high asset turnover — it sells everyday goods at low prices and moves stock fast. A luxury or premium consumer brand earns high margins on slower-moving goods. Banks such as HDFC Bank earn a return on assets of only around 1–2% and reach mid-teen ROEs through leverage of roughly 7–10x — normal for banks, alarming for a manufacturer. Software firms like Infosys and TCS run high margins with little debt and large cash balances. The lesson: **benchmark against the right peer group**.

notes.h: Accounting standards: Ind AS, IFRS and US GAAP
notes.p:
**IFRS** (set by the IASB in London) is used in well over 100 jurisdictions. India chose **convergence** rather than direct adoption: **Ind AS** largely mirror IFRS with some carve-outs, and became mandatory in phases from 1 April 2016 for large companies (initially those with net worth of ₹500 crore or more), followed by NBFCs from 2018–19, while implementation for commercial banks was deferred. Smaller unlisted companies may still follow older Indian GAAP (Accounting Standards).

**US GAAP** (set by the FASB) is often described as more rules-based, IFRS as more principles-based. Notable differences: US GAAP allows **LIFO** inventory, IFRS does not; IFRS allows **revaluation** of PP&E to fair value, US GAAP does not; IFRS permits capitalising **development costs** once criteria are met, US GAAP generally expenses them. These choices can shift margins and asset values, so adjust before comparing an Indian firm with a US one.

notes.h: Common mistakes, and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p:
Mixing year-end balances with full-year flows (better: use averages); comparing across industries; celebrating high ROE without checking leverage; ignoring that buybacks shrink equity and mechanically lift ROE. Negative-equity companies produce meaningless ROEs.

In interviews you will be handed two companies' statements and asked which is better run — DuPont is the cleanest structure for that answer. Credit analysts use coverage and leverage covenants; private-equity associates live on ROCE and cash conversion; consultants use days metrics in working-capital projects.

points: Four families: profitability, liquidity, leverage, efficiency.
ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier (DuPont).
ROCE = EBIT/(Equity + Debt) — financing-neutral.
Interest coverage = EBIT/interest; quick ratio excludes inventory.
CCC = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.
Compare with history and the right peers; leverage-driven ROE is fragile.
Ind AS ≈ IFRS; US GAAP allows LIFO and bans PP&E revaluation.

chapters.title: Cost behaviour, contribution margin & break-even

cards.title: Costs that move, costs that don't
cards.body: **Variable costs** rise with each unit (ingredients, packaging, delivery commission). **Fixed costs** stay the same within a range of activity (rent, salaried staff, software licences). **Semi-variable** costs have both parts, like a phone bill with a rental plus usage.

cards.title: Contribution margin
cards.body: **Contribution per unit = Price − Variable cost per unit.** It is what each sale contributes first towards fixed costs and then to profit. **CM ratio = Contribution ÷ Price.**

cards.title: Break-even
cards.body:
**Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit.**
**Break-even sales (₹) = Fixed costs ÷ CM ratio.**
**Units for target profit = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ Contribution per unit.**

cards.title: A cloud kitchen
cards.body: Biryani sells at ₹250; variable cost ₹150 → contribution ₹100 (CM ratio 40%). Fixed costs ₹3 lakh a month. Break-even = 3,00,000 ÷ 100 = **3,000 plates** (₹7.5 lakh sales). For ₹1 lakh profit: 4,00,000 ÷ 100 = **4,000 plates**.

cards.title: Margin of safety & operating leverage
cards.body: **Margin of safety** = (Actual sales − Break-even sales) ÷ Actual sales. **Degree of operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ Operating profit. At 4,000 plates, DOL = 4,00,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = **4** — a 10% rise in volume lifts profit 40%.

cards.title: The price-cut trap
cards.body: Cut price 10% to ₹225: contribution drops to ₹75. Break-even jumps to 4,000 plates, and to keep ₹1 lakh profit you need 5,334 plates — **33% more volume** for a 10% discount. Discounts look small to customers and huge to the P&L.

cards.title: Fixed vs variable is a choice
cards.body: Airlines, telecom and software have high fixed costs: brutal losses below break-even, huge profits above it. Asset-light models (renting kitchens, paying commissions) lower break-even but cap upside. Strategy often means choosing your cost structure.

cards.q: Price ₹500, variable cost ₹300, fixed costs ₹10 lakh. Break-even units?
CM ratio 25%, fixed costs ₹50 lakh. Break-even revenue?
cards.explain: Break-even sales = 50 lakh ÷ 0.25 = ₹200 lakh = ₹2 crore.

cards.q: Contribution ₹60 lakh, operating profit ₹15 lakh. If sales volume rises 5%, operating profit rises by about…
cards.explain: DOL = 60 ÷ 15 = 4. Profit change ≈ 4 × 5% = 20%.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Financial accounting reports to outsiders; **managerial accounting** helps insiders decide. Its first and most useful tool is separating costs by how they **behave** when volume changes. Once you know which costs move with each unit and which stay put, you can answer the questions managers actually ask: How many must we sell to stop losing money? What happens to profit if we cut prices? Should we take this bulk order at a lower price?

points: **Variable costs**: total rises in proportion to volume; per-unit cost is constant. Raw materials, packaging, payment-gateway fees, sales commissions, aggregator commission on each order.
**Fixed costs**: total is constant within a **relevant range**; per-unit cost falls as volume grows. Rent, salaried staff, insurance, depreciation.
**Step costs**: fixed until capacity runs out, then jump — hiring a second chef when orders cross a level.
**Mixed (semi-variable)**: a fixed base plus a variable part — electricity with a fixed demand charge, a phone plan with usage. Managers split them using the **high-low method** or regression.
The **relevant range** matters: 'fixed' costs are fixed only within it. Double the volume and you may need a new kitchen.

notes.p:
Profit = (Price − Variable cost per unit) × Units − Fixed costs. Everything in CVP follows from this one line:

**Contribution per unit** = P − V
**CM ratio** = (P − V) ÷ P
**Break-even units** = F ÷ (P − V)
**Break-even revenue** = F ÷ CM ratio
**Target units** = (F + target profit) ÷ (P − V)
**Margin of safety** = (Actual − Break-even) ÷ Actual
**Degree of operating leverage (DOL)** = Contribution ÷ Operating profit

CVP assumes constant price and unit variable cost, and a constant sales mix for multi-product firms. For several products, use a **weighted-average contribution** based on the expected mix.

notes.h: Fully worked example: a cloud kitchen
notes.p: A Bengaluru cloud kitchen (illustrative numbers) sells biryani at **₹250** a plate. Variable cost per plate: ingredients ₹80, packaging ₹15, aggregator commission and payment fees ₹55 → **₹150**. Fixed costs per month: kitchen rent ₹1,00,000, staff ₹1,50,000, utilities and software ₹50,000 → **₹3,00,000**.
points: Contribution = 250 − 150 = **₹100**; CM ratio = **40%**.
Break-even = 3,00,000 ÷ 100 = **3,000 plates/month** (about 100 a day), or ₹7,50,000 of sales.
Price cut to ₹225: contribution ₹75; break-even = **4,000** plates; for ₹1 lakh profit you need 4,00,000 ÷ 75 = **5,334** plates (33% more).
Alternative: negotiate commission down by ₹10 → contribution ₹110 → break-even ≈ **2,728** plates. Cost levers can beat price levers.

notes.p:
High fixed-cost businesses — airlines like IndiGo, telecom operators like Reliance Jio, software companies — have high operating leverage. Below break-even they bleed; above it, almost every extra rupee of contribution becomes profit. This explains why Jio priced aggressively to fill its network quickly: the network cost was largely fixed, so volume was everything.

Low fixed-cost businesses are safer but scale less dramatically. Many startups deliberately convert fixed into variable costs (renting cloud servers rather than buying them, paying commissions rather than salaries) to lower break-even while uncertain, then reverse the choice once volume is predictable.

Treating **allocated fixed costs as variable**: if head-office cost is spread at ₹40 a unit, managers wrongly believe cutting a unit saves ₹40. Assuming fixed costs stay fixed far outside the relevant range. Ignoring sales mix — pushing high-revenue but low-contribution products can increase sales and reduce profit. And forgetting that discounts reduce **contribution**, not just price, so the volume needed to compensate is far larger than intuition suggests.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Case interviews love break-even: 'Should the client launch this product?' usually needs a fixed cost, a contribution margin and a volume sanity check. GMAT word problems test the same algebra. In real jobs, every pricing review, promotion plan and capacity decision at a consumer company starts with a CVP model in a spreadsheet.

points: Variable costs move with volume; fixed costs don't (within the relevant range).
Contribution = Price − Variable cost; CM ratio = Contribution ÷ Price.
Break-even units = Fixed ÷ Contribution per unit; revenue = Fixed ÷ CM ratio.
Target units = (Fixed + Target profit) ÷ Contribution per unit.
DOL = Contribution ÷ Operating profit; % change in profit ≈ DOL × % change in volume.
Price cuts need disproportionately more volume to break even.
Cost structure (fixed vs variable) is a strategic choice.

chapters.title: Costing methods: absorption, variable & activity-based

cards.title: What does a product really cost?
cards.body: Direct materials and labour are easy to trace. The hard part is **overhead** — factory rent, supervisors, setups, quality checks. How you spread overhead can make a product look profitable or loss-making. That shapes pricing, product mix and which lines get cut.

cards.title: Absorption costing
cards.body: **Absorption (full) costing** assigns all manufacturing costs — including **fixed** factory overhead — to each unit. It is required for external reporting (Ind AS 2 / IAS 2 inventory). Unsold units carry part of the fixed overhead onto the balance sheet as inventory.

cards.title: Variable costing
cards.body: **Variable (marginal) costing** treats only variable manufacturing costs as product cost and expenses all fixed overhead in the period. It is used internally because it shows contribution clearly and profit moves with **sales**, not with production.

cards.title: Same firm, two profits
cards.body: Produce 10,000, sell 8,000 at ₹100. Variable manufacturing ₹40/unit, fixed factory overhead ₹2 lakh, variable selling ₹5/unit, fixed admin ₹1 lakh. Variable costing profit: **₹1,40,000**. Absorption profit: **₹1,80,000**. The ₹40,000 gap = 2,000 unsold units × ₹20 fixed overhead parked in inventory.

cards.title: The overproduction trick
cards.body: Under absorption costing a manager can raise reported profit simply by **producing more than demand** — fixed overhead hides in inventory. Watch for rising inventory alongside rising profits, especially near bonus time.

cards.title: Activity-based costing (ABC)
cards.body: Developed by **Robin Cooper and Robert Kaplan** at Harvard in the late 1980s, ABC assigns overhead using the **activities** that cause it — number of setups, inspections, orders — rather than one blunt base like labour or machine hours.

cards.title: Hidden cross-subsidy
cards.body: Overhead allocated by machine hours charges a high-volume standard pen ₹9 per unit and a low-volume custom pen ₹20. ABC, tracing setups and inspections, finds ₹4.50 and ₹110. The custom line was quietly being subsidised by the standard one.

cards.q: Under absorption costing, if production exceeds sales, reported profit compared with variable costing is…
cards.explain: Part of fixed overhead is carried into closing inventory instead of being expensed, so absorption profit is higher.

cards.q: Which is the best cost driver for machine-setup overhead under ABC?
cards.explain: Setup cost is caused by the number of setups, regardless of how many units each run produces.

cards.q: Fixed factory overhead ₹6 lakh, 30,000 units produced, 25,000 sold. Fixed overhead in closing inventory under absorption costing?
cards.explain: Fixed overhead per unit = ₹20; 5,000 unsold units × ₹20 = ₹1,00,000.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: 'What does this product cost us?' sounds simple. It isn't. Materials and direct labour are traceable, but a large and growing share of cost is **overhead** — engineering, setups, quality control, IT, warehousing. There is no single correct way to divide it among products, and each method tells a different story. Managers who don't understand the method end up dropping profitable products, keeping loss-makers, and mispricing custom work.

points: **Absorption costing**: product cost = direct materials + direct labour + variable overhead + **fixed manufacturing overhead** (allocated at a predetermined rate). Required for financial reporting and tax. Profit depends on both sales and **production volume**.

**Variable (marginal) costing**: product cost = direct materials + direct labour + variable overhead only. All fixed costs are period expenses. The income statement shows **contribution margin**, perfect for CVP and short-term decisions.
Rule: when **production > sales**, absorption profit > variable profit; when **production < sales** (inventory falls), absorption profit < variable profit; when equal, they match.
Difference = change in inventory units × fixed overhead rate per unit.

notes.h: Worked example: two profits, one factory
notes.p:
Data: 10,000 units produced, 8,000 sold at ₹100. Variable manufacturing cost ₹40/unit; fixed manufacturing overhead ₹2,00,000; variable selling cost ₹5/unit sold; fixed selling & admin ₹1,00,000.

**Variable costing:** Sales 8,00,000 − variable costs (8,000 × ₹45 = 3,60,000) = **contribution 4,40,000** − fixed costs (2,00,000 + 1,00,000) = **profit ₹1,40,000**.

**Absorption costing:** fixed overhead per unit = 2,00,000 ÷ 10,000 = ₹20, so unit product cost = ₹60. Sales 8,00,000 − COGS (8,000 × 60 = 4,80,000) = gross profit 3,20,000 − selling & admin (40,000 + 1,00,000) = **profit ₹1,80,000**.

**Reconciliation:** 2,000 units in closing inventory × ₹20 = **₹40,000** ✓. Nothing real changed — just where the fixed cost sits. Produce 15,000 units with no extra sales and absorption profit rises further, while the warehouse fills with unsold stock.

Traditional systems allocate all overhead using one volume-based driver (labour hours, machine hours). That worked when overhead was small and products similar. In the 1980s **Robin Cooper and Robert S. Kaplan** showed that it systematically **overcosts high-volume, simple products** and **undercosts low-volume, complex ones**, because complexity — setups, special inspections, engineering changes — drives overhead, not volume.

ABC steps: (1) identify activities; (2) pool their costs; (3) choose a **cost driver** for each; (4) compute a rate per driver unit; (5) charge products by their use of each driver. Kaplan and Steven Anderson later proposed **time-driven ABC** (2004) to make it cheaper to maintain.

notes.h: Worked example: standard vs custom pens
notes.p: A pen maker has ₹10,00,000 of overhead. Standard pens: 1,00,000 units, 9,000 machine hours, 20 setups, 100 inspections. Custom pens: 5,000 units, 1,000 machine hours, 80 setups, 200 inspections.
points: **Traditional** (₹10,00,000 ÷ 10,000 machine hours = ₹100/hour): Standard ₹9,00,000 → **₹9/unit**; Custom ₹1,00,000 → **₹20/unit**.
**ABC pools**: setups ₹4,00,000 ÷ 100 = ₹4,000/setup; inspections ₹3,00,000 ÷ 300 = ₹1,000/inspection; machining ₹3,00,000 ÷ 10,000 = ₹30/hour.
If custom pens sell at ₹80, the old system said they were very profitable; ABC shows they lose money unless repriced or simplified.

notes.p: Using absorption profit to evaluate plant managers invites overproduction. Treating ABC unit costs as avoidable: if you drop custom pens, the setup team may still be on payroll — ABC tells you where cost is **consumed**, not automatically what you save. Building an ABC model so detailed that nobody maintains it. And forgetting that customer and channel costs matter too: ABC applied to customers often reveals that a few demanding accounts destroy profit.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to reconcile absorption and variable profits. Consulting cases ask 'why are profits falling even though sales are rising?' — a product-mix and cost-allocation question. Banks, hospitals and telecom firms use ABC-style **cost-to-serve** analysis to price services and decide which customers to serve.

points: Absorption costing includes fixed factory overhead in product cost (required externally).
Variable costing expenses fixed overhead; profit tracks sales.
Production > sales → absorption profit higher; difference = Δ inventory × fixed OH rate.
Overproduction can inflate absorption profit — a governance red flag.
ABC (Cooper & Kaplan) allocates overhead by activity drivers.
Volume-based allocation overcosts simple high-volume products and undercosts complex ones.
Allocated cost ≠ avoidable cost.

chapters.title: Budgeting, variance analysis & relevant costs (make or buy)

cards.title: A budget is a plan in rupees
cards.body: A **budget** translates strategy into numbers for the coming year: sales, production, purchases, staff, capex and cash. It coordinates departments, allocates resources and sets a yardstick. The **master budget** chains them: sales budget → production → materials and labour → overhead → budgeted P&L, balance sheet and cash.

cards.title: Static vs flexible budget
cards.body: A **static budget** is fixed at one planned volume. A **flexible budget** re-computes what costs **should** have been at the volume actually achieved. Comparing actual costs with a static budget mixes up two questions: did we sell more, and did we spend efficiently?

cards.title: Material variances
cards.body:
**Price variance** = (Standard price − Actual price) × Actual quantity.
**Usage variance** = (Standard quantity for actual output − Actual quantity) × Standard price.
Positive = **favourable (F)**, negative = **adverse (A)**. Labour has the same pair: rate and efficiency variances.

cards.title: Cheap steel, costly waste
cards.body: Standard: 2 kg/unit at ₹50/kg. Output 1,000 units; used 2,100 kg at ₹48. Price variance = (50 − 48) × 2,100 = **₹4,200 F**. Usage = (2,000 − 2,100) × 50 = **₹5,000 A**. Net **₹800 A**. Purchasing 'saved' money by buying cheaper material that the factory then wasted.

cards.title: Relevant costs
cards.body: For any decision, only **future costs that differ between options** matter. **Sunk costs** (already spent) are irrelevant. **Opportunity costs** (the best alternative given up) are relevant even though they never appear in the books.

cards.title: Make or buy
cards.body: Making a part costs ₹60 variable + ₹25 allocated fixed = ₹85. A supplier quotes ₹72. Of the fixed cost, only ₹1 lakh (on 10,000 units) disappears if we buy. Make = 6,00,000 + 1,00,000 = **₹7 lakh**; buy = **₹7.2 lakh** → make. But if freed space can be rented for ₹50,000, buying wins by ₹30,000.

cards.title: Beware budget games
cards.body: When bonuses depend on beating budget, managers **pad** cost estimates and **sandbag** sales targets, and spend leftover money in March ('use it or lose it'). Zero-based budgeting and rolling forecasts are two responses.

cards.q: Standard price ₹20/kg, actual price ₹22/kg, actual quantity 5,000 kg. Material price variance?
cards.explain: (20 − 22) × 5,000 = −₹10,000, i.e. adverse — we paid more than standard.

cards.q: A firm spent ₹40 lakh on R&D for a product last year. In deciding whether to launch it now, the ₹40 lakh is…
options: A sunk cost to be ignored
cards.explain: Money already spent cannot be recovered by either choice, so it is sunk and irrelevant to the launch decision.

cards.q: Which budget adjusts expected costs to the actual level of activity achieved?
cards.explain: A flexible budget restates allowed costs at actual volume so efficiency can be judged fairly.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Managerial accounting has three jobs after costing: **plan** (budgets), **control** (compare actual results with the plan and explain the gaps), and **decide** (choose between options using only the numbers that matter). All three are habits of thought as much as techniques. A manager who can explain *why* costs exceeded plan, and who never lets sunk costs steer a decision, is worth a lot to any organisation.

A budget does several jobs at once: it forces planning, coordinates departments (sales cannot promise what production cannot make), allocates scarce cash, communicates priorities and provides a benchmark for performance. The **master budget** is built in sequence:
points: **Sales budget** — volume × price, by product and region. Everything else depends on it.
**Production budget** — sales + desired closing inventory − opening inventory.
**Materials, labour and overhead budgets** — derived from production.
**Operating expense budget** — marketing, admin, R&D.
**Capital budget** — major asset purchases (see corporate finance).
**Cash budget** — timing of receipts and payments; reveals when you will need a credit line.
**Budgeted income statement and balance sheet**.

Alternatives: **zero-based budgeting** (every cost justified from zero each cycle — associated with Peter Pyhrr at Texas Instruments in the 1970s and used by some consumer companies to drive cost cuts); **rolling forecasts**; and the **Beyond Budgeting** movement, which argues fixed annual targets cause more gaming than they prevent.

notes.p: A **standard cost** is what a unit *should* cost under efficient conditions: e.g. 2 kg of material at ₹50/kg. **Variances** split the gap between actual and standard into causes, so the right person is asked the right question.
points: **Material price variance** = (SP − AP) × AQ — usually purchasing's responsibility.
**Material usage variance** = (SQ − AQ) × SP — usually production's responsibility. SQ = standard quantity allowed for actual output.
**Labour rate variance** = (SR − AR) × AH; **labour efficiency variance** = (SH − AH) × SR.
**Sales volume variance** (in contribution terms) = (Actual units − Budgeted units) × standard contribution per unit.
Always use a **flexible budget**: judge costs against what they should be at the volume actually achieved.

notes.p:
Standard: 2 kg per unit at ₹50/kg = ₹100 of material per unit. Actual output 1,000 units. Actual purchases and usage 2,100 kg at ₹48/kg.

Standard cost of actual output = 1,000 × 2 × 50 = **₹1,00,000**
Actual cost = 2,100 × 48 = **₹1,00,800**
Total variance = **₹800 adverse**

Price variance = (50 − 48) × 2,100 = **₹4,200 favourable**
Usage variance = (2,000 − 2,100) × 50 = **₹5,000 adverse**
Check: 4,200 F − 5,000 A = 800 A ✓

The headline (₹800 over) hides the story. The purchasing team bought cheaper, lower-grade material and earned a favourable variance; the shop floor then wasted 100 kg because of it. Rewarding purchasing on price variance alone would encourage exactly this. Good variance analysis looks for **interdependence**, not culprits.

notes.h: Relevant costs and the make-or-buy decision
notes.p:
For any decision, ask: **which future cash flows change depending on what I choose?** Ignore **sunk costs** (already spent) and **allocated fixed costs that will continue anyway**. Include **opportunity costs** — the benefit of the best alternative forgone.

Worked example: a component needed in 10,000 units a year. Making it costs direct materials ₹30, direct labour ₹20, variable overhead ₹10, and allocated fixed overhead ₹25 — ₹85 per unit 'full cost'. A supplier offers ₹72.
points: Naive view: ₹72 < ₹85, so buy and 'save' ₹1,30,000.
Of the ₹2,50,000 fixed overhead allocated, only a supervisor's ₹1,00,000 salary disappears if we buy; the rest (factory rent, depreciation) continues.
Now suppose the freed space could be leased to a neighbour for ₹50,000 a year. That is an opportunity cost of making: make = ₹7,50,000 vs buy ₹7,20,000 → **buy**, saving ₹30,000.

Qualitative factors: supplier reliability, quality, IP protection, strategic control. Apple outsources assembly but tightly controls design and key components; Toyota keeps close, long-term supplier relationships.

notes.h: Common mistakes, and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p: Letting sunk costs drive decisions (**sunk cost fallacy** — 'we have already spent ₹50 crore on this plant, so we must finish it'). Dropping a product line because its **allocated** costs exceed revenue, when its contribution was covering fixed costs that will remain. Judging managers on static budgets. In consulting and general-management roles you will repeatedly build 'option A vs option B' analyses — the discipline of relevant costing keeps them honest. CMA, CA and MBA exams test variance formulas directly.

points: Master budget: sales → production → inputs → cash → budgeted statements.
Flexible budget restates costs at actual volume.
Price variance = (SP − AP) × AQ; usage variance = (SQ − AQ) × SP.
Favourable variances in one area can cause adverse ones in another.
Relevant costs are future and differ between options.
Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs.
Make or buy: compare buy price with avoidable make cost plus forgone opportunities.

chapters.title: Time value of money: PV, FV, annuities & EMIs

cards.title: A rupee today beats a rupee tomorrow
cards.body: Money today can be invested to earn a return, it is safe from inflation's bite, and it is certain. So ₹1 lakh today is worth more than ₹1 lakh in five years. **All of finance** — valuing a bond, a factory or a startup — rests on this one idea.

cards.title: Future and present value
cards.body:
**FV = PV × (1 + r)ⁿ**
**PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ**
r = rate per period, n = number of periods. Moving money forward is **compounding**; bringing it back is **discounting**. ₹1 lakh at 8% for 10 years grows to about **₹2.16 lakh**.

cards.title: Annuities and perpetuities
cards.body:
**Annuity PV** = C × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r — equal payments for n periods.
**Perpetuity PV** = C ÷ r — forever.
**Growing perpetuity PV** = C₁ ÷ (r − g), valid only if r > g. This last formula is the heart of the Gordon growth model.

cards.title: Your home-loan EMI
cards.body:
₹50 lakh loan, 9% a year, 20 years, monthly. r = 0.75%, n = 240.
**EMI = P × r × (1+r)ⁿ ÷ [(1+r)ⁿ − 1] ≈ ₹44,986.** Total paid ≈ ₹1.08 crore — interest of about **₹58 lakh**, more than the loan itself.

cards.title: Shorter tenure, smaller interest
cards.body: Same ₹50 lakh at 9% over **10 years**: EMI ≈ ₹63,338 — 41% higher — but total interest falls to about **₹26 lakh**. Early EMIs are mostly interest; prepaying in the first years saves the most.

cards.title: Rule of 72
cards.body: Years to double ≈ **72 ÷ interest rate %**. At 8%, about 9 years; at 12%, about 6. Also works for inflation: at 6% inflation, prices double in about 12 years — so your ₹1 crore retirement corpus buys half as much.

cards.title: Nominal vs effective rates
cards.body: A loan at '12% compounded monthly' costs **(1 + 0.12/12)¹² − 1 ≈ 12.68%** a year. Always compare **effective annual rates**. Banks quote whichever looks better — APR on loans, effective yield on deposits.

cards.q: PV of ₹10 lakh received in 5 years at 10% a year?
A preferred share pays ₹8 a year forever. Required return 10%. Value?
cards.explain: Perpetuity PV = C ÷ r = 8 ÷ 0.10 = ₹80.

cards.q: By the rule of 72, at 9% a year money doubles in about…
cards.explain: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Would you rather have ₹1 lakh today or ₹1 lakh in five years? Today — because you could put it in a fixed deposit and have more in five years, because inflation will erode what it buys, and because the future promise may not be kept. The **time value of money** turns this intuition into arithmetic so we can compare cash flows that arrive at different times. Every valuation, loan, insurance policy and pension calculation is built on it.

points: **Future value**: FV = PV × (1 + r)ⁿ. Interest earning interest — **compounding** — is what makes long horizons so powerful.
**Present value**: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. The rate r is the **discount rate** or **opportunity cost of capital** — the return you could earn elsewhere at similar risk.
**Annuity** (equal payments C for n periods): PV = C × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r; FV = C × [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1] ÷ r.
**Perpetuity**: PV = C ÷ r. **Growing perpetuity**: PV = C₁ ÷ (r − g), where C₁ is next period's cash flow.
**Effective annual rate** = (1 + i/m)ᵐ − 1 for a nominal rate i compounded m times a year.
**Real rate** ≈ nominal rate − inflation (exactly: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1).

notes.p:
An **EMI** (equated monthly instalment) is just an annuity whose present value equals the loan. Rearranging the annuity formula gives:

**EMI = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ ÷ [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]**

For a ₹50,00,000 loan at 9% a year for 20 years: r = 0.09 ÷ 12 = 0.0075; n = 240; (1.0075)²⁴⁰ ≈ 6.009.
EMI = 50,00,000 × 0.0075 × 6.009 ÷ 5.009 ≈ **₹44,986**.
Total paid = 44,986 × 240 ≈ **₹1.08 crore**; interest ≈ **₹58 lakh**.

In month 1, interest is 50,00,000 × 0.75% = ₹37,500, so only about ₹7,486 reduces principal. That is why prepayments early in a loan save so much, and why a 10-year tenure (EMI ≈ ₹63,338, interest ≈ ₹26 lakh) costs far less in total even though the monthly burden is higher.

notes.h: Worked example: the power of a SIP
notes.p:
A 25-year-old invests ₹10,000 a month in an equity mutual fund SIP for 20 years. If it earns 1% a month (about 12.7% a year effective — an **illustrative** assumption, not a promise), the future value is:

FV = 10,000 × [(1.01)²⁴⁰ − 1] ÷ 0.01 ≈ **₹98.9 lakh**

She contributed only ₹24 lakh; roughly ₹75 lakh is compounding. Start ten years later and invest for 10 years only, and the same SIP grows to about ₹23 lakh. **Time in the market, not timing the market**, is the lesson that fund houses repeat — and the maths supports it.

The growing perpetuity, **PV = C₁ ÷ (r − g)**, is the engine of the **Gordon growth model** (Myron Gordon) and the 'terminal value' in almost every DCF model. If a company will pay a dividend of ₹10 next year, growing 5% forever, and investors require 12%, the share is worth 10 ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) ≈ **₹143**. Change g to 7% and value jumps to ₹200. Small changes in growth or discount rate move value hugely — a warning to treat any DCF output with humility.

Mixing annual rates with monthly periods. Comparing nominal rates with different compounding frequencies. Using r − g when g ≥ r (the formula breaks down). Ignoring inflation when planning goals: a ₹20 lakh education cost today will be about ₹36 lakh in 10 years at 6% inflation. And confusing 'flat' interest rates — common in some consumer and vehicle loans — with reducing-balance rates: a 10% flat rate costs much more than 10% on a reducing balance.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: GMAT and CAT quant sections test compound interest directly. Finance interviews ask: 'What is a perpetuity worth?' and 'How would you value a bond?' (PV of coupons + PV of principal). In banking, insurance, real estate and corporate finance, PV and annuity calculations are daily work. Spreadsheet functions PV, FV, PMT, RATE and NPER do the arithmetic; you must still understand what they mean.

points: FV = PV(1 + r)ⁿ; PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.
Annuity PV = C[1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ]/r; perpetuity = C/r; growing perpetuity = C₁/(r − g).
Effective rate = (1 + i/m)ᵐ − 1; compare effective, not quoted, rates.
Rule of 72: doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ rate.
Real return ≈ nominal − inflation.
Valuations are very sensitive to r and g.

chapters.title: Capital budgeting: NPV, IRR & payback

cards.title: Which projects deserve money?
cards.body: **Capital budgeting** decides which long-term investments to make — a new plant, a product launch, an acquisition. The test: does the project return more, in today's money, than investors could earn elsewhere at similar risk? If yes, it creates value.

cards.title: Net present value
cards.body: **NPV = Σ CFₜ ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ − Initial investment.** Discount every future **cash flow** (not profit) at the project's cost of capital. **Accept if NPV > 0.** NPV is the rupee amount by which the project raises the firm's value.

cards.title: IRR and profitability index
cards.body: **IRR** is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0; accept if IRR > cost of capital. **Profitability index** = PV of future cash flows ÷ initial investment; accept if > 1. Useful when capital is rationed.

cards.title: Payback
cards.body: **Payback** = years to recover the investment from undiscounted cash flows. Above: 30 + 35 = 65 after year 2; 35 more needed of year 3's 40 → **2.9 years**. **Discounted payback** ≈ 3.9 years. Simple, popular, but ignores everything after the cutoff.

cards.title: When NPV and IRR disagree
cards.body: For mutually exclusive projects of different size or timing, IRR can rank wrongly — a 40% return on ₹1 lakh is worth less than 20% on ₹100 crore. Unusual cash flow patterns can give **multiple IRRs**. **When in doubt, trust NPV.**

cards.title: Use incremental cash flows
cards.body: Include only cash flows that change because of the project: extra revenue, costs, capex, **working capital**, tax effects, and **cannibalisation** of existing products. Exclude sunk costs and **financing costs** (they are already in the discount rate).

cards.q: A project costs ₹50 lakh and has a PV of future cash flows of ₹56 lakh. NPV?
cards.explain: NPV = 56 − 50 = +₹6 lakh. Accept.

cards.q: A project's IRR is 14% and its cost of capital is 16%. Its NPV at 16% is…
cards.explain: For a normal project, discounting at a rate above the IRR gives negative NPV — reject.

cards.q: Which should be EXCLUDED from a project's cash flows?
options: Lost sales of an existing product
Interest on the loan that funds it
cards.explain: Financing costs are captured in the discount rate (WACC); including interest too would double-count.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: A company is a portfolio of investments. Each time it builds a plant, opens stores or buys a business, it gives up cash today for uncertain cash later. **Capital budgeting** asks whether that trade creates value. The answer comes from the time value of money: bring all future cash flows back to today at a rate that reflects their risk, and compare with what you spend. Good capital allocation is, many investors argue, the single most important job of a CEO.

points: **NPV** = −I₀ + CF₁/(1 + r) + CF₂/(1 + r)² + … + CFₙ/(1 + r)ⁿ. Accept if positive. It is additive, uses all cash flows, and measures value created in rupees — the textbook-preferred rule.

**IRR**: the r that sets NPV to zero. Intuitive ('this project earns 18.6%'), but can mislead for mutually exclusive projects, scale differences and non-conventional cash flows; it also implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR. **MIRR** fixes the reinvestment problem.
**Payback period**: years to recover cost. Ignores time value and post-payback cash. Still widely used as a risk screen, especially where the future is very uncertain.
**Discounted payback**: payback using discounted cash flows — better, but still ignores later cash.
**Profitability index (PI)**: PV of inflows ÷ investment. Ranks projects when capital is limited (choose highest PI until the budget runs out).

notes.p: A packaging company considers a ₹100 crore line. Expected after-tax cash flows (₹ crore): Y1 30, Y2 35, Y3 40, Y4 30, Y5 25. Cost of capital 12%.
points: **IRR**: at 20%, NPV ≈ −3.0; at 12%, +16.4. Solving precisely gives **IRR ≈ 18.6%**.
**Payback**: cumulative −70, −35, +5 → 2 + 35/40 = **2.9 years**.
**Discounted payback**: cumulative PV −73.2, −45.3, −16.8, +2.2 → 3 + 16.84/19.07 ≈ **3.9 years**.

notes.p:
Garbage in, garbage out. The right cash flows are **incremental, after-tax and operating**:

Operating cash flow = EBIT × (1 − t) + Depreciation − Capex − Increase in working capital

Include: extra working capital (and its recovery at the end), the **depreciation tax shield**, **opportunity costs** (land you already own could be sold), **cannibalisation** (a new Maggi variant may eat into existing Maggi sales), and **terminal or salvage value**. Exclude: **sunk costs** (feasibility study already paid), **allocated overheads** that do not change, and **interest** (the discount rate already prices financing). Use **nominal cash flows with a nominal rate**, or real with real — never mix.

Run **sensitivity analysis** (what if volumes are 20% lower?), **scenario analysis** (bear/base/bull), and break-even NPV analysis. Big projects contain **real options** — the option to expand, delay or abandon — which simple NPV undervalues; an early-stage market entry can be worth more than its standalone NPV because it buys the right to scale later.

Surveys of CFOs (for example, Graham and Harvey's well-known 2001 survey of US firms) found that NPV and IRR are the most widely used methods, with payback still common. Many Indian conglomerates also apply a hurdle rate above WACC to cushion optimism bias.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how managers misuse it
notes.p: Inflating cash flows to clear the hurdle ('the spreadsheet always says yes'). Using one company-wide discount rate for projects of very different risk — a safe expansion and a risky new-country entry deserve different rates. Preferring high-IRR small projects over large value-creating ones. Forgetting working capital, which can sink otherwise attractive retail and manufacturing projects. And ignoring that **empire-building** incentives push managers towards growth even at negative NPV.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Exams: compute NPV, IRR, payback, and explain NPV–IRR conflicts. Interviews: 'Why is NPV better than IRR?' or 'What discount rate would you use for this project?' Real jobs: corporate-strategy and FP&A teams build these models for every major capex request; PE and project-finance teams do it for every deal.

points: NPV > 0 creates value; it is the most reliable rule.
IRR is the rate where NPV = 0; can mislead on scale, timing, unusual cash flows.
Payback ignores time value and later cash; useful only as a rough risk screen.
PI = PV inflows ÷ investment; use under capital rationing.
Use incremental, after-tax cash flows; include working capital and cannibalisation.
Exclude sunk costs and interest.
Match the discount rate to the project's risk.

chapters.title: Risk & return, diversification, CAPM & beta

cards.title: No free lunch
cards.body: Investors demand **higher expected return for bearing more risk**. Government bonds pay less than corporate bonds, which pay less (on average, over long periods) than equities. The question is: which risk gets rewarded?

cards.title: Measuring risk
cards.body: Expected return = probability-weighted average of outcomes. Risk is commonly measured by **standard deviation (σ)** of returns. Two-asset portfolio variance: **σₚ² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂**, where ρ is the correlation.

cards.title: Diversification in numbers
cards.body: Stock A: 12% return, σ 20%. Stock B: 16%, σ 30%. Correlation 0.2. A 50/50 mix returns **14%** with σ ≈ **19.6%** — **less risky than A alone**, despite adding riskier B. That is the free lunch Harry Markowitz identified in 1952.

cards.title: Two kinds of risk
cards.body: **Unsystematic (specific) risk** — a factory fire, a CEO scandal — can be diversified away by holding many stocks. **Systematic (market) risk** — recessions, interest rates, wars — cannot. Since diversification is nearly free, **markets reward only systematic risk**.

cards.title: Beta
cards.body: **β = Cov(stock, market) ÷ Var(market).** β = 1 moves with the market; β = 1.5 tends to move 1.5× as much; β = 0.6 is defensive (utilities, FMCG). β measures the risk a diversified investor actually bears.

cards.title: CAPM
cards.body:
**E(r) = r_f + β × (E(r_m) − r_f).**
Risk-free rate plus beta times the **equity risk premium**. Developed by **William Sharpe** (1964) and others including Lintner and Mossin. Example: r_f 7%, market 13%, β 1.2 → 7% + 1.2 × 6% = **14.2%**.

cards.title: Use CAPM, but humbly
cards.body: CAPM is the most-used model for the **cost of equity**, but its empirical fit is imperfect: Fama and French showed size and value factors also explain returns. Treat its answer as a reasoned estimate, not a law of nature.

cards.q: r_f = 6%, market return = 12%, β = 0.8. CAPM expected return?
Which risk can be eliminated by diversification?
cards.explain: Firm-specific events are unsystematic and diversify away; macro risks are systematic.

cards.q: Adding a stock with correlation of +1.0 to your portfolio…
