cards.explain: With perfect positive correlation, portfolio σ is just the weighted average of σs — no risk reduction.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: If two investments offer the same expected return, rational investors choose the safer one. So riskier assets must offer a higher expected return to attract buyers. But not all risk is equal. Some risk you can make disappear by spreading your money across many assets; the market will not pay you for bearing risk you could have shed for free. Only the risk that remains in a well-diversified portfolio — **market risk** — earns a premium. That single insight, which won several Nobel prizes, underpins how companies set their cost of capital and how index funds came to dominate.

points: **Expected return** E(r) = Σ pᵢ × rᵢ.
**Variance** σ² = Σ pᵢ × (rᵢ − E(r))²; **standard deviation** σ is its square root.
**Portfolio return** is the weighted average of asset returns.
**Portfolio risk is not the weighted average** of risks: σₚ² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρ₁₂σ₁σ₂.
Lower **correlation (ρ)** → more diversification benefit. ρ = +1 gives none; ρ = −1 can eliminate risk entirely.
**Harry Markowitz** (1952, 'Portfolio Selection') showed investors should choose portfolios on the **efficient frontier** — highest return for each level of risk.

notes.p:
Stock A: E(r) 12%, σ 20%. Stock B: E(r) 16%, σ 30%. Correlation ρ = 0.2. Portfolio 50% A, 50% B.

E(rₚ) = 0.5 × 12% + 0.5 × 16% = **14%**
σₚ² = 0.25 × 0.04 + 0.25 × 0.09 + 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.20 × 0.30
= 0.0100 + 0.0225 + 0.0060 = 0.0385
σₚ = √0.0385 ≈ **19.6%**

The portfolio earns more than A (14% vs 12%) with **less** risk (19.6% vs 20%). With 20–30 stocks across sectors, most specific risk disappears; what remains is market risk.

Total risk = **systematic** (market-wide) + **unsystematic** (firm-specific). A diversified investor only cares about how a stock adds to portfolio risk, which is measured by **beta**: β = Cov(rᵢ, r_m) ÷ σ²_m, estimated by regressing a stock's returns on index returns (Nifty 50 or Sensex in India).

The **Capital Asset Pricing Model**, developed by William Sharpe (1964), John Lintner and Jan Mossin (building on Markowitz and James Tobin), says:

**E(rᵢ) = r_f + βᵢ × [E(r_m) − r_f]**

Graphed against β, this is the **security market line**. Indicative inputs for India: risk-free rate from the 10-year government bond yield, and an equity risk premium that practitioners commonly place somewhere around 5–8% depending on method and source.

**Worked example**: r_f = 7%, E(r_m) = 13%, so the premium is 6%.
Defensive FMCG stock, β = 0.6 → 7% + 3.6% = **10.6%**
Market-like bank, β = 1.0 → **13%**
Cyclical metals stock, β = 1.5 → 7% + 9% = **16%**

notes.h: What CAPM gets right and wrong
notes.p: It is clean, intuitive and widely used — most companies estimate cost of equity with it. But **Eugene Fama and Kenneth French** (1992–93) showed that small-cap and high book-to-market (value) stocks earned more than beta predicted, leading to their **three-factor model**; later work added profitability, investment and momentum factors. Betas are unstable over time and depend on the index and period chosen. In practice, analysts use **industry (unlevered) betas** re-levered for the company's debt to reduce noise.

Confusing high volatility with high beta — a biotech stock can swing wildly for company reasons yet have low beta. Believing that owning 10 stocks in one sector is diversified. Chasing past returns. For individuals, the strongest practical lesson is low-cost diversification: index funds, which John Bogle's Vanguard popularised and which have spread rapidly in India through Nifty and Sensex index funds and ETFs.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Expect: 'What is beta?', 'Why does diversification work?', and CAPM calculations in finance exams (CFA Level 1 covers this heavily). Portfolio managers, risk analysts and corporate-finance teams use beta and CAPM daily to set hurdle rates and judge performance (alpha = actual return − CAPM return).

points: Higher expected return compensates for risk that can't be diversified away.
Portfolio σ depends on correlations; low correlation = strong diversification.
Markowitz (1952): efficient frontier; Sharpe (1964): CAPM.
Systematic risk is priced; unsystematic risk is not.
β = Cov(i, m)/Var(m).
CAPM: E(r) = r_f + β(E(r_m) − r_f).
Fama–French: size and value also explain returns; CAPM is a useful approximation.

chapters.title: Cost of capital & WACC

cards.title: The price of money
cards.body: Every rupee a company uses comes from lenders or shareholders, and each expects a return. The **cost of capital** is that expected return — the **hurdle** a project must beat. Earn less and you destroy value even while reporting profits.

cards.title: WACC
cards.body:
**WACC = (E/V) × Kₑ + (D/V) × K_d × (1 − t)**
E = market value of equity, D = market value of debt, V = E + D, Kₑ = cost of equity, K_d = pre-tax cost of debt, t = tax rate. Interest is tax-deductible, hence the (1 − t).

cards.title: Cost of equity and debt
cards.body: **Kₑ** via CAPM: r_f + β × equity risk premium. **K_d**: the yield the company would pay on new borrowing today (not the old coupon). After-tax K_d = K_d × (1 − t). Equity always costs more than debt because shareholders are paid last.

cards.title: Market values, target weights
cards.body: Use **market** values, not book values — shareholders' opportunity cost is based on what their stake is worth today. Better still, use the firm's **target** capital structure, since WACC is applied to future projects.

cards.title: Project risk beats company WACC
cards.body: A conglomerate's WACC suits average-risk projects only. A Tata group company entering a new risky business should use a rate reflecting **that** business's beta. Using one WACC everywhere overfunds risky ideas and starves safe ones.

cards.title: Value creation test
cards.body: **EVA (economic value added) = NOPAT − WACC × capital employed**, a measure popularised by Stern Stewart. ROCE above WACC creates value; below it destroys value, however large the profit.

cards.q: E/V = 70%, Kₑ = 14%, D/V = 30%, pre-tax K_d = 10%, tax 30%. WACC?
Why is the cost of debt multiplied by (1 − t)?
options: Interest is tax-deductible for the company
cards.explain: Interest reduces taxable profit, so the effective cost to the firm is lower.

cards.q: Which weights should normally be used in WACC?
options: Book values from the balance sheet
cards.explain: WACC reflects investors' current opportunity cost, so market or target weights are appropriate.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: When you run a company, you are using other people's money. Lenders want interest. Shareholders want dividends and share-price growth that compensate them for the risk of being paid last. The **weighted average cost of capital (WACC)** blends those demands into one percentage. It is the minimum return the firm's average project must earn to keep its investors whole. It is also the discount rate in most company valuations, so a one-point error can swing value by 10–20%.

points: **Cost of equity (Kₑ)** — not observable; estimated. Most common method: **CAPM**, Kₑ = r_f + β × ERP. Alternatives: **dividend growth model** Kₑ = D₁/P₀ + g, and bond yield plus a risk premium.
**Risk-free rate** — in India, typically the 10-year Government of India bond yield; in the US, the 10-year Treasury.
**Beta** — regression of stock vs index, or better, an **industry beta** unlevered and relevered: β_U = β_L ÷ [1 + (1 − t)D/E], then β_L = β_U × [1 + (1 − t)D/E] (the **Hamada** relation).
**Cost of debt (K_d)** — the current yield on the company's bonds or the rate banks would charge for new loans; rating-based spreads help for unlisted firms.

**Tax rate** — the marginal rate at which interest saves tax. India's concessional corporate rate under Section 115BAA is 22% plus surcharge and cess (about 25.2%); illustrative examples often use 25%.
**Weights** — market or target values of equity and debt.

notes.p: An illustrative listed manufacturer has 10 crore shares at ₹60 (market equity **₹600 crore**) and debt of **₹400 crore**. V = ₹1,000 crore.
points: r_f = 7%; equity risk premium = 6%; levered β = 1.1 → **Kₑ = 7% + 1.1 × 6% = 13.6%**.
New borrowing would cost **9%**; tax 25% → after-tax K_d = 9% × 0.75 = **6.75%**.
Weights: E/V = 60%, D/V = 40%.
Unlevered (asset) beta = 1.1 ÷ [1 + 0.75 × (400/600)] = 1.1 ÷ 1.5 ≈ **0.73** — the business risk without financing effects. A competitor with no debt should show a beta near this.
If the firm earns ROCE (post-tax) of 15% on ₹1,000 crore, it creates roughly (15% − 10.86%) × 1,000 ≈ **₹41 crore** of economic profit a year.

notes.h: Why debt looks cheap — and isn't free
notes.p: Debt's after-tax cost (6.75%) is half the cost of equity (13.6%), so it is tempting to borrow more and 'lower WACC'. But as debt rises, both lenders and shareholders face more risk: K_d rises, and β and Kₑ rise too. Beyond some point, financial-distress costs overwhelm the tax benefit. The capital-structure chapter explains this trade-off. The key point here: **WACC is not a free lever**; changing the mix changes the components.

Indian firms have historically faced higher costs of capital than US peers because of higher risk-free rates and inflation. That explains why Indian valuations rely heavily on growth and why infrastructure, which needs cheap long-term money, depends on government support and specialised lenders. Large conglomerates such as Tata, Reliance and Aditya Birla run capital-allocation processes that compare business-unit returns against hurdle rates; investors reward groups that exit businesses persistently earning below their cost of capital. Global managers popularised **EVA** (Stern Stewart) in the 1990s to tie bonuses to returns above WACC rather than to accounting profit.

Using book weights; using the coupon on old debt instead of today's yield; plugging a short-term T-bill rate into a long-term valuation; adding arbitrary 'company risk premia' to inflate the rate and kill projects; mixing nominal cash flows with a real discount rate; and applying one WACC to every division. Another trap: treating a low cost of capital period (cheap money) as permanent — when rates rose sharply in 2022–23 globally, many high-growth valuations fell for exactly this reason.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: 'Walk me through a WACC calculation' is a staple investment-banking question. 'Which is cheaper, debt or equity, and why?' tests the logic of priority and tax. Valuation, M&A, project finance and strategy teams all set and defend discount rates. Expect to defend each input — especially beta and the equity risk premium — rather than just compute the formula.

points: WACC = (E/V)Kₑ + (D/V)K_d(1 − t).
Kₑ via CAPM; K_d = current borrowing yield; use the after-tax K_d.
Use market or target weights, not book values.
Unlever/relever beta: β_L = β_U[1 + (1 − t)D/E].
Match the discount rate to project risk, not to the company average.
Value is created only when returns exceed WACC (EVA = NOPAT − WACC × capital).
More debt raises both Kₑ and K_d — WACC is not a free lever.

chapters.title: Capital structure: MM, tax shields & the trade-off

cards.title: Debt or equity?
cards.body: **Capital structure** is the mix of debt and equity that funds the firm. Debt is cheaper and tax-deductible but must be repaid no matter what. Equity is patient but expensive and dilutes owners. Getting the mix wrong can sink an otherwise good business.

cards.title: MM 1958: it doesn't matter (in theory)
cards.body: **Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller** proved that in a perfect market — no taxes, no bankruptcy costs, symmetric information — firm value is **independent of capital structure**. Slicing a pizza differently doesn't make more pizza. Debt makes equity riskier, so Kₑ rises exactly enough to keep WACC constant.

cards.title: MM with taxes (1963)
cards.body: Interest is tax-deductible, so debt creates a **tax shield**. **V_L = V_U + t × D** for permanent debt. Each ₹100 crore of permanent debt at a 25% tax rate adds ₹25 crore of value — in theory, implying 100% debt.

cards.title: Trade-off theory
cards.body: Real firms don't borrow to the hilt because debt brings **financial-distress costs**: lost customers, fleeing suppliers, fire-sale assets, legal fees, management distraction. Optimal debt balances the marginal tax benefit against marginal distress cost.

cards.title: Pecking order
cards.body: **Stewart Myers and Nicolas Majluf** (1984): managers know more than investors, so issuing equity signals 'our shares are overpriced'. Firms therefore prefer **internal cash first, then debt, then equity as a last resort.** It explains why profitable firms often carry little debt.

cards.title: Leverage cuts both ways
cards.body: Assets ₹1,000 crore. All-equity, EBIT ₹150, tax 25% → ROE 11.25%. With ₹500 crore debt at 9%: ROE **15.75%**. In a bad year (EBIT ₹50): all-equity ROE 3.75%; levered ROE **0.75%**. Debt magnifies good and bad years.

cards.title: Industry norms tell a story
cards.body: Stable cash flows and hard assets (utilities, toll roads) support high debt. Volatile, intangible-heavy businesses (software, pharma R&D, startups) carry little. Indian IT majors have historically run almost debt-free; infrastructure firms run heavily levered.

cards.q: Per MM with corporate taxes, permanent debt of ₹200 crore at a 30% tax rate adds how much value?
cards.explain: PV of tax shield = t × D = 0.30 × 200 = ₹60 crore.

cards.q: According to pecking-order theory, the LAST resort for financing is…
cards.explain: New equity carries the strongest negative signal and highest information cost.

cards.q: Which firm can typically sustain the MOST debt?
cards.explain: Stable, predictable cash flows and tangible assets lower distress risk, so utilities support high leverage.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: A business's value comes from its assets and operations — the factory, the brand, the customers. Capital structure decides **who gets what share** of the cash those assets produce: lenders first, shareholders after. The deep question in corporate finance is whether changing the split can change the total. The answer — developed over decades — is: not in a perfect world, yes a little through taxes, and decisively through the costs of distress and the information signals managers send.
In 1958 **Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller** (both later Nobel laureates) showed that under perfect markets:
points: **Proposition I**: firm value is independent of leverage. V_L = V_U.

**Proposition II**: cost of equity rises linearly with leverage: Kₑ = K_A + (K_A − K_d) × D/E, where K_A is the return on assets. Cheaper debt is exactly offset by riskier equity; WACC stays constant.
Intuition: investors can create 'homemade leverage' by borrowing themselves, so they won't pay extra for a firm that borrows for them.
**1963 correction for taxes**: interest is deductible, so V_L = V_U + PV(tax shield). For permanent debt D at tax rate t, PV(tax shield) = t × D.
MM is valuable not because markets are perfect but because it tells you **where to look** for real effects: taxes, distress costs, information and incentives.

notes.h: Worked example: tax shield and ROE
notes.p:
An illustrative company has operating assets worth ₹1,000 crore unlevered and steady EBIT of ₹150 crore. Tax 25%.

**Tax shield**: it borrows ₹400 crore permanently and uses it to buy back shares. PV(tax shield) = 0.25 × 400 = **₹100 crore**, so theoretical V_L = **₹1,100 crore** (ignoring distress costs).

**Effect on ROE** (book assets ₹1,000 crore):
points: ₹500 crore debt at 9%: interest 45 → PBT 105 → tax 26.25 → PAT 78.75 → equity 500 → ROE **15.75%**.
Bad year, EBIT 50. All equity: PAT 37.5 → ROE **3.75%**. Levered: PBT 5 → PAT 3.75 → ROE **0.75%**.
Disaster year, EBIT 30: levered PBT −15 — a loss, and interest still has to be paid in cash.
Leverage raises average ROE and its volatility — exactly what MM Proposition II predicts.

notes.p:
**Static trade-off theory**: optimal leverage where marginal tax benefit equals marginal expected cost of financial distress. Distress costs are higher for firms whose value lies in intangibles, growth options or customer trust (a software firm or an airline customers fear may vanish) and lower for firms with saleable hard assets.

**Pecking-order theory** (Myers & Majluf, 1984): because of **information asymmetry**, managers prefer internal funds, then debt, then equity. Share prices typically fall when firms announce equity issues — consistent with the signal.

**Agency view**: **Michael Jensen** (1986) argued that debt disciplines managers of cash-rich firms by forcing out free cash flow that might otherwise be wasted on empire-building — the logic behind leveraged buyouts. Too much debt, however, creates **debt overhang** and incentives to gamble with lenders' money.

India's twin-balance-sheet problem of the 2010s showed the cost of over-leverage: several infrastructure, power and steel groups borrowed heavily in the 2000s boom, cash flows disappointed, and bad loans piled up at banks. The **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016)** gave creditors a time-bound resolution process, shifting power from defaulting promoters to lenders. In contrast, firms like Infosys and TCS have historically kept little or no debt, returning surplus cash via dividends and buybacks. Globally, Apple borrowed heavily from 2013 despite holding large cash balances — partly for tax and repatriation reasons — illustrating that capital structure decisions are often about taxes and flexibility, not need.

Believing debt is 'cheap' because its rate is lower than Kₑ — it raises Kₑ. Judging leverage by debt/equity alone rather than by **debt/EBITDA and interest coverage**. Ignoring refinancing risk: short-term debt funding long-term assets (an asset–liability mismatch) caused the IL&FS crisis in 2018. And assuming the optimal structure is static; it should move with business risk, interest rates and growth plans.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Exams test MM propositions and t × D. Interviews ask: 'Why don't firms use 100% debt?' (distress costs, flexibility, signalling). In banking and private equity you will size debt using leverage and coverage ratios; CFOs debate the trade-off with rating agencies such as CRISIL and ICRA.

points: MM (1958): no taxes, perfect markets → capital structure irrelevant.
MM Prop II: Kₑ rises with leverage, keeping WACC constant.
With taxes (1963): V_L = V_U + t × D.
Trade-off: tax shield vs financial-distress costs.
Pecking order (Myers–Majluf 1984): internal cash → debt → equity.
Jensen: debt disciplines free cash flow; too much debt causes overhang.
Leverage magnifies ROE in both directions.

chapters.title: Payout policy: dividends & buybacks

cards.title: What to do with surplus cash
cards.body: A profitable firm can **reinvest** (if it has projects earning above its cost of capital), **pay dividends**, **buy back shares**, or **repay debt**. Payout policy is really an investment decision in disguise: return cash when you can't use it better than shareholders can.

cards.title: MM dividend irrelevance (1961)
cards.body: **Miller and Modigliani** showed that in perfect markets dividend policy doesn't change firm value: a ₹10 dividend lowers the share price by ₹10, and an investor who wants cash can sell shares instead ('homemade dividends'). Real-world frictions — taxes, signals, agency — are what make payout matter.

cards.title: Dividends as signals
cards.body: **John Lintner** (1956) found managers **smooth** dividends and raise them only when confident the higher level is sustainable. So markets read a dividend increase as good news and a cut as bad news. Cutting a dividend is something boards dread.

cards.title: Buybacks: flexible payouts
cards.body: A **buyback** returns cash by repurchasing shares. It's flexible (no implicit promise to repeat), concentrates ownership for remaining holders, and can signal undervaluation. Indian IT companies such as Infosys, TCS and Wipro have used repeated buybacks alongside dividends.

cards.title: Does a buyback raise EPS?
cards.body: PAT ₹100 crore, 10 crore shares (EPS ₹10), price ₹200. Spend ₹200 crore idle cash (earning 4.5% after tax) to buy 1 crore shares. Lost income ₹9 crore → PAT 91; shares 9 crore → **EPS ₹10.11**. EPS rises because the earnings yield (5%) beats the cash yield (4.5%).

cards.title: EPS up ≠ value up
cards.body: A buyback creates value only if shares are bought **below intrinsic value** or if it stops managers wasting cash. Buying overpriced shares transfers wealth from remaining to selling shareholders, whatever happens to EPS.

cards.title: Indian tax twist
cards.body: Since April 2020 dividends are taxed in shareholders' hands at their slab rates (dividend distribution tax was abolished). From 1 October 2024 buyback proceeds are also taxed as **deemed dividends** for shareholders. Tax changes have repeatedly reshaped Indian payout choices — always check current rules.

cards.q: Under MM dividend irrelevance, a company pays a ₹5 dividend on a ₹100 share. Ex-dividend price should be about…
cards.explain: Cash leaves the firm, so value per share falls by the dividend: ₹95 plus the ₹5 in hand equals the original ₹100.

cards.q: Lintner's research found that managers typically…
options: Pay out all earnings each year
Prefer equity issues over retained earnings
Smooth dividends and change them slowly
cards.explain: Managers target a long-run payout ratio and adjust gradually, avoiding cuts.

cards.q: Earnings yield 8%, after-tax yield on idle cash 4%. Using cash for a buyback will…
options: Raise the dividend payout ratio to 100%
cards.explain: When the earnings yield on retired shares exceeds the forgone after-tax return on cash, the buyback is EPS-accretive.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Shareholders own the cash a company generates. Managers can keep it to invest, or give it back. The right choice depends on one test: **can the company earn more than its cost of capital on the money?** A young company with abundant opportunities should reinvest nearly everything; a mature company with more cash than good ideas should return it. **Payout policy** — how much, and whether via dividends or buybacks — is how companies answer that test publicly.

points: **MM irrelevance (1961)**: in perfect markets, payout policy doesn't affect value; investors can manufacture their own payout by selling or reinvesting.

**Bird-in-the-hand**: some argue investors value certain dividends over uncertain future gains (associated with Myron Gordon and John Lintner); MM called this a fallacy since risk comes from the business, not the payout.
**Signalling**: dividend changes convey management's private view of future earnings; buybacks can signal undervaluation.
**Agency / free cash flow (Jensen 1986)**: paying out cash stops managers wasting it on low-return projects or vanity acquisitions.
**Clientele effect**: retirees may prefer steady dividends; growth investors prefer reinvestment or buybacks. Firms attract the shareholders whose preferences match their policy.
**Tax**: where dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains, buybacks are more efficient — and tax law changes shift behaviour.

notes.p: Key terms: **payout ratio** = dividends ÷ PAT; **dividend yield** = DPS ÷ price; **record date** (who gets it), **ex-dividend date** (price drops roughly by the dividend). Lintner's 1956 interviews with US managers found they target a long-run payout ratio and adjust only part of the way each year, so dividends are much smoother than earnings. Government-owned Indian companies (PSUs such as Coal India or ONGC) have often paid high dividends partly because the government, as majority owner, relies on that income. Cash-rich consumer companies such as Hindustan Unilever, Nestlé India and ITC have historically paid out a large share of profits because their asset-light models need relatively little reinvestment.

An illustrative company: PAT ₹100 crore, 10 crore shares → EPS ₹10; share price ₹200 → P/E 20, **earnings yield 5%**. It holds ₹200 crore of surplus cash in deposits earning 6% pre-tax (**4.5%** after 25% tax).
points: Buyback: ₹200 crore ÷ ₹200 = **1 crore shares** retired → 9 crore remain.
Lost after-tax interest = 200 × 4.5% = **₹9 crore** → PAT falls to ₹91 crore.
Rule: buyback is EPS-accretive when **earnings yield (E/P) > after-tax yield on cash** (5% > 4.5%).
If instead the stock traded at ₹400 (earnings yield 2.5%), the same ₹200 crore buys 0.5 crore shares; PAT 91 ÷ 9.5 crore = ₹9.58 → EPS falls.
Value test: the buyback helps continuing shareholders only if ₹200 is below what each share is truly worth.

notes.h: Buybacks: tender offer vs open market
notes.p: Indian buybacks (governed by SEBI's Buy-back Regulations) have mostly been via the **tender-offer route**, typically at a premium to market price, where shareholders tender shares and the company accepts them proportionately, with a reservation for small shareholders. The **open-market route** through stock exchanges has been progressively restricted by SEBI. In the US, open-market buybacks dominate; US companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars a year on them, with Apple the largest single buyer over the past decade. Critics argue buybacks can be timed to boost EPS-linked executive pay; supporters argue they efficiently recycle capital from mature firms to growing ones.

Judging a buyback by EPS alone. Borrowing to fund buybacks while the business needs investment. Maintaining a dividend the firm can't afford — paying out of borrowings rather than free cash flow. Ignoring tax changes: India's switch to taxing buyback proceeds as dividend for shareholders (from 1 October 2024) made buybacks much less attractive for many investors compared with the earlier regime in which the company paid the tax. Rules change often; verify the current position before advising.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: 'Should this company pay a dividend or buy back shares?' is a classic case-and-interview question: answer through investment opportunities, valuation, tax, signalling and flexibility. Exams test MM irrelevance and EPS accretion. Investor-relations, treasury and board-advisory roles deal with payout policy directly; equity analysts track payout ratios to judge capital discipline.

points: Reinvest if returns exceed cost of capital; otherwise return cash.
MM (1961): payout irrelevant in perfect markets; frictions make it matter.
Lintner: managers smooth dividends; cuts signal trouble.
Buybacks are flexible and can signal undervaluation.
Buyback is EPS-accretive if earnings yield > after-tax yield on cash.
EPS accretion ≠ value creation — price paid vs intrinsic value decides.
India: dividends taxed in shareholders' hands since 2020; buyback proceeds taxed as dividend since 1 Oct 2024.

chapters.title: Working capital management & the cash conversion cycle

cards.title: Growth eats cash
cards.body: A business pays suppliers, holds stock and waits for customers to pay. Every rupee stuck in inventory or receivables is a rupee you must finance. **Working capital management** decides how much cash the operating cycle swallows — and it kills more small firms than losses do.

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle
cards.body:
**CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO**
DIO (inventory days) = Inventory ÷ COGS × 365
DSO (receivable days) = Receivables ÷ Sales × 365
DPO (payable days) = Payables ÷ COGS × 365
It measures how long cash is tied up from paying suppliers to collecting from customers.

cards.title: Freeing ₹25 crore
cards.body: Sales ₹365 crore (₹1 crore/day), COGS ₹255.5 crore (₹0.7 crore/day). DIO 60, DSO 45, DPO 30 → **CCC 75 days**. Cut DSO to 30 and stretch DPO to 45: receivables fall ₹15 crore, payables rise ₹10.5 crore → **₹25.5 crore released**; CCC drops to 45 days.

cards.title: Negative CCC
cards.body: Some firms collect from customers before paying suppliers: Amazon's retail business, Dell's build-to-order PCs in the 1990s, supermarkets that sell for cash and buy on credit. Their suppliers fund growth, so expansion **generates** cash instead of consuming it.

cards.title: Cost of skipping a cash discount
cards.body: Terms '2/10, net 30': pay in 10 days for 2% off, else full in 30. Skipping the discount means borrowing 98 for 20 days at a cost of 2. Annualised ≈ (2/98) × (365/20) ≈ **37%**. Almost always take it.

cards.title: Three levers
cards.body: **Inventory**: forecasting, EOQ, just-in-time (Toyota's lean system). **Receivables**: credit policy, invoicing speed, collections, factoring. **Payables**: negotiate terms — but don't squeeze small suppliers to death; it damages the supply chain and, in India, can now cost tax deductions.

cards.title: India: MSME payment rules
cards.body: Under the MSMED Act buyers should pay micro and small suppliers within 45 days, and since FY2023–24 **Section 43B(h)** of the Income-tax Act disallows the expense deduction for late payments to them. **TReDS** platforms let MSMEs sell invoices on large buyers for early cash.

cards.q: DIO 50, DSO 40, DPO 35. Cash conversion cycle?
Which change SHORTENS the cash conversion cycle?
cards.explain: Higher DPO reduces CCC. The other options increase DSO or DIO or reduce DPO.

cards.q: Annual sales ₹730 crore; receivables ₹80 crore. DSO?
cards.explain: Daily sales = 730/365 = ₹2 crore; DSO = 80 ÷ 2 = 40 days.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Picture a garment exporter in Tiruppur. It pays for yarn, holds fabric for weeks while stitching, ships to a European retailer, and waits 90 days to be paid. During all that time its own cash is locked up. The bigger the order book, the bigger the cash hole. That is **working capital**: the money trapped in the operating cycle. Manage it well and growth funds itself; manage it badly and a profitable business runs out of cash.

points: **Operating cycle** = DIO + DSO — days from buying inputs to collecting cash.
**Cash conversion cycle (CCC)** = DIO + DSO − DPO — the part of that cycle you finance yourself.
**Net working capital (operating)** ≈ Inventory + Receivables − Payables. Each day of CCC costs roughly one day's COGS or sales in funding.
**Financing** working capital: cash credit and overdraft lines, working-capital demand loans, bill discounting, factoring, commercial paper (for large firms), and supply-chain finance.
**Conservative vs aggressive policy**: holding more inventory and cash lowers stock-out and liquidity risk but costs returns; lean policies boost ROCE but leave less buffer.

notes.p: An illustrative FMCG distributor: sales **₹365 crore** (₹1 crore a day), COGS **₹255.5 crore** (₹0.7 crore a day). Current position: DIO 60, DSO 45, DPO 30.
points: Inventory = 0.7 × 60 = ₹42 crore; Receivables = 1 × 45 = ₹45 crore; Payables = 0.7 × 30 = ₹21 crore.
Operating working capital = 42 + 45 − 21 = **₹66 crore**; CCC = 60 + 45 − 30 = **75 days**.
Plan: tighter credit and digital collections cut DSO to 30 → receivables ₹30 crore (frees ₹15 crore).
Negotiating 45-day supplier terms → payables 0.7 × 45 = ₹31.5 crore (frees ₹10.5 crore).
Total released = **₹25.5 crore**; new CCC = 60 + 30 − 45 = **45 days**.
At a 10% cost of funds, that saves about **₹2.55 crore a year** — on a business with perhaps ₹15–20 crore of profit.
Trade-offs: tighter credit may lose some customers; longer payables may raise supplier prices. Model both before acting.

notes.p:
**Inventory**: better demand forecasting, fewer SKUs, the **economic order quantity** model (EOQ = √(2DS/H), where D = annual demand, S = order cost, H = holding cost per unit), safety stock based on demand variability, and **just-in-time** production pioneered by Toyota (Taiichi Ohno's Toyota Production System). JIT's fragility was exposed during the 2020–21 pandemic and chip shortage, pushing many firms towards 'just-in-case' buffers.

**Receivables**: credit scoring of customers, clear terms, prompt and accurate invoicing (e-invoicing under GST helps), early-payment discounts, and **factoring** or invoice discounting.

**Payables**: negotiate longer terms, centralise purchasing, use supply-chain finance — while respecting MSME rules. Large Indian buyers delaying payments to small suppliers has been a long-standing policy concern, which is why the government added the Section 43B(h) tax disallowance and pushed TReDS (RBI-authorised Trade Receivables Discounting System platforms).

notes.h: Cases: who wins on working capital
notes.p: **Amazon** has long highlighted in shareholder letters that it collects from customers before paying many suppliers, giving it a negative cash conversion cycle that funded growth. **Dell** in the 1990s built PCs only after customers paid, holding very little inventory. In India, FMCG majors such as Hindustan Unilever have been noted for very low or negative working capital thanks to bargaining power with distributors; quick-commerce and e-commerce platforms work on similar float. By contrast, capital-goods and EPC firms that serve government clients often struggle with long receivable cycles.

Celebrating sales growth without watching DSO; offering longer credit to hit quarterly targets; ignoring obsolete stock buried in inventory; stretching payables until suppliers raise prices or stop supplying; and using short-term working-capital loans to fund long-term assets. Also, year-end CCC can be window-dressed — use averages across the year.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Case question: 'Our client is profitable and growing but needs a bank loan every quarter — why?' Answer: working capital. Exams test CCC and cash-discount maths. Finance managers, supply-chain leaders and credit analysts track DIO/DSO/DPO monthly; private-equity value-creation plans almost always include a working-capital release.

points: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO.
DIO = Inv/COGS × 365; DSO = AR/Sales × 365; DPO = AP/COGS × 365.
Each day of CCC ties up roughly one day's sales or COGS in cash.
Negative CCC (Amazon, Dell, strong FMCG) lets suppliers finance growth.
Skipping 2/10 net 30 costs about 37% annualised.
Levers: forecasting/JIT/EOQ, credit policy/collections/factoring, supplier terms.
India: MSME 45-day rule, Section 43B(h), TReDS.

chapters.title: Demand, supply & elasticity for pricing decisions

cards.title: Demand and supply
cards.body: **Demand**: how much buyers want at each price — usually less as price rises. **Supply**: how much sellers offer — usually more as price rises. Where they cross is the **equilibrium** price and quantity. Shifts (a new rival, a heatwave, a tax) move the curves and the equilibrium.

cards.title: Movement vs shift
cards.body: A change in the product's **own price** moves you **along** the demand curve. A change in anything else — income, tastes, rivals' prices, advertising, population — **shifts** the whole curve. Mixing these up is the most common error in managerial economics.

cards.title: Price elasticity of demand
cards.body: **PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.** |PED| > 1: **elastic** (buyers very responsive). |PED| < 1: **inelastic**. Use the **midpoint method** for big changes: divide each change by the average of the old and new values.

cards.title: The revenue rule
cards.body: If demand is **elastic**, cutting price **raises** revenue; if **inelastic**, raising price raises revenue. Revenue peaks where |PED| = 1. But managers maximise **profit**, not revenue — the **Lerner rule**: (P − MC) ÷ P = 1 ÷ |PED|.

cards.title: A streaming price cut
cards.body: Plan cut from ₹199 to ₹149; subscribers grow from 10 lakh to 14 lakh. Midpoint PED = (4/12) ÷ (50/174) ≈ **−1.16**, elastic. Revenue: ₹19.9 crore → **₹20.86 crore**. But if each subscriber costs ₹60 a month to serve, contribution drops from ₹13.9 crore to ₹12.46 crore.

cards.title: What makes demand inelastic?
cards.body: Few substitutes, necessity, small share of budget, short time horizon, and strong brands or habits. Cigarettes, petrol in the short run and essential medicines are inelastic; a particular brand of biscuit is elastic because rival packs sit beside it.

cards.title: Other elasticities
cards.body: **Income elasticity**: necessities (0–1), luxuries (>1), inferior goods (<0). **Cross-price elasticity**: positive for substitutes (Pepsi vs Coke), negative for complements (printers and ink). Use them to forecast demand as incomes grow and to spot real competitors.

cards.q: Price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 4%. Demand is…
cards.explain: |PED| = 0.4 < 1, inelastic; quantity falls less than price rises, so revenue rises.

cards.q: Cross-price elasticity between two goods is −0.8. They are…
cards.explain: A negative cross elasticity means a price rise in one reduces demand for the other — complements.

cards.q: Lerner rule: |PED| = 4, marginal cost ₹300. Profit-maximising price?

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Every pricing meeting is really a debate about one number managers rarely measure: **how much will customers buy at different prices?** Microeconomics gives the vocabulary — demand, supply, elasticity — and a few rules that stop expensive mistakes. The big lesson: price changes move quantity, and whether that helps depends on how sensitive customers are and on your margin, not on gut feeling.

points: **Law of demand**: other things equal, higher price → lower quantity demanded (income and substitution effects).
**Demand shifters**: income, prices of substitutes and complements, tastes, expectations, number of buyers, advertising.
**Supply shifters**: input costs, technology, number of sellers, taxes and subsidies, weather (for farm goods).
**Equilibrium**: where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Price above it → surplus and pressure to cut; below it → shortage and queues.
Example: an unusually poor onion harvest shifts supply left — prices spike, which is why onion prices periodically become political news in India.

**Price controls**: a ceiling below equilibrium (e.g. rent control) creates shortages; a floor above it (e.g. minimum support price without matching demand) creates surpluses that must be stored or disposed of.

notes.p:
**Price elasticity of demand** = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP (negative; we usually quote its absolute value). Midpoint formula: [(Q₂ − Q₁)/((Q₁ + Q₂)/2)] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁)/((P₁ + P₂)/2)].

**Revenue rule**: when |PED| > 1, price and revenue move in opposite directions; when |PED| < 1, the same direction. **Profit rule** — the Lerner condition from economist Abba Lerner — says a profit-maximising firm sets (P − MC)/P = 1/|PED|. Very elastic demand (|PED| = 10) supports only a 10% margin over price; less elastic (|PED| = 2) supports 50%. This is why commodity sellers earn thin margins and strong brands earn fat ones.

Elasticity rises with time: drivers can't immediately change cars when petrol prices rise, but over years they switch to efficient models, CNG or EVs.

An Indian OTT service (illustrative numbers) considers cutting its monthly plan from ₹199 to ₹149. Market tests suggest subscribers rise from 10 lakh to 14 lakh. Serving each subscriber (content delivery, payment fees, support) costs about ₹60 a month.
points: Verdict: the cut raises revenue but **lowers profit** — unless more subscribers bring other value (advertising, data, lower churn, scale for content deals).
Break-even volume at ₹149: 13.9 crore ÷ 89 ≈ **15.6 lakh** subscribers needed — 56% more than today.
Lesson: elasticity tells you about revenue; contribution margin tells you about profit. Use both.

notes.p: **Reliance Jio (2016)** priced mobile data extremely low and offered free voice; India's data consumption exploded, showing how elastic demand for data was at the old prices — and how high fixed-cost networks benefit from volume. **Sin taxes** on cigarettes raise revenue for governments precisely because demand is relatively inelastic, though higher taxes also reduce consumption among price-sensitive young smokers. Consumer companies use **sachet pricing** (₹1–₹5 shampoo packs, popularised in India) to reach price-sensitive buyers without cutting per-ml prices. Global airlines use dynamic pricing to charge business travellers (inelastic) more than leisure travellers (elastic) for the same seat.

Treating the demand curve as fixed when it shifts (blaming a price rise for a fall in sales caused by a competitor launch). Using elasticity from small changes to predict large ones. Assuming rivals won't react — a price cut that rivals match gives you no extra share, just lower margins (see game theory). Confusing revenue growth with profit growth. Ignoring reference prices: customers anchor on past prices, so cuts are easier than restoring prices later.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Consulting cases: 'Should the client raise prices?' — talk elasticity, competitor response, contribution and brand. GMAT critical reasoning often hides demand-shift vs movement confusion. Product managers, category managers and pricing analysts estimate elasticities with A/B tests, conjoint surveys and sales data regressions.

points: Own price → movement along the curve; other factors → shift.
PED = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP; use midpoint for big changes.
Elastic: price cut raises revenue; inelastic: price rise raises revenue.
Profit-max markup: (P − MC)/P = 1/|PED| (Lerner).
Substitutes: + cross elasticity; complements: −.
Elasticity is higher over longer periods and with more substitutes.
Always check contribution, not just revenue, before cutting price.

chapters.title: Costs, economies of scale & scope

cards.title: The economist's cost lens
cards.body: Economists count **opportunity costs**, not just accounting costs. The founder who quits a ₹30 lakh job to run a startup earning ₹20 lakh profit has made an **economic loss** of ₹10 lakh. **Economic profit** = revenue − all costs, including the return capital could earn elsewhere.

cards.title: Short-run cost curves
cards.body: **TC = FC + VC.** **Average total cost** ATC = TC ÷ Q. **Marginal cost** MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the cost of one more unit. MC first falls then rises (diminishing returns), and MC cuts ATC at ATC's **minimum**.

cards.title: Produce where MR = MC
cards.body: A firm maximises profit by producing until the extra revenue from one more unit equals its extra cost. In a competitive market MR = price, so expand output while **P ≥ MC**. Sunk and fixed costs don't change this choice.

cards.title: Economies of scale
cards.body: In the long run all inputs can change. **Economies of scale**: average cost falls as output grows — spreading fixed costs, specialisation, bulk buying, cheaper capital. Beyond some size, **diseconomies** (bureaucracy, coordination) push costs up. The output where costs stop falling is the **minimum efficient scale**.

cards.title: Learning curve
cards.body: Costs also fall with **cumulative** experience. Boston Consulting Group's **experience curve** (Bruce Henderson, 1960s) observed costs falling a roughly constant percentage — often 20–30% — each time cumulative output doubled. Early volume leaders can lock in a cost advantage.

cards.title: Economies of scope
cards.body: Producing **several products together** is cheaper than separately when they share inputs: ITC using its distribution network for foods and personal care; Amazon renting its computing infrastructure as AWS; Reliance cross-selling across Jio and retail. Scope is the logic behind many diversified firms.

cards.title: 80% learning curve
cards.body: First aircraft wing takes 100 hours. With an **80% curve**, unit 2 takes 80 hours, unit 4 takes 64, unit 8 takes 51.2, unit 16 about 41. Each doubling cuts unit time by 20% — powerful for bids on long production runs.

cards.q: A price-taking firm faces price ₹70. MC of the 5th unit is ₹60 and of the 6th unit ₹80. It should produce…
cards.explain: Produce while P ≥ MC: the 5th unit adds ₹10 profit; the 6th would lose ₹10.

cards.q: Which is an economy of SCOPE?
options: A bank selling insurance through its existing branches
A larger cement kiln with lower cost per tonne
Costs falling as workers gain experience
cards.explain: Using shared assets (branches, customers) across products is scope; the others are scale or learning effects.

cards.q: With a 90% learning curve, if unit 1 takes 200 hours, unit 4 takes…
cards.explain: Two doublings: 200 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 162 hours.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Price is set in the market, but cost is in your control. Understanding how costs **behave** as you produce more — in the short run with a fixed factory, and in the long run when you can build anything — explains why some industries end up with a few giants, why startups chase growth, and why big companies sometimes get worse rather than better.

notes.h: Short-run costs and the marginal principle
points: **Fixed costs (FC)** don't vary with output; **variable costs (VC)** do; **TC = FC + VC**.
**Average fixed cost** falls continuously as fixed costs spread over more units.
**Marginal cost (MC)** usually falls at first then rises due to the **law of diminishing marginal returns** — adding workers to a fixed kitchen eventually means they get in each other's way.
**MC intersects ATC at its minimum**: if the next unit costs less than the average, it pulls the average down; if more, it pushes it up.
**Decision rule**: produce where **marginal revenue = marginal cost**. Fixed and sunk costs are irrelevant to how much to produce, though they matter for whether to stay in business in the long run.
**Shutdown rule** (short run): keep operating if price covers average variable cost.

notes.p: An illustrative workshop has fixed costs of ₹100 a day. Variable costs at outputs 1–6: ₹50, 90, 120, 160, 220, 300.
points: Marginal cost: 50, 40, 30, 40, 60, 80 — falls, then rises.
At a market price of ₹70: produce 5 units (MC of 5th = 60 < 70; MC of 6th = 80 > 70). Revenue 350 − cost 320 = **profit ₹30**.

At ₹50: produce 4 units? MC of 4th (40) < 50, of 5th (60) > 50 → 4 units; revenue 200 − cost 260 = loss ₹60. But VC at 4 units is 160 < revenue 200, so operating still covers some fixed cost — stay open in the short run (closing loses the full ₹100).
Note how the decision never uses average fixed cost.

notes.h: Long run: scale, learning and scope
notes.p:
**Economies of scale** arise from indivisible fixed costs (a ₹20,000 crore refinery, a national ad campaign, an R&D lab), specialisation (Adam Smith's pin factory), purchasing power, and the physics of volume (a pipe or tank's capacity grows faster than its surface area). They explain why cement, steel, refining and telecom tend to concentrate. **Network effects** — the product becomes more valuable as more people use it (UPI, WhatsApp) — are a demand-side cousin of scale economies.

**Diseconomies of scale**: layers of management, slow decisions, weaker incentives, communication costs. Many large conglomerates create separate business units or spin-offs to keep units nimble.

**Learning/experience curves**: BCG's Bruce Henderson popularised the idea that unit costs fall by a constant percentage with each doubling of cumulative output. With learning rate L, unit cost of the nth unit = first-unit cost × n^(log₂L). It drove 1970s strategies of chasing market share — sometimes too far.

**Economies of scope**: cost savings from producing multiple products using shared resources — distribution (ITC's network carrying cigarettes, then foods and personal care), technology (Amazon's infrastructure becoming AWS), customer relationships (HDFC Bank cross-selling loans, cards and insurance) or brand (Tata across many categories).

Scale is a cost advantage only if rivals can't match it. In India, **Asian Paints**' scale in distribution and its demand-forecasting systems have often been cited as hard-to-copy advantages. **Amul**'s cooperative structure aggregates millions of small dairy farmers into enough scale to build processing plants and a national brand. But scale invites complacency; new entrants with different models (D2C brands, quick-commerce, new paint entrants backed by large groups) can attack incumbents where scale doesn't help.

Letting sunk costs affect output decisions. Assuming bigger is always cheaper — ignoring diseconomies and the cost of complexity. Over-diversifying in the name of 'synergy' when scope economies are imaginary; many conglomerate mergers promised synergies that never came. Pricing below cost on the hope of learning-curve gains that never materialise, or that competitors can access via cheaper technology.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Expect MR = MC questions in micro exams and 'why are profits falling as we grow?' cases (diseconomies, step costs). Operations and strategy roles constantly weigh scale vs flexibility — one big plant or several small ones near customers. M&A teams must estimate cost synergies (scale and scope) credibly.

points: Economic cost includes opportunity cost.
MC first falls then rises; MC crosses ATC at its minimum.
Produce where MR = MC; ignore sunk/fixed costs for output decisions.
Short run: operate if P ≥ AVC.
Economies of scale: AC falls with size; minimum efficient scale; diseconomies beyond.
Experience curve: costs fall a constant % per doubling of cumulative output.
Economies of scope: shared resources make multi-product firms cheaper.

chapters.title: Market structures: from perfect competition to monopoly

cards.title: Structure shapes profit
cards.body: How much a firm can earn depends heavily on the market it's in: how many sellers, how different the products are, and how hard it is to enter. Economists line markets up on a spectrum: **perfect competition → monopolistic competition → oligopoly → monopoly**.

cards.title: Perfect competition
cards.body: Many sellers, identical products, free entry and exit, full information. Each firm is a **price taker**; price = marginal cost and, in the long run, **economic profit is zero**. Close real examples: wholesale vegetable mandis, many farm commodities, currency markets.

cards.title: Monopolistic competition
cards.body: Many sellers with **differentiated** products and easy entry — restaurants, salons, apparel brands. Each has a little pricing power from its brand or location, but profits attract imitators, eroding them over time. Theory from **Edward Chamberlin** and **Joan Robinson** (1933).

cards.title: Oligopoly
cards.body: A **few large firms** whose decisions affect each other: telecom, cement, airlines, cola, aircraft (Boeing–Airbus). Profits depend on rivals' moves, so strategy and game theory matter. Collusion raises profits but is illegal — India's **Competition Commission (CCI)** has penalised cartels.

cards.title: Monopoly pricing
cards.body: A monopolist sets **MR = MC** and charges the price demand allows at that output. With demand P = 100 − Q and MC = 20: MR = 100 − 2Q = 20 → **Q = 40, P = 60**, profit ₹1,600. Competition would give P = 20, Q = 80. Lost surplus (**deadweight loss**) = ½ × 40 × 40 = **₹800**.

cards.title: Barriers to entry
cards.body: Profits persist only behind barriers: **economies of scale**, **network effects**, patents and licences, control of scarce inputs, switching costs, brand, and regulation. Warren Buffett calls durable barriers a **moat**. No moat, no lasting excess profit.

cards.title: Measuring concentration
cards.body: The **Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)** sums squared market shares (in %). Four firms at 25% each → 4 × 625 = **2,500**. Competition regulators treat higher HHIs and large increases from a merger as warning signs.

cards.q: In long-run perfect competition, firms earn…
cards.explain: Free entry competes away excess profit until price equals minimum average cost.

cards.q: Demand P = 120 − 2Q, MC = 40. Monopoly output?
Market shares 50%, 30%, 20%. HHI?
cards.explain: 2,500 + 900 + 400 = 3,800 — a highly concentrated market.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Two equally talented managers can earn very different returns simply because of the **industry structure** they operate in. A brilliant tomato farmer still sells at the mandi price. A mediocre manager with a government licence or a dominant network can earn handsome profits. Understanding market structure tells you **how much pricing power is possible** and **what will happen to profits** when they appear. Michael Porter's Five Forces, which you will meet in strategy, is built on this industrial-organisation economics.

points: **Perfect competition**: many firms, homogeneous product, free entry, price takers. P = MC; long-run P = minimum ATC; zero economic profit. Efficient for society, brutal for producers.

**Monopolistic competition**: many firms, differentiated products, free entry. Downward-sloping demand for each firm → some markup; long-run economic profit tends to zero as entrants copy successes. Think of the hundreds of momo stalls in Delhi or apparel brands online.

**Oligopoly**: few firms, high entry barriers, interdependence. Outcomes range from cosy price leadership to vicious price wars. Indian telecom consolidated from a dozen operators to three large private players plus state-owned BSNL; cement and aviation are other oligopolies.

**Monopoly**: single seller, no close substitutes, high barriers. Sets output where MR = MC and price above MC, producing less than society would want. Examples: Indian Railways in passenger rail, utility distribution in a licensed area; near-monopolies in some digital platforms.
**Monopsony**: a single dominant buyer (e.g. a sole sugar mill buying cane in a region) with power over suppliers' prices.

notes.h: Fully worked example: monopoly vs competition
notes.p:
Market demand: **P = 100 − Q**; constant marginal cost **₹20**, no fixed costs.

**Competition**: P = MC = 20 → Q = 80. Consumer surplus = ½ × 80 × (100 − 20) = **₹3,200**. Producer profit = 0.

**Monopoly**: TR = 100Q − Q² → MR = 100 − 2Q. Set MR = MC: 100 − 2Q = 20 → **Q = 40**; **P = 100 − 40 = 60**.
Profit = (60 − 20) × 40 = **₹1,600**.
Consumer surplus = ½ × 40 × (100 − 60) = **₹800**.
Total surplus = 2,400 vs 3,200 under competition.
**Deadweight loss = ₹800** = ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) — value that simply disappears because mutually beneficial trades don't happen.

Note the elasticity link: at the monopoly point, |PED| = (P/Q) × (1/slope) = 60/40 = 1.5, and the Lerner markup (60 − 20)/60 = 0.67 = 1/1.5 ✓. Monopolists always price on the elastic part of demand.

Oligopoly is the most common structure for big business and the hardest to predict. Classic models: **Cournot** (firms choose quantities), **Bertrand** (firms choose prices — with identical products, even two firms can drive price to marginal cost), **Stackelberg** (a leader moves first), and the **kinked demand curve** (rivals match cuts but not increases, so prices stay sticky). Firms often avoid price competition and compete on advertising, distribution and product features instead — think Coca-Cola vs PepsiCo or Hindustan Unilever vs P&G.

**Collusion** — explicit or tacit — raises profits at consumers' expense. India's **Competition Act, 2002**, enforced by the **CCI**, prohibits anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominance; the CCI has imposed large penalties on cement manufacturers for cartelisation and investigated dominant digital platforms. In 2023 the Act was amended to add a deal-value threshold for merger review, targeting acquisitions of data-rich startups.

Excess returns survive only behind barriers to entry: scale economies (refining, cement), **network effects** (UPI apps, marketplaces), regulation and licences (banking, telecom spectrum), patents (pharma), brand and habit (Amul, Parle-G), **switching costs** (enterprise software), and control of distribution (FMCG reach in lakhs of kirana stores). The managerial question is always: **which of these does my business have, and how quickly is it eroding?**

Defining the market too narrowly ('we are the only premium electric-scooter maker in Pune') and concluding you have a monopoly. Assuming monopolies are permanent — Nokia's dominance in phones and Kodak's in film collapsed. Believing high market share automatically means high profit; share without a cost or differentiation advantage just means a bigger target. And forgetting that tacit coordination can still breach competition law.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Micro exams test MR = MC and deadweight loss. Case interviews ask 'Is this an attractive market to enter?' — answer with structure: number of players, concentration, differentiation, barriers, likely competitor reaction. In real jobs, strategy teams assess market attractiveness; regulatory and legal teams handle CCI filings for mergers.

points: Spectrum: perfect competition → monopolistic competition → oligopoly → monopoly.
Perfect competition: P = MC, zero long-run economic profit.
Monopoly: MR = MC, P > MC, deadweight loss.
Monopolistic competition: differentiation gives brief pricing power; entry erodes it.
Oligopoly: interdependence — Cournot, Bertrand, Stackelberg, kinked demand.
Barriers/moats: scale, network effects, regulation, patents, brand, switching costs.
HHI = Σ(share %)²; CCI enforces the Competition Act, 2002.

chapters.title: Game theory for managers: dilemmas, Nash & commitment

cards.title: Your payoff depends on them
cards.body: **Game theory** studies decisions where your result depends on what others do — pricing against a rival, bidding for spectrum, negotiating a deal. The key habit: **put yourself in your rival's shoes** and ask how they will respond to each of your moves.

cards.title: Nash equilibrium
cards.body: A set of strategies where **no player can do better by changing only their own move**, given what others are doing. Named after **John Nash** (1950). It is a stable outcome — not necessarily a good one for the players.

cards.title: The pricing prisoner's dilemma
cards.body: Two airlines on one route. Both price High: ₹50 crore profit each. One Low, one High: Low gets ₹70 crore, High gets ₹10 crore. Both Low: ₹25 crore each. **Low is dominant** for each, so they end at **(Low, Low) = 25 each** — even though (High, High) = 50 each was available.

cards.title: Why price wars happen
cards.body: In a one-shot game the dilemma is hard to escape. But firms interact **repeatedly**. When the future matters, cooperation can be sustained by the threat of retaliation. **Robert Axelrod**'s tournaments (1980s) found that simple **tit-for-tat** — cooperate first, then copy the rival's last move — did remarkably well.

cards.title: Commitment and credibility
cards.body: **Thomas Schelling** (The Strategy of Conflict, 1960) showed that **limiting your own options** can strengthen your position. Building excess capacity, signing long-term contracts or publicly promising to match any price makes threats credible. A threat you would not carry out is just noise.

cards.title: Sequential games
cards.body: When moves are in order, solve by **backward induction**: start at the end and ask what each player would rationally do, then work back. An incumbent's threat to start a price war against an entrant is credible only if fighting is better for it **after** entry has happened.

cards.title: Change the game
cards.body: **Brandenburger and Nalebuff** (*Co-opetition*, 1996) argue the biggest wins come from changing the game itself — its players, added values, rules, tactics or scope — not from playing better. Loyalty programmes and 'most-favoured customer' clauses change the payoffs of a price war.

cards.q: In the airline example, why do both firms end at (Low, Low)?
options: Low is each firm's dominant strategy
High is each firm's dominant strategy
cards.explain: Whatever the rival does, pricing Low gives each firm a higher payoff, so both choose Low — a Nash equilibrium worse for both.

cards.q: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where…
options: No player gains by unilaterally changing strategy
cards.explain: Nash equilibrium is about unilateral stability, not joint optimality.

cards.q: A price-match guarantee by all retailers in a town tends to…
options: Reduce the number of products sold
Make price cuts pointless, supporting higher prices
cards.explain: If any cut is instantly matched, no one gains share by cutting — so the guarantee can soften competition.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Most business decisions are not made against nature but against other thinking people: competitors, suppliers, regulators, unions, acquirers. **Game theory** is the discipline of thinking about decisions when payoffs are **interdependent**. It doesn't give a magic formula; it gives structure — who are the players, what can they do, what do they want, what do they know, and in what order do they move?

points: **Players, strategies, payoffs**: the building blocks; a **payoff matrix** captures simultaneous games, a **game tree** sequential ones.
**Dominant strategy**: best for you no matter what others do. If you have one, play it.
**Nash equilibrium** (John Nash, 1950): each player's strategy is a best response to the others'. Nash shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for this work.
**Prisoner's dilemma**: individually rational choices produce a collectively worse outcome. Formalised at RAND around 1950 (Flood and Dresher; named by Albert Tucker).
**Repeated games**: when the game repeats indefinitely, cooperation can be sustained by the threat of future punishment.
**Sequential games and backward induction**: solve from the last move back. Only **credible** threats matter (subgame perfection, Reinhard Selten).
**Commitment** (Thomas Schelling): irreversible moves that change rivals' expectations.

notes.h: Fully worked example: a pricing dilemma
notes.p: Two airlines fly Delhi–Goa and each chooses a High or Low fare for the season. Annual route profits (₹ crore, illustrative):
points: A Low, B High: **(70, 10)** — A steals passengers.
For A: if B is High, Low gives 70 > 50; if B is Low, Low gives 25 > 10. **Low dominates.** Same for B.
Nash equilibrium: **(Low, Low)** with 25 each, though (High, High) gives 50 each — a classic prisoner's dilemma.

Escape routes: repeated interaction with tit-for-tat; differentiation (loyalty, schedules, service) so customers don't switch purely on price; capacity discipline; and changing payoffs via frequent-flyer programmes. Explicit agreements to fix fares are illegal cartels.

notes.p:
Price wars usually start because a firm misreads a rival's move, is desperate for volume (high fixed costs), or wants to change market structure. Indian telecom is the textbook modern case: Jio's 2016 entry with very low prices triggered intense competition, losses and consolidation; once the market had fewer players, the major operators raised tariffs in December 2019 and on later occasions. The outcome matched game-theoretic logic: aggressive moves are rational when they reshape the game for the long run, and cooperation (tacit, through signalling) becomes easier with fewer players.

In **sequential entry games**, an incumbent may threaten a price war. Backward induction asks: once the entrant is in, is fighting actually more profitable than accommodating? If not, the threat isn't credible. Incumbents make threats credible through **commitment** — sunk investment in spare capacity, long-term contracts with key customers, or a reputation for fighting built over many markets.

notes.h: Cooperation, signalling and changing the game
notes.p:
Repeated games explain why rival firms often avoid destructive competition: each knows that undercutting today invites retaliation tomorrow. **Robert Axelrod**'s computer tournaments (*The Evolution of Cooperation*, 1984) found tit-for-tat — nice, retaliatory, forgiving, clear — performed very well. Firms also **signal**: pre-announcing price changes, publicly stating capacity plans, or matching rivals instantly.

**Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff** (*Thinking Strategically*, 1991) and **Adam Brandenburger and Barry Nalebuff** (*Co-opetition*, 1996) brought these ideas to managers. Their core message: think about the whole **value net** — customers, suppliers, competitors and **complementors** (firms whose products make yours more valuable, like app developers for a phone platform). Sometimes competitors cooperate to grow the pie (setting industry standards) while competing to divide it.

Assuming rivals won't react ('we'll cut price 10% and take share'). Assuming rivals are irrational — or perfectly rational — without evidence. Making threats you won't carry out, which destroys credibility. Ignoring that winning an auction may mean overpaying (the **winner's curse** — relevant to spectrum and IPL franchise auctions). And confusing legal tacit coordination with illegal collusion: discussing prices with competitors is a serious offence.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Case interviews often include 'How will competitors respond?' — interviewers reward structured thinking about rivals' incentives. Exams ask you to find dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in 2×2 matrices. Real jobs: pricing strategy, bids and auctions, negotiations, M&A, and regulatory strategy all require game-theoretic thinking.

points: Interdependence: your payoff depends on others' choices.
Dominant strategy: best regardless of others; play it if you have one.
Nash equilibrium: no unilateral profitable deviation (Nash, 1950).
Prisoner's dilemma: rational individual choices, worse joint outcome — price wars.
Repeated games and tit-for-tat (Axelrod) can sustain cooperation.
Backward induction; only credible threats count; commitment creates credibility (Schelling).
Change the game: players, added value, rules, tactics, scope (Brandenburger & Nalebuff).

chapters.title: GDP, growth, inflation & business cycles

cards.title: Why managers need macro
cards.body: Your company can execute perfectly and still have a bad year if the economy slows, interest rates jump or the rupee falls. **Macroeconomics** explains the tide that lifts or sinks all boats — demand, costs, credit and currency.

cards.title: GDP by expenditure
cards.body:
**GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)**
Private consumption + investment (gross fixed capital formation and inventories) + government spending + net exports. In India, private consumption is the largest component — well over half of GDP.

cards.title: Nominal vs real
cards.body: **Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** uses base-year prices, stripping out inflation. Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation (exactly: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + deflator inflation) − 1). Nominal 10%, deflator 4% → real ≈ **5.8%**.

cards.title: India's statistics
cards.body: GDP is estimated by the **National Statistics Office (MoSPI)**. In February 2026 MoSPI released a new series with base year **2022–23**, replacing the 2011–12 base, and a new CPI series. Base revisions update the basket and methods, so compare growth rates within one series.

cards.title: Inflation: CPI vs WPI
cards.body: **CPI** tracks prices households pay (food has a large weight) and is what the **RBI targets**. **WPI** tracks wholesale and producer prices. **Core inflation** excludes volatile food and fuel. Moderate inflation is normal; high or unpredictable inflation destroys planning and savings.

cards.title: Business cycles
cards.body: Economies move through **expansion → peak → slowdown/recession → trough → recovery**. Leading indicators — PMI surveys, credit growth, auto and two-wheeler sales, GST collections, electricity demand — help managers see turns early.

cards.title: Cycle-proof your plans
cards.body: Sales of cars, cement, steel and luxury goods swing with the cycle; FMCG staples and utilities are steadier. Good managers stress-test budgets for a downturn and keep enough cash and flexibility to invest when competitors retrench.

cards.q: Nominal GDP grows 11% and the GDP deflator rises 5%. Approximate real growth?
Which index does the RBI's inflation target refer to?
cards.explain: The flexible inflation-targeting framework targets headline CPI (combined) inflation.

cards.q: Which is a LEADING indicator of the business cycle?
cards.explain: PMI new orders signal future production before it shows up in GDP.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period. It is the economy's income statement. When GDP grows faster, incomes rise, firms sell more and governments collect more tax. **Inflation** is the rate at which the general price level rises — it determines whether higher incomes buy more. Together, growth and inflation set the backdrop for every business plan: how fast markets grow, what wages to budget, and what interest rates to expect.
There are three equivalent approaches:
points: **Expenditure**: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M). Most quoted in the news.

**Production / value added**: sum of gross value added (GVA) across agriculture, industry and services, plus product taxes minus subsidies. India publishes GVA by sector; services form the largest share.
**Income**: wages + profits + rent + interest (+ taxes less subsidies, depreciation).
**GDP vs GNI**: GNI adds net income from abroad (e.g., profits earned by Indian firms overseas minus those of foreign firms in India).
**Per-capita GDP** and **PPP**-adjusted figures matter for comparing living standards: India is among the world's largest economies by total GDP but still a lower-middle-income country per person.

India's NSO releases quarterly GDP estimates about two months after each quarter ends, with advance, provisional and revised estimates for each year; new 2022–23-base series released in February 2026.

notes.h: Worked example: nominal, real and the deflator
notes.p:
Imagine an economy that makes only phones and tea (illustrative).
Base year: 100 phones at ₹10,000 + 10,000 kg tea at ₹200 = ₹10,00,000 + ₹20,00,000 = **₹30 lakh**.
Next year: 110 phones at ₹10,500 + 10,200 kg tea at ₹210.
**Nominal GDP** = 11,55,000 + 21,42,000 = **₹32.97 lakh** (+9.9%).
**Real GDP** (base prices) = 110 × 10,000 + 10,200 × 200 = 11,00,000 + 20,40,000 = **₹31.4 lakh** (+4.67%).
**GDP deflator** = nominal ÷ real × 100 = 32.97 ÷ 31.4 × 100 ≈ **105.0** → prices up about 5%.
Check: 1.099 ÷ 1.0467 ≈ 1.050 ✓.

So almost half the 'growth' in rupee terms was just higher prices. For a company, the same logic applies: if your revenue grew 9% while your category's prices rose 6%, your **volume** grew only about 3%.

**Demand-pull** inflation occurs when spending outruns the economy's capacity; **cost-push** when input costs rise (oil, a poor monsoon raising food prices, a weaker rupee raising import costs). **Expectations** matter: if workers and firms expect high inflation, they build it into wages and prices.

India's headline **CPI** (published by MoSPI; new series with base year 2024 released in 2026) has a large food weight, so monsoons and vegetable prices swing it. **WPI** (Office of the Economic Adviser) reflects producer prices, closer to costs for manufacturers. Costs of inflation: eroded savings and fixed incomes, uncertainty that discourages investment, and redistribution from lenders to borrowers. Deflation is also dangerous — consumers delay purchases and real debt burdens rise, as Japan's long stagnation showed.

notes.h: Business cycles and what drives them
notes.p: Cycles come from shocks (oil prices, pandemics, financial crises), credit booms and busts, inventory swings and policy changes. India's major recent episodes include the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2016 demonetisation and 2017 GST transition disruptions, and the sharp COVID-19 contraction in 2020–21 followed by a strong rebound. **Okun's law** (Arthur Okun) links slower growth to higher unemployment. Leading indicators — PMI, bank credit, auto sales, e-way bills, core-sector output — turn before GDP; lagging indicators (unemployment, NPAs) turn after.

Comparing nominal company growth with real GDP growth. Comparing growth rates across GDP series with different base years. Treating one quarter's figure as a trend — early estimates get revised. Ignoring that averages hide divergence: rural and urban demand, or premium and mass segments, can move in opposite directions (a 'K-shaped' recovery). And extrapolating boom-time demand into capacity plans.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Interviews: 'What is India's GDP growth outlook and how would it affect this client?' — know the latest headline numbers before any interview. Exams: compute real growth and deflators. Jobs: strategy and FP&A teams build revenue forecasts on GDP and inflation assumptions; banks' economists brief clients on the cycle; marketers separate price and volume growth.

points: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); India's largest component is private consumption.
Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation; deflator = nominal/real × 100.
India: new GDP base year 2022–23 (released Feb 2026); new CPI base 2024.
CPI (targeted by RBI) vs WPI vs core inflation.
Inflation: demand-pull, cost-push, expectations.
Cycle: expansion → peak → recession → trough → recovery; watch leading indicators.
Split your own growth into price and volume.

chapters.title: Monetary & fiscal policy: RBI, MPC and the Union Budget

cards.title: Two levers on the economy
cards.body: **Monetary policy** (the central bank) works through interest rates, liquidity and credit. **Fiscal policy** (the government) works through spending, taxes and borrowing. Both aim at stable growth with low inflation — but they often pull in different directions.

cards.title: India's inflation target
cards.body: Under the amended **RBI Act (2016)**, India follows **flexible inflation targeting**. The target is **4% CPI inflation with a band of 2–6%**, set by the government in consultation with the RBI. In March 2026 it was **retained for April 2026 – March 2031**.

cards.title: The Monetary Policy Committee
cards.body: The **MPC** has **six members**: three from the RBI (including the Governor, who has a casting vote) and three external members appointed by the government. It meets at least four times a year (in practice about every two months) and votes on the **policy repo rate**.

cards.title: The rate corridor
cards.body: **Repo rate**: rate at which the RBI lends to banks overnight against government securities — the policy rate. **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** = repo − 0.25% (floor). **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** = repo + 0.25% (ceiling). Other tools: **CRR**, **SLR**, open-market operations, forex operations.

cards.title: Transmission
cards.body: A repo cut lowers banks' funding costs; since 2019, new floating-rate retail and MSME loans must be linked to an **external benchmark**, usually the repo rate, so EMIs adjust faster. Lower rates lift borrowing, asset prices and spending — with a lag of several quarters.

cards.title: Deficits in the Budget
cards.body: **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = the government's borrowing need. **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments.

cards.title: Fiscal policy trade-offs
cards.body: Spending on roads and railways (**capex**) tends to have a larger multiplier than subsidies. But heavy borrowing can **crowd out** private investment and raise interest rates. India's FRBM framework sets the rules; recent budgets shifted the anchor towards a falling **debt-to-GDP** ratio.

cards.q: The repo rate is 6.00%. Under the current corridor, the SDF rate is…
cards.explain: SDF = repo − 25 bps = 5.75%; MSF = repo + 25 bps = 6.25%.

cards.q: How many members does India's Monetary Policy Committee have?
cards.explain: Six: three RBI officials (including the Governor) and three external members.

cards.q: Fiscal deficit ₹16 lakh crore; interest payments ₹12 lakh crore. Primary deficit?
cards.explain: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest = 16 − 12 = ₹4 lakh crore.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: When an economy overheats, prices rise too fast; when it stalls, jobs and profits vanish. Two institutions try to steer between these. The **Reserve Bank of India** uses **monetary policy** — mainly the price of short-term money — to manage inflation while supporting growth. The **Union Government** uses **fiscal policy** — the Budget's spending, taxes and borrowing — to support growth, redistribute and build public goods. For managers, these decide the cost of loans, consumer demand, government orders and the tax on every rupee of profit.

points: **Legal basis**: the RBI Act was amended in 2016 to adopt **flexible inflation targeting** and create the **MPC**. The first MPC meeting was in October 2016.

**Target**: 4% headline CPI inflation, tolerance band 2–6%, notified by the government for five years at a time. Notified for 2016–21, retained for 2021–26, and in March 2026 retained again for **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031**.
**Failure clause**: if average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government explaining why and what it will do (this first happened in 2022).

**MPC**: six members — RBI Governor (chair, casting vote), a Deputy Governor, one RBI officer, and three external experts appointed by the government for four-year terms. Decisions by majority vote; minutes published.

**Instruments**: policy **repo rate**; the **liquidity adjustment facility** corridor with **SDF** (introduced in April 2022 as the floor, at repo − 25 bps) and **MSF** (ceiling, repo + 25 bps); **CRR** (cash banks keep with the RBI); **SLR** (government securities banks must hold); **open market operations**; variable-rate repo/reverse repo auctions; forex intervention.
Policy rates change often — check the RBI website for the current repo rate rather than memorising it.

notes.h: Worked example: how a rate cut reaches your EMI
notes.p:
Suppose the MPC cuts the repo rate by 0.50 percentage points. A home loan linked to the repo rate (EBLR) moves from 9.00% to 8.50% at its next reset.
For a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan, the EMI falls from about **₹44,986 to about ₹43,391** — roughly ₹1,600 a month. Alternatively, banks often keep the EMI and shorten the tenure.

Now the business side: a firm with ₹500 crore of floating-rate debt saves 0.5% × 500 = **₹2.5 crore** a year of interest. Multiply across the economy and you see the channels: lower borrowing costs, higher asset prices (equities and real estate tend to rise when rates fall), a softer rupee as capital seeks higher yields elsewhere, and more consumer spending on credit-financed goods like cars and homes. Transmission takes time — the RBI and most economists think in terms of several quarters.

notes.h: Fiscal policy and the Union Budget
notes.p: The **Union Budget**, presented by the Finance Minister on 1 February each year, sets out receipts (taxes such as income tax, corporate tax, GST share, customs; non-tax revenue such as RBI dividends; disinvestment) and expenditure (revenue spending on salaries, subsidies, interest; capital spending on assets).
points: **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts). India's fiscal deficit jumped above 9% of GDP in 2020–21 during COVID and has since been brought down step by step towards roughly 4–4.5% of GDP.
