**Revenue deficit**: borrowing to fund day-to-day spending — the worst kind.
**Primary deficit**: fiscal deficit minus interest — shows whether current policy, excluding past debt, is adding to borrowing.
**FRBM Act, 2003** (amended 2018) set the fiscal rules; from 2026–27 the government has said it will target a declining **debt-to-GDP** path rather than a fixed annual deficit number.

**Multiplier**: capital expenditure on infrastructure tends to have a larger and longer-lasting multiplier than revenue spending — the rationale for India's sharp increase in public capex since 2020–21.
**Crowding out**: large government borrowing absorbs savings and can push up bond yields, raising firms' borrowing costs.

notes.p: The ideal mix depends on the problem. In a demand slump (2020), both loosened: rate cuts, liquidity support and government guarantees for MSME loans. In an inflation surge driven by supply (oil, food), monetary tightening reduces demand but cannot grow more vegetables — so fiscal measures like cutting fuel taxes or managing food stocks help. Economists emphasise **central-bank independence** and a credible target because when people trust that inflation will stay near 4%, they don't rush to raise prices and wages, making the target self-fulfilling. **Milton Friedman**'s insight that monetary policy works with 'long and variable lags' remains a caution against over-reacting to one month's data.

Thinking the RBI 'sets' all interest rates (it sets the policy rate; markets and banks set the rest). Assuming rate cuts immediately boost demand. Treating all deficits as bad — borrowing for productive capex in a slump can pay for itself, while borrowing for subsidies in a boom is risky. Quoting an out-of-date repo rate or deficit number in an interview.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Banking and consulting interviews: 'What did the last MPC decide and why?', 'What were the key fiscal numbers in the last Budget?' Exams: definitions of deficits, MPC structure, policy tools. Jobs: treasury teams manage interest-rate risk; real-estate, auto and banking firms track every MPC meeting; companies with government clients read the Budget's capex allocations line by line.

points: Monetary policy = RBI (rates, liquidity); fiscal = government (spending, taxes, borrowing).
Inflation target: 4% CPI, band 2–6%, retained for April 2026 – March 2031.
MPC: 6 members, Governor's casting vote, about six meetings a year.
Corridor: SDF = repo − 25 bps (floor); MSF = repo + 25 bps (ceiling).
Repo-linked (EBLR) loans transmit rate changes to EMIs faster.
Fiscal deficit = borrowing need; primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest.
Capex multipliers > subsidy multipliers; watch crowding out.

chapters.title: Exchange rates, trade & the balance of payments

cards.title: Prices of currencies
cards.body: An **exchange rate** is the price of one currency in another — e.g. ₹ per US$. When it takes **more** rupees to buy a dollar, the rupee has **depreciated**. Exporters (IT services, pharma, textiles) gain in rupee terms; importers (oil, electronics, gold) pay more.

cards.title: Balance of payments
cards.body: The **BoP** records all transactions between residents and the rest of the world. **Current account**: trade in goods and services, income, and transfers (remittances). **Capital and financial account**: FDI, portfolio flows, loans. Plus **changes in reserves**. Overall it must balance.

cards.title: India's typical pattern
cards.body: India usually runs a **merchandise trade deficit** (oil, electronics, gold imports), partly offset by a large **services surplus** (IT and business services) and **remittances** — India is the world's largest remittance recipient. The resulting modest **current account deficit** is financed by FDI and portfolio inflows.

cards.title: Interest-rate parity
cards.body: **Forward rate = Spot × (1 + i_home) ÷ (1 + i_foreign).** Spot ₹85/$, Indian rate 7%, US rate 4.5% → 1-year forward ≈ 85 × 1.07 ÷ 1.045 ≈ **₹87.03**. Higher-interest currencies trade at a forward discount — no free lunch from borrowing cheap dollars.

cards.title: PPP and the real exchange rate
cards.body: **Purchasing power parity** says identical goods should cost the same across countries after conversion; over the long run, high-inflation currencies tend to depreciate. The Economist's **Big Mac index** is a light-hearted PPP test. The **real exchange rate** adjusts for inflation differences — it decides true competitiveness.

cards.title: The impossible trinity
cards.body: A country can't simultaneously have a **fixed exchange rate**, **free capital movement** and an **independent monetary policy** (Mundell–Fleming). India runs a **managed float**: the market sets the rupee, and the RBI uses its large forex reserves to smooth excessive volatility.

cards.title: Managers must hedge
cards.body: Currency moves can wipe out a year's margin. Exporters and importers use **forwards, options and natural hedges** (matching costs and revenues in the same currency). Decide a hedging policy in advance rather than speculating.

cards.q: The rupee moves from ₹84/$ to ₹88/$. For an Indian IT exporter billing in dollars, rupee revenue…
cards.explain: Each dollar now converts into more rupees — the rupee has depreciated, helping exporters.

cards.q: Remittances from Indians working abroad are recorded in the…
cards.explain: Personal transfers are part of the current account, under secondary income (private transfers).

cards.q: Per the impossible trinity, a country with free capital flows and an independent monetary policy must give up…
cards.explain: Only two of the three can be held at once; with open capital and independent rates, the currency must float.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: No Indian business is purely domestic. Your phone's chips, your petrol, your software client in New Jersey and the foreign investor in your company's shares all connect you to the world through **exchange rates**, **trade** and **capital flows**. The **balance of payments** is the country's ledger with the rest of the world; the exchange rate is the price that helps keep it in balance. Managers who understand them can price exports, plan imports and manage currency risk instead of being surprised by it.

notes.h: The balance of payments in detail
points: **Current account**: (a) **goods** trade balance; (b) **services** (IT, travel, transport, financial services); (c) **primary income** (interest, dividends, wages across borders); (d) **secondary income** (remittances, grants).

**Capital account**: small items like capital transfers. **Financial account**: **FDI** (lasting ownership stakes), **FPI** (portfolio equity and debt), external commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, trade credit.
**Reserves**: if inflows exceed outflows, the RBI typically adds to forex reserves; if not, reserves fall.
Identity: current account + capital/financial account + change in reserves (with sign conventions) + errors and omissions = 0.
A **current account deficit** means a country invests more than it saves and must borrow or attract investment from abroad to fund the gap.
India's pattern: goods deficit, services surplus led by software and business services, large remittance inflows; CAD usually around 0–3% of GDP depending on oil prices.

notes.p: In the short run, currency values respond to **capital flows**, interest-rate differentials, risk appetite and news; in the long run, to **relative inflation** (PPP), productivity and the current account. Key ideas:
points: **Purchasing power parity (PPP)**: in the long run, the currency of a high-inflation country tends to depreciate by roughly the inflation gap. If India's inflation runs about 2–3 points above the US's, a gradual rupee depreciation is unsurprising.
**Covered interest parity**: Forward = Spot × (1 + i_INR)/(1 + i_USD). Forward premiums reflect interest differentials, not forecasts.
**Real effective exchange rate (REER)**: the trade-weighted exchange rate adjusted for inflation. A rising REER means exports are becoming less competitive even if the nominal rate looks stable.
**Regimes**: fixed/pegged (Gulf currencies to the dollar), free float (US dollar, euro), **managed float** (India).
**Impossible trinity** (Mundell–Fleming): you can pick only two of fixed exchange rate, open capital account, independent monetary policy.

notes.h: Worked example: currency risk for two Indian firms
notes.p: **Exporter**: an IT services firm bills **$100 million** a year with rupee costs of ₹6,800 crore.
points: At ₹85/$: revenue ₹8,500 crore → operating profit ₹1,700 crore (20% margin).
At ₹88/$: revenue ₹8,800 crore → profit ₹2,000 crore (22.7% margin) — **+17.6%** from a 3.5% currency move.
At ₹82/$: revenue ₹8,200 crore → profit ₹1,400 crore (−17.6%).

**Importer**: an electronics assembler buys $50 million of components and sells only in India. A move from ₹85 to ₹88 raises costs by 50m × ₹3 = **₹150 crore** unless it can pass the increase to customers.

**Forward hedge** (from the parity formula, illustrative rates): with spot 85, Indian rate 7% and US rate 4.5%, the 1-year forward ≈ 85 × 1.07 ÷ 1.045 ≈ **₹87.03**. The exporter can lock this in for next year's receipts; the importer can lock in costs. Hedging removes uncertainty — it doesn't promise a profit.

notes.p: India's **1991 balance-of-payments crisis** — when forex reserves fell to only a few weeks of import cover and the government had to pledge gold — led to rupee devaluation and the liberalisation reforms that opened the economy. In the **2013 'taper tantrum'**, when the US Federal Reserve signalled it would slow bond purchases, capital fled emerging markets and the rupee fell sharply; India was labelled one of the 'Fragile Five' and responded with measures including attracting NRI deposits. Since then India has built much larger forex reserves, giving the RBI more firepower to smooth volatility. On trade, the US–China tariff conflicts since 2018 and global 'China plus one' sourcing have created opportunities — for example in electronics assembly, where government production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes helped make India a significant exporter of smartphones.

Calling a weaker rupee simply 'bad' — it hurts importers and consumers but helps exporters and remittance-receiving households. Treating forward rates as forecasts. Ignoring **translation** exposure when consolidating foreign subsidiaries, and **economic** exposure — a domestic seller can be hurt by a cheap foreign rival when the rupee is strong. Speculating instead of hedging under the label of 'treasury management'.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and real jobs
notes.p: Interviews: 'How does a rupee depreciation affect Infosys versus an oil marketing company?' Exams: BoP classification, parity calculations, impossible trinity. Jobs: treasury and FP&A teams set hedge ratios; export-oriented firms price contracts in dollars; strategy teams assess sourcing locations by labour cost, tariffs and currency.

points: Rupee depreciation = more ₹ per $; helps exporters, hurts importers.
BoP = current account + capital/financial account + reserve changes.
India: goods deficit, services surplus, top remittance recipient, modest CAD.
Forward = Spot × (1 + i_home)/(1 + i_foreign).
PPP: high-inflation currencies depreciate over time; REER measures competitiveness.
Impossible trinity: choose two of fixed rate, free capital, independent policy.
Hedge with forwards/options/natural hedges according to a set policy.

chapters.title: Descriptive statistics & data visualisation for managers

cards.title: Why managers need statistics
cards.body: A manager never sees 'the business' — only numbers about it. **Descriptive statistics** compress thousands of data points into a few numbers you can reason with: a centre (typical value), a spread (how much it varies) and a shape (is it lopsided, are there outliers?). Get these three right and most dashboards suddenly make sense.

cards.title: Mean vs median
cards.body: The **mean** is the arithmetic average; the **median** is the middle value when sorted. The mean is pulled by extreme values; the median is not. Delivery times of 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14 and 41 minutes give a mean of **14** but a median of **11.5**. One late order moved the mean by three minutes. Report both when data is skewed.

cards.title: Measuring spread
cards.body: **Range** = max − min. **Variance** = average squared distance from the mean (sample: divide by n − 1). **Standard deviation (SD)** = √variance, in the original units. **Coefficient of variation** = SD ÷ mean, useful for comparing spread across different scales. **IQR** = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50%, robust to outliers.

cards.title: Same average, different business
cards.body: Store A sells ₹48k, ₹50k, ₹52k on three days; Store B sells ₹20k, ₹50k, ₹80k. Both average **₹50k**. Sample SD: A = **₹2k**, B = **₹30k**. CV: A = 4%, B = 60%. Store B needs far more safety stock and staff flexibility. The average alone would have told you they are identical.

cards.title: Pick the chart for the question
cards.body: Comparing categories → **bar chart**. Change over time → **line chart**. Distribution of one variable → **histogram or box plot**. Relationship between two variables → **scatter plot**. Part of a whole with 2–3 parts → maybe a pie; with more, a bar is almost always clearer.

cards.title: Spot a misleading chart
cards.body: Check three things before you believe a chart: does the **y-axis start at zero** (for bars it must)? Are there **two y-axes** that can be scaled to show any 'relationship'? Is the time window **cherry-picked**? Edward Tufte's rule: maximise the share of ink that shows data, and cut decoration.

cards.title: Anscombe's quartet
cards.body: In 1973 statistician Francis Anscombe built four small datasets with almost the same mean, variance, correlation and regression line — yet their scatter plots look completely different (a line, a curve, an outlier-driven line, a single extreme point). Lesson: **always plot the data** before trusting summary numbers.

cards.q: A city's household incomes are heavily right-skewed. Which single number best describes a 'typical' household?
cards.explain: Skewed data drags the mean towards the long tail (a few very rich households). The median is the middle household and is not pulled by extremes.

cards.q: Two sales reps both average 20 deals a month. Rep X has SD 2, Rep Y has SD 8. What can you conclude?
options: Y's monthly results are far less predictable
cards.explain: Same mean, different spread. A larger SD means more month-to-month volatility, so Y is less predictable.

cards.q: You want to show how monthly revenue changed over the last 24 months. Best chart?
options: Scatter plot of revenue vs region
cards.explain: Change over time is the classic job of a line chart; the eye reads slope as trend.

notes.p:
Every business generates more data than any human can read: every UPI payment, every Swiggy order, every machine reading on a shop floor. **Descriptive statistics** are the tools that shrink a pile of numbers into a handful of facts you can hold in your head. They do not explain *why* something happened — that is the job of inference and regression — but they tell you *what* happened, accurately and honestly.

Think of any dataset as having three properties. **Centre**: what is a typical value? **Spread**: how much do values differ from each other? **Shape**: is the data symmetric, lopsided (skewed), or does it have unusual points (outliers)? A good manager asks about all three before making a decision. Most bad decisions from data come from looking only at the centre.

The **mean** adds everything and divides by the count. It uses every data point, which is a strength and a weakness: one extreme value can drag it a long way. The **median** is the middle value after sorting, so it ignores how extreme the extremes are. The **mode** is the most frequent value, useful for categories (the most popular shoe size, the most common complaint).

When data is **right-skewed** — incomes, house prices, order values, time-to-resolve tickets — the mean sits above the median. That is why government and serious analysts quote median household income. If someone quotes only an average salary for an MBA batch, ask for the median: a few very high international offers can inflate the average.
points: Mean = Σx ÷ n
Median = middle value (average of the two middle values if n is even)
Skew rule of thumb: mean > median → right-skewed; mean < median → left-skewed

notes.p:
Spread is where risk lives. The **variance** is the average of squared deviations from the mean; for a sample we divide by **n − 1** rather than n to correct a slight underestimate. The **standard deviation** is its square root, which brings us back to the original units (rupees, minutes).

**Worked example.** Store A's daily sales: ₹48k, ₹50k, ₹52k. Store B: ₹20k, ₹50k, ₹80k.
Step 1 — Means: both are 150 ÷ 3 = **₹50k**.
Step 2 — Deviations: A: −2, 0, +2. B: −30, 0, +30.
Step 3 — Squared deviations summed: A: 4 + 0 + 4 = 8. B: 900 + 0 + 900 = 1,800.
Step 4 — Sample variance (÷ 2): A = 4, B = 900.
Step 5 — SD: A = **₹2k**, B = **₹30k**.
Step 6 — Coefficient of variation: A = 2/50 = 4%; B = 30/50 = 60%.

An operations manager would staff, stock and forecast these two stores completely differently, though their averages are identical. The **interquartile range (IQR)** — the gap between the 25th and 75th percentiles — gives a spread measure that, like the median, ignores outliers. A **box plot** draws exactly this: a box from Q1 to Q3, a line at the median, and whiskers to the typical range, with outliers shown as dots.

notes.h: Shape, outliers and the 'always plot it' rule
notes.p:
Two datasets can share the same mean and SD yet behave very differently. Francis Anscombe made this point in 1973 with four tiny datasets — now called **Anscombe's quartet** — that have nearly identical means, variances, correlations and fitted lines, but look nothing alike when plotted. One is a clean line, one a curve, one a line bent by a single outlier, one a vertical stack with a single distant point.

An **outlier** is not automatically an error. A ₹5 lakh order on a grocery app might be a data-entry mistake — or a bulk buyer worth a dedicated sales team. Investigate before you delete. A common rule flags points more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles as worth a look.

The chart should answer a specific question. Use **bars** to compare categories (sales by state), **lines** for trends over time (monthly active users), **histograms** for the distribution of one variable (basket sizes), **scatter plots** for relationships (discount vs volume), and **box plots** to compare distributions across groups (delivery times by city).

Edward Tufte, in *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, argued for a high **data-ink ratio**: remove 3-D effects, heavy gridlines and decoration so the data stands out. Put the key message in the title ("Delivery times rose after the monsoon"), not a label ("Delivery times"). Sort bars by size. Label lines directly instead of using a distant legend.
Most misleading charts are accidents, but they still mislead.
points: **Truncated axes**: a bar chart starting at 95 makes a 2% difference look like 200%
**Dual y-axes**: you can rescale either axis to manufacture or hide a relationship
**Average of averages**: averaging store-level conversion rates ignores that stores have very different traffic; weight by volume
**Ignoring spread**: 'average delivery time 25 minutes' hides the 10% of orders taking over an hour that drive complaints
**Cherry-picked windows**: starting a chart at the low point of a cycle to show 'growth'
**Pie charts with ten slices**: the eye cannot compare angles; use a sorted bar chart

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: In consulting and product interviews you will be handed a table and asked "what do you see?" Strong answers name the centre, spread and outliers, then ask about the shape ("is the average order value skewed by a few bulk orders?"). In exams, expect to compute mean, median, SD and CV, and to explain why the median is preferred for skewed data. On the job, nearly every weekly business review is a set of descriptive charts; the manager who asks "what does the distribution look like, not just the average?" usually finds the real problem.

points: Describe any data by **centre, spread and shape**
Mean is pulled by outliers; **median** is robust — prefer it for skewed data like incomes and order values
SD = √variance; sample variance divides by **n − 1**; CV = SD ÷ mean compares spread across scales
IQR = Q3 − Q1; box plots show median, IQR and outliers
Bar = compare, line = trend, histogram = distribution, scatter = relationship
Anscombe's quartet: identical summaries, different pictures — **always plot**
Watch for truncated axes, dual axes, cherry-picked windows and averages of averages

chapters.title: Probability & distributions: binomial, normal and Bayes

cards.title: Probability is the language of uncertainty
cards.body: Every business decision is a bet: will the customer buy, will the shipment arrive, will the loan default? **Probability** puts a number between 0 and 1 on each outcome so you can compare bets. Two rules carry most of the weight: **P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)** and **P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)**.

cards.title: Conditional probability
cards.body: **P(A|B)** is the probability of A *given* that B has happened. P(default) for all borrowers might be 3%, but P(default | missed last two EMIs) could be 40%. Credit scoring, fraud detection and churn models are all machines for estimating conditional probabilities.

cards.title: Bayes: the fraud-alert trap
cards.body: 1% of transactions are fraud. The alert catches 90% of fraud but also flags 5% of genuine ones. Out of 10,000 transactions: 100 fraud → 90 flagged; 9,900 genuine → 495 flagged. Of 585 alerts, only 90 are fraud: **P(fraud | alert) ≈ 15%**. A '90% accurate' system is mostly false alarms when the event is rare.

cards.title: The binomial distribution
cards.body: Use it for a count of successes in **n independent trials**, each with the same probability **p**. P(exactly k) = C(n,k) · pᵏ · (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. Mean = **np**. SD = **√(np(1−p))**. Examples: how many of 20 sales calls convert, how many of 500 parcels arrive damaged.

cards.title: Binomial at work
cards.body: A telecaller converts 10% of calls. Out of 5 calls, P(exactly 2 sales) = C(5,2) × 0.1² × 0.9³ = 10 × 0.01 × 0.729 = **7.3%**. P(at least one sale) = 1 − 0.9⁵ = 1 − 0.590 = **41%**. Expected sales per 5 calls = np = **0.5**.

cards.title: The normal distribution
cards.body: The bell curve, described by its mean μ and SD σ. **68%** of values lie within ±1σ, **95%** within ±2σ (precisely ±1.96σ), **99.7%** within ±3σ. Convert any value to a **z-score**: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ, the number of SDs from the mean. Heights, measurement errors and averages of many small effects tend to be roughly normal.

cards.title: Not everything is normal
cards.body: Stock returns have **fat tails**: extreme crashes happen far more often than the normal curve predicts. Order sizes and incomes are skewed. Before using normal-based formulas, plot a histogram. Misusing the normal curve for tail risk was one ingredient in the 2008 financial crisis.

cards.q: Daily demand is normal with mean 500 and SD 100. Roughly what share of days will demand exceed 700?
cards.explain: 700 is 2 SDs above the mean. About 95% of values lie within ±2σ, so about 5% lie outside, split equally: about 2.5% above.

cards.q: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches 99% of cases but has a 2% false-positive rate. If you test positive, the chance you have the disease is closest to:
cards.explain: Per 100,000 people: 100 sick → 99 positive; 99,900 healthy → 1,998 positive. 99 ÷ 2,097 ≈ 4.7%. Rare events + imperfect tests = mostly false positives.

cards.q: Each of 200 shipments is independently late with probability 0.05. The expected number of late shipments is:
cards.explain: Binomial mean = np = 200 × 0.05 = 10.

notes.p:
Managers live with uncertainty: demand next month, whether a customer pays, whether a new drug passes trials. **Probability** is a disciplined way to quantify that uncertainty so it can be compared, added up and priced. A probability of 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and everything interesting happens in between.

A **probability distribution** lists every possible outcome with its probability. Once you know the distribution of, say, daily demand, you can answer practical questions: how much stock gives a 95% chance of not running out? How many call-centre agents keep the wait under two minutes on most days? Distributions turn vague worry into numbers you can plan around.
Four rules cover most business problems.
points: **Complement**: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Often the easiest route: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)
**Addition**: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); drop the last term if A and B cannot both happen
**Multiplication**: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A); if independent, simply P(A) × P(B)
**Bayes' rule**: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) ÷ P(B) — it lets you reverse a conditional probability

notes.p:
Bayes' rule is named after the 18th-century minister Thomas Bayes and is the most practically important formula most managers never learn. It answers: given the evidence I just saw, how should I update my belief?

**Worked example (illustrative numbers).** A bank's fraud model flags transactions. Base rate of fraud: 1%. The model flags 90% of frauds (sensitivity) and wrongly flags 5% of genuine transactions (false-positive rate).
Imagine 10,000 transactions.
Step 1 — Frauds: 1% × 10,000 = 100. Flagged: 90.
Step 2 — Genuine: 9,900. Wrongly flagged: 5% × 9,900 = 495.
Step 3 — Total flags: 90 + 495 = 585.
Step 4 — P(fraud | flag) = 90 ÷ 585 ≈ **15.4%**.

So 85% of alerts are false alarms. This is the **base-rate fallacy**: people hear '90% accurate' and assume a flagged transaction is 90% likely to be fraud. The practical consequence is huge — if you block every flagged card, you annoy hundreds of good customers to catch 90 fraudsters. Banks therefore use flags to trigger a cheap check (an OTP or a call) rather than an outright block. The 'natural frequencies' method used above — imagine 10,000 cases and count — was championed by psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer because people reason far better with counts than with percentages.

Use the **binomial** when you count successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials with the same probability each time. Its formula is P(X = k) = C(n,k) pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, where C(n,k) = n! ÷ (k!(n−k)!) counts the ways to arrange k successes among n trials.

**Worked example.** A telecaller converts 10% of calls. In 5 calls:
P(0 sales) = 0.9⁵ = 0.590
P(exactly 2) = 10 × 0.1² × 0.9³ = 10 × 0.01 × 0.729 = 0.073
P(at least 1) = 1 − 0.590 = 0.410
Mean = np = 0.5 sales; SD = √(5 × 0.1 × 0.9) = √0.45 ≈ 0.67.

Why it matters: a new caller with zero sales in the first five calls is entirely normal (59% chance) and is not evidence of poor skill. Managers who fire people on small samples are reacting to binomial noise. With 100 calls, expected sales are 10 with SD = √9 = 3, so anything from about 4 to 16 is unremarkable.

The **normal distribution** is symmetric and bell-shaped, fully described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. The **central limit theorem** explains why it appears so often: averages and sums of many independent effects tend towards normal, whatever the shape of the individual effects. That is why sample means, measurement errors and aggregated demand across many customers are often close to normal.

To use it, convert to a **z-score**: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ.

**Worked example.** Weekly demand for a product at a warehouse averages 500 units with SD 100 (assume normal). What is the chance demand exceeds 650? z = (650 − 500) ÷ 100 = 1.5. From the standard normal table, P(Z > 1.5) ≈ **6.7%**. If you stock 650 units, you stock out roughly one week in fifteen. To cut that to 5% you need z = 1.645, i.e. 500 + 164.5 ≈ 665 units. This is exactly the logic behind safety stock in operations.
points: 68–95–99.7 rule: share within ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ
z = 1.645 → 5% in one tail; z = 1.96 → 2.5% in each tail (95% two-sided)
Other useful distributions: **Poisson** for counts of arrivals per period (calls per hour), **exponential** for time between arrivals

notes.p: Probability errors are expensive because they feel intuitive.
points: **Base-rate neglect**: ignoring how rare the event is (fraud, disease, star hires)
**Gambler's fallacy**: 'we've had five bad months, a good one is due' — independent events have no memory
**Assuming independence** when outcomes are linked: home loans defaulted together in 2008 because they shared a housing market
**Assuming normality** in the tails: market crashes, viral hits and supply shocks are fat-tailed
**Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)**: 'most fraudsters use new devices' does not mean 'most new-device users are fraudsters'

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: GMAT and CAT include probability and combinatorics questions; MBA statistics exams test binomial and normal calculations and Bayes. Consulting and fintech interviews love the fraud or medical-test puzzle because it separates people who calculate from people who guess. In jobs — credit risk at HDFC or Bajaj Finance, fraud at Paytm or Razorpay, demand planning at HUL — you will use conditional probabilities and normal approximations weekly, usually inside a spreadsheet or model.

points: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) — the most useful shortcut
Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) ÷ P(B); with a low base rate, most positives are false
Binomial: n trials, prob p; mean np, SD √(np(1−p))
Normal: 68–95–99.7; z = (x − μ)/σ; z = 1.645 for a 5% one-tail
Central limit theorem: averages of many independent effects tend to be normal
Small samples are noisy — don't judge people or products on five trials
Real-world tails are often fatter than normal

chapters.title: Sampling, confidence intervals & hypothesis tests (A/B testing)

cards.title: Why we sample
cards.body: You can't ask every Indian what toothpaste they use. A **sample** of a few thousand, chosen well, can describe a population of crores remarkably accurately. The key word is *well*: a **random** sample beats a huge biased one. Precision depends on sample size, not on population size.

cards.title: Sampling bias beats sample size
cards.body: In 1936 the *Literary Digest* polled over two million Americans, mostly from phone directories and car registrations, and confidently predicted Roosevelt would lose. He won in a landslide — the sample over-represented richer voters. Watch for **selection**, **non-response** and **survivorship** bias.

cards.title: Standard error and confidence intervals
cards.body: The **standard error** of a sample mean is SE = s ÷ √n. A **95% confidence interval** is x̄ ± 1.96 × SE. For a proportion, SE = √(p(1−p)/n). Quadrupling the sample size only **halves** the error — precision gets expensive.

cards.title: A survey interval
cards.body: 400 customers surveyed, average monthly spend ₹520, SD ₹200. SE = 200 ÷ √400 = **₹10**. 95% CI = 520 ± 1.96 × 10 = **₹500 to ₹540** (roughly). You can tell the CFO: our best estimate is ₹520, and we're fairly confident the true average lies between ₹500 and ₹540.

cards.title: The logic of a hypothesis test
cards.body: Start by assuming nothing changed — the **null hypothesis (H₀)**. Ask: if H₀ were true, how likely is data at least this extreme? That probability is the **p-value**. If it's below a threshold (often 0.05), reject H₀. A p-value is **not** the probability that H₀ is true.

cards.title: A/B test, worked
cards.body: Page A: 500 conversions from 10,000 visitors (5.0%). Page B: 580 from 10,000 (5.8%). Pooled rate 5.4%. SE of the difference = √(0.054 × 0.946 × (1/10,000 + 1/10,000)) ≈ 0.0032. z = 0.008 ÷ 0.0032 ≈ **2.5**, two-sided p ≈ **0.012**. Significant at 5%: ship B, assuming the test ran cleanly.

cards.title: Don't peek
cards.body: Checking an A/B test every day and stopping the moment p < 0.05 inflates false positives badly. Fix the sample size **before** the test, run full weeks (weekday and weekend behaviour differ), and ask whether the lift is big enough to matter — statistically significant is not the same as commercially significant.

cards.q: To halve the margin of error of a survey, you must multiply the sample size by:
cards.explain: Margin of error ∝ 1/√n. Halving it needs √n to double, so n must quadruple.

cards.q: An A/B test gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new design is worse
There is a 97% chance the new design is better
If there were truly no difference, data this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
The new design improves conversion by 3%
cards.explain: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that either hypothesis is true.

cards.q: A Type I error in an A/B test means:
options: Launching a change that actually has no effect
Missing a change that really works
Testing two variants instead of one
cards.explain: Type I = false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis. Type II = false negative: failing to detect a real effect.

notes.p:
Managers almost never see the whole population — every customer, every unit off the line, every possible visitor to a website. They see a **sample** and must infer the whole from the part. **Inferential statistics** gives two tools for doing that honestly: the **confidence interval**, which says how precise an estimate is, and the **hypothesis test**, which asks whether an observed difference is real or could easily be noise.

The modern face of this is the **A/B test**: show half your users version A and half version B, then compare. Amazon, Netflix, Booking.com, Flipkart and practically every app company run large numbers of such experiments. The maths is a century old — much of it from Ronald Fisher, Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson — but it has never been more commercially important.

A sample is useful only if it resembles the population. **Simple random sampling** gives every member an equal chance of selection. **Stratified sampling** first splits the population into groups (say, metro, tier-2 and rural) and samples within each, guaranteeing representation. **Cluster sampling** picks whole groups (villages, stores) to save travel cost.

The classic warning is the 1936 *Literary Digest* poll: an enormous sample drawn from phone directories and car registrations — lists that skewed towards richer voters in Depression-era America — predicted the wrong winner. A far smaller but better-designed poll by George Gallup got it right.
points: **Selection bias**: the way you collect data excludes some groups (online surveys miss offline customers)
**Non-response bias**: the people who reply differ from those who don't (angry or delighted customers answer feedback forms)
**Survivorship bias**: studying only the survivors — copying the habits of successful start-ups while ignoring the thousands with the same habits that failed

notes.p:
A sample mean will rarely equal the true mean exactly. The **standard error (SE)** measures how much sample means bounce around from sample to sample: SE = s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation. By the central limit theorem, sample means are roughly normal, so about 95% of them fall within 1.96 SE of the true mean.

**Worked example.** A D2C skincare brand surveys 400 randomly chosen customers. Average monthly spend: ₹520; SD: ₹200.
Step 1 — SE = 200 ÷ √400 = 200 ÷ 20 = ₹10.
Step 2 — Margin of error = 1.96 × 10 = ₹19.6.
Step 3 — 95% CI = ₹500.4 to ₹539.6.

Interpretation: if we repeated this survey many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true average. For proportions, use SE = √(p(1−p)/n). With 1,000 respondents and p = 0.5, SE ≈ 1.6%, so the margin of error is about ±3 percentage points — which is why so many opinion polls quote ±3%.
A hypothesis test is a structured argument by contradiction.
points: **1. State H₀ and H₁.** H₀: the new checkout page converts at the same rate as the old. H₁: it converts at a different rate
**2. Choose α**, the false-positive rate you will tolerate — usually 5%
**3. Compute a test statistic** (a z or t value) measuring how far the data are from H₀ in standard-error units
**4. Find the p-value**: the probability of a result at least this extreme if H₀ were true
**5. Decide**: if p < α, reject H₀; otherwise you have not shown a difference (which is not proof of no difference)
**Type I error** = false positive (launch something useless); **Type II error** = false negative (kill something that works). **Power** = 1 − P(Type II), raised mainly by larger samples

notes.p:
**Illustrative numbers.** An e-commerce app tests a new product page. Control A: 10,000 visitors, 500 orders (5.0%). Variant B: 10,000 visitors, 580 orders (5.8%).
Step 1 — Difference = 0.8 percentage points.
Step 2 — Pooled rate p = (500 + 580) ÷ 20,000 = 0.054.
Step 3 — SE = √(0.054 × 0.946 × (1/10,000 + 1/10,000)) = √(0.0000102) ≈ 0.0032.
Step 4 — z = 0.008 ÷ 0.0032 ≈ 2.5.
Step 5 — Two-sided p-value ≈ 0.012, below 0.05. Reject H₀.

Now the business question: a 16% relative lift in conversion on a high-traffic page could be worth crores a year — worth shipping. But if the same z came from a test of 50 lakh visitors with a 0.05-point lift, it might be statistically significant yet commercially trivial. Always report the **effect size with a confidence interval**, not only the p-value.
Experiments are easy to run and easy to fool yourself with.
points: **Peeking**: stopping a test as soon as p dips below 0.05 dramatically raises false positives; fix the sample size in advance
**Multiple comparisons**: test 20 button colours and one will be 'significant' by chance at 5%
**Novelty effects**: users click a new design because it is new; run long enough for this to fade
**Running partial weeks**: weekday and weekend users behave differently
**Confusing 'not significant' with 'no effect'**: a small test may simply lack power
**Sample ratio mismatch**: if a 50/50 split delivers 52/48, something in the assignment is broken — fix it before reading results

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Product-manager interviews at Indian tech firms routinely ask "how would you test whether this feature works?" — they want a clear metric, a hypothesis, a randomisation unit, a pre-set sample size and a guardrail metric (e.g. cancellations). Exams ask you to compute confidence intervals and z-tests and to interpret p-values correctly. In marketing and research roles you will design surveys; in operations, you will test process changes. The single most valued instinct is scepticism: "could this be noise or bias?"

points: Bias is worse than small size: a random sample of 1,000 beats a biased sample of 2 million
SE = s/√n; 95% CI ≈ estimate ± 1.96 SE; for proportions SE = √(p(1−p)/n)
Quadruple n to halve the error
p-value = P(data this extreme | H₀ true) — not P(H₀ true)
Type I = false positive; Type II = false negative; power rises with sample size
A/B tests: fix sample size first, no peeking, full weeks, watch multiple comparisons
Report effect size and its interval; statistical ≠ practical significance

chapters.title: Regression, correlation & the causation trap

cards.title: Correlation in one number
cards.body: The **correlation coefficient r** runs from −1 to +1 and measures how tightly two variables move together in a **straight line**. r = 0.8: strong positive. r = −0.3: weak negative. r = 0 means no *linear* link — there could still be a curve. Correlation says nothing about which variable drives which.

cards.title: What regression does
cards.body: **Regression** fits the line (or plane) that best predicts an outcome Y from one or more drivers X, by minimising the sum of squared prediction errors (**ordinary least squares**). Y = a + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + error. Each coefficient b tells you how much Y changes per unit of X, **holding the other X's constant**.

cards.title: Reading a regression output
cards.body: Illustrative: Monthly sales (₹ lakh) = 120 + **3.2** × Ad spend (₹ lakh) − **8.5** × Price (₹). R² = 0.72. Ad: SE 0.8, t = 4.0, p < 0.001. Price: SE 5.0, t = −1.7, p ≈ 0.09. Each extra ₹1 lakh of ads is associated with ₹3.2 lakh more sales, price held constant.

cards.title: Key numbers in the output
cards.body: **Coefficient** = estimated effect per unit. **Standard error** = uncertainty in it. **t-stat** = coefficient ÷ SE; |t| above about 2 ≈ significant at 5%. **p-value** = chance of a t this large if the true effect were zero. **R²** = share of Y's variation explained by the model (0 to 1).

cards.title: Correlation is not causation
cards.body: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together — because both rise in summer. A hidden **confounder** drives both. Other traps: **reverse causality** (do happy employees cause profits, or do profitable firms make employees happy?) and **selection** (people who choose premium plans differ from those who don't).

cards.title: Getting to causation
cards.body: The gold standard is a **randomised experiment** (an A/B test): random assignment breaks the link to confounders. When you can't randomise, use **natural experiments**, **difference-in-differences** (compare change in treated vs untreated groups) or carefully controlled regressions. The 2021 Nobel in economics honoured this toolkit.

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.body: A trend can reverse when you combine groups. In a famous 1973 study of UC Berkeley graduate admissions, men appeared to be admitted at a higher overall rate, yet within most departments women did as well or better — women had applied more to highly competitive departments. Always ask: what happens **within** each segment?

cards.q: A regression shows a coefficient of 3.2 with standard error 0.8. The t-statistic is:
cards.explain: t = coefficient ÷ standard error = 3.2 ÷ 0.8 = 4.0, comfortably significant.

cards.q: Cities with more police officers have more crime. The most likely explanation is:
options: Reverse causality or confounding: high-crime cities hire more police
cards.explain: Cities respond to crime by hiring police (reverse causality), and big cities have both (confounding). Correlation alone cannot show the direction.

cards.q: R² = 0.72 means:
options: The model explains about 72% of the variation in the outcome
cards.explain: R² is the proportion of variance in Y explained by the model. In simple regression R² = r², so r would be about 0.85.

notes.p:
Business questions are often about relationships. Does more advertising raise sales? Does a price cut raise volume enough to raise revenue? Do employees who get training stay longer? **Correlation** measures how strongly two variables move together. **Regression** goes further: it builds an equation to predict one variable from others and estimates how much each driver matters.

But both are just descriptions of patterns in data. Whether X **causes** Y is a separate and harder question. Some of the costliest mistakes in business come from treating a correlation as a lever you can pull.

The **Pearson correlation coefficient r** ranges from −1 to +1. Positive means the variables rise together, negative means one falls as the other rises, and the magnitude measures how close the points lie to a straight line. Rough guide: |r| below 0.3 is weak, 0.3–0.7 moderate, above 0.7 strong — though context matters.

Three warnings. First, r captures only **linear** relationships; a perfect U-shape can have r = 0. Second, r is very sensitive to **outliers** — one extreme point can create or destroy a correlation. Third, r is unit-free and says nothing about **size of effect**: a strong correlation can come with a tiny slope.

**Ordinary least squares (OLS)** regression chooses the intercept and slopes that minimise the sum of squared differences between actual and predicted Y. With one driver, the slope equals r × (SD of Y ÷ SD of X). With several drivers (**multiple regression**), each coefficient measures the effect of that driver **holding the others constant** — the main reason managers use it.
points: **Coefficient (b)**: change in Y for a one-unit change in X, others held constant
**Standard error**: how precisely b is estimated
**t-statistic** = b ÷ SE; roughly, |t| > 2 means significant at 5% with a decent sample
**p-value**: probability of seeing a t this extreme if the true b were zero
**R²**: share of Y's variance the model explains; adjusted R² penalises adding useless variables
**Residuals**: actual − predicted; plot them to check for curves and outliers

notes.h: Worked interpretation of a regression output
notes.p:
**Illustrative data.** A beverage brand regresses monthly sales across 60 city-months on advertising spend and shelf price.

Sales (₹ lakh) = 120 + 3.2 × Ad (₹ lakh) − 8.5 × Price (₹)
Ad: coefficient 3.2, SE 0.8, t = 4.0, p < 0.001
Price: coefficient −8.5, SE 5.0, t = −1.7, p ≈ 0.09
R² = 0.72

**Reading it.** Holding price fixed, each extra ₹1 lakh of advertising is associated with about ₹3.2 lakh of extra sales, and that estimate is precise (t = 4). A rough 95% interval is 3.2 ± 2 × 0.8 = 1.6 to 4.8 — even the low end suggests ads pay back in revenue, though you must still check gross margin: at a 30% margin, ₹3.2 lakh of sales yields only about ₹0.96 lakh of gross profit per ₹1 lakh of ads, which does **not** pay back. Every ₹1 rise in price is associated with ₹8.5 lakh lower sales, but the estimate is noisy (p ≈ 0.09), so we can't confidently distinguish it from zero at the 5% level. The model explains 72% of the month-to-month variation.

**Prediction.** With ads of ₹10 lakh and price ₹6: 120 + 32 − 51 = ₹101 lakh. Do not predict at ads of ₹200 lakh if the data only ranged up to ₹20 lakh — that is **extrapolation**, and diminishing returns almost certainly kick in.

Advertising may correlate with sales because firms advertise more in festive months when sales would rise anyway — the classic **confounder** (here, seasonality). Including a festive-season variable helps, but you can never control for everything you didn't measure; this is **omitted variable bias**.

The reliable route is **randomisation**. If ad spend is randomly varied across comparable cities, confounders are balanced on average and the difference in sales is causal. When randomisation is impossible, economists use **natural experiments** (a policy that hit some regions but not others), **difference-in-differences** and **instrumental variables**. David Card, Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens shared the 2021 economics Nobel for showing how to draw causal conclusions from such data.

**Simpson's paradox** is the sharpest warning. In the 1973 UC Berkeley admissions data, men had a higher aggregate admission rate, yet within most departments women were admitted at similar or higher rates; women had disproportionately applied to more competitive departments. Aggregating hid the real pattern.

points: Treating a regression coefficient as causal without an experiment or a credible design
Reading a high R² as 'the model is right' — a model can have high R² and be causally meaningless, or low R² and still estimate a useful effect precisely
Ignoring **multicollinearity**: if TV and digital spend always move together, the model can't separate their effects and SEs balloon
**Extrapolating** beyond the range of the data
**Data dredging**: running dozens of regressions and reporting the one that 'worked'
Forgetting that 'not significant' may just mean too little data

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams hand you a regression table and ask you to interpret coefficients, t-stats, p-values and R², and to make a prediction. Consulting and analytics interviews probe causation: "Customers who use our app weekly churn less — should we push notifications to make everyone use it weekly?" (Answer: maybe engaged customers both use the app and stay; test it.) On the job, marketing-mix models, pricing models and HR attrition models are all regressions; your value lies in asking what is confounding the result.

points: r ∈ [−1, 1] measures linear association; sensitive to outliers; blind to curves
OLS minimises squared errors; each coefficient = effect holding other variables constant
t = b ÷ SE; |t| > ~2 ≈ significant at 5%; R² = share of variance explained
Prediction: plug in values; never extrapolate far beyond the data
Correlation ≠ causation: confounders, reverse causality, selection
Randomised experiments establish causation; natural experiments and diff-in-diff help when you can't randomise
Simpson's paradox: always check within segments

chapters.title: Decision analysis: expected value, decision trees & the value of information

cards.title: Decisions under uncertainty
cards.body: A good decision is not the same as a good outcome. You can choose wisely and get unlucky. **Decision analysis** separates the two: lay out options, possible outcomes, their probabilities and payoffs, then choose the option with the best risk-adjusted value. Judge decisions by the process, not the result.

cards.title: Expected value (EV)
cards.body: **EV = Σ (probability × payoff)** across all outcomes. A launch with 40% chance of ₹50 cr profit and 60% chance of ₹20 cr loss: EV = 0.4 × 50 + 0.6 × (−20) = 20 − 12 = **₹8 cr**. EV is the average result if you could repeat the bet many times.

cards.title: Decision trees
cards.body: Draw **squares** for decisions you control and **circles** for chance events, with probabilities on each branch and payoffs at the ends. Then **roll back** from right to left: at a circle, take the EV; at a square, pick the best branch. The tree forces you to name every assumption.

cards.title: Expected value of perfect information
cards.body: **EVPI = EV with perfect information − EV without it.** With a crystal ball you'd launch only when demand is high: 0.4 × 50 + 0.6 × 0 = ₹20 cr. Without it, best EV = ₹8 cr. EVPI = **₹12 cr** — the ceiling on what any market research could be worth.

cards.title: Is a test market worth it?
cards.body: A test costs money and is imperfect: it says 'positive' 80% of the time when demand is high, 25% when low. Rolling back the tree: launch only after a positive test, giving EV ≈ **₹13 cr** before the test's cost. Value of the sample information = 13 − 8 = **₹5 cr**. Pay up to ₹5 cr for the test, not more.

cards.title: Risk attitude
cards.body: EV assumes you're **risk-neutral**. A start-up with ₹25 cr in the bank should not take a 60% chance of losing ₹20 cr just because EV is positive. **Utility** and the **certainty equivalent** (the sure amount you'd accept instead of the gamble) capture risk aversion. Big diversified firms can act closer to risk-neutral.

cards.title: Sensitivity analysis
cards.body: Ask: at what probability does the decision flip? Launch EV = 50p − 20(1 − p) = 70p − 20, which is positive when p > **2/7 ≈ 29%**. If your team is confident demand-success is well above 29%, launch; if it's close, invest in information. This 'break-even probability' is often more useful than the EV itself.

cards.q: An option has a 30% chance of ₹100 profit and a 70% chance of ₹20 loss. Its expected value is:
EV of best action without information is ₹8 cr; EV with perfect information is ₹20 cr. A consultant offers a perfect forecast for ₹15 cr. You should:
options: Accept: perfect forecasts are always worth buying
Reject: it costs more than the ₹12 cr value of perfect information
cards.explain: EVPI = 20 − 8 = ₹12 cr. No information, even perfect, is worth paying more than that.

cards.q: In a decision tree, when rolling back, at a chance node you should:
options: Take the probability-weighted average of the branches
cards.explain: Chance nodes are outside your control, so you take the expected value. You only choose (max) at decision nodes.

notes.p:
Managers are paid to decide before the facts are in. Should Tata Motors invest in a new EV platform? Should a pharma company fund Phase III trials? Should a D2C brand open offline stores? **Decision analysis** is a set of tools — expected value, decision trees, value of information, sensitivity analysis — that make such choices explicit and comparable.

The first principle, emphasised by Annie Duke in *Thinking in Bets* and by decision scientists for decades: separate the **quality of a decision** from the **quality of the outcome**. A sensible bet that loses was still sensible. Organisations that punish every bad outcome teach managers to avoid all risk, including the good kind.

**Expected value** is the probability-weighted average payoff: EV = Σ pᵢ × xᵢ. It is the right criterion when the bet is small relative to your resources and you face many similar bets — an insurer pricing thousands of policies, a VC with a portfolio of 30 start-ups, a bank making lakhs of loans.

It is the wrong criterion, on its own, when one bad outcome could be ruinous. Daniel Bernoulli noticed in the 18th century that people value money with diminishing marginal **utility**: losing ₹1 crore hurts more than gaining ₹1 crore helps. The **certainty equivalent** is the guaranteed amount that feels as good as a gamble; for a risk-averse decision-maker it is below the EV, and the gap is the **risk premium**. Kahneman and Tversky's **prospect theory** adds that people feel losses roughly twice as strongly as equal gains and evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point — useful for predicting how managers and customers actually behave.

notes.h: Building and rolling back a decision tree
notes.p: A **decision tree** maps a sequential decision.
points: **Squares** = decision nodes (you choose)
**Circles** = chance nodes (nature chooses, with probabilities summing to 1)
**Triangles or end values** = payoffs, net of all costs on that path
**Roll back** from right to left: at circles compute EV; at squares keep the best branch and prune the rest
The final answer is a **strategy**: what to do first and how to respond to each piece of news

notes.h: Worked example: launch, test, or walk away
notes.p:
**Illustrative numbers.** A consumer company is considering a national launch of a new ready-to-eat range.
If demand is high (prior probability 0.4): profit ₹50 cr. If low (0.6): loss ₹20 cr. Not launching: ₹0.

**Step 1 — No information.** EV(launch) = 0.4 × 50 + 0.6 × (−20) = 20 − 12 = ₹8 cr. EV(don't) = 0. Best: launch, EV ₹8 cr.

**Step 2 — Perfect information.** If you knew demand in advance, you'd launch only when it's high: 0.4 × 50 + 0.6 × 0 = ₹20 cr. **EVPI = 20 − 8 = ₹12 cr.**

**Step 3 — A real test market.** It says 'positive' with probability 0.8 if demand is high and 0.25 if low.
P(high and positive) = 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.32; P(low and positive) = 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.15; P(positive) = 0.47.
P(high and negative) = 0.08; P(low and negative) = 0.45; P(negative) = 0.53.
After a positive test: EV(launch) = (0.32 × 50 − 0.15 × 20) ÷ 0.47 = 13 ÷ 0.47 ≈ ₹27.7 cr → launch.
After a negative test: EV(launch) = (0.08 × 50 − 0.45 × 20) ÷ 0.53 = −5 ÷ 0.53 ≈ −₹9.4 cr → don't launch (₹0).
EV with test = 0.47 × 27.7 + 0.53 × 0 ≈ ₹13 cr.
**Expected value of sample information (EVSI) = 13 − 8 = ₹5 cr.**

**Decision.** If the test costs less than ₹5 cr, run it, then launch only on a positive result. Notice that the test's value comes entirely from letting you **avoid** the bad launch — information is valuable only if it could change what you do.

Probabilities in business are judgement calls, so test how robust the answer is. Here, EV(launch) = 50p − 20(1 − p) = 70p − 20, positive when p > 2/7 ≈ 0.29. If the team's estimate is 0.4, the decision is moderately robust; if they're really unsure whether it's 0.25 or 0.45, information is worth a lot. A **tornado chart** shows which inputs swing the result most and therefore deserve research money.

Trees also reveal **real options**: the right to expand, delay, stage or abandon. Launching in two states first, with the option to go national, is a tree with a learning step built in. Staged investment is why venture capital is paid in rounds and why drug development has trial phases.

points: Judging past decisions only by outcomes (**resulting**)
Using EV for bet-the-company decisions and ignoring ruin risk
Plucking probabilities from thin air and then treating the EV as precise — always run sensitivity
Double-counting sunk costs: money already spent should not enter the tree
Paying for research that cannot change the decision — its value is zero
**Overconfidence**: managers' 90% ranges contain the truth far less than 90% of the time; widen them

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams love the full tree with EVPI and EVSI — practise rolling back cleanly. Consulting cases often reduce to an EV calculation ("should the client bid for this contract?"), and interviewers reward candidates who also ask about downside risk. In jobs — pharma portfolio management, oil and gas exploration, venture capital, product launches, M&A — decision trees and scenario EVs are standard, and the break-even probability is often the number that ends the debate in the room.

points: Good decision ≠ good outcome; judge the process
EV = Σ p × payoff; right for repeated or small bets
Tree: squares = decide (take max), circles = chance (take EV); roll back right to left
EVPI = EV with perfect info − EV without; the ceiling on research spend
EVSI = value of an imperfect test; information is worth something only if it can change the decision
Risk aversion: certainty equivalent < EV; avoid ruin even with positive EV
Find the break-even probability; run sensitivity; value staged options

chapters.title: What marketing really is: needs, value and the marketing mix

cards.title: Marketing is not advertising
cards.body: Most people think marketing means ads. Philip Kotler, whose textbook *Marketing Management* has trained generations of MBAs, defines it far more broadly: identifying and meeting human and social needs **profitably**. Ads are the last, visible 10%. The real work is deciding whom to serve, what to offer and how to capture value.

cards.title: Needs, wants, demands
cards.body: A **need** is a basic human requirement (hunger). A **want** is a need shaped by culture and individuals (a masala dosa, or a burger). **Demand** is a want backed by ability to pay. Marketers don't create needs; they shape wants and convert them into demand by making offers available and affordable.

cards.title: Customer value
cards.body: Customers buy **perceived value**: total benefits (functional, emotional, social) minus total costs (price, time, effort, risk). Ted Levitt's line, as it's usually paraphrased: people don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole. Sell the hole.

cards.title: Marketing myopia
cards.body: In his 1960 *HBR* article 'Marketing Myopia', Theodore Levitt argued that US railroads declined because they saw themselves in the railroad business, not the **transportation** business. Define your market by the customer need, not your product — or a competitor from outside your 'industry' will take it.

cards.title: The 4Ps (and 7Ps)
cards.body: E. Jerome McCarthy's **4Ps**: **Product**, **Price**, **Place** (distribution), **Promotion**. Services add three (Booms & Bitner): **People**, **Process**, **Physical evidence**. The customer-side mirror (Lauterborn's 4Cs): customer solution, cost, convenience, communication. The Ps must fit each other and the target segment.

cards.title: Nirma vs HUL
cards.body: In 1969 Karsanbhai Patel launched Nirma, a cheap detergent powder sold to lower-income households that HUL's premium Surf largely ignored. Nirma grew rapidly. HUL responded with **Wheel**, a low-priced brand with a leaner cost structure. Lesson: an underserved segment, a coherent mix (low price, wide reach, simple product) and a fit cost model.

cards.title: Interview framing
cards.body: When asked 'how would you market X?', don't start with ads. Go in order: **customer and need → segment and target → positioning → 4Ps → metrics**. Interviewers reward structure that begins with the customer.

cards.q: Levitt's 'marketing myopia' warns firms against:
options: Defining their business by product instead of customer need
Charging prices that are too low
cards.explain: Levitt's railroads example: they thought they were in railroads, not transportation, and lost customers to cars, trucks and planes.

cards.q: Which of these is a 'want' rather than a 'need'?
cards.explain: Thirst is a need; a specific branded drink is a want shaped by culture and preference.

cards.q: The three extra Ps used for services are:
cards.explain: Booms and Bitner added People, Process and Physical evidence because services are intangible and produced with the customer present.

notes.p:
**Marketing** is the discipline of understanding what customers need and organising the whole business to deliver it profitably. Philip Kotler's short definition — meeting needs profitably — captures both halves: the customer side (needs, value) and the business side (profit). Peter Drucker went further in *Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices*: the aim of marketing is to know the customer so well that the product fits and sells itself, making selling almost superfluous.

That is why marketing sits at the centre of strategy. Decisions about which customers to serve, what to build, what to charge and where to sell are marketing decisions, even when made by the CEO or the product team. Advertising is only the most visible output.

Kotler distinguishes **needs** (universal: food, belonging, status), **wants** (culturally shaped ways to satisfy needs) and **demand** (wants backed by purchasing power). An Indian family's need for transport becomes a want for a scooter or a small car, and becomes demand when EMIs make it affordable — which is why auto finance is as much a marketing tool as advertising is.

Customers choose the offer with the highest **perceived value**: benefits minus costs, as the customer sees them. Benefits include function (it cleans), emotion (it feels premium), and social signal (people see me using it). Costs include price but also search time, effort, switching hassle and risk. You can raise value by adding benefits *or* cutting non-price costs — Swiggy and Zomato mostly sold time and effort savings, not cheaper food.
points: **Customer satisfaction** = performance vs expectations; over-promising destroys it
**Customer lifetime value** matters more than one transaction (see the metrics chapter)
**Exchange** is the core act: both sides must feel better off

notes.h: Five orientations a company can take
notes.p: Kotler describes how companies have historically approached markets.
points: **Production concept**: customers want cheap, available products — focus on efficiency (early Ford Model T)
**Product concept**: customers want the best quality — risk: building over-engineered products nobody asked for
**Selling concept**: customers must be pushed to buy — common for unsought goods like insurance
**Marketing concept**: find needs first, then build the right product for chosen customers
**Holistic/societal marketing**: also account for long-run consumer and social welfare, employees, partners and society

notes.p:
Theodore Levitt's 1960 *Harvard Business Review* article argued that growth industries stall because managers define their business too narrowly. American railroads saw themselves as running trains, not moving people and goods, and so ceded the market to cars, trucks and aircraft. Hollywood, he argued, nearly made the same mistake with television.

Indian examples are easy to find. Camera-film makers lost to digital and then to smartphones. SMS revenue for telecom operators was eaten by WhatsApp. A business defined by the customer need — capturing memories, staying in touch — would have seen the threat earlier. The practical test: write your market definition as a customer need in one line. If a start-up could serve that need without being in your 'industry', it's a competitor.
E. Jerome McCarthy popularised the **4Ps** around 1960. They are the levers a marketer controls.
points: **Product**: features, quality, design, brand, packaging, pack sizes, warranty
**Price**: list price, discounts, credit terms, price architecture across variants
**Place**: channels, coverage, logistics, availability at the moment of need
**Promotion**: advertising, sales promotion, PR, personal selling, digital and social
**People, Process, Physical evidence** (Booms & Bitner, 1981) for services: staff behaviour, the service journey, and tangible cues like store design or an app's interface
Robert Lauterborn's **4Cs** (1990) reframes them from the customer's side: customer solution, cost to the customer, convenience, communication

notes.h: Case: Nirma, HUL and a coherent mix
notes.p:
In 1969 Karsanbhai Patel began selling a yellow detergent powder in Gujarat, reportedly door-to-door at first, at a fraction of the price of HUL's Surf. **Nirma** targeted lower- and middle-income households that premium brands underserved. Its mix fitted that customer: a basic but adequate product, a very low price, a lean cost structure and wide distribution through small shops, backed by mass advertising with a memorable jingle. It grew into one of India's largest detergent brands.

HUL's response, launching **Wheel** as a low-cost brand with a separate, leaner supply model, became a widely taught example of competing at the bottom of the pyramid (C.K. Prahalad discusses it in *The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid*). The lessons: big markets exist below the premium tier; the whole mix (including the cost model) must fit the segment; and incumbents often respond with a fighter brand rather than cutting the price of their flagship.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p:
Common mistakes: starting with the product instead of the customer; treating marketing as a communications department; choosing Ps that contradict each other (a premium price with discount-store distribution); and copying a competitor's mix without its cost structure.

In interviews — especially for FMCG roles at HUL, P&G, ITC, Nestlé or Marico, and in consulting — you'll be asked to launch or revive a product. Start with the customer and need, define the segment, state a positioning, walk through the 4Ps, and close with two or three metrics. In exams, expect definitions (needs/wants/demands, the orientations), Levitt's myopia, and a short case applying the mix.

points: Marketing = meeting needs profitably (Kotler); ads are a small, visible part
Needs → wants → demand (want + ability to pay)
Customers choose highest perceived value: benefits minus all costs, not just price
Levitt's 'Marketing Myopia' (1960): define the business by customer need
4Ps (McCarthy) + People, Process, Physical evidence (Booms & Bitner); 4Cs from the customer's view
The mix must be internally consistent and fit the target segment
Nirma vs Wheel: underserved segments and fighter brands

chapters.title: Segmentation, targeting & positioning (STP)

cards.title: You can't serve everyone
cards.body: **STP** is the heart of marketing strategy. **Segment**: split the market into groups with similar needs. **Target**: choose which groups to serve. **Position**: decide what you want to mean in those customers' minds versus alternatives. Skip it and you end up with a product that is a bit of everything and first choice for no one.

cards.title: Ways to segment
cards.body: **Demographic**: age, income, family size. **Geographic**: metro vs tier-2 vs rural, north vs south. **Psychographic**: lifestyle, values, personality. **Behavioural**: usage rate, occasion, benefit sought, loyalty. Behavioural and needs-based segments usually predict buying best; demographics are easier to reach.

cards.title: A good segment is…
cards.body: Kotler's tests: **Measurable** (can you size it?), **Substantial** (big and profitable enough?), **Accessible** (can you reach it via media and channels?), **Differentiable** (does it respond differently to the mix?), **Actionable** (can you build a programme for it?). Fail any one and it's not a usable segment.

cards.title: Targeting choices
cards.body: **Undifferentiated**: one offer for all (rare now). **Differentiated**: different offers for different segments — Maruti Suzuki runs Arena and the more premium **Nexa** showrooms. **Concentrated**: dominate one niche. **Micro/1:1**: personalised offers, as in app-based recommendations.

cards.title: Titan's portfolio
cards.body: Titan Company serves different segments with distinct brands: **Sonata** for value-conscious watch buyers, **Titan** for the mainstream-to-premium watch buyer, **Fastrack** for youth, and **Tanishq** for jewellery, built on trust in purity. Separate brands let each one hold a clear position without confusing the others.

cards.title: Positioning statement
cards.body: For **[target]** who **[need]**, **[brand]** is the **[frame of reference]** that **[point of difference]** because **[reason to believe]**. Example: For busy urban parents who want healthy snacks fast, Brand X is the breakfast mix that's ready in 3 minutes because it uses pre-cooked millets.

cards.title: Own one word
cards.body: Al Ries and Jack Trout (*Positioning*, 1981) argued that positioning happens in the customer's mind, and the strongest brands own a single idea: Volvo — safety; Fevicol — an unbreakable bond. Use a **perceptual map** (two axes customers care about) to find an empty, valuable spot.

cards.q: A bank offers one product to frequent travellers and another to students. This is:
cards.explain: Serving several segments with different offers is differentiated targeting.

cards.q: Segmenting phone buyers by 'gamers', 'camera lovers' and 'battery-anxious users' is mainly:
cards.explain: Grouping by the benefit sought from the product is behavioural/benefit segmentation.

cards.q: Which of Kotler's segment criteria fails if you cannot find any media or channel that reaches the group?
cards.explain: Accessible means you can reach and serve the segment through channels and media.

notes.p:
No product can be everything to everyone. A shampoo that's gentle, cheap, salon-grade and anti-dandruff will be the best at none of them. **STP** — segmentation, targeting, positioning — is how marketers decide whom to serve and what to stand for. It comes before the 4Ps, because the right price, product and channel depend entirely on who the customer is.

The logic is economic. Customers differ in what they value and what they'll pay. Treating them as one mass leaves money on the table with some and loses others entirely. Grouping them into **segments** with similar needs lets you design an offer that wins decisively with the groups you choose.

notes.h: Segmentation: how to split a market
notes.p: There are four classic bases, usually combined.
points: **Demographic**: age, gender, income, occupation, life stage — easy to measure and buy media against
**Geographic**: region, city tier, urban/rural, climate — crucial in India where language, diet and income vary by state
**Psychographic**: values, lifestyle, personality — the 'health-conscious striver' vs the 'traditional family-first' buyer
**Behavioural**: usage occasion, benefits sought, usage rate (heavy vs light users), loyalty, readiness to buy
For B2B: industry, company size, buying process, purchase criteria

notes.p:
Kotler's criteria screen whether a segment is usable: **measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable, actionable**. Then rank the survivors by **attractiveness** (size, growth, margins, competitive intensity) and **fit** (does your company have the capabilities and brand permission to win there?).

**Illustrative sizing.** A packaged-foods company considers 'working professionals in the top 8 metros who skip breakfast'. Suppose 1.2 crore working professionals in those cities, 30% skip breakfast at least three days a week → 36 lakh people. If 10% can be won at ₹600 a month of spend, that's 3.6 lakh × ₹600 × 12 = ₹259 crore a year in revenue potential. Rough, but enough to compare against other segments.

Targeting strategies range from **undifferentiated** (one offer for all), to **differentiated** (separate offers per segment), **concentrated** (dominate a niche — many D2C brands start here), and **micro-marketing** (local or individual offers, now cheap thanks to data and apps).

notes.h: Positioning: owning a place in the mind
notes.p:
Al Ries and Jack Trout's *Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind* (1981) made the key point: positioning is not what you do to a product, it's what you do to the prospect's mind. Customers file brands under simple ideas, and the first or clearest brand to own an idea is hard to dislodge.

A positioning has three parts: a **frame of reference** (what category are we compared with?), **points of parity** (what we must match to be considered), and **points of difference** (why choose us). Kevin Lane Keller developed this language in his brand-management work. A **perceptual map** plots brands on two dimensions customers care about — say, price and 'natural vs clinical' for skincare — to reveal crowded and empty spaces.
points: Volvo has long been associated with **safety**
Fevicol built its 'unbreakable bond' idea with humorous ads for decades
Dettol (Reckitt) stands for germ protection. Within one company, HUL keeps positions distinct: Lifebuoy for health and hygiene, Lux for beauty

notes.p:
**Maruti Suzuki** sells mass models through its Arena network and launched the separate **Nexa** retail channel in 2015 for more premium models, giving a different experience to a different segment without diluting either.

**Titan Company** runs a portfolio: Sonata for value, Titan for the core watch buyer, Fastrack for youth, Tanishq for jewellery. Tanishq's positioning — trust and certified purity in a market where buyers worried about being cheated on gold — is a textbook point of difference built on a reason to believe.

**Bajaj Auto** repositioned around performance motorcycles with the Pulsar in 2001, targeting young men who wanted more power and style than commuter bikes offered. Rather than compete head-on with Hero in the mass commuter segment, it found a segment where it could lead.

points: **Segmenting by what's easy, not what matters**: age bands that don't predict behaviour
**Targeting everyone** to maximise reach, ending with a muddled position
**Positioning on a claim you can't support** — no reason to believe
**Constantly changing positioning** with every new campaign or brand manager
**Ignoring points of parity**: a unique benefit doesn't help if you fail a basic requirement (taste, safety)
**Brand overlap** in a portfolio, where your own brands cannibalise each other

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Every marketing case starts with STP. Interviewers want you to propose two or three meaningful segments, pick one with a reason (size × fit), and write a sharp positioning statement. Exams test segmentation bases, Kotler's criteria, targeting strategies and perceptual maps. On the job, brand managers revisit positioning yearly in brand plans, and product managers do the same thing under the name 'user personas' and 'ideal customer profile'.

points: STP comes before the 4Ps
Bases: demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioural (benefit, occasion, usage)
Kotler's tests: measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable, actionable
Target by attractiveness × fit; undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated, micro
Positioning = frame of reference + points of parity + points of difference + reason to believe
Ries & Trout: positioning lives in the customer's mind; own one idea
Indian cases: Maruti Arena/Nexa, Titan's brand portfolio, Bajaj Pulsar

chapters.title: Consumer behaviour & the buying journey

cards.title: Why people buy
cards.body: Customers rarely buy for the reasons they state. They buy to solve a problem, express identity, reduce risk or fit in. **Consumer behaviour** studies the cultural, social, personal and psychological forces behind choice — and the predictable shortcuts the brain uses to decide quickly.

cards.title: The five-stage process
cards.body: The classic model: **need recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase → post-purchase behaviour**. For a car, every stage is long and deliberate. For a biscuit, the whole thing collapses into a two-second glance at a shelf. Marketing tasks differ at each stage.

cards.title: High vs low involvement
cards.body: **High involvement** (car, phone, insurance, education): expensive, risky, infrequent — buyers research, compare and seek reassurance. **Low involvement** (salt, soap, tea): cheap, habitual — buyers rely on familiarity, availability and packaging. Most FMCG battles are won on **mental and physical availability**, not persuasion.

cards.title: The journey is a loop
cards.body: McKinsey's consumer decision journey (2009) replaced the narrowing funnel with a loop: an initial set of brands, **active evaluation** where brands can be added or dropped, the moment of purchase, then the post-purchase experience that either creates a **loyalty loop** or sends the customer back to shopping.

cards.title: Fix the leakiest stage
cards.body: Illustrative app funnel: 10 lakh ad impressions → 2% click = 20,000 visits → 25% add to cart = 5,000 → 40% complete checkout = **2,000 orders**. Raising checkout completion from 40% to 50% gives 2,500 orders (+25%) — often cheaper than buying 25% more traffic.

cards.title: Mental shortcuts
cards.body: Behavioural science (Kahneman, Tversky, Thaler) shows predictable biases: **loss aversion** (losses loom larger than gains), **anchoring** (the first number sets expectations), **social proof** (bestseller tags, ratings), **defaults** (pre-ticked options stick), **scarcity** ('only 2 left'). Used honestly, they reduce friction; abused, they become dark patterns.

cards.title: Jobs to be done
cards.body: Clayton Christensen asked: what **job** is the customer hiring the product to do? His milkshake story found many morning buyers 'hired' a thick milkshake to make a long, boring commute bearable and keep them full till lunch. Compete with whatever else does that job — not only other milkshakes.

cards.q: A customer feels anxious after buying an expensive laptop and keeps reading reviews to reassure herself. This is:
cards.explain: Post-purchase doubt is cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger's concept). Marketers reduce it with reassurance, warranties and onboarding.

cards.q: For a low-involvement product like table salt, which matters most?
options: Being familiar and easily available at the point of purchase
cards.explain: Low-involvement purchases are habitual; availability and familiarity drive choice.

cards.q: Showing a ₹4,999 'original price' struck out next to a ₹2,999 offer price mainly uses:
cards.explain: The higher reference price anchors the buyer's sense of value, making ₹2,999 feel like a bargain.

notes.p:
Marketing strategy depends on a theory of why customers buy. **Consumer behaviour** borrows from psychology, sociology and economics to explain how people notice needs, search, choose, buy and feel afterwards.
