The key insight of the last fifty years is that people are not the cold calculators of economics textbooks: they use shortcuts, follow others, fear losses and are shaped by culture.

For a manager, the practical questions are: where in the journey are we losing customers, what drives choice in our category, and what can we change — product, message, price, channel — to tilt the decision?
Kotler groups the influences into four layers.
points: **Cultural**: culture, sub-culture, social class — vegetarianism, festivals like Diwali and Onam, and regional tastes shape demand in India
**Social**: family, reference groups, opinion leaders and influencers — in India, family often co-decides big purchases like a car or a house
**Personal**: age, life stage, occupation, income, lifestyle, personality
**Psychological**: motivation (Maslow's hierarchy, from physiological needs to self-actualisation), perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes

notes.p:
The five-stage model — **need recognition, information search, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase** — is a useful map, but involvement changes its shape. In high-involvement purchases (a two-wheeler, a home loan, an MBA), buyers research extensively, build a **consideration set** of a few brands, compare on attributes and seek reassurance from family and online reviews. After buying, many feel **cognitive dissonance** — Leon Festinger's term for the discomfort of holding conflicting thoughts ("did I overpay?"). Good marketers reduce it with onboarding, warranties and follow-up.

In low-involvement purchases, there is little search: buyers pick familiar brands they can see. Byron Sharp's *How Brands Grow* (2010) argues, from large datasets, that brands grow mainly by increasing **mental availability** (being easily thought of in buying situations) and **physical availability** (being easy to find and buy), and by reaching light buyers — not by deepening loyalty among existing ones.

The traditional **AIDA** funnel (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) suggested customers narrow steadily from many brands to one. McKinsey's 2009 'consumer decision journey' research found something different: buyers start with a small initial set, then **add** brands during active evaluation (through search, reviews, friends), and after buying either enter a **loyalty loop** or re-open the journey next time. Post-purchase experience therefore feeds directly into the next sale and into others' reviews.

**Worked funnel example (illustrative).**
Impressions: 10,00,000
Click-through 2% → 20,000 visits
Add-to-cart 25% → 5,000 carts
Checkout completion 40% → 2,000 orders
Overall conversion from visit = 2,000 ÷ 20,000 = 10%.
If the team removes friction at payment (saved cards, UPI intent, fewer form fields) and completion rises to 50%, orders rise to 2,500 — the same gain as a 25% bigger ad budget, at a fraction of the cost. The lesson: measure every stage and fix the leakiest one first.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's work on heuristics and **prospect theory**, and Richard Thaler's work on nudges, explain much buying behaviour.
points: **Loss aversion**: 'Don't lose your ₹500 cashback' beats 'Earn ₹500 cashback'
**Anchoring**: MRP, struck-through prices and the first price seen set the reference
**Decoy effect**: a deliberately unattractive option makes another look better (see pricing)
**Defaults**: auto-renewal and pre-selected add-ons stick because changing takes effort
**Social proof**: ratings, 'bestseller' badges, '2,000 people bought this today'
**Scarcity and urgency**: limited stock or time windows
**Mental accounting**: people treat money differently by source and purpose — festival bonuses get spent more freely

notes.h: Jobs to be done and real cases
notes.p:
Clayton Christensen's **jobs-to-be-done** lens asks what progress the customer is trying to make. In his often-told milkshake study, a fast-food chain found many milkshakes were bought early in the morning by commuters who wanted something filling, slow to consume and one-handed for a long drive. The competition wasn't other milkshakes; it was bananas, bagels and boredom.

Indian examples: **Reliance Jio**'s 2016 launch with free voice and very cheap data removed the cost barrier that had kept many Indians from heavy mobile internet use, rapidly changing behaviour across the market. **UPI** succeeded partly because paying became simpler than handling cash — friction removal, not persuasion. Quick-commerce apps sell the job 'I forgot something and need it now'.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p:
Mistakes: trusting what customers *say* in surveys over what they *do*; assuming all buyers deliberate like engineers; optimising only the top of the funnel; ignoring post-purchase experience; and using **dark patterns** (hidden charges, confusing cancellations), which win a sale and lose trust — regulators, including India's Central Consumer Protection Authority, have issued guidelines against them.

In interviews, you'll be asked to diagnose falling conversion or design a launch; map the journey, find the drop-off, propose a fix and a metric. Exams test the five-stage model, influences, involvement and dissonance. In jobs, consumer insight teams at FMCG firms and growth teams at start-ups do this daily.

points: Influences: cultural, social, personal, psychological
Five stages: need → search → evaluate → buy → post-purchase
High involvement = deliberate; low involvement = habit, availability, familiarity
Journey is a loop (McKinsey 2009): brands can be added during evaluation; post-purchase drives loyalty
Measure every funnel stage; fix the leakiest
Biases: loss aversion, anchoring, defaults, social proof, scarcity, decoys
Jobs to be done: compete with anything that does the customer's job

chapters.title: Product & brand decisions: life cycle, extensions and brand equity

cards.title: Three levels of a product
cards.body: Kotler's layers: **core benefit** (what problem it solves — clean teeth), **actual product** (features, design, brand, packaging), **augmented product** (warranty, delivery, service, app). Competition in mature markets increasingly happens at the augmented level — think of a car's service network.

cards.title: The product life cycle
cards.body: Sales follow an S-curve: **introduction** (slow sales, high cost, educate the market), **growth** (rapid adoption, competitors enter), **maturity** (sales plateau, price competition, fight for share), **decline** (substitutes win; harvest, reposition or exit). Strategy, pricing and spend should shift by stage.

cards.title: Line vs brand extension
cards.body: A **line extension** adds variants under the same brand in the same category (new flavours, pack sizes). A **brand extension** takes the brand into a new category (Amul from butter into ice cream and chocolate). Extensions are cheaper to launch but can dilute the brand or cannibalise existing products.

cards.title: Cannibalisation maths
cards.body: Illustrative: a new small pack sells 1,00,000 units a month at ₹12 contribution = ₹12 lakh. But 30,000 of those buyers would have bought the big pack (₹20 contribution): lost ₹6 lakh. Net gain = **₹6 lakh**, minus ₹2 lakh of extra fixed costs = **₹4 lakh**. Always count what you take from yourself.

cards.title: Brand equity
cards.body: **Brand equity** is the extra value a name adds over an unbranded equivalent — why people pay more for Tata Salt or an iPhone. David Aaker's components: **awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty**. Kevin Lane Keller's pyramid: salience → performance and imagery → judgements and feelings → resonance.

cards.title: Maggi's 2015 crisis
cards.body: In 2015 India's food regulator ordered Maggi noodles off shelves over safety concerns. Nestlé withdrew the product. After court-ordered retests, Maggi returned later that year and, over the following years, won back much of its leadership. Decades of brand equity — trust, habit, nostalgia — gave it a cushion that a new brand would not have had.

cards.title: Extension fit test
cards.body: Before extending, ask: does the brand's core association **transfer** to the new category? Amul's dairy expertise fits ice cream. A brand known for 'tough and industrial' may not fit skincare. Poor fit confuses customers and can weaken the parent brand's meaning.

cards.q: A company adds a mango flavour to its existing juice brand. This is a:
cards.explain: Same brand, same category, new variant = line extension.

cards.q: In which life-cycle stage is price competition and fighting for market share usually most intense?
cards.explain: In maturity, total demand plateaus, so growth must come from rivals — hence price battles, promotions and differentiation.

cards.q: A new SKU earns ₹10 lakh contribution, but ₹7 lakh of that is diverted from the company's existing SKUs. Incremental contribution is:
cards.explain: Incremental = new contribution − cannibalised contribution = 10 − 7 = ₹3 lakh.

notes.p:
The **product** is the centre of the marketing mix: everything else — price, place, promotion — assumes something worth buying. Product decisions include what to make, how many variants to offer, when to launch or retire items, and how to brand them. A **brand** is the set of associations and promises attached to a name; it's what turns a commodity into something people seek out and pay more for.

Good product and brand managers think in portfolios and over time: which products are rising or fading, how they fit together, and how each decision adds to or subtracts from the brand's meaning.

notes.h: Product levels and the product mix
notes.p:
Kotler describes products in layers: the **core benefit** (a phone's core benefit is staying connected), the **actual product** (screen, camera, design, brand name, packaging) and the **augmented product** (warranty, service centres, software updates, EMI options). In crowded categories the core and actual products converge, so firms compete on augmentation — Asian Paints, for example, has expanded beyond paint into home-painting and décor services.

A company's **product mix** has **width** (number of product lines — HUL has soaps, detergents, tea, foods, personal care), **length** (total items), and **depth** (variants per item — sizes, flavours). Indian FMCG makes heavy use of **small packs and sachets**, which allow low-income buyers to purchase in affordable units; shampoo sachets are a classic example of designing the product around the customer's cash flow.
The **product life cycle (PLC)** describes sales of a category or product over time.
points: **Introduction**: low sales, high costs per unit, heavy spending to build awareness and trial; few competitors
**Growth**: rapid adoption, profits rise, competitors enter; invest in distribution and capacity
**Maturity**: sales plateau, intense price and promotional competition, margins squeezed; differentiate, extend lines, find new uses or segments
**Decline**: substitutes win (CRT TVs, landline phones, film cameras); cut costs and harvest, reposition, or exit

Caveat: Nariman Dhalla and Sonia Yuspeh's 1976 *HBR* article 'Forget the Product Life Cycle Concept!' warned that treating the PLC as destiny can become self-fulfilling — cut support for a 'mature' brand and it will decline

notes.h: Line extensions, brand extensions and cannibalisation
notes.p:
**Line extensions** add variants within a category: flavours, sizes, formats. They're cheap to launch and defend shelf space, but too many create complexity and confuse buyers. **Brand extensions** stretch a brand into a new category. **Amul** extended from butter and milk into cheese, ice cream, chocolate and more, all consistent with its dairy identity and its co-operative promise of value. Successful extensions rest on **fit**: the parent brand's associations must make sense in the new category.

**Worked cannibalisation example (illustrative).** A detergent brand launches a ₹10 small pack.
New pack volume: 1,00,000 units a month × ₹12 contribution = ₹12 lakh.
Cannibalised: 30% of buyers would otherwise have bought the 1 kg pack, contributing ₹20 each: 30,000 × ₹20 = ₹6 lakh lost.
Net incremental contribution = 12 − 6 = ₹6 lakh.
Extra fixed costs (packaging line changeover, listing fees): ₹2 lakh.
Incremental profit = **₹4 lakh a month**. Positive — launch. But if cannibalisation were 60%, the loss would be ₹12 lakh and the launch would destroy value. Cannibalisation is not always bad: if a competitor would take those customers anyway, it's better to cannibalise yourself.

**Brand equity** is the differential effect brand knowledge has on customer response. David Aaker (*Managing Brand Equity*, 1991) identified four assets: **brand awareness**, **perceived quality**, **brand associations**, and **brand loyalty**. Kevin Lane Keller's **customer-based brand equity** pyramid builds upward from **salience** (do people think of you?), through **performance** and **imagery**, to **judgements** and **feelings**, and finally **resonance** (loyalty, attachment, community).

Strong equity shows up as price premiums, resilience in crises, easier distribution and cheaper extensions. The 2015 **Maggi** episode is the Indian example: after the regulator's ban and Nestlé's withdrawal of the product, Maggi returned after court-ordered retests and gradually rebuilt its leading position — something hard to imagine for a brand without decades of habit and trust behind it. Globally, **Apple** and **Coca-Cola** sustain premiums on products that rivals can functionally match.

points: **Ignoring cannibalisation** — counting gross rather than incremental sales from a new SKU
**SKU proliferation**: dozens of variants raise supply-chain cost and confuse shelves; prune the tail
**Stretching a brand too far** into categories where its associations don't fit
**Treating the PLC as fate** and starving 'mature' brands of investment
**Short-term promotions** that erode perceived quality and train buyers to wait for discounts
Measuring brand only by awareness, not by preference and price premium

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: FMCG brand-management interviews often ask: 'should we launch this variant?' Strong answers size the opportunity, estimate cannibalisation, check brand fit and propose a test. Exams test product levels, PLC strategies, extension types and Aaker/Keller frameworks. On the job, brand managers own a P&L and spend much of their time on portfolio decisions — which SKUs to launch, which to cut, how to renovate the core.

points: Product levels: core benefit, actual product, augmented product
Mix: width, length, depth; India uses sachets and small packs to match cash flows
PLC: introduction, growth, maturity, decline — shift strategy by stage, but don't treat it as destiny
Line extension = same category; brand extension = new category; fit is everything
Incremental profit = new contribution − cannibalised contribution − extra fixed costs
Aaker: awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty; Keller: salience → resonance
Strong equity = price premium and crisis resilience (Maggi 2015)

chapters.title: Pricing: value-based, cost-plus, psychological and price discrimination

cards.title: Price is the sharpest lever
cards.body: Price is the only P that brings money in; the others cost money. Because many companies earn single-digit operating margins, a small price rise that holds volume can lift profit by a much larger percentage. Yet many firms set prices by habit or by copying rivals.

cards.title: Three ways to set price
cards.body: **Cost-plus**: cost × (1 + markup) — simple, ignores customers. **Competition-based**: price relative to rivals — ignores your differentiation. **Value-based**: price from what the product is worth to the customer — hardest, but captures the most. Costs set the **floor**, customer value the **ceiling**, competition the reference.

cards.title: Economic value to the customer
cards.body: Illustrative: a rival's industrial pump costs ₹10 lakh. Ours saves ₹4 lakh of electricity over its life (in present-value terms). **EVC = ₹14 lakh**. Price anywhere between ₹10 and ₹14 lakh splits the extra value between us and the buyer. Pricing at cost-plus (say ₹9 lakh) would give away the whole advantage.

cards.title: Will a price cut pay?
cards.body: Required volume rise to keep the same contribution after a price cut = **ΔP ÷ (CM − ΔP)**, where CM is the original unit contribution. Price ₹100, variable cost ₹60 → CM ₹40. A ₹10 cut needs 10 ÷ 30 = **33% more volume** just to break even. Price cuts are much more expensive than they look.

cards.title: Price elasticity
cards.body: **Elasticity** = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price. If |e| > 1 demand is **elastic**: a price cut raises revenue. If |e| < 1 it's **inelastic**: a price rise raises revenue. Essentials, addictive goods and products with few substitutes are inelastic; commodities with many substitutes are elastic.

cards.title: Psychological pricing
cards.body: **Charm prices** (₹99, ₹499) are read as 'under 100'. **Anchors** (a high MRP or premium tier shown first) make other prices feel reasonable. The **decoy effect**: Dan Ariely described *The Economist* offering web-only, print-only and print+web at the same price as print-only — the decoy pushed many towards the bundle.

cards.title: Price discrimination
cards.body: Charging different customers different prices for the same thing. **First degree**: each pays their maximum (negotiated B2B deals). **Second**: price varies with quantity or version (bulk packs, economy vs business class). **Third**: by group (student, senior-citizen fares). Railways' Tatkal quotas and dynamic airfares are everyday Indian examples.

cards.q: Price ₹200, variable cost ₹150. By roughly how much must volume rise to keep total contribution unchanged after a 10% price cut?
cards.explain: CM = ₹50. A 10% cut is ₹20, so new CM = ₹30. Required rise = ΔP ÷ (CM − ΔP) = 20 ÷ 30 ≈ 67%.

cards.q: Price rises 10% and quantity falls 5%. Demand is:
cards.explain: Elasticity = −5% ÷ 10% = −0.5, so |e| < 1: inelastic. Revenue = 1.10 × 0.95 = 1.045, a 4.5% rise.

cards.q: Cinema tickets that are cheaper for weekday morning shows than for Saturday night are an example of:
cards.explain: Same product, different prices for customers with different willingness to pay at different times — a form of price discrimination (also called peak-load pricing).

notes.p:
**Price** captures the value a company creates. Every other part of the marketing mix — product, distribution, promotion — creates value or costs money; price is how the firm gets paid. Because operating margins in many industries are thin, pricing has outsized leverage: a 1% price rise with no volume loss on a business with a 10% operating margin raises operating profit by 10%. Hermann Simon of Simon-Kucher, in *Confessions of the Pricing Man*, argues that price is the most powerful and most neglected profit driver.

The central principle: **costs set the floor, customer value sets the ceiling, and competitors' prices shape where in between you can land.**

points: **Cost-plus**: unit cost × (1 + markup). Easy to justify, common in retail and contracting. Weakness: ignores what customers will pay — leaves money on the table for differentiated products and over-prices commodities
**Competition-based**: set price relative to rivals (match, premium, discount). Realistic, but assumes your offer is equivalent and can trigger price wars
**Value-based**: estimate the customer's **economic value** and price to share it. Requires customer research but captures differentiation
**Skimming vs penetration**: launch high and lower over time (new iPhones), or launch low to grab share and scale (Reliance Jio's 2016 entry with free calls and very cheap data)

notes.p:
**Economic value to the customer (EVC)** = price of the next-best alternative + value of your extra benefits (or minus extra costs).

**Illustrative example.** A factory compares two industrial pumps. The competitor's costs ₹10 lakh. Ours costs us ₹6 lakh to make and uses less power, saving ₹4 lakh over its life in present-value terms.
Step 1 — Reference value (the alternative): ₹10 lakh.
Step 2 — Differentiation value: +₹4 lakh.
Step 3 — EVC = ₹14 lakh.
At any price between ₹10 lakh and ₹14 lakh, the buyer is better off choosing us. A price of ₹12 lakh splits the gain: we earn ₹6 lakh margin instead of the ₹3 lakh a cost-plus 50% markup would give (₹9 lakh price), and the customer still gains ₹2 lakh. Cost-plus pricing here would have given our entire efficiency advantage away.

The job of sales then is to **prove** the ₹4 lakh saving to the buyer — value only counts if the customer believes it.

notes.h: Price changes: elasticity and break-even volume
notes.p:
**Price elasticity of demand** e = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price. When |e| > 1, demand is elastic and cutting price raises revenue; when |e| < 1, it's inelastic and raising price raises revenue. But revenue is not profit. The managerial question is about **contribution**.

**Worked example.** Price ₹100, variable cost ₹60, contribution margin (CM) ₹40, current volume 10,000 units → total contribution ₹4,00,000.
Proposal: cut price 10% to ₹90. New CM = ₹30.
Volume needed to keep ₹4,00,000: 4,00,000 ÷ 30 = 13,333 units, a **33% increase**.
General formula: required % volume change = ΔP ÷ (CM − ΔP) = 10 ÷ (40 − 10) = 33%.
Conversely, a 10% price rise (CM becomes ₹50) can lose up to 1 − 40/50 = **20%** of volume before contribution falls.

The asymmetry is striking: price cuts need large volume gains; price rises tolerate sizeable volume losses. And rivals usually match cuts, so the volume gain often never arrives.
Buyers don't process prices like calculators.
points: **Charm pricing**: ₹99 and ₹1,999 are read by their left digit — they feel meaningfully cheaper than ₹100 and ₹2,000
**Anchoring**: showing a premium plan first or a high MRP struck through makes the target price feel reasonable

**Decoy effect**: Dan Ariely (*Predictably Irrational*) described an *Economist* offer where print-only cost the same as print+web; almost nobody chose the decoy, but it pushed buyers from web-only to the bundle
**Good–better–best tiers**: many buyers choose the middle option; design tiers so the middle is the one you want sold
**Price-quality inference**: a too-low price can signal poor quality, especially for gifts, cosmetics and medicine
**Partitioned pricing**: low headline price plus fees; effective short term, but hidden charges anger customers and can attract regulators

notes.p: Charging different prices to different customers for essentially the same product, based on **willingness to pay** rather than cost. Economists (following A.C. Pigou) distinguish three degrees.
points: **First degree**: each customer pays close to their maximum — negotiated enterprise software deals, bargaining in a bazaar
**Second degree**: customers self-select by quantity or version — bulk packs, economy vs business class, freemium vs pro plans
**Third degree**: different prices by observable group — student discounts, senior-citizen concessions, lower prices in rural packs, regional pricing of streaming plans
Conditions: segments with different willingness to pay, a way to separate them, and limited resale (arbitrage)
**Dynamic pricing**: prices change with demand — airline fares, ride-hailing surge, Indian Railways' Tatkal and flexi-fare schemes
Fences must feel fair; perceived unfairness (surge pricing during emergencies) triggers backlash

notes.h: Common mistakes and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p: Common mistakes: pricing purely on cost; matching every competitor's cut; ignoring elasticity differences across segments; discounting so often that the list price loses meaning; and setting price once and never revisiting it. In interviews, pricing cases ask 'how should we price this new product?' — answer with the floor (cost), the ceiling (customer value/EVC), the reference (competitors), then strategy (skim/penetrate) and a test. Exams love the break-even volume calculation and elasticity. On the job, pricing and revenue-management teams in airlines, hotels, SaaS and FMCG run exactly these analyses.

points: Costs = floor, customer value = ceiling, competitors = reference
Value-based pricing via EVC = next-best alternative's price + differentiation value
Required volume rise for a cut = ΔP ÷ (CM − ΔP); cuts need big volume gains
Elasticity = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP; |e| > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic
Skimming vs penetration (Jio 2016)
Psychological: charm prices, anchors, decoys, tiers
Price discrimination: 1st (individual), 2nd (quantity/version), 3rd (group); needs fences and no resale

chapters.title: Distribution & channels: kirana, modern trade, e-commerce and quick commerce

cards.title: Place is often the hardest P
cards.body: A great product is worthless if it's not there when the customer wants it. **Distribution** decides where, how and at what cost your product reaches the buyer. In India, with crores of households spread across cities, towns and villages, distribution reach is often a bigger moat than the product itself.

cards.title: Channel levels
cards.body: **Zero-level**: direct to consumer (D2C websites, company stores). **One-level**: company → retailer → consumer (large modern-trade chains). **Two-level**: company → distributor → retailer. **Three-level**: company → distributor/stockist → wholesaler → small retailer — the classic route to rural and small-town kiranas.

cards.title: General trade: the kirana
cards.body: **General trade (GT)** means India's vast network of small, mostly family-run shops — commonly estimated at over a crore. Kiranas offer proximity, credit to regular customers, home delivery and loose or small-pack items. Most FMCG volume in India still moves through GT, served by distributors and salesmen on fixed 'beat' routes.

cards.title: Modern trade and e-commerce
cards.body: **Modern trade (MT)**: organised chains like DMart, Reliance Retail and More — big formats, central buying, sharper negotiation. **E-commerce**: Amazon and Flipkart (operating as marketplaces under India's FDI rules), JioMart, D2C brand sites. **Quick commerce**: Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart deliver in minutes from **dark stores**.

cards.title: Where does the ₹100 go?
cards.body: Illustrative, ignoring taxes: MRP ₹100. Retailer margin ~₹12 → retailer buys at ₹88. Distributor margin ~₹5 → distributor buys at ₹83. The company realises **₹83**, before paying for trade promotions, freight and salesmen. Channel costs can take a fifth or more of the consumer price.

cards.title: Distribution metrics
cards.body: **Numeric distribution** = % of stores that stock you. **Weighted distribution** = % of category sales that happen in stores that stock you. Present in 40% of stores that do 70% of category sales → ND 40, WD **70**. Also track **out-of-stocks**, **lines per bill** and **cost-to-serve** per channel.

cards.title: Channel conflict
cards.body: When the same pack is cheaper on an app than at the kirana, distributors and retailers protest — sometimes by de-prioritising your brand. Manage it with **channel-specific packs or SKUs**, consistent pricing rules, and clear roles for each channel. Indian distributor associations have publicly pushed back against quick-commerce pricing.

cards.q: A product is stocked in 30% of outlets, but those outlets sell 60% of the category. Its weighted distribution is:
cards.explain: Weighted distribution counts each outlet by its share of category sales: 60.

cards.q: Why do most foreign-owned e-commerce companies in India operate as marketplaces?
options: FDI rules restrict foreign-owned multi-brand e-commerce from holding its own inventory
GST applies only to inventory models
cards.explain: India's FDI policy allows foreign investment in the marketplace model but not the inventory-based model for multi-brand e-commerce.

cards.q: HUL's Project Shakti primarily aimed to:
options: Reach small villages through rural women entrepreneurs
cards.explain: Launched around 2001, Project Shakti recruits rural women as micro-entrepreneurs who sell HUL products in villages that conventional distribution reaches poorly.

notes.p:
**Distribution** — the 'Place' in the 4Ps — is the system that makes a product available where and when customers want to buy it. Channels perform real work: holding inventory, breaking bulk into small quantities, extending credit, transporting, displaying and promoting, collecting cash and returns. Someone has to do these jobs; the only question is who does them most efficiently, and how the margin is shared.

In India distribution is unusually decisive. A product must reach metros, tier-2 towns and lakhs of villages, often through small shops with limited space and cash. Companies like HUL, ITC, Dabur, Nestlé and Coca-Cola have built competitive moats partly from reach: being in more shops, more reliably, than rivals.
Channels are described by their number of intermediary **levels**.
points: **Zero-level (direct)**: brand website, company-owned stores (Apple stores, Titan's World of Titan showrooms) — maximum control and data, high cost
**One-level**: company sells to retailers directly — common with large modern-trade chains and e-commerce
**Two-level**: company → distributor → retailer — the backbone of urban FMCG
**Three-level**: company → super-stockist/stockist → wholesaler → retailer — needed to reach small towns and villages
**Intensive** (everywhere: biscuits, soap), **selective** (some outlets: appliances), **exclusive** (one dealer per area: luxury, premium cars) distribution
**Push** (incentivise the trade to stock and sell) vs **pull** (create consumer demand so the trade must stock you)

notes.p:
**General trade (GT)**: the kirana and paan shop. Commonly estimated at over a crore outlets, they are close to home, give credit to known customers, deliver locally and sell loose and small packs. Company salesmen or distributor salesmen visit on fixed weekly **beats**, take orders and merchandise. Most FMCG sales still flow through GT, though its share is gradually falling in cities.

**Modern trade (MT)**: organised retail chains — DMart (Avenue Supermarts, known for an everyday-low-price, cost-focused model), Reliance Retail, More, Spencer's. Larger assortments, central buying and stronger bargaining power over brands.

**E-commerce**: Amazon, Flipkart, JioMart, Nykaa, plus D2C brand websites. India's FDI policy allows foreign-owned multi-brand e-commerce players to run **marketplaces** connecting sellers and buyers, but not to hold their own inventory for sale. The government-backed **ONDC** network (launched 2022) aims to let any seller be discovered on any buyer app.

**Quick commerce**: Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart deliver groceries and essentials in roughly 10–20 minutes from **dark stores** — small warehouses close to dense neighbourhoods, not open to walk-in shoppers. It has grown fast in large cities and is changing impulse and top-up shopping, with visible tension with traditional distributors.

**Rural reach**: HUL's **Project Shakti**, launched around 2001, recruits rural women as micro-entrepreneurs who sell to their communities — extending reach while creating income.

**Illustrative margin chain (ignoring GST).** A shampoo bottle has an MRP of ₹100.
Retailer margin: about 12% of MRP → retailer's buying price ₹88.
Distributor margin: about ₹5 → distributor's buying price ₹83.
Company realisation: ₹83 per unit.
From this, the company still pays trade schemes (say ₹3), primary freight (₹2) and its own sales force costs.

So nearly a fifth of the consumer price goes to channel partners, and more to serve the channel. Compare channels on **cost-to-serve** (logistics, margins, promotions, returns) and **what each channel does for you** (reach, visibility, data).

**Coverage metrics.** If your product is stocked in 40% of grocery outlets (numeric distribution 40) but those outlets account for 70% of category sales, weighted distribution is 70: you're in the big, busy stores but missing many small ones. Sales teams set targets on both, plus out-of-stock rates and the number of SKUs per outlet.

Channel design starts from the customer: where do target buyers shop, how often, in what pack sizes, and what service do they expect? Then compare channel options on reach, cost, control and fit with positioning — a luxury brand that sells through discount chains erodes its premium.

**Channel conflict** arises when channels compete for the same customer. Typical flashpoints in India: deep online discounts undercutting kirana prices; quick-commerce apps negotiating directly with brands; distributors losing modern-trade accounts to direct supply. Remedies include channel-specific SKUs and pack sizes, clear pricing corridors, territory rules, and treating distributors as partners with fair returns on their capital.

points: Chasing the newest channel while neglecting the one that delivers most volume
Comparing channels on gross margin alone, ignoring cost-to-serve and returns
Launching without enough distribution, so advertising drives people to empty shelves
Uniform pricing across channels that have very different cost structures, causing conflict
Ignoring distributor ROI — under-earning distributors stop investing in your brand
Over-stocking the trade at quarter-end ('channel stuffing'), which inflates sales now and depresses them later

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: FMCG sales and marketing interviews ask how to expand rural reach, whether to launch on quick commerce, or how to resolve a distributor revolt. Expect questions on GT vs MT vs e-commerce economics and on numeric vs weighted distribution. Many FMCG management trainees begin with a sales stint — managing distributors and beats in a territory — precisely because distribution is where the business is won. Exams test channel levels, intensive/selective/exclusive, push vs pull and channel conflict.

points: Channels do real work: inventory, breaking bulk, credit, transport, display
Levels: zero (direct), one, two, three; intensive, selective, exclusive coverage
India: general trade (kirana, crore-plus outlets), modern trade (DMart, Reliance Retail), e-commerce marketplaces, quick commerce via dark stores
FDI rules: foreign multi-brand e-commerce = marketplace, not inventory
Margin chain: channel partners can take a fifth or more of MRP
Numeric vs weighted distribution; track out-of-stocks and cost-to-serve
Manage conflict with channel-specific SKUs and pricing rules

chapters.title: Integrated marketing communication, digital & marketing metrics (CAC, CLV, NPS)

cards.title: One voice, many channels
cards.body: **Integrated marketing communication (IMC)** means every touchpoint — TV, Instagram, packaging, store, sales rep, customer service — tells one consistent story. The tools: **advertising, sales promotion, PR, personal selling, direct and digital marketing, events**. Each plays a role; IMC makes them add up rather than compete.

cards.title: Paid, owned, earned
cards.body: **Paid** media: ads you buy (TV, search, social ads). **Owned**: channels you control (app, website, email, packaging). **Earned**: what others say (reviews, press, word of mouth, shares). Paid buys reach; owned builds relationships cheaply; earned is the most credible and the least controllable.

cards.title: Brand vs performance
cards.body: Performance marketing (search, retargeting) harvests demand that already exists and is easy to measure. Brand building creates future demand and is harder to attribute. Les Binet and Peter Field's analysis of advertising effectiveness data suggested that, on average, a split of roughly **60% brand, 40% activation** works best — over-investing in what's measurable starves growth.

cards.title: Digital funnel maths
cards.body: Illustrative: 10 lakh impressions at ₹150 **CPM** = ₹1.5 lakh. CTR 1% → 10,000 clicks, so **CPC** = ₹15. 3% of clicks convert → 300 customers. **CAC** = 1,50,000 ÷ 300 = **₹500**. Now the only question that matters: is a customer worth more than ₹500?

cards.title: Customer lifetime value
cards.body: With annual margin **m**, retention rate **r** and discount rate **d** (margins received at each year-end): **CLV = m ÷ (1 + d − r)**. m = ₹2,000, r = 80%, d = 10%: CLV = 2,000 ÷ 0.3 ≈ **₹6,667**. Undiscounted, expected life = 1 ÷ (1 − r) = 5 years → ₹10,000.

cards.title: Unit economics rules of thumb
cards.body: **CLV ÷ CAC**: many investors look for about **3 or more**. **CAC payback** = CAC ÷ monthly margin per customer — under a year is often seen as healthy for subscription businesses. A business with CLV below CAC loses more money the faster it grows.

cards.title: NPS and market share
cards.body: **Net Promoter Score** (Fred Reichheld, *HBR* 2003): ask 'How likely are you to recommend us?' (0–10). NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6). **Market share** can be by volume or value. **Relative market share** = your share ÷ largest rival's share.

cards.q: Annual margin ₹3,000, retention 75%, discount rate 15%. CLV using m ÷ (1 + d − r) is:
Survey: 45% give 9–10, 35% give 7–8, 20% give 0–6. NPS is:
cards.explain: NPS = promoters − detractors = 45 − 20 = 25. Passives (7–8) are ignored.

cards.q: A brand spends ₹20 lakh on ads and acquires 4,000 customers. Each customer's CLV is ₹1,200. What's the problem?
options: CAC is ₹500 so CLV/CAC is only 2.4
CAC is ₹50, too low to be real
cards.explain: CAC = 20,00,000 ÷ 4,000 = ₹500. CLV/CAC = 1,200 ÷ 500 = 2.4 — positive, but below the common benchmark of about 3.

notes.p:
Communication is how a company tells its chosen customers what it offers and why they should care. **Integrated marketing communication (IMC)** is the discipline of making every message — an ad, a pack, a push notification, a delivery executive's behaviour — consistent with one positioning, so that each exposure reinforces the others.

The second half of this chapter is about **measurement**. Marketing spends big money, and a manager must be able to say what it bought. The core metrics — CAC, CLV, NPS, market share — turn marketing from an art into an investment decision.
The tools of the communication mix each do a different job.
points: **Advertising** (TV, print, digital, outdoor): reach and memory at scale
**Sales promotion** (discounts, coupons, cashback, contests): short-term trial and switching; overuse trains buyers to wait for deals
**Public relations**: credibility via third parties; vital in crises
**Personal selling**: complex or high-value sales — B2B, insurance, cars
**Direct and digital**: email, WhatsApp, app notifications, search, social, influencers — targeted and measurable
**AIDA** (Attention → Interest → Desire → Action) remains a handy way to check a campaign does each job
**Paid, owned, earned** media framework: buy reach, build owned audiences, earn advocacy

notes.p:
Digital tools made it easy to measure the last click before a purchase, and many firms shifted budgets to search ads and retargeting. Les Binet and Peter Field, analysing the UK's IPA effectiveness database in *The Long and the Short of It* (2013), found that short-term activation produces quick, measurable sales spikes, while emotional brand campaigns build long-term growth and pricing power; across their data, a split of roughly 60% brand and 40% activation tended to perform best on average.

Indian examples of long-running brand platforms include Amul's topical 'Amul girl' advertising, running for decades, and Fevicol's humorous 'strong bond' films. Many D2C brands that relied heavily on performance ads found CAC rising as competition for the same audiences grew — a reminder that harvesting demand is not the same as creating it.

**Illustrative campaign.** A D2C coffee brand runs a social campaign.
Impressions: 10,00,000 at a CPM (cost per thousand impressions) of ₹150 → spend = 1,000 × ₹150 = ₹1,50,000.
Click-through rate (CTR): 1% → 10,000 clicks. Cost per click (CPC) = 1,50,000 ÷ 10,000 = ₹15.
Conversion rate: 3% → 300 first orders.
**CAC** (customer acquisition cost) = 1,50,000 ÷ 300 = ₹500.
If average first-order margin is ₹200, this campaign loses money on the first order. Whether it's a good campaign depends entirely on repeat purchase — that is, on lifetime value. Note: a full CAC should also include agency fees, discounts, and sales salaries — 'blended' vs 'paid' CAC is a frequent source of confusion.

**CLV** is the present value of the margin a customer will generate over their relationship with you. A simple model assumes constant annual margin m, retention probability r each year, discount rate d, and margins received at the end of each year; then CLV = m ÷ (1 + d − r). (Textbooks use slightly different timing conventions — e.g. Gupta and Lehmann's version multiplies by r when the first year isn't guaranteed — so check the assumption.)

**Worked example.** The coffee brand's retained customers generate ₹2,000 margin a year; 80% stay each year; discount rate 10%.
CLV = 2,000 ÷ (1 + 0.10 − 0.80) = 2,000 ÷ 0.30 ≈ ₹6,667.
Check by summing: ₹1,818 (year 1) + ₹1,322 (year 2) + ₹962 (year 3) + … converges to ₹6,667.
Undiscounted: expected lifetime = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5 years → ₹10,000.
CLV ÷ CAC = 6,667 ÷ 500 ≈ 13 — excellent. Raising retention to 85% gives 2,000 ÷ 0.25 = ₹8,000: a five-point retention gain lifts CLV 20%, which is why retention is often the highest-return marketing investment.

**Benchmarks**: CLV/CAC of about 3 or more and a CAC payback period under 12 months are common rules of thumb in subscription and D2C businesses, not laws.

**Net Promoter Score**, introduced by Fred Reichheld in his 2003 *HBR* article 'The One Number You Need to Grow', asks how likely a customer is to recommend you on a 0–10 scale. Promoters score 9–10, passives 7–8, detractors 0–6. NPS = % promoters − % detractors, ranging from −100 to +100. With 50% promoters, 30% passives and 20% detractors, NPS = 30. Its strengths are simplicity and a follow-up 'why?'; its weaknesses are that it's noisy, varies by culture and industry, and is easily gamed when staff are paid on it.

**Market share** = your sales ÷ total market sales, measured by **volume** (units, tonnes) or **value** (₹). A premium brand can have a higher value share than volume share. **Relative market share**, used in the BCG growth-share matrix, = your share ÷ the largest competitor's share: 15% against a leader's 30% gives 0.5. Share should be read alongside **penetration** (% of households buying) and **purchase frequency**.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how it shows up in jobs
notes.p:
Mistakes: counting only paid-media CAC and ignoring discounts and salaries; calculating CLV on revenue instead of margin; assuming retention stays high forever; optimising last-click attribution and cutting brand spend; reading NPS without the verbatim reasons; and quoting share without defining the market.

In interviews — especially for start-ups, growth and D2C roles — expect unit-economics questions: compute CAC, CLV, payback, and say whether a business can scale. In FMCG, you'll discuss media mix, share and penetration. Exams test the communication mix, AIDA, CLV and NPS calculations.

points: IMC: one consistent story across advertising, promotion, PR, selling, digital
Paid, owned, earned media
Binet & Field: balance brand building and activation (~60:40 on average)
CPM, CTR, CPC, conversion → CAC = total acquisition spend ÷ new customers
CLV = m ÷ (1 + d − r) with year-end margins; use margin, not revenue
CLV/CAC ≳ 3 and payback < 12 months are rules of thumb
NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6); relative share = your share ÷ leader's share

chapters.title: Process analysis: capacity, bottlenecks, utilisation & Little's Law

cards.title: Every business is a process
cards.body: A bank turns applications into loans; a cloud kitchen turns orders into meals; a factory turns steel into cars. **Process analysis** maps the steps, measures how fast each can work, and finds what limits the whole. It's the foundation of operations management — and of fixing almost any slow, costly workflow.

cards.title: Capacity and the bottleneck
cards.body: **Capacity** of a step = number of resources ÷ time per unit. The step with the **lowest capacity** is the **bottleneck**, and it sets the capacity of the entire process. **Flow rate** = min(demand, process capacity). **Utilisation** = flow rate ÷ capacity of a step.

cards.title: Cloud kitchen, worked
cards.body: Prep: 2 cooks × 4 min/order → 30 orders/hr. Cooking: 1 station × 3 min → **20/hr**. Packing: 1 person × 1.5 min → 40/hr. Bottleneck = cooking; process capacity = 20/hr. With demand 18/hr, utilisation: prep 60%, cooking **90%**, packing 45%. Adding a packer does nothing; adding a stove does.

cards.title: Little's Law
cards.body: **Inventory = Flow rate × Flow time**, or L = λ × W. It holds for almost any stable process, whatever the variability. Know any two, get the third. A clinic sees 30 patients an hour and has 15 in the building on average → each spends **0.5 hr** there.

cards.title: Little's Law in finance
cards.body: A company holds ₹50 crore of inventory and its cost of goods sold is ₹300 crore a year. Flow time = 50 ÷ 300 = 1/6 year ≈ **2 months**; **inventory turns** = 300 ÷ 50 = **6** a year. Cutting inventory to ₹25 crore at the same throughput halves flow time and frees ₹25 crore of cash.

cards.title: Theory of Constraints
cards.body: Eliyahu Goldratt's novel *The Goal* (1984) popularised five steps: **identify** the constraint, **exploit** it (never let it idle), **subordinate** everything else to it, **elevate** it (add capacity), then **repeat** — because a new bottleneck will appear. An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole system.

cards.title: Don't chase 100% everywhere
cards.body: Managers love high utilisation on every machine. But non-bottleneck steps running flat out just build piles of work-in-process in front of the bottleneck. Only the bottleneck needs to be busy all the time; elsewhere, spare capacity is cheap insurance.

cards.q: Step A: 50 units/hr, Step B: 35 units/hr, Step C: 45 units/hr, in series. Demand is 40 units/hr. Process output is:
cards.explain: Output = min(demand, bottleneck capacity) = min(40, 35) = 35 units/hr. Step B is the bottleneck.

cards.q: A visa office processes 120 applications a day; average 600 applications are pending inside. Average processing time per application is:
cards.explain: Little's Law: W = L ÷ λ = 600 ÷ 120 = 5 days.

cards.q: Adding capacity to a non-bottleneck step will usually:
options: Always reduce flow time by half
cards.explain: Output is set by the bottleneck; extra capacity elsewhere just raises idle time.

notes.p:
Every organisation is a set of **processes** that transform inputs into outputs: patients into treated patients, applications into approved loans, raw materials into finished goods. **Process analysis** asks three questions. How much can this process produce per hour (**capacity**)? How long does a unit take to go through (**flow time**)? How much work is sitting inside it (**inventory** or work-in-process)?

The answers drive cost, speed and customer experience. A slow loan process loses applicants to faster fintechs; a factory with too much work-in-process ties up cash; a hospital with a bottleneck in diagnostics leaves expensive surgeons idle. Most process problems are found with a whiteboard, a stopwatch and the ideas in this chapter.

points: **Process flow diagram**: boxes for activities, triangles for inventory/buffers, arrows for flow
**Activity time (processing time)**: how long a resource takes per unit
**Capacity of a resource** = 1 ÷ activity time (× number of parallel resources)
**Bottleneck**: the resource with the lowest capacity; it sets process capacity
**Flow rate (throughput)** = min(demand, process capacity)
**Utilisation** = flow rate ÷ capacity; the bottleneck has the highest utilisation
**Cycle time**: time between successive units leaving the process = 1 ÷ flow rate
**Flow time**: total time a unit spends in the process, including waiting

notes.p:
A cloud kitchen has three steps for each order.
Prep: 2 cooks, 4 minutes per order each → capacity = 2 × 60/4 = 30 orders/hr.
Cooking: 1 station, 3 minutes per order → 60/3 = 20 orders/hr.
Packing: 1 person, 1.5 minutes per order → 60/1.5 = 40 orders/hr.

**Bottleneck**: cooking, at 20 orders/hr. That's the capacity of the whole kitchen.
At a demand of 18 orders/hr, flow rate = 18. Utilisations: prep 18/30 = 60%, cooking 18/20 = 90%, packing 18/40 = 45%. Cycle time = 60/18 ≈ 3.3 minutes.
In the dinner peak, demand hits 26 orders/hr. Flow rate is capped at 20; the kitchen is **capacity-constrained**, and 6 orders an hour are lost or delayed.

**What to do?** Hiring another packer adds nothing. Options that work: add a second cooking station (capacity rises to min(30, 40, 40) = 30/hr — and prep becomes the new bottleneck), move some cooking work upstream into prep (pre-cooking components), or simplify the menu so cooking takes 2.5 minutes (capacity 24/hr). This is exactly how operations consultants approach a factory or a hospital.

John Little proved in 1961 that for any stable system, **average inventory (L) = average flow rate (λ) × average flow time (W)**. It needs no assumptions about distributions — which is why it's one of the most useful equations in management.
points: **Hospital**: 30 patients/hr arrive, 15 are inside on average → each spends 0.5 hr
**Loans**: 200 applications/week, 600 in process → 3 weeks to decide. To cut to 1 week at the same volume, WIP must fall to 200
**Inventory turns**: ₹50 cr inventory, ₹300 cr annual COGS → flow time 2 months; turns = 300/50 = 6 per year; days of inventory ≈ 365/6 ≈ 61
**Receivables**: ₹30 cr receivables on ₹360 cr annual credit sales → customers take 30/360 of a year ≈ 30 days to pay
Lesson: to make a process faster without changing throughput, **reduce the work-in-process** sitting in it

notes.h: Process types and the Theory of Constraints
notes.p:
Robert Hayes and Steven Wheelwright's **product-process matrix** (1979) links volume and variety to process choice: **job shops** for low-volume, high-variety work (a tailor, a tool room), **batch** processes (a pharma plant making several drugs), **assembly lines** (car plants), and **continuous flow** (refineries, cement). Mismatching process to product — a job shop trying to mass-produce — is costly.

Eliyahu Goldratt's *The Goal* (1984), a business novel, made the **Theory of Constraints (TOC)** famous. Its five steps: identify the constraint; exploit it (keep it working on the right things, never starved or blocked); subordinate everything else to its pace; elevate it (buy capacity); repeat. TOC also introduced 'drum-buffer-rope': let the bottleneck set the pace (drum), protect it with a buffer of work, and release new work only as fast as the bottleneck consumes it (rope).

points: Adding capacity at non-bottleneck steps (often the most visible or loudest department)
Measuring every department on utilisation, which piles up WIP and lengthens flow time
Ignoring setup times, rework loops and shared resources when computing capacity
Using average demand when peaks drive the real constraint
Assuming the bottleneck is a machine — often it's an approval step, a specialist, or a software system
Fixing a bottleneck and not noticing the new one

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Operations cases in consulting interviews often ask 'why is this plant/hospital/call centre missing targets?' Draw the process, compute capacities, find the bottleneck, then suggest exploiting and elevating it. Exams test capacity, utilisation, cycle time and Little's Law. On the job — in manufacturing at Tata Steel or Maruti, in operations at Swiggy or Delhivery, in back-offices at banks — you'll use Little's Law to link WIP, throughput and lead time, and bottleneck logic to decide where investment pays.

points: Capacity of a step = resources ÷ activity time; process capacity = bottleneck capacity
Flow rate = min(demand, capacity); utilisation = flow rate ÷ capacity
Little's Law: L = λ × W — works for inventory, patients, loans, receivables
Inventory turns = COGS ÷ inventory; days of inventory = 365 ÷ turns
Theory of Constraints: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat
Extra capacity at a non-bottleneck adds no output
Product-process matrix: job shop → batch → line → continuous as volume rises and variety falls

chapters.title: Queues & service operations

cards.title: Why queues form even with spare capacity
cards.body: A bank teller who can serve 12 customers an hour, facing 10 arrivals an hour, still builds queues. Why? **Variability**: customers arrive in clumps and some transactions take much longer than others. Queues come from the combination of **high utilisation** and **variability**, not just from too little capacity.

cards.title: The utilisation curve
cards.body: Waiting time scales with **ρ ÷ (1 − ρ)**, where ρ = utilisation. At 50% that factor is 1; at 80% it's 4; at 90% it's 9; at 95% it's 19. Waits **explode** as utilisation approaches 100%. Running service staff 'fully busy' guarantees long queues.

cards.title: Kingman's approximation
cards.body: Average wait in queue ≈ **service time × [ρ ÷ (1 − ρ)] × [(CVa² + CVs²) ÷ 2]**, where CV = coefficient of variation of arrival and service times. Three levers: shorter service time, lower utilisation, less variability. For random (Poisson) arrivals and exponential service, both CVs = 1.

cards.title: The teller, worked
cards.body: Service averages 5 minutes (12/hr); 10 customers arrive per hour at random. ρ = 10/12 ≈ 0.83. Wait ≈ 5 × (0.83/0.17) × 1 ≈ **25 minutes**. If arrivals rise to 11/hr (ρ ≈ 0.92), wait ≈ 5 × 11 ≈ **55 minutes**. A 10% rise in demand more than doubled the wait.

cards.title: Pooling
cards.body: One shared queue feeding several servers beats separate queues for each — it's why banks and airports use a single snaking line. Pooling cuts waits because no server sits idle while another's line is long. The same logic drives shared call centres and centralised inventory.

cards.title: The psychology of waiting
cards.body: David Maister's 1985 essay 'The Psychology of Waiting Lines': unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time; uncertain and unexplained waits feel longer; unfair waits feel longest. Showing an estimated wait time, a token number and a progress update can raise satisfaction without adding a single server.

cards.title: Aravind Eye Care
cards.body: Aravind, founded in Madurai in 1976 by Dr G. Venkataswamy, performs very high volumes of cataract surgery by designing the process like an assembly line: specialised staff for each step, standardised procedures and surgeons kept on the bottleneck task — surgery itself. High volume and productivity allow it to treat many poor patients free or at very low cost.

cards.q: Utilisation rises from 80% to 90%. The ρ/(1−ρ) factor in waiting time goes from:
cards.explain: 0.8/0.2 = 4; 0.9/0.1 = 9. Waits more than double for a 10-point rise in utilisation.

cards.q: Which change does NOT reduce average queue waiting time?
cards.explain: Higher utilisation increases waiting time sharply — the opposite of what you want.

cards.q: A restaurant puts mirrors near the lift and shows estimated wait times. According to Maister, this mainly works by:
options: Making waiting feel occupied and certain
cards.explain: Occupied, explained and certain waits feel shorter, even if actual wait is unchanged.

notes.p:
Queues are everywhere in services: bank branches, hospital OPDs, call centres, toll plazas, food-delivery kitchens, even an email inbox. **Queueing theory**, which began with the Danish engineer Agner Krarup Erlang's work on telephone exchanges in the early 1900s, explains why queues form and how to manage them.

The central insight surprises most people: queues form even when capacity exceeds demand on average. They come from **variability** — in when customers arrive and how long each takes — combined with **high utilisation**. As a resource gets close to fully busy, waiting time doesn't rise gently; it explodes. Managers who try to keep service staff 100% busy create the long lines customers hate.

points: **Arrival rate (λ)**: customers per hour
**Service rate (μ)**: customers one server can handle per hour; service time = 1/μ
**Utilisation (ρ)** = λ ÷ (number of servers × μ); must be below 1 or the queue grows without limit
**Wq**: average waiting time in queue; **W** = Wq + service time
**Lq**: average number waiting; by Little's Law, Lq = λ × Wq
For one server with random arrivals and exponential service (the M/M/1 queue): Wq = ρ ÷ (μ − λ), Lq = ρ² ÷ (1 − ρ)
**Kingman's formula** for the general case: Wq ≈ service time × ρ/(1−ρ) × (CVa² + CVs²)/2

notes.p:
A branch has one teller. Average service time 5 minutes (μ = 12/hr). Customers arrive at random, 10 per hour (λ = 10/hr).
Step 1 — ρ = 10/12 = 0.833.
Step 2 — Wq = ρ ÷ (μ − λ) = 0.833 ÷ 2 = 0.417 hr ≈ **25 minutes**.
Step 3 — Lq = 0.833² ÷ (1 − 0.833) = 0.694 ÷ 0.167 ≈ **4.2 customers** waiting on average. Check with Little: λ × Wq = 10 × 0.417 = 4.2 ✓.
Step 4 — If arrivals rise to 11/hr: ρ = 0.917, Wq = 0.917 ÷ 1 = 0.917 hr ≈ **55 minutes**.

A 10% increase in demand more than doubled the wait. Now cut service-time variability (standardise forms, move complex cases to an appointment desk): if CVs falls from 1 to 0.5, Kingman's variability term falls from (1 + 1)/2 = 1 to (1 + 0.25)/2 = 0.625, and the 25-minute wait drops to about 16 minutes — with no new staff.

**Pooling**: two tellers with separate lines, each at ρ = 0.83, perform worse than one combined line served by both. In the combined system, no teller is idle while customers wait in the other line, so average waits fall substantially.

notes.h: Managing capacity and demand in services
notes.p: Services cannot be stored: an empty seat on tonight's flight or an idle doctor-hour is lost forever. So service operations manage both sides.
points: **Capacity side**: shift scheduling matched to forecast demand, cross-trained staff who move to the bottleneck, part-time staff for peaks, self-service (ATMs, UPI, app check-in)
**Demand side**: appointments and slots, off-peak pricing, reservations, triage that routes simple cases to fast lanes
**Revenue (yield) management**: airlines and hotels vary prices and allocate capacity by segment to fill perishable inventory profitably
**Service blueprint**: maps customer actions, front-stage staff actions, back-stage actions and support systems, with a 'line of visibility' — used to find failure points
**Customer contact**: high-contact steps are less efficient but drive experience; move non-contact work back-stage where it can be standardised

notes.h: The psychology of waiting and a case
notes.p:
David Maister's 1985 essay 'The Psychology of Waiting Lines' gave service managers a set of propositions: occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time; pre-process waits feel longer than in-process waits; anxiety makes waits seem longer; uncertain and unexplained waits feel longer than known, explained ones; unfair waits feel longer than equitable ones. That's why token-number displays, estimated wait times, live delivery-tracking maps and 'your order is being prepared' messages matter so much.

**Case: Aravind Eye Care System.** Founded in 1976 in Madurai by Dr G. Venkataswamy, Aravind is widely studied (including in Harvard Business School cases) for applying process thinking to surgery. Staff are specialised by step — screening, counselling, preparation — so that highly trained surgeons spend their time on the bottleneck activity: operating. Standardised procedures reduce variability; high volume lowers unit cost. Paying patients subsidise free or low-cost care for the poor. It's a vivid demonstration that operations excellence can serve a social mission.

points: Planning staff to average demand and running at very high utilisation — waits explode at peaks
Ignoring variability; standardising service and smoothing arrivals is often cheaper than adding staff
Separate queues per server instead of pooling
Measuring only average wait, not the tail (the 90th-percentile wait drives complaints)
Adding capacity without fixing the psychology — an unexplained 10-minute wait can feel worse than an explained 15-minute one
Confusing busy staff with good service

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Interviewers ask: 'Lines at our stores are long — hire more cashiers?' Good answers separate utilisation, variability and perception: add capacity at peaks, pool queues, introduce express lanes, and manage the waiting experience. Exams test M/M/1 calculations, Little's Law applications and the utilisation curve. On the job, call-centre workforce management, hospital OPD design, airport operations and quick-commerce dispatch all use these models daily.

points: Queues come from utilisation + variability, not only from too little capacity
M/M/1: Wq = ρ/(μ − λ); Lq = ρ²/(1 − ρ); Lq = λ × Wq
Kingman: Wq ≈ ts × ρ/(1−ρ) × (CVa² + CVs²)/2 — cut time, utilisation or variability
Pool queues; use appointments, off-peak pricing and self-service
Maister: occupied, explained, certain, fair waits feel shorter
Aravind: specialise steps, keep the scarce resource on the bottleneck

chapters.title: Quality & lean: TQM, Six Sigma (DMAIC) and the Toyota Production System

cards.title: Quality is a system, not inspection
cards.body: Inspecting bad products at the end is expensive and too late. The quality movement — led by **W. Edwards Deming**, **Joseph Juran** and **Philip Crosby** — argued that most defects come from the **system** (process, materials, training), not careless workers, so management must fix the system. Deming's lectures in post-war Japan were hugely influential there.

cards.title: Cost of quality
cards.body: Four buckets: **prevention** (training, design), **appraisal** (inspection, testing), **internal failure** (scrap, rework), **external failure** (warranty claims, recalls, lost customers). Spending more on prevention usually cuts total cost sharply. Crosby summed it up in his book title: *Quality Is Free*.

cards.title: Six Sigma
cards.body: Developed at **Motorola** in the 1980s and made famous by **GE** under Jack Welch. Goal: reduce variation so defects are extremely rare — **3.4 defects per million opportunities** at 'six sigma' (allowing for a 1.5σ drift). Projects follow **DMAIC**: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control.

cards.title: Measuring defects and capability
cards.body: **DPMO** = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit) × 10⁶. **Cp** = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ: can the process fit inside the spec? **Cpk** = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ: also checks centring. Cp or Cpk ≥ 1.33 is a common minimum target.

cards.title: Capability, worked
cards.body: A 500 g pack has specs 494–506 g. Process SD = 1.5 g. Cp = 12 ÷ 9 = **1.33** — fine if centred. But the mean has drifted to 502 g: Cpk = min(506 − 502, 502 − 494) ÷ 4.5 = 4 ÷ 4.5 = **0.89**. Too many overweight packs. Fix: re-centre the filler — no new machine needed.

cards.title: The Toyota Production System
cards.body: Built at Toyota by **Taiichi Ohno** and others. Two pillars: **Just-in-Time** (make only what's needed, when needed, in the amount needed — pulled by **kanban** signals) and **jidoka** (automation with a human touch: stop the line at the first defect, e.g. the **andon** cord). Foundation: standard work and **kaizen**, continuous improvement.

cards.title: The seven wastes (muda)
cards.body: Ohno's wastes: **transport, inventory, motion, waiting, over-production, over-processing, defects** (memory aid: TIM WOOD). Over-production is the worst: it hides all the others. Lean thinking, as described by Womack and Jones, starts by mapping the **value stream** and cutting everything the customer wouldn't pay for.

cards.q: 5,000 invoices, each with 4 opportunities for error, show 60 errors. DPMO is:
In DMAIC, the step that makes sure gains are sustained (control charts, SOPs, ownership) is:
cards.explain: Control locks in the improvement with monitoring and standards so the process doesn't drift back.

cards.q: A worker pulls the andon cord to stop the line when she spots a defect. This reflects:
cards.explain: Jidoka: build in quality by stopping at the first abnormality so the root cause is fixed immediately.

notes.p:
**Quality** means meeting customer requirements consistently. For decades, firms tried to achieve it by inspecting finished goods and scrapping the bad ones. The quality revolution of the 20th century showed this is backwards: defects are mostly created by the **process**, so quality must be designed and built in, and the people doing the work must be empowered to improve it.

Three overlapping toolkits came out of this revolution: **Total Quality Management (TQM)**, a management philosophy; **Six Sigma**, a data-driven method for reducing variation; and **lean**, derived from the **Toyota Production System**, which attacks waste and speeds flow. Today most companies use a blend, often called 'Lean Six Sigma'.

**W. Edwards Deming**, an American statistician, lectured Japanese managers from 1950 on statistical quality control and management's responsibility for systems; Japan's Deming Prize is named after him. His **14 points** include ceasing dependence on mass inspection, driving out fear, and breaking down barriers between departments. He promoted the **PDCA** (Plan–Do–Check–Act) improvement cycle, which built on Walter Shewhart's work.

**Joseph Juran** stressed the **quality trilogy** — planning, control, improvement — and the Pareto principle in quality ('the vital few' causes behind most defects). **Philip Crosby** argued for 'zero defects' and that quality is free because preventing defects costs less than fixing them.

**TQM** combines these ideas: customer focus, company-wide involvement, process thinking, fact-based decisions and continuous improvement. Indian firms embraced it from the 1990s; several Indian companies, including Tata Steel, have won the Deming Prize.
points: **Cost of quality**: prevention + appraisal + internal failure + external failure
External failures (recalls, lost trust) are by far the most expensive
Tools: Pareto charts, fishbone (Ishikawa) diagrams, control charts, 5 Whys

notes.p: **Six Sigma** began at Motorola in the mid-1980s and was scaled by GE in the late 1990s. A 'six sigma' process, allowing for a long-run drift of 1.5σ in the mean, produces about **3.4 defects per million opportunities**. Projects are run by trained 'Green Belts' and 'Black Belts' using **DMAIC**.
points: **Define**: the problem, customer requirement (CTQ — critical to quality), scope and goal
**Measure**: current performance; validate the measurement system; compute DPMO or capability
**Analyse**: find root causes with data — Pareto, fishbone, regression, hypothesis tests
**Improve**: design and pilot solutions; confirm the improvement statistically
**Control**: lock in gains — control charts, standard operating procedures, mistake-proofing (**poka-yoke**), clear owners

notes.p:
**DPMO.** An accounts-payable team processes 5,000 invoices a month. Each invoice has 5 opportunities for error (vendor, amount, tax code, PO match, date). Last month: 75 errors.
DPMO = 75 ÷ (5,000 × 5) × 1,000,000 = 75 ÷ 25,000 × 10⁶ = **3,000**. With the conventional 1.5σ shift, that's roughly a **4.2-sigma** process. Reaching 6 sigma would mean about 0.085 errors a month — perhaps one a year.

**Capability.** A biscuit line fills 500 g packs; legal and customer specs are 494–506 g. Process SD = 1.5 g.
Cp = (506 − 494) ÷ (6 × 1.5) = 12 ÷ 9 = **1.33** — the process is capable if centred.
But the mean has drifted to 502 g. Cpk = min(506 − 502, 502 − 494) ÷ (3 × 1.5) = 4 ÷ 4.5 = **0.89**.
The process is now producing too many overweight packs (giving away product). The fix is re-centring, not buying a new machine. Re-centre the mean at 500 g and Cpk returns to 1.33.

notes.h: Lean and the Toyota Production System
notes.p: The **Toyota Production System (TPS)** was developed at Toyota from the late 1940s onward, with **Taiichi Ohno** as its chief architect; James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos introduced it to Western readers as 'lean production' in *The Machine That Changed the World* (1990).
points: **Just-in-Time (JIT)**: produce only what the next process needs, when it needs it; **kanban** cards signal replenishment (a **pull** system)
**Jidoka**: machines and people stop at the first abnormality — the **andon** cord lets any worker halt the line so problems surface and get fixed at the root
**Heijunka**: level production volume and mix to avoid peaks
**Standard work** and **kaizen**: document the current best way, then improve it continually, led by the people doing the work
**Seven wastes**: transport, inventory, motion, waiting, over-production, over-processing, defects
**5S**: sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain
Inventory hides problems, like water hiding rocks in a river: lower the water and the rocks appear

notes.p:
**Maruti Suzuki** brought Japanese practices to Indian car-making from the 1980s through its partnership with Suzuki — supplier development, kaizen, and tight just-in-time links with nearby vendor parks around Gurugram and Manesar. Toyota Kirloskar brought TPS directly.

The **Mumbai dabbawalas**, who deliver lakhs of home-cooked lunches daily using a colour-and-number coding system, are often cited for an extraordinarily low error rate; the popular 'Six Sigma' label comes from media accounts rather than formal certification, but the lesson — simple, standardised, visual processes run by trained people — is genuine lean thinking.

Mistakes: treating quality as the QA department's job; launching Six Sigma as a certificate drive without leadership attention; copying lean tools (kanban boards, 5S posters) without the culture of stopping to fix problems; cutting inventory to JIT levels without fixing supplier reliability; and blaming workers for system problems.

Interviews for operations and manufacturing roles ask you to walk through DMAIC on a problem, or to spot wastes in a described process. Exams test the pioneers, cost of quality, DPMO, Cp/Cpk and TPS concepts. On the job, Lean Six Sigma Green Belt projects are a common way for young managers in manufacturing, banking back-offices and IT services to show measurable impact.

points: Quality is built into the process, not inspected in (Deming, Juran, Crosby)
Cost of quality: prevention, appraisal, internal and external failure
Six Sigma: 3.4 DPMO; DMAIC = Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control
DPMO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities) × 10⁶
Cp = spec width ÷ 6σ; Cpk adds centring; 1.33 is a common target
TPS pillars: Just-in-Time (pull, kanban) and jidoka (andon); base of standard work and kaizen
Seven wastes: transport, inventory, motion, waiting, over-production, over-processing, defects

chapters.title: Inventory management: EOQ, safety stock and the newsvendor

cards.title: Why hold inventory at all?
cards.body: Inventory is money sitting on shelves. Firms hold it to get **economies of scale** in ordering (cycle stock), to protect against **uncertainty** in demand and supply (safety stock), to cover **transit** time (pipeline stock) and to prepare for **seasonal** peaks. The art is holding just enough — too little loses sales, too much burns cash and goes stale.

cards.title: Economic Order Quantity
cards.body: Balancing ordering cost against holding cost: **EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H)**, where D = annual demand, S = cost per order, H = holding cost per unit per year. At the EOQ, annual ordering cost equals annual holding cost. Attributed to Ford W. Harris (1913).

cards.title: EOQ, worked
cards.body: D = 12,000 units/yr, S = ₹500/order, H = ₹20/unit/yr. EOQ = √(2 × 12,000 × 500 ÷ 20) = √6,00,000 ≈ **775 units**. About 15.5 orders a year. Ordering cost ≈ ₹7,740, holding cost ≈ ₹7,750, total ≈ **₹15,500**. The total-cost curve is flat near the EOQ, so 700 or 800 is almost as good.

cards.title: Safety stock and reorder point
cards.body: **Safety stock = z × σ_d × √L**, where σ_d = SD of daily demand, L = lead time in days, z from the target service level (1.65 for 95%). **Reorder point = average demand during lead time + safety stock.** Higher service levels cost disproportionately more stock.

cards.title: Reorder point, worked
cards.body: Daily demand averages 50 units, SD 10; lead time 9 days; target 95% cycle service level (z ≈ 1.65). Safety stock = 1.65 × 10 × √9 ≈ **49–50 units**. Reorder point = 50 × 9 + 50 = **500**. When stock falls to 500, place the next order.

cards.title: The newsvendor model
cards.body: For one-shot perishable or seasonal items: **critical ratio = Cu ÷ (Cu + Co)**, where Cu = cost of under-stocking (lost margin per unit) and Co = cost of over-stocking (cost minus salvage). Order the quantity at which P(demand ≤ Q) equals the critical ratio.

cards.title: Newsvendor, worked
cards.body: Festive kurtas cost ₹600, sell at ₹1,500, unsold ones clear at ₹300. Cu = 900, Co = 300 → CR = **0.75**. Demand ~ normal, mean 1,000, SD 200. z for 0.75 ≈ 0.67. Order ≈ 1,000 + 0.67 × 200 ≈ **1,135**. High margin, cheap leftovers → order above the mean.

cards.q: If annual demand quadruples and other inputs stay the same, the EOQ:
cards.explain: EOQ ∝ √D, so quadrupling D multiplies EOQ by √4 = 2.

cards.q: A bakery's cake costs ₹200, sells for ₹500, and leftovers are thrown away (salvage 0). The critical ratio is:
cards.explain: Cu = 500 − 200 = 300; Co = 200 − 0 = 200. CR = 300 ÷ 500 = 0.60, so stock enough to cover demand 60% of the time.

cards.q: Lead time rises from 4 days to 16 days, with demand variability unchanged. Safety stock (same service level) will:
cards.explain: Safety stock ∝ √L. √16 ÷ √4 = 4 ÷ 2 = 2, so it doubles.

notes.p:
**Inventory** is one of the largest assets on many balance sheets — for retailers, distributors and manufacturers alike. It exists because supply and demand don't line up perfectly in time, quantity or certainty. Inventory management answers two questions for every item: **how much to order** and **when to order**.

Getting it right frees cash and protects sales. Getting it wrong shows up as stock-outs (lost sales, angry customers, idle production lines) or as excess stock (blocked cash, storage costs, obsolescence, markdowns). Retailers such as DMart are known for tight inventory and working-capital discipline; quick-commerce firms must stock thousands of items in tiny dark stores, which makes inventory decisions existential.

points: **Cycle stock**: results from ordering in batches — average cycle stock = Q/2
**Safety stock**: buffer against demand and lead-time uncertainty
**Pipeline (in-transit) stock**: = demand rate × transit time (Little's Law)
**Seasonal/anticipation stock**: built ahead of Diwali, monsoon or harvest peaks
**Holding cost** (typically expressed as a percentage of item value per year): capital cost, storage, insurance, shrinkage, obsolescence
**Ordering/setup cost**: paperwork, transport per shipment, machine changeovers
**Stock-out cost**: lost margin, lost customers, expediting
**ABC analysis**: a small share of items (A) usually accounts for most of the value — control them tightly; manage C items with simple rules

notes.p:
The **Economic Order Quantity** model (Ford W. Harris, 1913) assumes steady demand, a fixed cost per order and a constant holding cost. Ordering more each time means fewer orders (less ordering cost) but more average stock (more holding cost). Total relevant cost = (D/Q) × S + (Q/2) × H, minimised at **EOQ = √(2DS/H)**.

**Example.** A distributor sells 12,000 cartons a year. Each order costs ₹500 (admin and freight); holding costs ₹20 per carton per year.
EOQ = √(2 × 12,000 × 500 ÷ 20) = √6,00,000 ≈ 775 cartons.
Orders per year = 12,000 ÷ 775 ≈ 15.5 (about every 3.4 weeks).
Annual ordering cost = 15.5 × 500 ≈ ₹7,740; annual holding cost = 775/2 × 20 = ₹7,750; total ≈ ₹15,490.

Two insights. First, **EOQ grows with the square root** of demand, so doubling volume needs only about 41% bigger orders — a scale economy. Second, the cost curve is **flat near the optimum**: ordering 700 or 850 costs barely more, so round to practical pack and truck sizes. The lean response is to attack S itself — cheaper, quicker orders and setups (Shigeo Shingo's SMED for changeovers) make small batches economical.

notes.h: Safety stock and the reorder point
notes.p:
When demand during the replenishment lead time is uncertain, keep a buffer. If daily demand has SD σ_d and lead time is L days (assumed fixed), demand during lead time has SD σ_d√L. For a target **cycle service level** (probability of not stocking out in a cycle), safety stock = z × σ_d × √L.

**Example.** Daily demand mean 50, SD 10; lead time 9 days; target 95% (z ≈ 1.65).
Lead-time demand: mean 450, SD 10 × 3 = 30.
Safety stock ≈ 1.65 × 30 ≈ 49.5 → 50 units.
Reorder point = 450 + 50 = 500.
At 99% (z ≈ 2.33), safety stock rises to about 70 units: the last few percentage points of service are the most expensive.

Because safety stock scales with √L, **cutting lead time** (nearer suppliers, faster transport) and **reducing variability** (better forecasts, smaller and more frequent orders) are often better than simply holding more.

Some products are bought once for a single selling period: newspapers, festive apparel, Valentine's roses, mangoes, flight meals. Order too few and you lose margin; order too many and you dump leftovers. The **newsvendor model** balances the two.
Cu = cost of under-stocking one unit = price − cost.
Co = cost of over-stocking one unit = cost − salvage value.
Optimal order: the quantity Q where P(demand ≤ Q) = Cu ÷ (Cu + Co), the **critical ratio**.

**Example.** A retailer buys festive kurtas at ₹600, sells at ₹1,500, and clears leftovers at ₹300 after the season.
Cu = 900, Co = 300, critical ratio = 900 ÷ 1,200 = 0.75.
Demand is roughly normal with mean 1,000 and SD 200. The z for the 75th percentile ≈ 0.674.
Q* = 1,000 + 0.674 × 200 ≈ 1,135 kurtas.
If leftovers were worthless (Co = 600), CR = 0.6, z ≈ 0.25 → Q ≈ 1,050. High margins and good salvage push you to stock more; thin margins and worthless leftovers push you to stock less. Fashion retailers such as Zara attack the problem differently — by shortening lead times so they can order closer to the season and re-order what sells.

points: Using the same service level for every item — A items and critical spares deserve different targets
Ignoring lead-time variability, often a bigger source of risk than demand variability
Treating safety stock as a fixed number while demand and lead times change
Ordering to the average demand for one-shot items instead of using the critical ratio
Rewarding purchasing for low unit prices that come with huge minimum order quantities
Hiding inventory in the channel ('stuffing') to hit sales targets

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams give you EOQ, reorder point and newsvendor problems — practise all three until they're mechanical. Interviewers ask 'how much should we stock for the festive season?' or 'why is our working capital rising?' — answer with demand uncertainty, margins vs leftover costs, and lead times. On the job, supply-chain planners at FMCG firms, e-commerce category managers, pharma distributors and quick-commerce operators run these models, usually inside planning software, and spend their time challenging the inputs.
