points: Inventory types: cycle, safety, pipeline, seasonal; costs: holding, ordering, stock-out
EOQ = √(2DS/H); ordering cost = holding cost at the optimum; curve is flat near EOQ
EOQ ∝ √D — doubling demand raises order size by ~41%
Safety stock = z × σ_d × √L; reorder point = mean lead-time demand + safety stock
Shorter lead times and lower variability beat bigger buffers
Newsvendor: CR = Cu/(Cu + Co); order where P(D ≤ Q) = CR
ABC: control high-value items tightly

chapters.title: Supply chain strategy: bullwhip, MTS vs MTO, global sourcing & resilience

cards.title: Supply chain as strategy
cards.body: A **supply chain** links suppliers, factories, warehouses, distributors and retailers to the customer. Strategy question: what should it optimise — lowest cost, fastest response, or highest resilience? You can't maximise all three. The right choice depends on the product and the customer promise.

cards.title: Efficient vs responsive
cards.body: Marshall Fisher's 1997 *HBR* article: **functional** products (staples with stable demand, thin margins — salt, detergent) need **efficient**, low-cost chains. **Innovative** products (fashion, new phones — unpredictable demand, high margins) need **responsive** chains with buffers and speed. Mismatches destroy value.

cards.title: The bullwhip effect
cards.body: Small swings in consumer demand become **bigger swings** in orders the further upstream you go. Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang (1997) named four causes: **demand-signal processing** (each tier forecasts from its customers' orders), **order batching**, **price fluctuations** (promotions and forward buying), and **rationing and shortage gaming** (over-ordering when supply is tight).

cards.title: Taming the bullwhip
cards.body: Share point-of-sale data with suppliers, cut lead times, order in smaller and more frequent batches, replace temporary promotions with **everyday low pricing**, and allocate scarce stock based on past sales rather than current orders. Vendor-managed inventory hands replenishment to the supplier.

cards.title: MTS, ATO, MTO, ETO
cards.body: **Make-to-stock**: build to forecast, ship from shelf (FMCG). **Assemble-to-order**: hold components, assemble when ordered (Dell's PC model). **Make-to-order**: produce after the order (custom furniture). **Engineer-to-order**: design after the order (power plants). The **decoupling point** — where forecast-driven meets order-driven — is a key design choice.

cards.title: Total landed cost
cards.body: Illustrative: an import costs ₹100 vs a domestic ₹118. Add freight and insurance ₹8, duty 10% on ₹108 = ₹10.8, extra pipeline inventory ~₹3, quality and delay risk ~₹4 → import ≈ **₹125.8**. Domestic with ₹2 freight = **₹120**. The 'cheaper' supplier is dearer. Always compare **landed**, not invoice, cost.

cards.title: Resilience after the shocks
cards.body: COVID-19, the 2021 Suez Canal blockage by the *Ever Given*, and the 2021–22 chip shortage that cut car output (Maruti Suzuki among many others) showed the fragility of lean, single-source chains. Responses: **dual sourcing**, 'China+1', strategic buffers for critical parts, mapping suppliers several tiers deep, and nearshoring.

cards.q: Retail sales of nappies are fairly steady, but the manufacturer's orders to its raw-material suppliers swing wildly. This is best explained by:
cards.explain: Demand variability amplifies upstream — the bullwhip effect, famously observed in P&G's Pampers supply chain.

cards.q: According to Fisher, a fast-fashion line with short life and unpredictable demand needs:
options: A responsive chain with speed and buffers
Single sourcing from the cheapest supplier
cards.explain: Innovative products need responsive chains; the cost of stock-outs and markdowns outweighs production savings.

cards.q: Which policy is MOST likely to reduce the bullwhip effect?
options: Allocating scarce stock in proportion to current orders
cards.explain: Shared POS data lets every tier see true demand rather than amplified orders. The others all worsen bullwhip.

notes.p:
A **supply chain** is every organisation and step involved in getting a product to a customer — from raw-material suppliers through manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors and retailers. **Supply chain management** coordinates the flows of goods, information and money across these independent firms.

The strategic insight is that the supply chain must fit the competitive strategy. A company competing on low price needs a ruthlessly efficient chain; one competing on novelty or speed needs a responsive one; and every company now needs enough resilience to survive shocks. Many companies have found that their chain was optimised for a world that no longer exists.

notes.h: Matching chain to product: Fisher's framework
notes.p: In 'What Is the Right Supply Chain for Your Product?' (*HBR*, 1997), Marshall Fisher separated products into two types.
points: **Functional products**: stable, predictable demand, long life cycles, low margins, low variety — staples like salt, soap, basic groceries. Need an **efficient (physically efficient)** chain: high utilisation, low inventory, lowest-cost suppliers

**Innovative products**: unpredictable demand, short life cycles, high margins, high variety — fashion, new electronics. Need a **responsive (market-responsive)** chain: buffer capacity, strategic inventory, short lead times, suppliers chosen for speed and flexibility
Common failure: treating innovative products efficiently — cheap far-away production leads to stock-outs of hits and markdowns of misses

Zara (Inditex) is the classic responsive example: much of its fashion-sensitive production is kept close to its European base for short lead times, with frequent small shipments; basics can be sourced more cheaply further away

notes.p:
Jay Forrester at MIT showed in the late 1950s and 1960s that supply chains amplify demand fluctuations; MIT's **Beer Game** simulation lets students experience it — even with steady consumer demand, ordering decisions create wild swings upstream. Hau Lee, V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang named it the **bullwhip effect** in a 1997 article, noting P&G's observation that orders for Pampers nappies fluctuated far more than babies' fairly steady consumption.

**Four causes and fixes:**
1. **Demand-signal processing** — each tier forecasts from orders it receives, adding its own safety buffer. Fix: share point-of-sale data; collaborative forecasting.
2. **Order batching** — monthly orders or full-truck rules create lumps. Fix: smaller, frequent orders; mixed-load trucks.
3. **Price fluctuations** — trade promotions encourage forward buying. Fix: everyday low pricing.
4. **Rationing and shortage gaming** — customers inflate orders when supply is short, then cancel. Fix: allocate based on past sales, not current orders.

**Illustrative effect**: consumer sales of a product might vary by ±5% week to week, retailer orders by ±15%, distributor orders by ±25% and factory orders to raw-material suppliers by ±40% — each tier reacting to amplified signals.

notes.h: MTS, ATO, MTO and the decoupling point
notes.p: Where the chain switches from forecast-driven to order-driven activity is the **customer order decoupling point**.
points: **Make-to-stock (MTS)**: finished goods built to forecast — instant availability, but inventory and forecast risk (biscuits, shampoo)
**Assemble-to-order (ATO)**: components stocked, final assembly on order — Dell's direct PC model in the 1990s allowed customisation with low finished-goods stock
**Make-to-order (MTO)**: production starts after the order — custom furniture, many industrial parts; longer lead times, little finished stock
**Engineer-to-order (ETO)**: design starts after the order — ships, power plants
**Postponement**: delay differentiation as late as possible (generic product, local labelling or paint mixing) — Asian Paints' in-store tinting machines let a few bases become many shades on demand

notes.h: Global sourcing and total landed cost
notes.p:
Low unit prices abroad can disappear once the full cost is counted. **Total landed cost** = purchase price + freight and insurance + duties + inventory carrying cost for longer pipelines + quality, risk and coordination costs.

**Worked example (illustrative).** An Indian appliance maker compares a component from an overseas supplier at ₹100 with a domestic supplier at ₹118.
Import: ₹100 + freight/insurance ₹8 = ₹108; customs duty at 10% of ₹108 = ₹10.8; extra 8 weeks of pipeline and safety stock, carrying cost ≈ ₹3; expected quality, delay and currency risk ≈ ₹4. Landed ≈ **₹125.8**.
Domestic: ₹118 + freight ₹2 = **₹120**, plus a shorter lead time and easier collaboration.
The domestic option is cheaper and more responsive. Policy shapes these numbers too: India's **Production Linked Incentive (PLI)** schemes, launched from 2020, and firms' 'China+1' diversification have encouraged more manufacturing in India — most visibly the growth of iPhone assembly here by Apple's contract manufacturers.

Lean, single-source, globally stretched chains are efficient in calm times and fragile in shocks. COVID-19 lockdowns, the *Ever Given* blocking the Suez Canal in March 2021, and the semiconductor shortage of 2021–22, which forced carmakers worldwide including Maruti Suzuki to cut output, made resilience a board-level topic. After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, Toyota was reported to have built a detailed database of its suppliers several tiers deep and to have encouraged buffer stocks of critical parts — which reportedly helped it weather the chip shortage better than many rivals.
points: **Map** suppliers beyond tier 1; the bottleneck is often a tier-3 supplier you've never heard of
**Dual or multi-source** critical items; qualify alternates before a crisis
**Strategic buffers** for long-lead, single-point-of-failure parts — lean doesn't mean zero stock everywhere
**Nearshoring/regionalisation** to cut lead times and geopolitical risk
**Stress-test**: 'what if this port, plant or supplier is out for 8 weeks?'

notes.p:
Mistakes: choosing suppliers on unit price alone; running one chain design for products with very different demand patterns; using frequent trade promotions that whipsaw the factory; and either over-correcting into hoarding or cutting all buffers in the name of lean.

Interviews ask 'should we move sourcing to Vietnam/India?' (use landed cost and risk), 'why are our factory orders so volatile?' (bullwhip), or 'how should a D2C brand set up its chain?' (MTS vs MTO, decoupling point). Exams test Fisher's matrix, bullwhip causes and remedies, and landed-cost comparisons. Supply-chain roles at FMCG, auto, pharma, e-commerce and 3PL firms like Delhivery deal with these trade-offs daily.

points: Fit the chain to the product: functional → efficient; innovative → responsive (Fisher 1997)
Bullwhip: variability amplifies upstream; causes — signal processing, batching, price swings, shortage gaming
Fixes: share POS data, smaller frequent orders, everyday low pricing, allocate on past sales
MTS, ATO, MTO, ETO; the decoupling point and postponement
Compare suppliers on total landed cost, not invoice price
Resilience: map multi-tier suppliers, dual-source, buffer critical parts, nearshore
Cases: P&G Pampers (bullwhip), Zara (responsive), Dell (ATO), Toyota after 2011 (resilience)

chapters.title: Motivation: why people work hard (or don't)

cards.title: Motivation = direction, intensity, persistence
cards.body: Motivation is not a mood. Organisational behaviour defines it as three things: **where** effort goes (direction), **how hard** someone tries (intensity) and **how long** they keep at it (persistence). A manager's job is to shape all three — and the big theories each explain a different lever.

cards.title: Maslow's hierarchy
cards.body: Abraham Maslow (1943) proposed five needs: **physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation**. Lower needs dominate until reasonably satisfied. Lesson for managers: a fair salary and job security are the floor; recognition and growth motivate only once the floor is solid. Research does not support a rigid ladder — treat it as a useful map, not a law.

cards.title: Herzberg's two factors
cards.body: Frederick Herzberg found that **hygiene factors** (pay, policy, working conditions, supervision) cause dissatisfaction when bad but don't motivate when good. **Motivators** (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth) create real satisfaction. Fixing the canteen stops complaints; it doesn't make anyone love the job.

cards.title: Vroom's expectancy theory
cards.body:
**Motivational force = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence.**
Expectancy: 'If I try, can I perform?'
Instrumentality: 'If I perform, will I actually get the reward?'
Valence: 'Do I value that reward?'
Because it is multiplicative, if any one term is near zero, motivation collapses — no matter how big the bonus.

cards.title: Self-determination theory
cards.body: Deci and Ryan argue people are intrinsically driven when three needs are met: **autonomy** (choice over how), **competence** (getting better), **relatedness** (connection to others). Heavy control and pure carrot-and-stick incentives can **crowd out** intrinsic motivation on interesting work. Daniel Pink popularised this as autonomy, mastery and purpose in *Drive*.

cards.title: A sales team that stopped trying
cards.body: A bank sets a ₹50 lakh quarterly target with a big bonus. Reps think the target is impossible (expectancy ≈ 0.1) and last year bonuses were cut 'for budget reasons' (instrumentality ≈ 0.3). Even a valued bonus gives near-zero force. Fix: a reachable target with tiered payouts, and pay what was promised.

cards.title: Interview angle
cards.body: When asked 'How would you motivate a demotivated team member?', diagnose first: is it a hygiene problem (pay, unfair treatment), an expectancy problem (skills, resources), an instrumentality problem (broken promises) or a meaning problem (autonomy, purpose)? Naming the lever beats a generic 'I'd talk to them'.

cards.q: Under Herzberg's theory, which is a hygiene factor?
cards.explain: Salary is a hygiene factor: poor pay causes dissatisfaction, but good pay alone does not create lasting motivation. The others are motivators.

cards.q: Expectancy = 0.9, Instrumentality = 0.8, Valence = 0. What is the motivational force?
cards.explain: Vroom's model multiplies the terms. If the person doesn't value the reward (valence 0), the product is 0.

cards.q: Which set are the three basic needs in self-determination theory?
cards.explain: Deci and Ryan's SDT names autonomy, competence and relatedness. Achievement/power/affiliation is McClelland's needs theory.

notes.p:
Every manager eventually asks the same question: why does one person stay late to fix a problem while another, with the same pay and title, does the minimum? Motivation theory is the toolkit for answering it.

In organisational behaviour, **motivation** is the set of forces that determine the **direction**, **intensity** and **persistence** of effort. Notice what this definition leaves out: ability and opportunity. Performance is roughly ability × motivation × opportunity. A brilliant, motivated analyst with no data access still produces nothing. So before you blame motivation, check the other two.

**Maslow's hierarchy of needs** (1943) lists physiological, safety, belonging (social), esteem and self-actualisation needs. The intuition is powerful: a factory worker worried about rent will not be moved by a 'purpose' poster. Later research found people pursue several needs at once and the order varies by person and culture, so use it as a checklist, not a staircase.

**Herzberg's two-factor theory** (1959) came from interviews about good and bad days at work. **Hygiene factors** — company policy, supervision, pay, working conditions, relationships, job security — are 'extrinsic'. When they are poor, people are dissatisfied; when they are fine, people are merely 'not dissatisfied'. **Motivators** — achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth — are what actually create satisfaction. The practical message: you cannot pay your way to engagement, but you can underpay your way to attrition.

**McClelland's needs theory** adds that people differ in their need for **achievement**, **power** and **affiliation**. A high-achievement person wants moderate, measurable challenges and fast feedback — great in sales, sometimes poor as a manager because they want to do everything themselves.

notes.h: Process theories: how people decide to try
notes.p:
**Vroom's expectancy theory** (1964) treats effort as a calculation:

**Motivational force = Expectancy (E) × Instrumentality (I) × Valence (V)**

E is the belief that effort leads to performance; I is the belief that performance leads to the reward; V is how much the person values that reward. The multiplication matters: any term near zero kills motivation.

**Equity theory** (J. Stacy Adams) says people compare their own ratio of outcomes to inputs with a reference person. If a colleague gets the same raise for half the work, the 'under-rewarded' person may cut effort, ask for more, or leave. Perceived fairness, not absolute pay, drives the reaction.

**Goal-setting theory** (Locke and Latham) finds that **specific, difficult but accepted** goals with feedback beat 'do your best'. The 'accepted' part links back to expectancy: an impossible goal is ignored.
points: Worked example (illustrative numbers): Option A — bonus valued at V = 0.9, but E = 0.2 (target unrealistic) and I = 0.5 (payouts unreliable): force = 0.2 × 0.5 × 0.9 = 0.09.
Option B — smaller bonus V = 0.6, E = 0.7 (stretch but doable), I = 0.9 (always paid): force = 0.7 × 0.9 × 0.6 = 0.378.
The smaller, credible bonus produces roughly four times the motivational force.

notes.p:
Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's **self-determination theory (SDT)** separates **intrinsic** motivation (doing something because it is interesting or meaningful) from **extrinsic** motivation (doing it for a reward or to avoid punishment). People thrive when three needs are met: **autonomy**, **competence** and **relatedness**.

A well-known finding is the **crowding-out effect**: for tasks people already find interesting, tightly controlling rewards can reduce intrinsic interest. This doesn't mean incentives are bad. For routine, measurable work, incentives work well. For creative, complex work, managers get more by giving ownership, a clear purpose and room to master skills — the ideas Daniel Pink packaged as autonomy, mastery and purpose in *Drive* (2009).

**Google's** 20%-time tradition (now much diluted) and **3M's** older 15% rule were attempts to buy autonomy for engineers. **Tata Steel** is often cited for building strong hygiene foundations early — housing, healthcare and welfare for workers — which built loyalty over generations.

Compare a typical Indian **BPO** in the 2000s: decent pay, strict scripts, night shifts and little autonomy. Hygiene was adequate, motivators were thin, and attrition was famously high. Many firms responded with job rotation, internal promotions and skill certifications — adding motivators, not just money. **Zomato** and **Swiggy** delivery partners show the opposite design problem: pay-per-order incentives are pure extrinsic levers, so platform changes to payout rules hit instrumentality and trust directly.
Managers misuse these theories in predictable ways.
points: Using money for everything — raises fix hygiene problems but rarely buy discretionary effort for long.
Setting 'stretch' targets nobody believes in, which destroys expectancy.
Promising rewards and then moving the goalposts, which destroys instrumentality for years.
Assuming everyone values the same reward — a young analyst may value learning; a parent may value flexibility.
Micromanaging creative people, killing autonomy.
Ignoring comparisons: secret raises leak, and equity theory says perceived unfairness hurts more than low pay.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: In **MBA exams** you will be asked to classify factors (hygiene vs motivator), compute an expectancy score, or recommend a reward design for a case. In **interviews**, 'How would you motivate your team?' tests whether you can diagnose. In a **real job**, you'll design incentive plans, run appraisal conversations and decide who gets the stretch project. The best managers ask: what does this person value, do they believe they can do it, and do they trust that I'll deliver what I promise?

points: Motivation = direction + intensity + persistence; performance also needs ability and opportunity.
Maslow: physiological → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualisation; a map, not a strict ladder.
Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction.
Vroom: Force = E × I × V; any zero kills motivation.
Equity theory: people compare outcome/input ratios; fairness is perceived.
Locke & Latham: specific, hard, accepted goals + feedback.
SDT: autonomy, competence, relatedness; over-controlling rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation.

chapters.title: Personality, perception & decision biases at work

cards.title: Why OB cares about personality
cards.body: Personality predicts some work behaviour, modestly but reliably. The best-supported model is the **Big Five (OCEAN)**: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (emotional stability). **Conscientiousness** is the most consistent predictor of job performance across roles. MBTI is popular in workshops but has weak scientific support for hiring.

cards.title: Perception is not reality
cards.body: People act on what they **perceive**, not on facts. We filter information through expectations. Classic distortions: **halo effect** (one good trait colours everything), **stereotyping**, **selective perception** (seeing what fits your role), and **projection** (assuming others think like you).

cards.title: Attribution error
cards.body: When others fail, we blame their character ('he's lazy'); when we fail, we blame the situation ('the brief was unclear'). This is the **fundamental attribution error** plus **self-serving bias**. In appraisals it makes managers unfair to subordinates and blind to process problems.

cards.title: Bounded rationality
cards.body: Herbert Simon showed managers don't optimise — they **satisfice**: pick the first option that is good enough, because time, information and brainpower are limited. Kahneman's **System 1** (fast, intuitive) and **System 2** (slow, deliberate) explain when shortcuts help and when they hurt.

cards.title: Five biases that cost companies money
cards.body: **Anchoring** (first number sticks), **confirmation bias** (seek supporting evidence), **overconfidence** (forecasts too narrow), **sunk-cost fallacy** (throw good money after bad), **escalation of commitment** (defend past decisions). Each shows up in budgets, hiring and M&A.

cards.title: Sunk cost in action
cards.body: A firm has spent ₹40 crore on an IT system; finishing needs ₹25 crore more, and the finished system will save only ₹15 crore (present value). The ₹40 crore is gone either way. Decision rule: compare **future** cost (₹25 cr) with **future** benefit (₹15 cr). Stop — even though 'we've come so far' feels persuasive.

cards.title: De-biasing tools
cards.body: Use a **pre-mortem** (imagine the project failed — why?), assign a devil's advocate, use structured interviews with scoring rubrics, and write forecasts as ranges. Process beats willpower: you cannot 'try harder' not to be biased.

cards.q: Which Big Five trait most consistently predicts job performance across occupations?
cards.explain: Meta-analyses find conscientiousness — being organised, dependable and achievement-oriented — is the most consistent predictor.

cards.q: A manager rates an employee highly on every dimension because she presents well. This is:
cards.explain: One salient positive trait spilling over onto all judgements is the halo effect.

cards.q: You've spent ₹10 lakh on a campaign. Finishing costs ₹4 lakh and will bring ₹3 lakh of profit. What should you do?
options: Finish, since ₹10 lakh is already invested
Spend more to improve it regardless
Finish, because total spend is less than ₹15 lakh
Stop — future cost exceeds future benefit
cards.explain: The ₹10 lakh is sunk. Only compare ₹4 lakh future cost with ₹3 lakh future benefit — stop.

notes.p:
Organisations are made of people, and people are not calculators. They come with stable traits (personality), they interpret the world through filters (perception), and they make decisions with predictable shortcuts (biases). Organisational behaviour studies these so managers can hire better, judge more fairly and decide more wisely.

The big shift of the last 50 years, led by **Herbert Simon**, **Daniel Kahneman** and **Amos Tversky**, is the move from assuming 'rational economic man' to studying how people actually decide. Kahneman's *Thinking, Fast and Slow* (2011) is the best single book on it.
The **Big Five** or **OCEAN** model is the research standard:
points: **Openness to experience** — curious, imaginative; linked to creativity and training success.
**Conscientiousness** — organised, reliable, persistent; the most consistent predictor of job performance.
**Extraversion** — sociable, assertive; helps in sales and leadership emergence.
**Agreeableness** — cooperative, trusting; helps in teams and service roles, can hurt in tough negotiations.
**Neuroticism** (low emotional stability) — anxiety and moodiness; linked to lower job satisfaction.

notes.p:
Personality correlations with performance are real but modest, so they should be one input among several, never the sole basis for a hire. The **MBTI** (16 types like 'INTJ') is loved in team workshops as a conversation starter, but it has weak test-retest reliability and poor predictive validity — do not use it to select people.

Personality also interacts with the situation. A **strong situation** (clear rules, a checklist-driven cockpit) suppresses personality differences; a **weak situation** (a startup with vague roles) lets them show. Other useful constructs include **locus of control** (do I control outcomes or does luck?), **self-monitoring** (adapting to social cues) and **proactive personality**.

Perception is how we organise and interpret sensory information. Because attention is limited, we take shortcuts:

**Halo/horns effect** — one trait colours the overall judgement. **Contrast effect** — a candidate looks great after three weak ones. **Stereotyping** — judging by group membership. **Selective perception** — a finance head sees every problem as a cost problem.

**Attribution theory** (Harold Kelley) asks whether we explain behaviour internally (ability, effort) or externally (situation). We look at **distinctiveness** (does she do this in other tasks?), **consensus** (do others do it too?) and **consistency** (does she always do it?). The **fundamental attribution error** — over-blaming individuals and under-weighting the situation — makes appraisals unfair. The **self-serving bias** credits our wins to skill and our losses to luck.

notes.h: Decision biases, with a worked example
notes.p:
Kahneman's **System 1** is fast and automatic; **System 2** is slow and effortful. Most biases are System 1 shortcuts applied where System 2 was needed.

**Anchoring:** in salary talks, the first number shapes the outcome. **Availability:** we overrate risks that are vivid (a recent fraud) and underrate quiet ones. **Confirmation bias:** we seek data that supports our view. **Overconfidence:** project managers' '90% confidence' ranges routinely miss — the **planning fallacy**. **Framing:** '90% survival' and '10% mortality' produce different choices. **Escalation of commitment** (Barry Staw): managers pour more into failing projects they started.
points: Worked sunk-cost example (illustrative): ₹40 crore spent on an ERP rollout; ₹25 crore needed to finish; PV of savings after finishing = ₹15 crore.
Correct comparison: −₹25 cr + ₹15 cr = −₹10 cr NPV from continuing. Stopping costs ₹0 more.
The ₹40 crore is irrelevant to the decision. Continuing destroys another ₹10 crore of value.
Real-world echo: the Concorde project is so famous for this that economists call it the 'Concorde fallacy'.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how good firms de-bias
notes.p: Most firms assume smart people aren't biased. They are — often more confident, not less.
points: **Unstructured interviews** invite halo and similarity bias; structured interviews with fixed questions and scoring are more predictive.
**Pre-mortems** (Gary Klein): before launch, imagine it failed and list why. It legitimises dissent.
**Red teams / devil's advocate** for big bets such as acquisitions.
**Reference-class forecasting**: ask how long similar projects actually took, not how long this one 'should' take.
**Separate decision-makers**: the person who started a project shouldn't be the only one deciding to continue it.
**Blind review** of CVs or work samples to reduce stereotyping.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exam questions ask you to identify the bias in a mini-case or recommend a de-biasing method. Consulting and product interviews reward candidates who say 'let me check whether I'm anchoring on that number'. In real jobs you'll sit on hiring panels, review budgets and decide whether to kill projects — exactly where these biases live. Infosys, TCS and most large Indian employers now train managers on structured interviewing for this reason.

points: Big Five: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism; conscientiousness predicts performance best.
MBTI: fine for discussion, not for selection.
Perception biases: halo, contrast, stereotyping, selective perception, projection.
Fundamental attribution error: blame people, ignore situations.
Simon: bounded rationality → satisficing. Kahneman: System 1 vs System 2.
Key biases: anchoring, availability, confirmation, overconfidence, framing, sunk cost, escalation.
Decide on future costs vs future benefits only; sunk costs are irrelevant.
De-bias with process: pre-mortems, structured interviews, reference-class forecasts.

chapters.title: Teams & group dynamics

cards.title: Group vs team
cards.body: A **group** is people who share information; output is the sum of individual work. A **team** has a common goal, mutual accountability and complementary skills, so output can exceed the sum — **synergy**. Katzenbach and Smith's *The Wisdom of Teams* made this distinction famous.

cards.title: Tuckman's stages
cards.body: Bruce Tuckman (1965): **Forming** (polite, unclear), **Storming** (conflict over roles and ideas), **Norming** (agreed ways of working), **Performing** (high output). He later added **Adjourning**. Storming is normal — teams that skip it often never really agree.

cards.title: Psychological safety
cards.body: Amy Edmondson defines it as a shared belief that the team is **safe for interpersonal risk-taking** — admitting mistakes, asking questions, disagreeing. Google's **Project Aristotle** found it was the most important factor among its effective teams. It is not 'being nice'; it's being able to say hard things.

cards.title: Process losses
cards.body: Teams can underperform: **social loafing** (effort drops when individual output isn't visible — the Ringelmann effect), **groupthink** (Irving Janis — cohesion suppresses dissent) and **coordination costs** that grow with size. Amazon's 'two-pizza team' rule tries to keep teams small.

cards.title: Groupthink: the Bay of Pigs
cards.body: Janis's classic case: Kennedy's advisers in 1961 approved a flawed invasion of Cuba. Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters. Kennedy later changed the process for the Cuban Missile Crisis — leaving the room sometimes, inviting outside experts, assigning devil's advocates.

cards.title: Fix team problems with structure
cards.body: Make individual contributions visible to curb loafing. Have the leader speak **last**. Use written pre-reads so quiet members contribute. Rotate a devil's advocate. Agree team norms explicitly in the norming stage instead of hoping they emerge.

cards.q: In which of Tuckman's stages does conflict over roles and direction peak?
cards.explain: Storming is when members challenge ideas, roles and leadership. It's normal and necessary.

cards.q: What did Google's Project Aristotle find mattered most for effective teams?
cards.explain: Psychological safety topped the list, followed by dependability, structure and clarity, meaning and impact.

cards.q: Three people pulling a rope pull less than three times one person. This is best explained by:
cards.explain: The Ringelmann effect/social loafing: individual effort drops when contributions aren't identifiable.

notes.p:
Almost all serious work in companies — a product launch, a merger, an audit — is done by teams. Yet most people have experienced teams that were worse than the best person working alone. The study of group dynamics explains why some teams create **synergy** and others create **process loss**.

Ivan Steiner's simple formula captures it: **Actual productivity = Potential productivity − Process losses.** Potential comes from the members' skills; process losses come from poor coordination and motivation. Good team design raises potential and cuts losses.

Jon Katzenbach and Douglas Smith define a team as 'a small number of people with complementary skills who are committed to a common purpose, performance goals, and approach for which they hold themselves mutually accountable'. Each word matters: **small** (coordination cost grows fast — with n people there are n(n−1)/2 links, so 5 people have 10, 10 people have 45), **complementary skills**, **common purpose**, and **mutual accountability**.

Team types include functional teams, cross-functional teams (product squads), self-managed teams and virtual teams. **Meredith Belbin's team roles** (e.g. Plant, Shaper, Implementer, Completer-Finisher) are a popular, if debated, way to think about balancing contributions.
Bruce Tuckman's stages, from his 1965 review, are the best-known model of team development:
points: **Forming** — members are polite and dependent on the leader. Leader's job: clarify purpose, roles, timelines.
**Storming** — disagreement about goals, roles and leadership. Leader's job: surface conflict, keep it about tasks not people.
**Norming** — agreed working norms and growing trust. Leader's job: codify norms (how we decide, how we meet).
**Performing** — the team is self-directed and productive. Leader's job: delegate, remove obstacles.
**Adjourning** (added 1977 with Mary Ann Jensen) — wrap up and recognise contribution.

notes.p:
**Amy Edmondson** at Harvard began with a puzzle: hospital teams with better leadership reported **more** medication errors. The reason: they weren't making more errors, they were more willing to **report** them. She called the underlying climate **psychological safety**.

In 2012–2015, **Google's Project Aristotle** studied 180 teams and found that who was on the team mattered less than how the team worked together; psychological safety was the strongest factor. Practical signals: people admit mistakes early, ask 'dumb' questions, and the junior analyst challenges the VP's slide.

Psychological safety is **not** low standards. Edmondson pairs it with accountability: high safety + high standards = a learning zone; high safety + low standards = a comfort zone; low safety + high standards = an anxiety zone.

**Social loafing**: Max Ringelmann's rope-pulling experiments (late 1800s) showed individual effort falls as group size rises. Causes: diffusion of responsibility and invisible contribution. Fixes: identifiable individual tasks, peer evaluation, smaller teams.

**Groupthink** (Irving Janis, 1972): highly cohesive groups under pressure seek unanimity over realistic appraisal. Symptoms include an illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, stereotyping outsiders, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity and 'mindguards' who filter bad news. Janis's cases include the Bay of Pigs invasion.

Corporate example: post-mortems of many failed acquisitions and bank collapses describe boards where nobody challenged a dominant CEO. Remedies: leader speaks last, devil's advocate, outside experts, a 'second-chance' meeting before final decisions.

**Amazon** uses six-page written memos read silently at the start of meetings, so arguments are judged on substance rather than charisma, and its 'two-pizza team' heuristic keeps teams small.

points: Adding people to a late project — Fred Brooks's law: 'adding manpower to a late software project makes it later', because of ramp-up and coordination cost.
Treating all conflict as bad. **Task conflict** (about ideas) in moderation helps; **relationship conflict** (personal) hurts.
Rewarding only individuals in a team task, which encourages hoarding information.
Confusing harmony with performance — a quiet team may be an unsafe team.
Skipping explicit norms and assuming everyone shares the same idea of 'urgent' or 'done'.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Behavioural interviews ask 'Tell me about a team conflict you resolved' — answer with the stage (storming), the action (separating task from relationship conflict) and the result. Exams test Tuckman's stages, groupthink symptoms and loafing remedies. In consulting and product roles, you'll be on a new team every few months, so recognising forming and storming lets you shorten them.

points: Team = small, complementary skills, common purpose, mutual accountability.
Steiner: actual productivity = potential − process losses.
Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
Edmondson: psychological safety = safe to take interpersonal risks; pair it with high standards.
Project Aristotle: psychological safety mattered most at Google.
Social loafing (Ringelmann): fix with visible individual contributions.
Groupthink (Janis): fix with devil's advocates, leader speaks last, outside views.
Communication links grow as n(n−1)/2 — keep teams small.

chapters.title: Power, influence & organisational politics

cards.title: Power is the capacity to influence
cards.body: **Power** is the potential to change what others do; **influence** is power in action; **politics** is using power outside formal channels. Every organisation has politics because resources are scarce and goals conflict. Ignoring it doesn't make you ethical — it makes you ineffective.

cards.title: French & Raven's bases of power
cards.body: John French and Bertram Raven (1959): **Legitimate** (the title), **Reward**, **Coercive** (punishment) — all **positional**. **Expert** (knowledge) and **Referent** (being liked and admired) — **personal**. Raven later added **Informational**. Personal power produces commitment; coercive power produces compliance at best.

cards.title: Cialdini's principles of influence
cards.body: Robert Cialdini's *Influence* (1984): **Reciprocity**, **Commitment & consistency**, **Social proof**, **Authority**, **Liking**, **Scarcity** — and later **Unity** (shared identity). These shortcuts work because they are usually reliable cues; that's also why they can be exploited.

cards.title: Where power really comes from
cards.body: Beyond titles, power flows from **controlling scarce resources**, **reducing uncertainty** for others, being **hard to replace**, and **network centrality** — being the bridge between groups. The IT admin who alone understands the legacy billing system has more power than the org chart shows.

cards.title: Cialdini at a mobile store
cards.body: A salesperson offers you free chai (reciprocity), notes '3 people bought this today' (social proof), says 'only 2 left at this price' (scarcity), cites the company engineer's view (authority), and gets you to agree the camera matters most before showing the pricier model (commitment). Recognise the levers; then decide calmly.

cards.title: Influence tactics at work
cards.body: Yukl's research on tactics: **rational persuasion**, **inspirational appeals** and **consultation** are most effective; **pressure** and **legitimating** ('policy says so') are least. Build a **coalition** before the big meeting — decisions are often made in the corridor, not the boardroom.

cards.title: Interview framing
cards.body: Asked 'How did you get buy-in without authority?' — describe mapping stakeholders (who has power, who cares), using expert and referent power, consulting early, and building a coalition. Avoid stories where you won by going over someone's head.

cards.q: A senior engineer is followed because colleagues deeply respect her knowledge. Her main power base is:
cards.explain: Influence based on knowledge and skill is expert power — a personal, not positional, base.

cards.q: 'Only 3 seats left at this fare!' uses which Cialdini principle?
cards.explain: Limited availability makes options seem more valuable — the scarcity principle.

cards.q: Which influence tactic is generally found to be among the most effective?
cards.explain: Consultation, rational persuasion and inspirational appeals tend to build commitment; pressure and legitimating tend to produce resistance or bare compliance.

notes.p:
Fresh MBAs often believe good ideas win on merit. Then they watch a weaker proposal get funded because its sponsor had the CFO's ear. That is not corruption — it is how organisations work when resources are scarce and goals compete.

**Jeffrey Pfeffer** of Stanford, author of *Power: Why Some People Have It — and Others Don't* (2010), argues that understanding power is a core management skill. **Power** is the capacity to influence others; **influence** is the process; **organisational politics** is the use of power through informal channels to pursue interests. The aim of this chapter is to make you effective without becoming manipulative.
French and Raven's five bases remain the foundation:
points: **Legitimate** — authority from position ('I'm your manager'). Works for routine requests; weak for extra effort.
**Reward** — ability to give raises, projects, praise. Works while you control the rewards.
**Coercive** — ability to punish. Produces compliance and resentment.
**Expert** — knowledge others need. Grows with skill; travels with you across jobs.
**Referent** — people identify with or admire you. The basis of charisma.
**Informational** (Raven, 1965) — control of or access to information others need.

notes.p:
Power also comes from your position in the system. **Resource dependence theory** (Pfeffer and Salancik) says power flows to those who control what others need. The **strategic contingencies** view adds that units which **reduce critical uncertainty**, are **central** to workflows and are **non-substitutable** gain power. That is why the treasury team is powerful during a liquidity crunch and the compliance team becomes powerful after a regulatory scare.

**Network power** matters too. Sociologist Ronald Burt's work on **structural holes** shows that people who bridge otherwise disconnected groups get early information and more ideas — and tend to be promoted faster. In practice: have lunch outside your function.

Robert Cialdini spent years studying salespeople, fundraisers and recruiters. His principles:

**Reciprocity** — we feel obliged to return favours (free samples). **Commitment and consistency** — once we take a small public position, we act to stay consistent (foot-in-the-door). **Social proof** — we copy similar others ('most guests reuse towels'). **Authority** — we defer to credible experts. **Liking** — we say yes to people we like, who are similar to us or who compliment us. **Scarcity** — rare or disappearing options seem more valuable. **Unity** (added in *Pre-Suasion*, 2016) — shared identity, 'we are family'.

Indian marketing is full of these: 'India's most trusted brand' (social proof/authority), Diwali 'limited period' offers (scarcity), and free tastings at sweet shops (reciprocity). Inside companies, a manager who helps colleagues early builds a reciprocity bank she can draw on later.

notes.h: Worked case: getting a project approved
notes.p: Illustrative case: Priya, a product manager at a fintech, needs ₹2 crore for a fraud-detection feature. The CFO is sceptical; the risk head is supportive; the sales head fears delays.
points: Step 1 — Stakeholder map: plot each person on power (high/low) vs interest (high/low). CFO = high power, medium interest. Risk head = high power, high interest. Sales head = medium power, high interest.
Step 2 — Use expert power: quantify fraud losses (say ₹6 crore a year, illustrative) and show a 40% reduction would pay back ₹2 crore in under a year.
Step 3 — Consult the sales head early and adjust the rollout so no sales feature is delayed (consultation + reciprocity).
Step 4 — Get the risk head to co-present (authority + coalition).
Step 5 — Pre-wire the CFO with a one-page memo before the meeting so there are no surprises.
Outcome: the formal meeting becomes a confirmation, not a debate.

notes.h: Politics: ethical lines and common mistakes
notes.p:
Politics turns toxic when tactics serve personal interest at the organisation's expense — hoarding information, taking credit, sabotage. Research links high perceived politics with lower job satisfaction and higher turnover.

Common mistakes: relying only on legitimate power ('because I said so'); using coercion as a default; going over a boss's head without warning; ignoring informal networks; and naïvely assuming the best analysis wins. A useful ethical test: would you be comfortable if every person affected saw exactly what you did and why?

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams test French & Raven's bases and Cialdini's principles through short scenarios. Interviews probe 'influence without authority' — a daily reality in product management and consulting. In the job, the skills are stakeholder mapping, pre-wiring decisions, building coalitions and earning expert and referent power that survives reorganisations.

points: Power = capacity to influence; politics = informal use of power.
French & Raven: legitimate, reward, coercive (positional); expert, referent (personal); plus informational.
Personal power builds commitment; coercive power builds compliance and resentment.
Structural power: control scarce resources, reduce uncertainty, be central and hard to replace.
Burt's structural holes: bridging groups gives information advantage.
Cialdini: reciprocity, commitment/consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, unity.
Most effective tactics: rational persuasion, consultation, inspirational appeals.

chapters.title: Leadership theories: from traits to Level 5

cards.title: Leadership vs management
cards.body: John Kotter: **management** copes with complexity — planning, budgeting, organising, controlling. **Leadership** copes with change — setting direction, aligning people, motivating. Organisations need both; over-managed and under-led firms are efficient at doing the wrong thing.

cards.title: Trait and behaviour theories
cards.body: Early research hunted for **traits** of born leaders. Some correlate modestly (extraversion, conscientiousness, intelligence) but none guarantee success. The Ohio State and Michigan studies then focused on **behaviour**: **initiating structure** (task focus) and **consideration** (people focus). Both matter.

cards.title: Situational / contingency leadership
cards.body: **Fiedler**: match the leader's style to how favourable the situation is. **Hersey–Blanchard**: adapt style to follower readiness — **telling, selling, participating, delegating**. **Path-goal theory** (House): the leader clears the path to goals. One style does not fit all.

cards.title: Transformational leadership
cards.body: James MacGregor Burns and Bernard Bass contrasted **transactional** leadership (rewards for performance) with **transformational** leadership — the four I's: **Idealised influence**, **Inspirational motivation**, **Intellectual stimulation**, **Individualised consideration**. It tends to lift effort beyond what contracts specify.

cards.title: Servant and Level 5 leadership
cards.body: Robert Greenleaf's **servant leadership**: the leader exists to serve and grow the team. Jim Collins's **Level 5** leader (*Good to Great*, 2001) blends **personal humility** with **intense professional will** — credit goes out the window, blame goes in the mirror.

cards.title: Same leader, different situations
cards.body: A new hire in week one needs clear instruction (telling). A capable but nervous analyst needs encouragement (participating). A seasoned manager needs to be left alone (delegating). A manager who uses one style for all three will smother one person and abandon another.

cards.title: Answering 'Describe your leadership style'
cards.body: Don't say 'transformational'. Say: 'I adapt to the person and situation' and give one concrete example of being directive and another of delegating. Then name your default and its weakness. Self-awareness reads as leadership.

cards.q: Under Hersey–Blanchard, an able and willing, experienced team member calls for:
cards.explain: High readiness (able and willing) calls for delegating — low direction, low support.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of the 'four I's' of transformational leadership?
cards.explain: The four I's are idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. Incentives are transactional.

cards.q: Jim Collins's Level 5 leader combines:
cards.explain: Collins described Level 5 leaders as a paradoxical blend of personal humility and intense professional will.

notes.p:
Leadership is the most written-about topic in management and the most misunderstood. Popular culture pictures a heroic CEO with a big vision. Research tells a quieter story: effective leadership depends on the situation and the followers, and the best leaders often look unremarkable from outside.

A working definition: **leadership is the process of influencing a group towards achieving shared goals**. John Kotter's distinction is useful — management produces order and consistency; leadership produces change and movement. A good MBA graduate needs to do both.
The field has moved through five broad waves:
points: **Trait theories** (early 1900s–1940s) — 'great man' thinking. Ralph Stogdill's 1948 review found traits alone did not reliably predict leadership.

**Behavioural theories** (1950s–60s) — Ohio State: initiating structure vs consideration; Michigan: production-oriented vs employee-oriented. Blake and Mouton's managerial grid plotted concern for production against concern for people.
**Contingency / situational theories** (1960s–70s) — Fiedler, Hersey–Blanchard, path-goal (Robert House).
**Transformational and charismatic** (1978 onwards) — Burns, Bass.
**Values-based** — servant leadership (Greenleaf, 1970), authentic leadership, Level 5 (Collins, 2001).

notes.p:
**Fiedler's contingency model** measures a leader's style with the 'least preferred co-worker' scale (task- or relationship-oriented) and argues style is fairly fixed, so you should match leaders to situations. Situation favourability depends on leader–member relations, task structure and position power. Task-oriented leaders do best in very favourable or very unfavourable situations; relationship-oriented leaders in the middle.

**Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership** argues the leader should flex. Follower **readiness** (ability + willingness) sets the style:

R1 unable & unwilling/insecure → **Telling** (high task, low relationship)
R2 unable but willing → **Selling** (high task, high relationship)
R3 able but unwilling/insecure → **Participating** (low task, high relationship)
R4 able & willing → **Delegating** (low task, low relationship)

**Path-goal theory** says the leader's job is to clarify the path to goals and remove obstacles, choosing directive, supportive, participative or achievement-oriented behaviour as needed. **Leader–member exchange (LMX)** notes leaders form 'in-groups' and 'out-groups', and the out-group gets less support.

**Transactional** leaders exchange rewards for performance and manage by exception. **Transformational** leaders change how followers see their work through the four I's. Meta-analyses link transformational leadership with higher follower satisfaction and performance, though it can tip into personality cults.

**Servant leadership** (Robert Greenleaf, 'The Servant as Leader', 1970) flips the pyramid: the leader's first job is to help followers grow. **Level 5 leadership** comes from Jim Collins's study of companies that went from good to great: their CEOs were described as modest, quietly determined and focused on building the institution, not their own image. Collins's hierarchy runs from Level 1 (capable individual) to Level 5 (executive).

**Daniel Goleman's** research on leadership styles (coercive, authoritative, affiliative, democratic, pacesetting, coaching) and **emotional intelligence** add that the best leaders switch styles fluidly.

**Ratan Tata** is widely seen in India as a values-driven leader who combined humility with bold moves — the Corus and Jaguar Land Rover acquisitions, and the Tata Nano attempt — and prioritised the group's reputation for integrity. **N. R. Narayana Murthy** at Infosys is often cited for leading by personal example and for setting governance standards in an Indian IT firm.

Globally, **Satya Nadella** at Microsoft (CEO since 2014) is a common example of transformational leadership: he reframed the culture around a 'learn-it-all' growth mindset, drawing on Carol Dweck's work, and moved the company towards cloud. Contrast leaders whose charisma masked weak governance — the lesson that **charisma is not the same as effectiveness**.

points: Assuming leadership = the person at the top; leadership happens at every level.
Using one style everywhere — directing experts or delegating to novices.
Confusing charisma with competence; research on narcissistic leaders shows high emergence but mixed results.
Neglecting the out-group: unequal treatment kills team trust.
Leading only through transactions, then wondering why nobody goes beyond the job description.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to match a scenario to a theory (e.g. 'which Hersey–Blanchard style?') or compare transactional and transformational leadership. Interviews ask about your leadership style and a time you led without authority. In your first managerial role, the most useful idea will probably be situational leadership: diagnose each person's readiness for each task, and flex accordingly.

points: Kotter: management = complexity; leadership = change.
Traits matter modestly; behaviours: initiating structure vs consideration.
Fiedler: match leader to situation; Hersey–Blanchard: flex style to readiness (telling, selling, participating, delegating).
Path-goal: clarify the path, remove obstacles.
Transformational four I's: idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration.
Servant leadership (Greenleaf): lead by serving.
Level 5 (Collins): humility + professional will.
Charisma ≠ effectiveness.

chapters.title: Organisational culture & design

cards.title: Culture: 'how we do things here'
cards.body: Edgar Schein defines culture in three levels: **Artefacts** (visible: dress, office layout, rituals), **Espoused values** (stated: mission statements), and **Basic underlying assumptions** (unspoken beliefs that really drive behaviour). Change the artefacts without the assumptions and nothing changes.

cards.title: Strong cultures cut both ways
cards.body: A strong culture aligns behaviour without rules — Toyota's continuous improvement, Tata's trust. But it can block change: the same shared assumptions that made a firm great can make it blind when markets shift. Culture is a **strategic asset and a strategic risk**.

cards.title: Structure: the core choices
cards.body: Every design answers: **specialisation** (how narrow are jobs?), **chain of command**, **span of control** (how many reports per manager?), **centralisation** (where are decisions made?), and **formalisation** (how many rules?). Wide spans and decentralisation = flatter, faster, but needs capable people.

cards.title: Common structures
cards.body: **Functional** (by expertise — efficient, but silos). **Divisional** (by product/geography — accountable, but duplication). **Matrix** (two bosses — flexible, but confusing). **Network/team-based** (flexible squads). Chandler: '**structure follows strategy**'.

cards.title: Span of control arithmetic
cards.body: 1,000 front-line staff. With a span of 5: 200 supervisors, 40 managers, 8 seniors, 2 heads, 1 CEO → 251 managers, 6 levels. With a span of 10: 100 + 10 + 1 = 111 managers, 4 levels. Wider spans cut layers and cost — but each manager has less time per person.

cards.title: Mechanistic vs organic
cards.body: Burns and Stalker: **mechanistic** organisations (rigid hierarchy, many rules) suit stable environments; **organic** ones (flat, flexible, lateral communication) suit fast-changing ones. A government bank and a fintech startup sit at opposite ends — and both can be right for their context.

cards.title: Exam & interview tip
cards.body: When a case says 'the company is slow to respond to local markets', think decentralisation or divisional structure. 'Duplication and inconsistent quality' → centralise or move toward functional. Always state the trade-off, never just the fix.

cards.q: In Schein's model, which level is hardest to observe and change?
cards.explain: Basic underlying assumptions are taken-for-granted beliefs, often unconscious, and they drive real behaviour.

cards.q: A firm where staff report to both a product head and a country head has a:
cards.explain: Dual reporting lines define a matrix structure.

cards.q: With 1,000 staff and a uniform span of control of 10, about how many managers are needed above the front line?

notes.p: Two companies can have the same strategy, the same technology and similar talent, yet perform very differently. Often the difference is **culture** (the shared assumptions about how things are done) and **design** (how work, authority and information are arranged). Peter Drucker is often credited with the line 'culture eats strategy for breakfast' — the attribution is uncertain, but the idea is sound: a strategy that clashes with the culture usually loses.

**Edgar Schein** of MIT, in *Organizational Culture and Leadership*, defined culture as a pattern of shared basic assumptions a group learned while solving its problems, that worked well enough to be taught to new members.
points: **Artefacts** — what you see and hear: office layout, dress, jargon, stories, rituals, awards. Easy to observe, hard to interpret.
**Espoused beliefs and values** — what the company says it values: 'customer first', 'integrity'. May or may not match behaviour.
**Basic underlying assumptions** — the unspoken, taken-for-granted beliefs: 'the boss is always right', 'failure ends careers', 'engineering decides'. These actually drive behaviour.

notes.p:
The **Competing Values Framework** (Quinn and Cameron) sorts cultures into **Clan** (collaborative, family-like), **Adhocracy** (creative, entrepreneurial), **Market** (competitive, results-driven) and **Hierarchy** (controlled, process-driven). Most firms are a mix; mergers often fail when, say, a clan culture meets a market culture.

**Geert Hofstede's** national culture dimensions (power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, and others) explain why management practices travel badly. India is typically scored as relatively high on power distance, which helps explain why junior staff may hesitate to contradict seniors — directly relevant to psychological safety.

Culture is transmitted through **selection** (hiring for fit), **socialisation** (onboarding, stories), **leader behaviour** (what leaders pay attention to, reward and punish) and **symbols**.

Organisation design answers six questions: work specialisation, departmentalisation, chain of command, **span of control**, **centralisation vs decentralisation**, and **formalisation**.

Main structure types:
points: **Simple** — owner decides everything; typical of a small kirana or early startup.
**Functional** — grouped by expertise (finance, marketing, operations). Deep skills and efficiency, but silos and slow cross-functional decisions.

**Divisional** — grouped by product, customer or region (e.g. a conglomerate with separate businesses). Clear accountability, but duplicated functions. Alfred Chandler's study of firms like DuPont and General Motors gave us 'structure follows strategy'.
**Matrix** — dual reporting (product × region). Balances two priorities, but creates conflict and slow decisions without strong norms.
**Network / team-based** — small autonomous squads (e.g. 'Spotify model'-style squads and tribes) or heavy outsourcing. Fast and flexible, harder to coordinate.

notes.p:
Illustrative: a retail chain has 1,000 store staff.

**Span of 5:** 1,000/5 = 200 first-line supervisors; 200/5 = 40 area managers; 40/5 = 8 regional heads; 8/5 ≈ 2 zonal heads; 1 CEO. Total managers ≈ 200 + 40 + 8 + 2 + 1 = **251**, with 6 levels including the front line.

**Span of 10:** 1,000/10 = 100; 100/10 = 10; 10/10 = 1. Total = **111** managers and 4 levels.

If a manager costs ₹15 lakh a year (illustrative), the wider span saves roughly 140 × ₹15 lakh = **₹21 crore a year**, and information moves through two fewer layers. The catch: a supervisor with 10 people needs trained staff, standard processes and good tools; otherwise quality drops. Wide spans suit routine, standardised work; narrow spans suit complex, novel work.

**Toyota**'s culture of kaizen and respect for people, embodied in the Toyota Production System, is widely studied; when GM tried to copy the tools at the NUMMI joint venture, the lesson often drawn was that tools without the underlying assumptions spread poorly elsewhere. **Netflix**'s published culture memo ('freedom and responsibility') is an example of explicitly codified values supported by policies such as minimal approval layers.

In India, the **Tata group** combines a divisional structure (independent listed companies) with a strong shared culture and brand governed through Tata Sons. **Hindustan Unilever** is known for a structured management-trainee programme that transmits culture through rotation and socialisation.

points: Changing the org chart and expecting culture to follow.
Writing values posters that leaders don't live — staff watch what gets rewarded, not what's printed.
Adopting a fashionable structure (matrix, squads) without the coordination skills it needs.
Hiring only for 'culture fit', which can become hiring people like us — reducing diversity of thought.
Ignoring national culture when expanding abroad or integrating an acquisition.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Expect exam questions on Schein's levels, mechanistic vs organic, and structure trade-offs. In consulting cases, re-organisation questions ask you to choose a structure and defend the trade-offs. In post-merger integration jobs, culture clash is often the biggest risk to value.

points: Schein: artefacts → espoused values → basic underlying assumptions.
Strong culture aligns behaviour but can resist change.
Competing values: clan, adhocracy, market, hierarchy.
Design choices: specialisation, departmentalisation, chain of command, span, centralisation, formalisation.
Structures: simple, functional, divisional, matrix, network.
Chandler: structure follows strategy.
Burns & Stalker: mechanistic for stable, organic for dynamic environments.
Wider spans = fewer layers and lower cost, but less time per person.

chapters.title: Hiring & talent management

cards.title: HR as strategy, not admin
cards.body: Modern HRM treats people as the main source of advantage in knowledge businesses. Dave Ulrich's model casts HR as **strategic partner, change agent, administrative expert and employee champion**. The question is not 'did we fill the seat?' but 'do we have the capabilities our strategy needs?'

cards.title: Workforce planning
cards.body: Start from strategy: what roles will we need in 2–3 years? Then: **build** (train internally), **buy** (hire), **borrow** (contractors, consultants) or **bot** (automate). Indian IT firms 'build' heavily — hiring freshers in bulk and training them for months.

cards.title: Selection methods that predict
cards.body: Large meta-analyses (Schmidt & Hunter and later updates) find **structured interviews**, **work-sample tests** and **cognitive ability tests** among the better predictors of job performance. **Unstructured interviews**, years of experience and graphology predict far less. Combine methods for best results.

cards.title: Cost of a bad hire / attrition
cards.body: **Cost of turnover ≈ recruitment + onboarding/training + lost productivity during ramp-up + vacancy cost.** For many roles this is commonly estimated at a sizeable fraction of a year's salary — sometimes more for senior or specialised roles. Use your own firm's numbers; the method matters more than any rule of thumb.

cards.title: Attrition maths
cards.body: A 500-person team has 20% annual attrition → 100 exits. If each replacement costs ₹4 lakh all-in (illustrative), that's **₹4 crore a year**. Cutting attrition to 15% saves 25 × ₹4 lakh = **₹1 crore** — often more than the cost of a mentoring programme or better managers.

cards.title: Talent management & the 9-box
cards.body: The **9-box grid** plots **performance** (low/medium/high) against **potential** (low/medium/high). Top-right = future leaders to stretch; bottom-left = performance issues to address. It feeds **succession planning** — who could replace each critical role, and when?

cards.title: Employer brand & EVP
cards.body: Your **employee value proposition** (EVP) is why a good candidate should choose you: pay, growth, culture, mission, flexibility. Be honest — a **realistic job preview** lowers early attrition because people who join know what they signed up for.

cards.q: Which selection method is generally a STRONGER predictor of job performance?
options: Structured interview with a scoring rubric
cards.explain: Structured interviews with standard questions and rubrics outperform unstructured chats, experience counts and graphology.

cards.q: A 1,000-person firm cuts attrition from 18% to 12%. At ₹3 lakh per replacement, annual savings are:
cards.explain: Exits fall from 180 to 120 = 60 fewer. 60 × ₹3 lakh = ₹180 lakh = ₹1.8 crore.

cards.q: In a 9-box grid, a high-performer with low potential is usually treated as:
options: A valued solid contributor to retain in role
cards.explain: High performance, low potential: reliable experts in their current roles — retain and recognise, but don't force them into leadership tracks.

notes.p:
In a steel plant the main assets are furnaces; in a consulting firm, bank or software company the main assets walk out of the door every evening. **Human resource management (HRM)** is the set of practices for attracting, developing, motivating and retaining those people so the organisation can execute its strategy.

The field has moved from 'personnel administration' (payroll, attendance) to **strategic HRM**: linking people practices to competitive advantage. Dave Ulrich's *Human Resource Champions* (1997) framed four HR roles — strategic partner, change agent, administrative expert, and employee champion — and many large firms now organise HR into business partners, centres of excellence and shared services.
Think of HR as a pipeline:
points: **Workforce planning** — forecast demand and supply of skills.
**Attraction** — employer brand, EVP, sourcing (referrals, campus, job boards, headhunters).
**Selection** — screening, tests, interviews, offers.
**Onboarding** — the first 90 days strongly shape early retention.
**Development** — training, rotation, mentoring, the 70-20-10 heuristic (most learning on the job).
**Performance & reward** — covered in the next chapter.
**Retention and succession** — keep critical talent; prepare successors.
**Exit** — exit interviews, alumni networks, rehiring.

notes.p:
Most hiring decisions are made with tools that predict poorly. Frank Schmidt and John Hunter's widely cited 1998 meta-analysis — and later re-analyses that revised some numbers — consistently rank **work samples**, **structured interviews** and **general mental ability tests** above unstructured interviews, reference checks and years of experience.

A **structured interview** asks every candidate the same job-relevant questions — often behavioural ('Tell me about a time you…') or situational ('What would you do if…') — and scores answers against a pre-agreed rubric. It reduces halo, similarity and contrast biases from the OB chapter.

**Assessment centres** (group exercises, in-tray tasks, role plays) are used by many Indian firms for management trainees. **Campus hiring** at IIMs, IITs and engineering colleges is a large-scale 'buy' strategy, and the big IT services firms run long training programmes for freshers — a 'build' strategy at scale.

Legal note (phrased generally): hiring decisions must avoid discrimination prohibited under Indian law, and data collected from candidates is subject to India's data-protection rules. Check current law and company policy.
Illustrative numbers for an Indian IT services delivery unit:
points: Headcount = 2,000; annual attrition = 22% → 440 exits.

Replacement cost per exit: recruitment ₹40,000 + training ₹80,000 + lost productivity during a 3-month ramp at 50% output on a ₹8 lakh salary (₹8 lakh × 3/12 × 50% = ₹1 lakh) + project penalties/vacancy ₹30,000 = ₹2.5 lakh.
Annual cost = 440 × ₹2.5 lakh = ₹11 crore.
A programme that cuts attrition to 17% (340 exits) saves 100 × ₹2.5 lakh = ₹2.5 crore a year.
If the programme (better managers, career paths) costs ₹1 crore a year, it pays back 2.5×.

notes.p:
**Talent management** focuses extra investment on critical roles and high-potential people. The **9-box grid** crosses performance with potential. High-performance, high-potential people ('stars') get stretch roles and visibility; high-performance, low-potential people are valued experts; low-performance, high-potential people may be in the wrong role or need coaching; low-low quadrants need a performance plan.

**Succession planning** names 'ready now' and 'ready in 1–2 years' successors for key roles. Its absence is a governance risk: boards of listed companies are expected to oversee succession for senior management. **Tata Sons**' leadership transitions and **Infosys**' CEO changes have been widely covered in the press — a reminder that succession is a board-level concern.

The gig and contract workforce (delivery partners, freelancers) is growing in India; firms must decide which capabilities are core (build and own) and which can be borrowed.

points: Hiring for the CV rather than for the capabilities the role needs.
Relying on gut-feel interviews and 'culture fit' that turn into cloning.
Over-selling the job, causing early exits; a realistic job preview helps.
Neglecting onboarding — a new hire left alone for weeks forms a lasting impression.
Labelling 'potential' based on visibility or similarity to the boss.
Treating attrition as an HR metric instead of a business cost.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask for the stages of HR planning, selection methods and their validity, and the 9-box. Case interviews ask 'Attrition is rising at our BPO — what would you do?' — answer with segmentation (who's leaving, when, why), cost quantification and targeted fixes. Every manager hires; doing it with structure is one of the highest-return skills you can build.

points: Strategic HRM links people practices to strategy; Ulrich's four HR roles.
Build, buy, borrow, bot.
Better predictors: work samples, structured interviews, cognitive tests; weaker: unstructured interviews, experience counts.
Turnover cost = recruitment + training + lost productivity + vacancy cost.
9-box: performance × potential → development decisions.
Succession planning: 'ready now' vs 'ready later'; a board-level concern.
Realistic job previews reduce early attrition.

chapters.title: Performance management & compensation

cards.title: What performance management is for
cards.body: Three jobs: **align** individual goals with strategy, **develop** people through feedback, and **decide** pay, promotion and exits fairly. Many systems fail because one annual rating tries to do all three at once — and the pay conversation drowns out the development one.

cards.title: Goal-setting: KPIs and OKRs
cards.body: **KPIs** track ongoing health (e.g. collection days, NPS). **OKRs** — Objectives and Key Results, from Andy Grove at Intel, popularised by John Doerr — set an ambitious objective with 3–5 measurable key results, often reviewed quarterly. Good goals are **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.

cards.title: Forced ranking: the debate
cards.body: GE under Jack Welch used a **20-70-10** 'vitality curve', managing out the bottom 10%. Critics: it fuels internal competition and assumes talent is normally distributed in every team. Many firms (Microsoft dropped stack ranking in 2013) moved to continuous feedback instead.

cards.title: Total rewards
cards.body: Compensation = **fixed pay** + **variable pay** (bonus, incentives) + **long-term incentives** (ESOPs, RSUs) + **benefits** (PF, gratuity, insurance) + **non-cash** (learning, flexibility). In India, offers quote **CTC** (cost to company), which is larger than take-home pay.

cards.title: CTC vs in-hand
cards.body: Illustrative CTC ₹12 lakh: basic ₹5 lakh, HRA ₹2.5 lakh, special allowance ₹3.05 lakh, employer PF (12% of basic) ₹60,000, gratuity provision ~₹24,000, target bonus ₹61,000. Monthly in-hand excludes employer PF, gratuity and unpaid bonus, then deducts employee PF and tax — often well under CTC ÷ 12.

cards.title: Pay structure design
cards.body: Firms set **pay bands** per grade using market benchmarks. **Compa-ratio = actual pay ÷ band midpoint.** A compa-ratio of 0.85 means paid 15% below midpoint — a retention risk if performance is strong. Internal equity (fair vs peers) and external competitiveness (fair vs market) both matter.

cards.title: Feedback that works
cards.body: Use **SBI**: Situation, Behaviour, Impact. 'In Tuesday's client call (S), you interrupted the CFO twice (B), and she disengaged for the rest of the meeting (I).' Specific, observable, no labels. Give it within days, not at the annual review.

cards.q: An employee earns ₹18 lakh; the band midpoint is ₹20 lakh. Compa-ratio is:
cards.explain: Compa-ratio = 18 ÷ 20 = 0.90 — paid 10% below midpoint.

cards.q: Who is credited with creating OKRs at Intel?
cards.explain: Andy Grove developed OKRs at Intel; John Doerr later spread them to Google and others. Drucker's earlier 'management by objectives' was an influence.

cards.q: Which component is part of CTC but NOT part of monthly take-home?
cards.explain: Employer PF contribution is counted in CTC but goes to the employee's PF account, not the monthly bank credit.

notes.p:
Performance management and compensation answer two questions every employee asks: 'How am I doing?' and 'Am I paid fairly?' Get them right and you reinforce the behaviour the strategy needs. Get them wrong and you get gaming, cynicism and attrition of exactly the people you wanted to keep.

The classic warning comes from Steven Kerr's article 'On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B' (1975): organisations often reward one behaviour while hoping for another — e.g. rewarding call-centre staff for short call times while hoping for solved customer problems.

**Management by Objectives (MBO)**, popularised by Peter Drucker in *The Practice of Management* (1954), asked managers and employees to agree objectives jointly. **OKRs** evolved at Intel under Andy Grove and were taken to Google by John Doerr (described in his book *Measure What Matters*, 2018). An OKR pairs a qualitative objective with measurable key results:
points: Objective: Make onboarding delightful for small merchants.
KR1: Cut time-to-first-transaction from 7 days to 2.
KR2: Raise 30-day activation from 45% to 65%.
KR3: Reduce onboarding support tickets per merchant by 40%.

notes.p:
Common methods: **graphic rating scales** (1–5 on competencies), **behaviourally anchored rating scales** (BARS — each score tied to described behaviour), **360-degree feedback** (input from peers, reports, customers), and **forced distribution/bell curve**.

Rater errors from the OB chapter reappear: **halo**, **leniency** (everyone gets 4/5), **central tendency** (everyone gets 3), **recency** (only the last month counts) and **similar-to-me** bias. Calibration meetings, where managers compare ratings across teams, reduce some of these.

**The forced-ranking debate.** GE under Jack Welch was famous for its 20-70-10 differentiation. Advocates say it forces honest conversations. Critics say it damages collaboration and fits poorly in small teams. Microsoft ended stack ranking in 2013, and several large firms — including some Indian IT companies — have publicly moved away from rigid bell curves toward more frequent check-ins. The trend is toward **continuous feedback** with lighter annual ratings.

A pay system balances three kinds of fairness: **internal equity** (similar jobs paid similarly — usually through **job evaluation** and grades), **external competitiveness** (benchmarks from salary surveys) and **individual equity** (better performers earn more).

Key tools:
points: **Pay bands**: each grade has a minimum, midpoint and maximum.
**Compa-ratio** = actual salary ÷ band midpoint.
**Variable pay**: annual bonus tied to company, team and individual scores; sales commissions.
**Long-term incentives**: ESOPs and RSUs with vesting (often over 3–4 years) to retain people and align them with shareholders. Common in Indian startups.
**Benefits**: in India, statutory items such as Provident Fund and gratuity, plus insurance and leave.
**Pay-mix**: sales roles may be 60:40 fixed:variable; back-office roles closer to 90:10.

notes.h: Worked example: bonus and merit matrix
notes.p:
Illustrative company bonus formula: **Bonus = Base salary × Target % × Company factor × Individual factor.**

Analyst: base ₹10 lakh, target bonus 10%, company achieved 90% of profit goal (factor 0.9), individual rating 'exceeds' (factor 1.2).
Bonus = ₹10,00,000 × 0.10 × 0.9 × 1.2 = **₹1,08,000**.

Merit raise matrix: raises depend on rating **and** compa-ratio, so under-paid strong performers catch up faster. Example: 'exceeds' rating at compa-ratio 0.85 → 12% raise; 'exceeds' at 1.10 → 7%; 'meets' at 0.85 → 8%; 'meets' at 1.10 → 4%. If the 'exceeds' analyst at 0.85 earns ₹17 lakh against a ₹20 lakh midpoint, a 12% raise takes pay to ₹19.04 lakh, compa-ratio ≈ 0.95.

**Wells Fargo**'s fake-accounts scandal (revealed 2016) is a textbook case of aggressive sales targets driving unethical behaviour — Kerr's folly in action. In India, mis-selling of insurance and financial products by staff under heavy cross-sell targets has repeatedly drawn regulatory attention.
