The lesson: what you measure and pay for shapes behaviour, including behaviour you never intended.
points: Rewarding only what's easy to measure (calls, sales volume) and ignoring quality.
Annual-only feedback — surprises at review time destroy trust.
Bell curves forced on teams of five.
Pay secrecy combined with visible inequities — equity theory predicts resentment.
Bonuses so small or so uncertain that they fail Vroom's expectancy test.
Quoting CTC to candidates without explaining take-home pay.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Expect exam questions on appraisal errors, MBO/OKRs, compa-ratio and pay-mix. Interviews may ask 'How would you design incentives for a sales team without encouraging mis-selling?' — answer: balanced scorecard of volume and quality (persistency, complaints), clawbacks, and team components. As a manager you'll write reviews and negotiate raises — use SBI feedback and data.

points: Performance management aligns, develops and decides — separate the development talk from the pay talk.
Kerr: beware rewarding A while hoping for B.
MBO (Drucker) → OKRs (Grove, Doerr); goals should be SMART.
Rater errors: halo, leniency, central tendency, recency, similar-to-me.
Forced ranking: sharp differentiation vs collaboration damage; trend toward continuous feedback.
Compa-ratio = actual pay ÷ band midpoint.
Total rewards: fixed, variable, long-term (ESOPs/RSUs), benefits, non-cash; CTC ≠ take-home.
SBI feedback: situation, behaviour, impact.

chapters.title: What strategy is (and isn't)

cards.title: Strategy is choosing
cards.body: Michael Porter's 1996 HBR article 'What Is Strategy?' argues strategy means **deliberately choosing a different set of activities** to deliver a unique mix of value. If everyone does the same things a bit better, nobody wins. Strategy is as much about **what not to do** as what to do.

cards.title: Operational effectiveness ≠ strategy
cards.body: **Operational effectiveness (OE)** = doing similar activities better than rivals: lean, Six Sigma, best practice. Necessary, but easy to copy, so gains get competed away. **Strategy** = performing **different** activities, or similar ones in **different ways**. OE is a race; strategy is choosing a different race.

cards.title: Trade-offs make strategy stick
cards.body: A **trade-off** is when more of one thing means less of another. Southwest Airlines' no-meals, no-assigned-seats, point-to-point model can't be copied by a full-service carrier without hurting its existing model. Trade-offs stop **straddling** — rivals trying to copy you while keeping their own position.

cards.title: Fit: activities that reinforce
cards.body: Porter describes three orders of **fit**: (1) **consistency** between each activity and the strategy, (2) activities that **reinforce** each other, (3) **optimisation of effort** across activities. A system of fitting activities is far harder to imitate than any single activity.

cards.title: IndiGo's low-cost system
cards.body: IndiGo (illustrating Porter's logic): a largely single aircraft family (simpler training and maintenance), high aircraft utilisation, quick turnarounds, a strong on-time focus, and a lean no-frills product. Each choice supports the others. Copying one piece — say, cheap fares — without the rest doesn't produce the same costs.

cards.title: Three positioning sources
cards.body: Porter: positions arise from **variety-based** (a narrow set of products, e.g. Jiffy Lube oil changes), **needs-based** (most needs of a particular group, e.g. private banking), or **access-based** (customers reachable differently, e.g. rural distribution) logic.

cards.title: The strategy test
cards.body: Ask of any 'strategy' slide: what are we choosing **not** to do? Which customers will we disappoint? If there's no trade-off, it's an aspiration ('be the best'), not a strategy. Richard Rumelt calls this 'bad strategy' — fluff and goals mistaken for a plan.

cards.q: Per Porter, adopting Six Sigma and lean practices that rivals also adopt is an example of:
cards.explain: Best practices that can be imitated improve operational effectiveness, not strategy.

cards.q: Why do trade-offs make a strategy sustainable?
options: They lower costs for all firms
They remove the need for fit
They stop rivals copying without damaging their own position
cards.explain: Trade-offs force rivals to choose; straddling both positions makes them worse at each.

cards.q: Which describes a needs-based position?
options: Serving most needs of a specific customer group
Producing a narrow subset of an industry's products
Reaching customers in a different way
cards.explain: Needs-based positioning serves most or all needs of a particular group of customers.

notes.p:
Ask ten managers what their strategy is and you'll hear 'become the market leader', 'grow 30%', 'be customer-centric'. Those are goals or slogans, not strategy. **Michael Porter**'s 1996 *Harvard Business Review* article 'What Is Strategy?' is the clearest antidote. His central claim: **competitive strategy is about being different** — deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value.

Richard Rumelt (*Good Strategy Bad Strategy*, 2011) adds a practical definition: good strategy has a **kernel** — a **diagnosis** of the challenge, a **guiding policy** for dealing with it, and **coherent actions** that carry it out.

**Operational effectiveness (OE)** means performing similar activities better than rivals — faster, cheaper, with fewer defects. Japanese manufacturers' lead in the 1970s–80s came largely from OE (TQM, just-in-time). OE is essential, but Porter warns that it is not enough:

**Best practices diffuse.** Consultants, benchmarking and staff turnover spread them. As every firm improves, the **productivity frontier** moves out for everyone and relative position stays the same.

**Competitive convergence.** When everyone copies best practice, firms start to look alike, customers choose on price, and margins fall. Porter called this a 'mutually destructive' race.

Strategy instead means choosing a **unique position**.

notes.h: The three pillars: position, trade-offs, fit
notes.p: Porter's argument rests on three ideas:
points: **Strategic position** — from variety-based, needs-based or access-based logic. IKEA targets young, price-conscious furniture buyers willing to self-assemble and transport.

**Trade-offs** — incompatible choices: image inconsistency, different activities requiring different equipment or skills, and limits on internal coordination. Continental Airlines' 'Continental Lite' tried to straddle low-cost and full-service and is Porter's cautionary tale.

**Fit** — first-order (each activity consistent with the strategy), second-order (activities reinforce each other), third-order (optimisation of effort across the system). Porter's examples include Southwest, IKEA and Vanguard.
**Activity-system maps** show the core themes as large circles and the reinforcing activities around them; the denser the links, the harder to copy.

notes.p: The following is an illustrative strategic analysis, not company disclosure. **IndiGo**, India's largest airline by domestic market share in recent years, has broadly pursued a low-cost-carrier model:
points: **Fleet**: largely built on the Airbus A320 family for most of its history → common pilot training, spare parts and maintenance → lower costs.
**High utilisation and quick turnarounds** → each aircraft flies more sectors a day → fixed costs spread over more seats.
**On-time focus** → reliability becomes a differentiator for business travellers even at low fares.
**Simple product** (no free meals, buy-on-board) → fewer catering costs and faster turnarounds, reinforcing utilisation.
**Large aircraft orders** → strong bargaining position with manufacturers.
Each activity supports the others. A full-service rival can cut fares (copying one piece), but without the same system its costs stay higher. This is second-order fit.

notes.p:
**Southwest Airlines** (USA) is Porter's main example: short-haul point-to-point routes, secondary airports, no meals, no assigned seats (historically), a standardised Boeing 737 fleet and rapid gate turnarounds. **IKEA** combines modular flat-pack design, self-service showrooms, suburban stores and customer self-assembly. **Vanguard** in mutual funds built a low-cost, index-focused position and avoided costly activities like aggressive marketing and frequent trading.

In India, **D-Mart** (Avenue Supermarts) is often analysed as a low-cost retail system: a strong preference for owning stores rather than renting, a focused assortment, fast inventory turns and paying suppliers early in exchange for better terms — a set of reinforcing choices rather than one trick.

points: Confusing goals ('₹1,000 crore revenue') with strategy.
Benchmarking rivals until everyone looks the same.
Straddling: adding premium features to a low-cost model, or discounting a premium brand.
Treating strategy as a one-off plan rather than a set of activity choices.
Pursuing growth by diluting the position — Porter warns growth pressure is a major threat to strategy.
Rumelt's 'bad strategy' signs: fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, bad objectives.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to distinguish OE from strategy, identify trade-offs, or draw an activity system. Consulting interviews reward candidates who ask 'Where does this company choose to compete, and what does it give up?' In jobs, strategy work is about saying no: which segments, channels and products are out, so resources can concentrate on what is in.

points: Porter (1996): strategy = being different through a chosen set of activities.
Operational effectiveness is necessary but easily imitated.
Competitive convergence leads to price wars and thin margins.
Positions: variety-based, needs-based, access-based.
Trade-offs prevent straddling and protect the position.
Fit: consistency, reinforcement, optimisation of effort.
Rumelt's kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions.
Test: what are we choosing not to do?

chapters.title: Industry analysis: Porter's Five Forces

cards.title: Why industries differ in profit
cards.body: Average returns vary hugely across industries — software and consumer brands often earn high margins; airlines and commodity steel struggle. Porter's **Five Forces** (1979) explains why: profitability depends on industry **structure**, not just on how good the managers are.

cards.title: The five forces
cards.body:
1. **Rivalry** among existing competitors.
2. **Threat of new entrants**.
3. **Threat of substitutes**.
4. **Bargaining power of buyers**.
5. **Bargaining power of suppliers**.
The stronger the forces, the more of the value created leaks away from the firms in the industry.

cards.title: What drives each force
cards.body: **Entry**: economies of scale, capital needs, brand, distribution access, regulation. **Buyers**: concentration, switching costs, price sensitivity. **Suppliers**: concentration, unique inputs. **Substitutes**: price-performance of alternatives. **Rivalry**: number of firms, growth, fixed costs, exit barriers.

cards.title: Indian telecom after Jio
cards.body: Jio's 2016 entry with free voice and very cheap data intensified rivalry sharply. Weak players exited or merged (Vodafone + Idea). Industry structure moved toward three private players. Buyers had low switching costs (number portability). Suppliers (spectrum from government) had huge power. Result: years of poor industry returns, later improving as consolidation allowed tariff hikes.

cards.title: Complements and the 'sixth force'
cards.body: Porter's 2008 update says government is not a sixth force but acts through the five. **Complements** (products that increase each other's value — phones and apps) matter too; Brandenburger and Nalebuff's 'value net' brings them into the picture.

cards.title: How to use it in a case
cards.body: Don't list all five mechanically. Rate each **high/medium/low**, give the one or two **drivers** that justify the rating, and finish with the so-what: 'This industry is unattractive for a new entrant unless it can…' The conclusion is the point.

cards.title: Common misuses
cards.body: Analysing a firm instead of an industry; defining the industry too broadly ('transport') or narrowly; treating the forces as static; forgetting that a firm can **reshape** forces — by raising switching costs, integrating backward, or creating new segments.

cards.q: Which factor would INCREASE the bargaining power of buyers?
options: Few buyers each purchasing large volumes
cards.explain: Concentrated buyers purchasing large volumes have more leverage. High switching costs, differentiation and fragmented buyers reduce buyer power.

cards.q: In the five forces model, video calls replacing business travel for airlines are an example of:
cards.explain: Substitutes meet the same need through a different product or technology.

cards.q: Which of these is a barrier to entry?
options: Strong economies of scale for incumbents
cards.explain: Economies of scale force entrants to come in big or accept a cost disadvantage — a barrier to entry.

notes.p:
Why do Indian cement companies, consumer-goods firms and IT services companies often earn healthy returns while airlines repeatedly struggle, even with capable managers? **Michael Porter**'s answer, first published in *HBR* in 1979 ('How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy') and updated in 2008 ('The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy'), is that the **structure of the industry** determines how the economic value it creates is divided.

The value an industry creates is split between customers (as consumer surplus), suppliers, rivals and would-be entrants. Five forces determine how much is left for incumbents. Analysing them tells you whether an industry is attractive, and where a firm can position itself to escape the strongest forces.

notes.h: The five forces and their drivers
points: **Threat of new entrants** — high when barriers are low. Barriers: supply-side economies of scale, demand-side benefits of scale (network effects), customer switching costs, capital requirements, incumbency advantages independent of size (brand, locations, patents), unequal access to distribution, restrictive government policy, and expected retaliation.

**Bargaining power of suppliers** — high when suppliers are more concentrated than buyers, the input is unique, switching suppliers is costly, there's no substitute input, or suppliers can integrate forward.

**Bargaining power of buyers** — high when buyers are few or buy in large volumes, products are standardised, switching costs are low, buyers could integrate backward, or the purchase is a large share of their costs (making them price-sensitive).
**Threat of substitutes** — high when a substitute offers an attractive price-performance trade-off and switching is cheap. Substitutes cap prices.

**Rivalry among existing competitors** — intense when competitors are many or similar in size, industry growth is slow, exit barriers are high, fixed costs are high (pressure to fill capacity), products are perishable or undifferentiated, and rivals are committed for non-economic reasons.

notes.p: A five forces analysis of Indian mobile telecom, roughly 2016–2023. Treat this as an illustrative teaching analysis.
points: **Rivalry — very high (2016–2019), moderating later.** Jio's entry in September 2016 with free voice and very cheap data triggered a price war. High fixed costs (networks, spectrum) push firms to fill capacity. Several operators exited or merged; Vodafone India and Idea Cellular merged in 2018.

**Threat of entry — low today.** Spectrum auctions, nationwide network rollout and the capital involved run to tens of thousands of crores. Jio was the exception — a very deep-pocketed parent willing to invest at massive scale.

**Buyer power — moderate-to-high individually, high collectively.** Each consumer is tiny, but mobile number portability makes switching easy and prepaid users are price-sensitive. Enterprise buyers negotiate hard.
**Supplier power — high.** The government controls spectrum; a few global vendors supply network equipment; tower companies are concentrated.
**Substitutes — moderate.** Wi-Fi and internet calling apps substitute for voice and SMS revenue, pushing operators to earn from data.

**So-what:** an unattractive industry during the price war; consolidation to three main private players (plus state-owned BSNL) later reduced rivalry, and tariff increases became possible. Lesson: structure, not just execution, drove industry returns.

notes.p:
**Airlines** are Porter's classic unattractive industry: powerful suppliers (two big aircraft makers, airports, unions, fuel), price-sensitive buyers using comparison sites, high fixed costs, high exit barriers, and frequent new entry backed by cheap aircraft leasing. Warren Buffett has joked that investors would have been better off if someone had shot down the Wright brothers.

**Soft drinks concentrate** (Coca-Cola, PepsiCo) is the opposite: strong brands, a scale-driven distribution system, cheap and plentiful inputs, and fragmented buyers. Similarly, Indian **paints** has historically been seen as attractive — strong brands, deep dealer networks and tinting systems create entry barriers — although new entrants with large capital have recently tested that.
Porter's 2008 article gives practical guidance:
points: **Define the industry correctly** — by product scope and geography. Cement is regional because transport is costly; enterprise software is global.
**Quantify where possible** — concentration ratios, margins, switching costs, growth rates.
**Focus on the strongest forces** — they set profitability.
**Look at trends** — how will forces shift in 3–5 years (regulation, technology)?
**Position the company** where forces are weakest; **reshape** forces (raise switching costs, build brand); **exploit change** in structure.
Government acts **through** the forces (e.g. licensing raises entry barriers). Complements matter but are not a force.
Listing forces without ratings or conclusions.
Confusing industry attractiveness with company advantage — a great firm can thrive in a bad industry and vice versa.
Equating 'industry growth' with attractiveness; fast growth can invite entry.
Treating technology or government as separate forces rather than asking how they affect the five.
Ignoring the value of complements (e.g. apps for smartphones, charging networks for electric vehicles).

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Market-entry case interviews ('Should our client enter the Indian quick-commerce market?') expect a structured view of attractiveness: Five Forces is the natural tool. Exam questions ask you to classify drivers or analyse a named industry. In strategy, PE and equity research jobs, Five Forces is a standard first lens on whether margins are sustainable.

points: Industry structure drives average profitability (Porter, 1979; 2008).
Five forces: rivalry, entry, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power.
Entry barriers: scale, network effects, switching costs, capital, brand, distribution, regulation.
Rivalry rises with many equal rivals, slow growth, high fixed costs, high exit barriers.
Government and complements act through the forces.
Rate each force, justify, and state the so-what.
Firms can position away from or reshape forces.
Indian telecom after 2016: rivalry shock → consolidation → pricing power later.

chapters.title: Generic strategies & competitive advantage

cards.title: Competitive advantage, defined
cards.body: A firm has **competitive advantage** when it earns persistently higher profits than rivals. Economically: it creates a bigger gap between **willingness to pay (WTP)** and **cost** than competitors do. Two routes: raise WTP (differentiation) or lower cost (cost leadership).

cards.title: The value wedge
cards.body:
**Value created = WTP − Cost.**
Customer surplus = WTP − Price.
Firm margin = Price − Cost.
A firm wins by widening the wedge — and then keeping enough of it as margin while still giving customers a better deal than rivals.

cards.title: Porter's three generic strategies
cards.body: From *Competitive Strategy* (1980): **Cost leadership** (lowest cost in the industry), **Differentiation** (unique value buyers pay a premium for) and **Focus** — cost focus or differentiation focus on a narrow segment. Scope (broad vs narrow) × source (cost vs uniqueness).

cards.title: Stuck in the middle
cards.body: Porter warned that a firm trying to be everything — not the cheapest, not clearly different — ends up **stuck in the middle** with below-average returns. Critics note some firms (Toyota historically, IKEA) achieve low cost and differentiation together, usually through innovation that shifts the frontier.

cards.title: Cost leader vs differentiator in India
cards.body: **D-Mart**: lean costs, everyday low prices, focused assortment — cost leadership. **Titan/Tanishq**: brand trust, design and certified purity — differentiation in jewellery. **Royal Enfield**: a differentiation focus on a mid-size leisure-motorcycle niche. Each makes coherent choices consistent with its route.

cards.title: Wedge maths
cards.body: Brand A: WTP ₹1,000, cost ₹600 → value ₹400. Brand B: WTP ₹800, cost ₹350 → value ₹450. B creates more value despite lower WTP. If B prices at ₹700, customer surplus = ₹100 and margin = ₹350; A at ₹900 gives surplus ₹100 and margin ₹300. B wins on margin.

cards.title: Case interview use
cards.body: When asked 'how should the client compete?', start by asking which customers it serves and whether its edge is in cost or WTP. Then check that pricing, operations and marketing all line up behind that choice — misaligned functions are the usual problem.

cards.q: A firm targets a narrow segment with a premium, tailored product. This is:
cards.explain: Narrow scope + uniqueness = differentiation focus.

cards.q: WTP = ₹500, cost = ₹300, price = ₹420. Customer surplus and firm margin are:
cards.explain: Customer surplus = 500 − 420 = ₹80. Margin = 420 − 300 = ₹120. Total value created = ₹200.

cards.q: 'Stuck in the middle' describes a firm that:
options: Has neither a cost nor a differentiation advantage
Operates in the middle of the value chain
cards.explain: Porter's term for firms without a clear advantage on either cost or differentiation.

notes.p: Five Forces tells you how attractive an industry is. **Competitive advantage** explains why some firms in the same industry earn much more than others. Michael Porter's *Competitive Strategy* (1980) and *Competitive Advantage* (1985) gave managers a simple map: a firm can outperform by having **lower costs** than rivals or by offering something **different** that buyers will pay more for — across the whole market or in a focused segment.

notes.h: The economics: willingness to pay and cost
notes.p:
The cleanest modern framing comes from Brandenburger and Stuart (1996) and is taught in most MBA strategy courses as the **value stick**:

**Willingness to pay (WTP)** — the maximum a customer would pay.
**Price** — what they actually pay.
**Cost** — what it costs the firm to make and deliver.
(Some versions add supplier willingness-to-sell below cost.)

Value created = WTP − Cost. Customer surplus = WTP − Price. Firm margin = Price − Cost.

A firm has a competitive advantage if it creates more value than rivals — by raising WTP more than cost (differentiation) or lowering cost more than WTP (cost leadership).
points: Worked example (illustrative, per unit):
Rival: WTP ₹1,000, cost ₹700 → value created ₹300. It prices at ₹900 → customer surplus ₹100, margin ₹200.
Our firm: WTP ₹1,100 (better design), cost ₹720 → value created ₹380.
To win customers we must offer at least the rival's ₹100 surplus: price ≤ ₹1,000.
At ₹1,000, our margin = ₹280 vs rival's ₹200 — a 40% higher margin per unit.
The extra ₹80 of value created is the advantage; we split it between margin and, if we wish, a better customer deal.

**Cost leadership** — become the lowest-cost producer at acceptable quality. Sources: scale, learning curve, process technology, cheap inputs, lean overheads, simple product design. Risks: technology shifts, imitation, losing sight of what customers value.

**Differentiation** — be unique on attributes buyers value: quality, brand, design, service, speed, features. The premium must exceed the extra cost. Risks: premium becomes too large, imitation, needs change.
**Cost focus** — lowest cost for a narrow segment, e.g. budget hotel chains for value travellers.
**Differentiation focus** — tailored value for a niche, e.g. luxury or specialist products.
Porter's warning: **stuck in the middle** — firms that try to straddle typically lack the trade-offs and fit that create advantage.

notes.p:
**Cost leaders**: Walmart globally built advantage through scale, logistics and supplier bargaining. In India, **D-Mart** is widely analysed as a cost-led retailer and **Reliance Jio** used scale and an all-4G network to price data aggressively.

**Differentiators**: **Apple** commands premium prices from design, ecosystem and brand. In India, **Titan's Tanishq** built trust in a fragmented jewellery market with certified purity and standardised exchange policies; **Asian Paints** differentiates through brand, colour-tinting systems and a dense dealer network, while also running a very efficient supply chain.

**Focus**: **Royal Enfield** revived itself by focusing on a leisure and touring niche in mid-size motorcycles rather than competing head-on in mass commuter bikes. **Ferrari** limits volumes to protect exclusivity.

**Hybrid cases**: **Toyota** for decades combined low cost and high reliability through the Toyota Production System — evidence that innovation can move the frontier, so 'stuck in the middle' is a risk, not a law.

Advantage erodes through imitation, substitution and shifts in what customers value. It lasts longer when based on: **economies of scale** that rivals can't reach, **learning-curve** effects, **network effects**, **switching costs**, **brand** built over years, **proprietary technology/patents**, and — most durably — the **activity system fit** from the previous chapter. The next chapter (resources and VRIO) asks which underlying resources make an advantage hard to copy.

points: Claiming 'differentiation' without evidence customers will pay more.
Cutting costs in ways that destroy WTP (e.g. cheaper materials in a premium brand).
Chasing every segment and ending up stuck in the middle.
Assuming low price = cost leadership. Low price without low cost is just a subsidy.
Forgetting that focus strategies can be squeezed if broad rivals decide to serve the niche.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to classify a firm's generic strategy, compute value created and margins, or explain 'stuck in the middle'. Case interviews ask how a client should respond to a cheaper entrant — the answer depends on whether its advantage is cost or WTP. In product and marketing jobs, pricing decisions are really decisions about splitting the value wedge.

points: Competitive advantage = creating more value (WTP − cost) than rivals.
Customer surplus = WTP − price; margin = price − cost.
Porter: cost leadership, differentiation, focus (cost or differentiation).
Stuck in the middle = no clear edge on either dimension.
Low price ≠ low cost.
Hybrids (Toyota) are possible when innovation shifts the frontier.
Sustain advantage via scale, learning, network effects, switching costs, brand, IP and fit.

chapters.title: Value chain & resource-based view (VRIO)

cards.title: Porter's value chain
cards.body: Porter (1985) splits a firm into activities. **Primary**: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, service. **Support**: firm infrastructure, HR, technology development, procurement. Advantage comes from how each activity adds WTP or cuts cost — and how they link.

cards.title: The resource-based view
cards.body: Instead of looking outward at industries, the **RBV** looks inward: advantage comes from **resources and capabilities** that are hard for rivals to get or copy. Key thinkers: Birger Wernerfelt (1984), Jay Barney (1991). Resources = tangible (plants) and intangible (brand, know-how).

cards.title: VRIO test
cards.body: Jay Barney's questions: Is the resource **Valuable** (exploits an opportunity or neutralises a threat)? **Rare**? Costly to **Imitate**? Is the firm **Organised** to capture value? V only → parity. V+R → temporary advantage. V+R+I+O → **sustained competitive advantage**.

cards.title: Why resources are hard to copy
cards.body: **Historical conditions** (built over decades), **causal ambiguity** (rivals can't tell what causes success), **social complexity** (culture, relationships), and **patents**. Toyota published much about its production system, yet many rivals struggled to replicate its results.

cards.title: Core competence
cards.body: C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel (1990): a **core competence** gives access to many markets, adds significantly to customer benefit, and is hard to imitate. Honda's engine expertise spans cars, motorcycles, generators and lawn mowers. Think of the firm as a tree: competencies are roots; products are fruit.

cards.title: VRIO on Asian Paints' distribution
cards.body: Illustrative: a dense dealer network with tinting machines and demand forecasting. Valuable? Yes — availability and choice. Rare? Few rivals matched its reach historically. Imitable? Costly — built over decades with dealer relationships and data. Organised? Yes — supply chain systems are tightly integrated. → Sustained advantage (but large well-funded entrants test it).

cards.title: Apply VRIO resource by resource
cards.body: Don't VRIO the whole company. List 4–6 specific resources (brand, a patent, a distribution network, a data asset), run each through the test, and conclude which are true sources of advantage. Then ask: are we investing to protect those?

cards.q: A resource that is valuable and rare but easy to imitate gives:
cards.explain: V + R without I gives a temporary advantage until rivals copy it.

cards.q: Which is a PRIMARY activity in Porter's value chain?
cards.explain: Outbound logistics is primary. Procurement, HRM and technology development are support activities.

cards.q: Prahalad and Hamel's core competence must satisfy all EXCEPT:
options: Access to a wide variety of markets
cards.explain: Core competences are about collective learning and skills, not owning physical assets.

notes.p: There are two great lenses in strategy. The **outside-in** lens (Five Forces, positioning) asks where to compete. The **inside-out** lens asks what the firm has that others can't easily copy. This chapter covers the inside-out tools: Porter's **value chain**, which breaks a firm into activities, and the **resource-based view (RBV)**, which asks which resources and capabilities produce lasting advantage.
In *Competitive Advantage* (1985), Porter divided a firm into nine generic activities:
points: **Primary activities**: inbound logistics (receiving, storing inputs), operations (turning inputs into products), outbound logistics (delivering), marketing & sales, and after-sales service.
**Support activities**: firm infrastructure (finance, legal, planning), human resource management, technology development (R&D, IT), and procurement.
**Margin**: the difference between the value the chain creates and its total cost.
**Linkages**: decisions in one activity affect others — better product design reduces service costs; better procurement improves operations quality.
**Value system**: the firm's chain sits inside a larger chain of suppliers, channels and buyers.

notes.p:
For each activity, ask: does it raise WTP, lower cost, or neither? Where is our cost structure out of line with rivals? Which activities should be done in-house and which outsourced?

Example (illustrative): for a quick-commerce company, **outbound logistics** (dark-store density, rider routing) is the core of the promise of fast delivery and likely a source of advantage; **procurement** scale drives margin; **marketing** buys growth; **technology development** (demand forecasting) links all of them by reducing stock-outs and waste. Outsourcing payroll processing is fine; outsourcing forecasting probably isn't.

In Indian IT services, the value chain explains the offshore model: operations (software delivery) moved to lower-cost Indian centres while sales and client-facing roles stayed near clients.

The RBV assumes resources are **heterogeneous** across firms and **imperfectly mobile**. Jay Barney's 1991 paper set out the conditions for **sustained** competitive advantage; his later **VRIO** framework turns them into four questions:

**V — Valuable**: does it let the firm exploit opportunities or neutralise threats?
**R — Rare**: do only a few competitors have it?
**I — Inimitable**: do firms without it face a cost disadvantage in obtaining it?
**O — Organised**: do the firm's structure, systems and incentives let it capture the value?
points: Not valuable → competitive disadvantage.
Valuable, not rare → competitive parity.
Valuable, rare, imitable → temporary advantage.
Valuable, rare, costly to imitate, but not organised → unexploited advantage.
All four → sustained competitive advantage.

notes.p:
Barney identifies four sources: **unique historical conditions** (path dependence — a brand or network built over decades), **causal ambiguity** (even insiders can't fully explain success), **social complexity** (culture, trust, relationships) and **patents**. **Dynamic capabilities** (David Teece) extend the idea: the ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure resources matters most in fast-changing industries.

**Toyota**'s production system is a classic case: it has been studied for decades, yet many rivals found it hard to replicate fully because it lives in culture and routines, not just tools. **Xerox PARC** illustrates the 'O' failure: it invented key elements of the modern computer interface (graphical user interface, Ethernet, the laser printer), but the company was not organised to commercialise most of them — Apple and others did.

**C.K. Prahalad** and **Gary Hamel**'s 1990 *HBR* article 'The Core Competence of the Corporation' argued that a diversified firm should be seen as a portfolio of competencies, not of business units. Three tests: a core competence (1) gives potential access to a wide variety of markets, (2) makes a significant contribution to perceived customer benefits, and (3) is difficult to imitate. Their examples included Honda (engines) and Canon (optics, imaging, microprocessor controls).

In India, one can argue **Tata Consultancy Services**' competence in managing large, distributed software delivery, or **Amul**'s cooperative milk procurement network, play similar roles — though such claims should always be tested with VRIO.

points: Calling everything a 'core competence'.
Running VRIO on vague items ('our people') rather than specific resources.
Ignoring the 'O' — great resources wasted by poor organisation.
Assuming advantages last forever; dynamic capabilities matter when industries change.
Outsourcing an activity that is actually a source of advantage because it looks costly on a spreadsheet.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to classify value-chain activities and complete VRIO tables. Case interviews use the value chain to locate cost problems ('where in the chain are costs out of line?') and VRIO for build/buy/partner decisions. In corporate strategy and PE due diligence, a VRIO view of a target's assets is a standard step.

points: Value chain: 5 primary (inbound, operations, outbound, marketing & sales, service) + 4 support (infrastructure, HRM, technology, procurement).
Linkages between activities often matter more than any single activity.
RBV: advantage from heterogeneous, imperfectly mobile resources (Wernerfelt, Barney).
VRIO: Valuable, Rare, Inimitable, Organised → sustained advantage.
Inimitability from history, causal ambiguity, social complexity, patents.
Core competence (Prahalad & Hamel): many markets, customer benefit, hard to imitate.
Dynamic capabilities (Teece): sense, seize, reconfigure.

chapters.title: Corporate strategy: diversification, portfolios & M&A

cards.title: Business vs corporate strategy
cards.body: **Business strategy**: how to win in one market. **Corporate strategy**: **which businesses** to be in and how the parent adds value. Michael Goold and Andrew Campbell call this **parenting advantage**: the parent should make each business worth more than it would be on its own.

cards.title: Ansoff matrix
cards.body:
Igor Ansoff (1957): products (existing/new) × markets (existing/new).
**Market penetration** — existing product, existing market (lowest risk).
**Product development** — new product, existing market.
**Market development** — existing product, new market.
**Diversification** — new product, new market (highest risk).

cards.title: BCG growth-share matrix
cards.body: Market growth × relative market share. **Stars** (high growth, high share) — invest. **Cash cows** (low growth, high share) — harvest cash. **Question marks** (high growth, low share) — invest or exit. **Dogs** (low growth, low share) — fix or divest. The **GE–McKinsey** 9-box uses richer axes: industry attractiveness × business strength.

cards.title: Porter's three tests for diversification
cards.body:
1. **Attractiveness**: is the new industry structurally attractive?
2. **Cost of entry**: will entry costs eat up future profits?
3. **Better-off**: will the new unit or the corporation gain advantage from the link?
Failing any test destroys shareholder value.

cards.title: Vertical integration
cards.body: Owning stages of your value chain: **backward** (toward suppliers) or **forward** (toward customers). Good when markets fail — few suppliers, specialised assets, hold-up risk (Williamson's transaction-cost logic). Bad when it locks you into an inferior or obsolete supplier and adds fixed costs.

cards.title: M&A value arithmetic
cards.body: Target standalone value ₹1,000 cr. Synergies (PV) ₹300 cr. Bidder pays ₹1,250 cr (25% premium). **Value to bidder = 1,000 + 300 − 1,250 = +₹50 cr.** Pay ₹1,400 cr and it's −₹100 cr: target shareholders capture all the synergy and more. The **winner's curse** is paying away the synergy.

cards.title: Conglomerates in India
cards.body: Indian groups (Tata, Aditya Birla, Mahindra, Reliance) remain diversified partly because, historically, weaker capital and talent markets let a group parent add value through capital, brand and management. Tarun Khanna and Krishna Palepu called these '**institutional voids**'. As markets mature, that logic weakens.

cards.q: Launching an existing product in a new country is, on the Ansoff matrix:
cards.explain: Existing product + new market = market development.

cards.q: A business with low market growth and high relative share is a:
cards.explain: Cash cows generate more cash than they need; use it to fund stars and question marks.

cards.q: Target standalone value ₹500 cr, synergies ₹150 cr, price paid ₹600 cr. Net value to the acquirer is:
cards.explain: 500 + 150 − 600 = +₹50 cr. The target's shareholders captured ₹100 cr of the synergy via the premium.

notes.p:
A single-business firm asks 'how do we win in this market?'. A multi-business corporation must also ask 'which markets should we be in, and why are these businesses better off together than apart?' That second question is **corporate strategy**.

Shareholders can diversify cheaply on their own by buying a mutual fund. So a corporation's diversification only creates value if the parent does something investors cannot: share resources, transfer skills, provide capital or management where markets fail. Goold, Campbell and Alexander (*Corporate-Level Strategy*, 1994) call this the **parenting advantage** test.
Igor Ansoff's 1957 *HBR* article 'Strategies for Diversification' gave the classic 2×2:
points: **Market penetration** — sell more of existing products to existing markets (pricing, promotion, distribution). E.g. a FMCG firm deepening rural reach.
**Market development** — existing products, new markets (new regions, segments, channels). E.g. an Indian two-wheeler maker exporting to Africa and Latin America.
**Product development** — new products for existing customers. E.g. a bank adding insurance and wealth products.
**Diversification** — new products in new markets. **Related** (shares resources, e.g. ITC moving from cigarettes into packaged foods using distribution) or **unrelated** (conglomerate).
Risk rises as you move away from the existing product and market.

notes.p:
The **BCG growth-share matrix** (Bruce Henderson, 1970) plots market growth rate against **relative market share** (your share ÷ largest rival's share). Its logic rests on the experience curve: high share → lower cost → more cash. Prescriptions: milk **cash cows** to fund **stars** and selected **question marks**; divest or reposition **dogs**.

Limits: share and growth are crude proxies; 'dogs' can be profitable; the matrix ignores synergies between units and can demotivate managers of labelled units.

The **GE–McKinsey matrix** uses composite axes — **industry attractiveness** (size, growth, margins, Five Forces) and **business unit strength** (share, brand, cost position, capabilities) — on a 3×3 grid with invest/grow, selectivity, and harvest/divest zones.

Porter's 1987 *HBR* article 'From Competitive Advantage to Corporate Strategy' found that many diversified US companies had later divested a large share of their acquisitions, and proposed three tests: **attractiveness**, **cost-of-entry** and **better-off**. Related diversification tends to outperform unrelated, because value comes from sharing activities and transferring skills.

**Vertical integration** decisions draw on **transaction cost economics** (Oliver Williamson): integrate when market contracting is costly — few trading partners, **asset specificity** (investments useful only for one partner), uncertainty and risk of hold-up. Examples: Reliance's backward integration from textiles into polyester and petrochemicals, then refining; Apple's move to designing its own chips. Risks: higher fixed costs, reduced flexibility, and protecting an internal supplier that is uncompetitive.

**Institutional voids** (Khanna & Palepu): in emerging markets with thin capital, talent and contract-enforcement institutions, business groups can fill gaps internally — one explanation for the persistence of diversified Indian groups.

notes.h: M&A logic with a worked example
notes.p: Acquisitions are the fastest way to execute corporate strategy and among the riskiest. Many studies find that a large share of deals fail to create value for the acquirer's shareholders, mostly because of overpayment and weak integration.
points: Illustrative deal: target's standalone equity value (market, undisturbed) = ₹2,000 crore.
Expected synergies: cost savings of ₹60 crore a year after tax, valued at 10× = ₹600 crore; integration costs ₹100 crore → net synergy PV = ₹500 crore.
Bid with a 30% premium: price = ₹2,600 crore.
Net value to acquirer = standalone value + net synergy − price = 2,000 + 500 − 2,600 = **−₹100 crore**.
Maximum justified premium = ₹500 crore (25%); at that point the acquirer gains nothing and the target captures all the synergy.
Lesson: decide the walk-away price before the auction starts; momentum and ego (hubris, Richard Roll, 1986) push bidders past it.

notes.p:
**Tata Steel's acquisition of Corus (2007)** expanded scale dramatically but is widely discussed as a case of a large premium paid near a cycle peak, followed by years of losses and restructuring in European operations. **Tata Motors' acquisition of Jaguar Land Rover (2008)** went through a hard early phase but became a major contributor to the group in later years — showing that results depend on the price paid and the post-merger turnaround. Globally, **AOL–Time Warner (2000)** remains the cautionary tale of value destruction, while **Disney's** purchases of Pixar and Marvel are often cited as successful capability-led deals.

Related diversification wins: **ITC** used its distribution reach and brand-building skills from cigarettes to build packaged foods and personal-care businesses.

points: Diversifying for 'risk reduction' — shareholders can do that themselves more cheaply.
Paying away synergies through high premiums; overestimating revenue synergies.
Ignoring integration costs and culture clash.
Using BCG labels mechanically.
Vertically integrating into a business you don't know how to run.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exam questions test Ansoff and BCG classification and acquisition value arithmetic. 'Should our client acquire X?' is a classic case interview: test strategic fit, synergies, price vs value, and integration risks. In corporate development, investment banking and PE, synergy valuation and walk-away prices are day-to-day work.

points: Corporate strategy = which businesses + how the parent adds value (parenting advantage).
Ansoff: penetration, market development, product development, diversification.
BCG: stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs; GE–McKinsey: attractiveness × strength.
Porter's tests: attractiveness, cost-of-entry, better-off.
Vertical integration: justified by transaction costs and hold-up risk.
Acquirer gain = standalone value + synergies − price paid.
Related diversification usually beats unrelated; institutional voids explain Indian groups.

chapters.title: Disruptive innovation & blue ocean strategy

cards.title: Sustaining vs disruptive innovation
cards.body: Clayton Christensen (*The Innovator's Dilemma*, 1997): **sustaining** innovations make good products better for existing customers. **Disruptive** innovations start **worse** on mainstream metrics but cheaper, simpler or more convenient, appealing to the low end or non-consumers — then improve until they take the mainstream.

cards.title: Why good companies fail
cards.body: Incumbents listen to their best customers and invest where margins are highest — exactly the right behaviour, which is why they **rationally ignore** the disruptor's small, low-margin market. By the time it matters, the entrant's capabilities have caught up. That's the 'dilemma'.

cards.title: Two types of disruption
cards.body: **Low-end disruption**: serve overserved customers with a good-enough cheaper offer (minimills vs integrated steel mills). **New-market disruption**: compete against **non-consumption** — people who couldn't use the product before (personal computers vs mainframes, cheap mobile data bringing first-time internet users online).

cards.title: Blue ocean strategy
cards.body: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne (2005): **red oceans** are crowded markets where rivals fight over existing demand. **Blue oceans** are uncontested market space created by **value innovation** — raising buyer value and lowering cost at the same time, breaking the value-cost trade-off.

cards.title: ERRC grid
cards.body:
Four actions framework:
**Eliminate** — which factors the industry takes for granted can go?
**Reduce** — which can be cut well below standard?
**Raise** — which should go well above standard?
**Create** — which factors has the industry never offered?
Plot the result on a **strategy canvas** against rivals.

cards.title: Cirque du Soleil
cards.body: Kim & Mauborgne's flagship case. **Eliminated** animal acts and star performers; **reduced** thrill and danger; **raised** the unique venue experience; **created** a theme, artistic music and dance. It drew adults and corporate clients who never went to circuses — new demand, not stolen demand.

cards.title: Don't overuse 'disruption'
cards.body: Christensen himself complained the word is abused. Uber, he argued with co-authors in HBR (2015), was not a classic disruption: it didn't start at the low end or with non-consumers. Ask: did it start worse-but-cheaper, or among non-consumers? If not, it's a sustaining or radical innovation.

cards.q: A product that starts inferior on mainstream metrics but serves non-consumers cheaply is:
cards.explain: New-market disruptions compete against non-consumption with simpler, cheaper offerings.

cards.q: In the ERRC grid, removing a factor the industry takes for granted is:
cards.explain: Eliminate: drop factors the industry has long competed on but buyers no longer value.

cards.q: Why do incumbents often ignore disruptive entrants?
options: The disruptor's early market is small and low-margin, and their best customers don't want it
Disruptors always have better technology from day one
cards.explain: Christensen's insight: rational resource allocation toward best customers and high margins leads incumbents to ignore low-end/new markets.

notes.p:
Some of the most famous business failures — integrated steel mills, film photography leaders, many disk-drive makers — were not caused by lazy management. They happened to well-run companies doing what good management recommends. Clayton Christensen's theory of **disruptive innovation** explains why. Kim and Mauborgne's **blue ocean strategy** is a complementary idea: instead of fighting rivals in crowded markets, create new demand.

Both push managers beyond Porter's 'choose a position in an existing industry' to ask: how might the industry itself be redrawn?
In *The Innovator's Dilemma* (1997), Christensen studied the disk-drive industry and found a pattern:
points: **Performance trajectories**: technology improves faster than mainstream customers can use it, so leaders end up **overshooting** — offering more than most customers need.
**Sustaining innovations** (incremental or radical) improve performance on dimensions mainstream customers value. Incumbents usually win these battles.
**Disruptive innovations** start worse on those dimensions but offer other benefits — cheaper, simpler, smaller, more convenient. They take root at the **low end** or in **new markets**.
Incumbents rationally ignore them: margins are thin, the market is small, and their best customers say they don't want it.
The disruptor improves along its own trajectory until it is 'good enough' for the mainstream — and its cost advantage wins.
Classic example: **steel minimills** began with low-quality rebar, which integrated mills were happy to abandon, then moved up into higher-grade products.

notes.p:
These are interpretive teaching examples; reasonable people classify them differently.

**Mobile data and Jio (2016)**: by making data extremely cheap, Jio brought hundreds of millions of Indians online for the first time — a strong **new-market** element, competing with non-consumption of mobile internet. However, it also attacked incumbents head-on with a better network, so it is not a pure disruption case.

**UPI payments**: a free, simple, interoperable system that served people and small merchants who didn't use cards — competing with cash and non-consumption rather than with credit cards on features.

**Low-cost airlines** brought many first-time flyers from trains and buses into aviation.

Globally, **Netflix**'s DVD-by-mail and early streaming started as worse than Blockbuster's instant in-store rental for many customers, then improved; Christensen and colleagues cited Netflix as a disruption example in their 2015 HBR article. **Personal computers** disrupted minicomputers; **digital cameras** and then smartphones disrupted film.

W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne of INSEAD (*Blue Ocean Strategy*, 2005) argue that companies spend too much energy beating rivals in **red oceans**. Their alternative is **value innovation**: simultaneously pursuing differentiation and low cost by reconstructing what the industry offers.

Tools:
**Strategy canvas** — a line chart of the key competing factors (x-axis) and offering level (y-axis) for you and rivals. A blue-ocean move shows a visibly different curve.
**Four actions / ERRC grid** — Eliminate, Reduce, Raise, Create.
**Six paths** — look across alternative industries, strategic groups, buyer groups, complementary offerings, functional/emotional appeal, and time.

**Worked ERRC example — a budget hotel chain (illustrative, modelled on the 'Formule 1' case Kim and Mauborgne describe):** Eliminate lounges and restaurants; Reduce room size and front-desk hours; Raise bed quality, hygiene and quietness; Create automated check-in. Result: cost per room well below a standard two-star hotel, while the factors guests value most for a night's sleep improve.

Both reject head-on competition, but they differ. **Disruption** is about a **trajectory over time** and incumbents' response. **Blue ocean** is about **designing an offering** that creates new demand now. A blue ocean move need not be inferior at launch; a disruption usually is. Critics note that both theories are easier to apply in hindsight, and that blue oceans attract imitators and eventually turn red.

notes.h: How incumbents should respond and common mistakes
notes.p: Christensen's advice: create an **autonomous unit** with its own cost structure and success metrics to pursue the disruptive business, rather than forcing it through the mainstream organisation's processes and values. His **resources, processes and values (RPV)** framework explains why: processes and values that serve the core business reject the new one.
points: Labelling every successful startup 'disruptive'.
Assuming disruption means 'better technology' — it's about business model and trajectory.
Responding to disruption by moving further upmarket (a short-term relief that cedes ground).
Copying a blue ocean move after it is already crowded.
Using ERRC only to add features (Raise/Create) without Eliminate/Reduce — that raises cost.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to classify innovations, build an ERRC grid or explain the innovator's dilemma. In interviews: 'How should a traditional bank respond to fintechs?' — discuss which segments are overserved, non-consumption, and the autonomous-unit response. In product and strategy roles, ERRC and strategy canvases are practical workshop tools.

points: Sustaining innovation improves products for existing customers; incumbents usually win.
Disruptive innovation starts worse but cheaper/simpler, in low-end or new markets.
Incumbents rationally ignore disruptors — the innovator's dilemma.
Low-end vs new-market disruption.
Respond with an autonomous unit (RPV framework).
Blue ocean: value innovation = higher value + lower cost, creating new demand.
ERRC: eliminate, reduce, raise, create; strategy canvas.
Don't call everything disruptive.

chapters.title: Platform strategy & network effects

cards.title: Pipelines vs platforms
cards.body: A **pipeline** business creates value linearly: buy inputs, make product, sell it (a car maker). A **platform** creates value by **connecting two or more groups** and facilitating interactions between them (buyers and sellers, riders and drivers, app developers and users). The platform often owns little of what's exchanged.

cards.title: Network effects
cards.body: A **network effect** exists when a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. **Direct (same-side)**: more WhatsApp users make WhatsApp more useful to each user. **Indirect (cross-side)**: more restaurants on Zomato attract more diners, and more diners attract more restaurants.

cards.title: The chicken-and-egg problem
cards.body: No buyers without sellers, no sellers without buyers. Solutions: **subsidise one side** (free for users, charge advertisers), **seed supply** yourself, start with a **single-side tool** that's useful alone, or **piggyback** on an existing network. Early Swiggy and Zomato invested heavily in restaurant onboarding and delivery fleets.

cards.title: Pricing: subsidy side and money side
cards.body: Platforms often make one side free (**subsidy side**) and charge the other (**money side**). Subsidise the side that is more price-sensitive and whose presence attracts the other. Google search is free for users; advertisers pay. Credit cards: consumers often get rewards; merchants pay fees.

cards.title: Winner-take-all? Not always
cards.body: Markets tip toward one platform when network effects are strong, **multi-homing** is costly and there's little room for differentiation. They stay contested when users easily multi-home (drivers on both Ola and Uber; diners on both Swiggy and Zomato), or when local network effects make scale less decisive.

cards.title: Value of a network
cards.body: Metcalfe's law (heuristic): potential connections = n(n−1)/2. 10 users → 45 links; 100 → 4,950; 1,000 → 499,500. Value grows much faster than users — but real platforms see diminishing returns and congestion, so treat it as intuition, not a valuation formula.

cards.title: Interview checklist for platforms
cards.body: Ask: Who are the sides? Which side is subsidised? Are network effects same-side or cross-side, local or global? Can users multi-home? What stops disintermediation (users meeting once, then transacting off-platform)? How is quality governed?

cards.q: More Android users attract more app developers, which attract more users. This is:
cards.explain: Value flows across two different groups (users and developers) — a cross-side network effect.

cards.q: Which condition makes a platform market LESS likely to be winner-take-all?
options: Users easily using several platforms at once
cards.explain: Easy multi-homing lets rival platforms coexist.

cards.q: Using n(n−1)/2, how many possible connections are there among 20 users?

notes.p:
The most valuable companies of the past two decades — Apple's App Store, Google, Amazon Marketplace, Meta, Visa — share one feature: they are **platforms**. In India, UPI, Flipkart's marketplace, Zomato, Swiggy, Ola, Urban Company and Naukri all run on platform logic.

A platform creates value by facilitating interactions between external producers and consumers. Its key asset is not a factory but a **network** and the **data and rules** that govern it. The key economic force is the **network effect**. Good references: *Platform Revolution* (Parker, Van Alstyne and Choudary, 2016), *Matchmakers* (Evans and Schmalensee, 2016), and Eisenmann, Parker and Van Alstyne's HBR article 'Strategies for Two-Sided Markets' (2006).

points: **Direct / same-side**: each additional user directly benefits other users of the same type (telephones, WhatsApp, LinkedIn connections).
**Indirect / cross-side**: users on one side benefit from more users on the other side (riders and drivers; shoppers and sellers; players and game developers).
**Negative network effects**: congestion, spam, too many sellers competing for attention, low-quality matches. Platforms must curate.
**Local vs global**: Zomato's network effects are largely **city-level** — a restaurant in Pune doesn't help a diner in Kolkata. Local effects make it easier for rivals to compete city by city.
**Data network effects**: more usage → better data → better product (search ranking, recommendations), a softer but real effect.

notes.p:
Every two-sided platform faces the **chicken-and-egg problem**. Common playbooks:

**Subsidise the harder side**: early ride-hailing companies guaranteed driver earnings; food delivery firms ran heavy discounts for users.
**Seed one side yourself**: build first-party inventory or supply.
**Single-user utility first**: build a tool useful on its own, then add the network (OpenTable's reservation software for restaurants is a classic case).
**Constrain the market**: launch in one city or one college (Facebook began with Harvard) to reach density quickly.
**Piggyback**: Airbnb's early growth hack of cross-posting listings to Craigslist is a famous example.

**UPI** solved chicken-and-egg differently: as public digital infrastructure run by NPCI, it was interoperable across banks and apps from the start, with zero merchant fees on most UPI person-to-merchant payments, which drove adoption by small merchants via QR codes.
A food-delivery platform in one city:
points: Average order value = ₹400; commission from restaurant = 20% → ₹80.
Customer delivery/platform fee = ₹30. Revenue per order = ₹110.
Delivery partner cost = ₹50; payment gateway and support = ₹15; discounts funded by platform = ₹25.
Contribution per order = 110 − 50 − 15 − 25 = **₹20**.
At 20,000 orders/day: daily contribution = ₹4,00,000 → about ₹1.2 crore over 30 days.
If city fixed costs (tech allocation, staff, marketing) are ₹1 crore/month, the city earns roughly ₹20 lakh/month.

Network logic: more density → shorter delivery distances → lower partner cost per order → better contribution. Cutting the discount from ₹25 to ₹10 lifts contribution to ₹35/order — but only if demand holds, which depends on how strong the network effects and habits really are.

notes.p:
Whether a market tips to one winner depends on: strength of network effects, **multi-homing costs** (how easy is it to use rivals at the same time?), **differentiation** possibilities, and **switching costs**. Uber and Ola drivers often run both apps; diners use both Swiggy and Zomato — so the markets stayed contested.

**Disintermediation** risk: once a client finds a good plumber or tutor, they may transact directly. Platforms fight this with insurance, guarantees, payment protection, ratings and ongoing value.

**Governance**: rules on who joins, quality controls, ratings, dispute resolution, and pricing. Apple's App Store review is an example of tight curation; open marketplaces trade quality for breadth.

**Regulation**: platforms face scrutiny on competition (self-preferencing, data use) worldwide; in India the Competition Commission of India has examined major digital platforms, and India's FDI rules restrict foreign-owned e-commerce marketplaces from holding inventory — phrase specifics carefully and check current rules.

points: Assuming any app with users has network effects — many have none; their users don't benefit from each other.
Burning cash on subsidies without a path to unit-economics profitability once subsidies end.
Ignoring local network effects and expecting national dominance from one city's success.
Neglecting supply quality; bad matches create negative network effects.
Charging the wrong side — taxing the side that is most price-sensitive and most needed.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Expect questions like 'How would you launch a B2B marketplace for kirana stores?' — cover sides, which to subsidise, density strategy, unit economics and disintermediation. Exams ask you to identify direct vs indirect network effects and explain winner-take-all conditions. In product, growth and VC roles, platform metrics such as liquidity (share of listings that transact), take rate and multi-homing are core.

points: Pipeline = linear value creation; platform = facilitating interactions between groups.
Direct (same-side) vs indirect (cross-side) network effects; can be negative.
Chicken-and-egg: subsidise, seed, single-user utility, constrain market, piggyback.
Subsidy side vs money side.
Tipping depends on network-effect strength, multi-homing costs, differentiation.
Local network effects make markets contestable city by city.
Watch disintermediation, governance and regulation.
Metcalfe: n(n−1)/2 connections — intuition, not valuation.

chapters.title: BATNA, reservation price & distributive bargaining

cards.title: BATNA: your real power
cards.body: **BATNA** = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement (Fisher & Ury, *Getting to Yes*, 1981). It's what you'll do if this deal fails. Your power in a negotiation comes less from arguments and more from how good your walk-away option is. Improve your BATNA **before** you sit down.

cards.title: Reservation price & target
cards.body: Your **reservation price** (walk-away point) is derived from your BATNA — the worst deal you'd accept. Your **target** is the ambitious-but-justifiable outcome you aim for. Never confuse the two; people who only know their reservation price tend to settle near it.

cards.title: ZOPA
cards.body:
**Zone of Possible Agreement** = the overlap between the seller's reservation price and the buyer's reservation price.
If buyer max ≥ seller min, ZOPA = [seller min, buyer max].
If buyer max < seller min, there's **no ZOPA** — no deal should happen. Distributive bargaining is the fight over where in the ZOPA you land.

cards.title: Job offer, worked
cards.body: Your BATNA: an offer at ₹18 lakh; moving costs and a worse commute make you value this job ₹1 lakh less, so your reservation = ₹19 lakh. The firm's budget max = ₹23 lakh. ZOPA = ₹19–23 lakh, worth ₹4 lakh. Anchor with a justified ₹24 lakh; settling at ₹22 lakh captures 75% of the zone.

cards.title: Anchoring and first offers
cards.body: The first credible number anchors the discussion (Galinsky & Mussweiler's research supports making the first offer when you have good information). Make it **ambitious but defensible** with a reason. If they anchor first, don't counter near their number — re-anchor with your own justified figure.

cards.title: Concession patterns
cards.body: Concede in **decreasing** steps (₹2 lakh, ₹1 lakh, ₹50,000) — it signals you're nearing your limit. Ask for something in return for each concession. Avoid splitting the difference early; it rewards whoever anchored more extremely.

cards.title: Never reveal your reservation price
cards.body: Share your **interests** and **justifications**, not your bottom line. And research theirs: market salary data, the cost of a vacant role, their other candidates. Information about the other side's BATNA is the most valuable thing you can bring.

cards.q: Seller's minimum is ₹45 lakh; buyer's maximum is ₹52 lakh. The ZOPA is:
cards.explain: The buyer's max exceeds the seller's min, so any price from ₹45 lakh to ₹52 lakh works for both.

cards.q: What does BATNA stand for?
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
Baseline Acceptable Terms of a Negotiated Arrangement
cards.explain: Coined by Roger Fisher and William Ury in Getting to Yes.

cards.q: Which concession pattern best signals you are approaching your limit?
cards.explain: Shrinking concessions signal you're near your walk-away point.

notes.p:
Every manager negotiates constantly — salaries, vendor contracts, budgets, deadlines, deals. Yet most people prepare by rehearsing arguments rather than by doing the structural analysis that actually determines outcomes. This chapter covers **distributive** (or 'claiming value') negotiation: a fixed pie where more for you means less for them, like the price of a used car.

The foundational ideas come from Roger Fisher and William Ury's *Getting to Yes* (1981, Harvard Negotiation Project) and from Howard Raiffa's *The Art and Science of Negotiation* (1982). Deepak Malhotra and Max Bazerman's *Negotiation Genius* (2007) is an excellent practical guide.
Before any negotiation, write down:
points: **Your BATNA** — what you will actually do if no agreement is reached. Not a wish; a concrete alternative.
**Your reservation price (RP)** — the point at which you'd rather take the BATNA. Derived from your BATNA, adjusted for all differences (risk, timing, non-cash factors).
**Your target / aspiration** — an ambitious, justifiable goal.
**Your estimate of their BATNA and RP** — research it. The ZOPA lies between the two reservation prices.

notes.p:
**ZOPA** (zone of possible agreement) exists when the buyer's reservation price is at or above the seller's. The size of the ZOPA is the **bargaining surplus**. Distributive negotiation is about how that surplus is split.

If there is no ZOPA, a rational negotiator walks away — the right outcome. A common mistake is 'deal fever': agreeing below your RP because you've invested time.
points: Worked example — buying a flat (illustrative):
Seller's BATNA: another buyer's firm offer at ₹82 lakh, closing in 60 days. Seller values a quick sale at ₹2 lakh (interest on her home loan for the next flat), so her RP ≈ ₹80 lakh.
Buyer's BATNA: a comparable flat for ₹88 lakh needing ₹3 lakh of repairs → effective ₹91 lakh. He prefers this flat's location by ₹2 lakh, so his RP = ₹93 lakh.
ZOPA = ₹80–93 lakh; surplus = ₹13 lakh.
Seller lists at ₹98 lakh (anchor). Buyer counters at ₹79 lakh citing recent sales per sq ft.
Concessions: buyer 79 → 83 → 85 → 86; seller 98 → 92 → 89 → 87.

Deal at ₹86.5 lakh. Seller captures 6.5 of 13 (50%); buyer captures 6.5 (50%). Had the buyer known the seller's BATNA was ₹82 lakh with a 60-day wait, he could have pushed nearer ₹82 lakh by offering a faster close.

notes.p:
**Anchoring.** The first offer pulls the final price toward it. Research by Adam Galinsky and colleagues suggests first movers often gain when they have good information. Anchor ambitiously but with a justification ('comparable flats in this society sold at ₹X per sq ft').

**Counter-anchoring.** If the other side opens first, don't react to their number; put your own justified anchor on the table quickly.

**Concessions.** Plan them. Make them smaller over time; make them conditional ('If you can close in 30 days, I can do ₹X').

**Improve your BATNA.** Get the other offer, the other vendor's quote. In salary talks, a competing offer is the strongest lever — but don't bluff about one you don't have.

**Use time and deadlines.** Deadlines create pressure for both sides; whoever's BATNA worsens faster with time is weaker.

**Salary negotiation in India**: candidates often negotiate on percentage hike over their current CTC. A better anchor is the market value of the role (from salary surveys and peers) rather than your past pay, which keeps you tied to an old reservation point.

**Procurement**: large Indian manufacturers and retailers run reverse auctions to make suppliers' BATNAs visible and push prices toward suppliers' reservation prices.

**Sports and media rights**: auction-based sales of cricket broadcast rights show the seller strengthening its position by creating competing bidders — every bidder's BATNA becomes 'lose the rights to a rival'.

points: Not knowing your own BATNA and RP before you start.
Revealing your RP ('my budget is ₹20 lakh max').
Opening too modestly for fear of offending.
Splitting the difference early.
Making unilateral concessions without asking for anything back.
Fixating on price and missing other terms (payment schedule, warranty, joining date) — the bridge to the next chapter.
Lying about alternatives — it damages reputation, and in many contexts misrepresenting material facts can carry legal consequences.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams give a scenario and ask for BATNA, ZOPA and a recommended opening. Interviews may include role-plays or 'Tell me about a negotiation you led'. In jobs — procurement, sales, banking, consulting, HR — you'll negotiate weekly. Write the four numbers on paper every time.

points: BATNA = what you'll do if no deal; strengthen it before negotiating.
Reservation price derives from BATNA; target is your ambitious goal.
ZOPA = overlap of reservation prices; no overlap → walk away.
Anchor first when well-informed; justify the anchor.
Concede in shrinking, conditional steps.
Never reveal your RP; research theirs.
Avoid splitting the difference early and deal fever.

chapters.title: Integrative negotiation: creating value

cards.title: Expand the pie before slicing it
cards.body: **Integrative** negotiation looks for deals that make both sides better off by trading on differences. Most real negotiations involve **several issues** — price, timing, quality, risk — so they are not fixed-pie. The skill is to create value first, then claim your share.

cards.title: Positions vs interests
cards.body: Fisher & Ury's principle: **focus on interests, not positions**. A position is what someone says they want ('₹10 lakh fee'); an interest is why ('we must show margin this quarter'). Classic story: two people fighting over an orange — one wanted the juice, the other the peel.

cards.title: Principled negotiation
cards.body: *Getting to Yes* gives four principles: **Separate the people from the problem**; **Focus on interests, not positions**; **Invent options for mutual gain**; **Insist on objective criteria** (market rates, precedent, expert valuation). Underpinned by knowing your BATNA.

cards.title: Sources of value: differences
cards.body: Value comes from differences in **priorities** (trade what you care less about for what you care more about — **logrolling**), **forecasts** (contingent deals/earn-outs), **risk tolerance**, and **time preferences** (one side wants cash now, the other later).

cards.title: Logrolling, scored
cards.body: Vendor and client score issues out of 100. Vendor: price 60, payment terms 30, delivery date 10. Client: price 30, payment 10, delivery 60. Trade: client concedes on price and terms; vendor gives the fast delivery the client needs. Both score far higher than splitting each issue in half.

cards.title: Contingent contracts
cards.body: When sides disagree about the future, **bet on it**. A buyer thinks a startup will earn ₹10 crore; founders say ₹20 crore. An **earn-out** pays extra if revenue hits ₹20 crore. Each side gets what it believes is a good deal, and incentives align.

cards.title: Practical moves
cards.body: Negotiate **multiple issues simultaneously**, not one at a time. Make **MESOs** — multiple equivalent simultaneous offers — to learn their priorities from which one they prefer. Ask 'why?' and 'what if?' often. Share some information to build trust; reciprocity follows.

cards.q: Two departments both demand the only conference room on Friday. One needs privacy; the other needs a projector. What's the integrative move?
options: Explore interests — give privacy elsewhere and the projector room to the other team
cards.explain: Interests (privacy vs projector) may be satisfiable separately — a classic integrative solution.

cards.q: Trading concessions on low-priority issues for gains on high-priority ones is called:
cards.explain: Logrolling creates value from differences in priorities.

cards.q: Which is one of Fisher & Ury's four principles?
cards.explain: Objective criteria (market data, precedent, expert opinion) make agreements fair and defensible.

notes.p:
Distributive bargaining assumes a fixed pie. But most business negotiations — a supply contract, a joint venture, a job offer — involve many issues, and the parties value them differently. That means there's value to **create**: deals where both sides are better off than a simple compromise.

This is **integrative** negotiation. Its intellectual home is the Harvard Negotiation Project: Fisher and Ury's *Getting to Yes* (1981) and David Lax and James Sebenius's *The Manager as Negotiator* (1986), which named the tension between **creating** and **claiming** value the 'negotiator's dilemma'.
Fisher and Ury proposed four principles:
points: **Separate the people from the problem** — address emotions and relationships directly; attack the problem, not the person.
**Focus on interests, not positions** — ask why. Interests include needs, fears, constraints and priorities.
**Invent options for mutual gain** — brainstorm before deciding; look for low-cost-to-you, high-value-to-them moves.
**Insist on objective criteria** — market prices, benchmarks, precedent, independent valuation, scientific standards.
Plus: **know your BATNA** — principled negotiation doesn't mean being soft.

notes.p:
**Different priorities** → logrolling. **Different forecasts** → contingent agreements. **Different risk preferences** → the less risk-averse side bears risk for a price. **Different time preferences** → one side gets money sooner, the other gets more later. **Complementary capabilities** → each does what it does cheaply.

A classic illustration is Mary Parker Follett's library story from the 1920s: one person wanted the window open, the other closed; the solution — open a window in the next room — gave fresh air without a draught. Interests, not positions.

notes.h: Worked example: a scored multi-issue deal
notes.p: Illustrative supplier negotiation between a packaging vendor and an FMCG client. Each side privately scores outcomes (points out of 100).
points: **Price** (₹10 vs ₹9 per unit): Vendor gets 50 pts at ₹10, 0 at ₹9. Client gets 20 at ₹9, 0 at ₹10.
**Payment terms** (30 vs 90 days): Vendor gets 30 at 30 days, 0 at 90. Client gets 10 at 90 days, 0 at 30.
**Contract length** (1 vs 3 years): Vendor gets 20 for 3 years, 0 for 1. Client gets 70 for 3 years (supply security), 0 for 1.
**Compromise deal** (midpoint on each: ₹9.50, 60 days, 2 years): Vendor ≈ 25 + 15 + 10 = 50; Client ≈ 10 + 5 + 35 = 50. Total 100.
**Integrative deal** (₹10, 30 days, 3 years): Vendor = 50 + 30 + 20 = 100; Client = 0 + 0 + 70 = 70. Total 170.

The client is better off (70 vs 50) **and** the vendor is better off (100 vs 50). The client could also claim some of the extra value — say ₹9.80 and 45 days — and both would still beat the compromise.

notes.p:
**Earn-outs in M&A**: buyers and founders often disagree about future growth; an earn-out ties part of the price to performance — common in Indian startup acquisitions and global deals alike. **Camp David Accords (1978)**: Egypt's interest was sovereignty over the Sinai; Israel's was security. A demilitarised Sinai returned to Egypt met both interests — a famous example cited in *Getting to Yes*.

**Long-term supply contracts** — for example, between automakers and component suppliers — often trade price concessions for volume commitments, which suppliers value because they can plan capacity.

Good tactics: negotiate a **package**, not issue by issue; ask diagnostic questions; make **MESOs** (two or three offers of equal value to you) and watch which they prefer; propose **post-settlement settlements** (after agreeing, ask 'can we both do better?').
points: The **fixed-pie bias** (Bazerman & Neale): assuming their gain is your loss.
Negotiating issues sequentially, which makes trades impossible.
Revealing everything — creating value requires information sharing, but claiming still matters.
Confusing being nice with being integrative; you can be warm and still insist on objective criteria.
Ignoring implementation — a clever deal the other side can't deliver is worthless.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams ask you to distinguish positions from interests or design a contingent contract. Interview role-plays often hide integrative potential — candidates who ask questions and trade across issues score highest. In jobs, vendor contracts, partnerships, internal budgeting and offer negotiations (salary vs joining bonus vs ESOPs vs start date) are all multi-issue.

points: Integrative = create value by trading on differences; distributive = claim value.
Lax & Sebenius: the negotiator's dilemma between creating and claiming.
Fisher & Ury: people vs problem, interests not positions, options for mutual gain, objective criteria.
Sources of value: priorities, forecasts, risk, time, capabilities.
Logrolling and contingent contracts (earn-outs).
Negotiate packages; use MESOs; try post-settlement settlements.
Beware the fixed-pie bias.

chapters.title: Structured communication: Minto pyramid, memos & executive presentations

cards.title: Answer first
